title: Fix observed token rate calculation
body:
## What changed

- record the time when upstream response headers arrive for each metered response
- calculate observed tok/sec from the streamed generation phase instead of full request wall time
- use only the latest 20 clean, successful replies so old sessions do not dominate the display
- exclude retries, empty completions, and historical rows without generation timing
- document the corrected metric

## Why

The tray divided all successful output tokens by total request duration across the full usage history. That mixed generation with prompt processing, queueing, and short tool-call overhead, so the displayed rate could be far below the model's actual decoding throughput.

## User impact

The tok/sec value now reflects recent post-header generation speed. After upgrading, it remains unmeasured until the first newly metered reply completes rather than reusing incompatible historical timing.

## Validation

- `npm run check`
- `npm test` — 1,079 passed, 0 failed, 8 skipped

title: feat: publish routed models into DeepSeek Harness as a second target
body:
## What

Adds `dsh` (DeepSeek Harness) as a second supported target. `--target dsh`
publishes every routed model into the harness's own settings document as one
provider route, so the models a user already has in Codex show up in the
harness with no extra configuration and no second set of API keys.

```sh
./install.sh --target dsh --auto --providers configured
# or, on a machine that already serves Codex:
./bin/model-router dsh enable
```

## Why it is small

The harness reads provider routes from `$DSH_HOME/settings.yaml`, which it
watches and hot-reloads, and its shipped bundle mounts the generic
`dsh-llm-pi-ai` adapter **dormant** — zero routes until a settings section
supplies some. So this is a settings write rather than a plugin or composition
change, and nothing has to restart.

The route points at the same `/v1/responses` caller endpoint Codex already
uses. That choice is the whole design: tool-result ageing, the vision bridge,
the substituted prompt-token count that keeps compaction working against
providers reporting zero, bounded upstream retries, and the usage and
throughput accounting all already sit on that routed path, so a harness turn
gets them without a second request path to keep correct.

## A target is a client, not a router

One installation serves both: one service, one gateway, one credential store,
one provider selection, one set of ports. `MODEL_ROUTER_TARGET` selects which
client's configuration a command writes and never forks the state directory or
the service — otherwise somebody who installs both is asked for every API key
twice and runs two gateways against one set of provider quotas.
`ROUTER_PLANE_TARGET` names that shared plane; the `/health` service name and
the environment aliases key on it rather than on the client, which is what
stops a second integration from looking like a foreign process squatting on the
router port. Installed integrations are republished together whenever the
routable set changes, so they cannot drift apart.

## What it will not touch

The two documents belong to the harness. It writes leaf-level diffs into
`settings.yaml` and preserves the user's comments, and its own Models page
writes provider routes beside ours, so this owns exactly one key in each file
(`llm-pi-ai.providers.codex-router` and `CODEX_ROUTER_CALLER_KEY`) and treats
every other byte as somebody else's work. Publishing twice is byte-identical;
removing the route restores the document exactly, comments and sibling routes
included. Both files are written 0600 under a 0700 directory, matching the
bound the harness holds them to, because the settings document carries the
managed base URL and the other carries the key it references.

`src/yaml-structure.mjs` is a fail-closed structural lexer for block-mapping
YAML, not a general parser. A tab indent, a duplicate key, a multi-document
stream, a sequence root, an unterminated flow collection, an anchored key, an
inline `providers` mapping: each is refused with the file untouched and the
line named. A refusal costs a command; a wrong guess rewrites a file whose only
copy is on somebody's disk.

## Deliberate limits

- **Only routed models are published.** An unregistered slug on
  `/v1/responses` is native GPT traffic needing the caller's own ChatGPT
  session, which a harness request does not carry, so advertising a native
  model would offer a turn that cannot authenticate. The vision-bridge engine
  candidates exclude native models here for the same reason.
- **No `compat` on the route.** pi-ai types those switches only on
  `openai-completions` and refuses a route-level switch elsewhere; each model's
  request profile is applied on the router's own side of the hop.
- **A reasoning level pi-ai cannot name is dropped and reported**, never
  approximated. A model with no levels declares `reasoningEfforts: false`
  rather than omitting the field, which would inherit whatever the installed
  catalog says about a colliding id.
- **The default model stays the user's.** Taking it over is opt-in
  (`--set-default-model`), snapshotted, and restored on uninstall — the
  discipline the Codex login-free mode already applies to `model` and
  `model_provider`.
- **Delegation stays the user's.** `dsh-tool-subagent` installs no settings
  section, so `./bin/model-router dsh subagent-preset` prints the block to
  paste rather than editing a preset this does not own. `bin/multi-agent` stays
  Codex-only, since it drives `multi_agent_version` and the Codex agents
  directory.

## Drive-by fix

`src/skills-install.mjs` ran its CLI block on `process.argv[2]` with no
entry-module guard, and `install-manifest.mjs` imports it — so any command
transitively pulling the manifest in while its own subcommand happened to be
`install` or `uninstall` installed the Codex skill pack and exited 0 before
doing its own work. Every other module in the repository already guarded this.

## Test plan

Automated — `npm run check` and `npm test`: **1117 pass, 0 fail**, including 39
new tests across `test/yaml-structure.test.mjs`, `test/dsh-catalog.test.mjs`,
and `test/dsh-config-manager.test.mjs`. The document-surgery tests run against a
settings file with somebody else's work in every position the router writes
near. `test/control.test.mjs` was also made hermetic: its target assertion read
the developer's own installation, so publishing to the harness on the machine
running the tests changed the expected list.

Manual, against a real `@deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.0-rc.6` install:

- [x] A headless turn routed through the gateway and appeared in the router's
      own usage events (`model=local/llama3.2:3b provider=local status=200`).
- [x] Pointing the route at a dead port broke it (`TRANSPORT: Connection
      error.`) and restoring it fixed it **with no restart**, proving both the
      dependency and the hot reload.
- [x] A model absent from the route failed `UNKNOWN_MODEL: pi-ai provider
      "codex-router" has no configured model …`, proving the published list is
      what the harness consults.
- [x] A 40KB aged tool result on that endpoint reported `toolResultsAged: 1,
      toolResultBytesSaved: 38470`.
- [x] Throughput accounting picked the turn up
      (`observedTokensPerSecond` on the routed model).
- [x] `MODEL_ROUTER_TARGET=dsh doctor` reports Harness routing config, caller
      credential, settings privacy, and catalog freshness.
- [ ] **The web Models page is not verified.** Its API is not REST, so this
      asserts on model registration rather than on rendering. Worth a human
      look before merge.

One bug came out of that live run and is fixed here: the harness rewrites
`settings.yaml` and its writer folds a long double-quoted value at its line
width, ending the line with a backslash so the break is lossless. The lexer
refused that as unterminated, so the router could not republish into any
document the harness had touched — which it does routinely. Quoted scalars are
now tracked across lines like block scalars and flow collections already were;
one left open at end of file is still refused.

title: feat: Simplified Chinese, and a tray language setting to choose it
body:
Builds on @Yuxin-Qiao's work in #181 and adds the piece it deliberately left out.

#181 localized the tray, the Island, and the desktop panel, and shipped a 292-entry Simplified Chinese catalog. It followed macOS's preferred language and added no setting on purpose — its own comment says *"without adding a second language setting."*

That leaves no answer for the common case: a Chinese speaker on an English macOS install, or an English speaker on a Chinese one. This adds the setting.

## The setting

`TrayLanguage { system, english, chinese }`, persisted under `ModelRouterTray.language`, as a segmented picker in tray Settings above the Dynamic Island row.

- **`system` stays the default** and keeps #181's exact behavior, so nobody who was already happy gets moved.
- **Each option is labelled in the language it selects** — "English", "中文" — not in the current one. Somebody who cannot read the current language still has to be able to find their way out.
- **`language` is `@Published`**, so the panel re-renders in place rather than waiting for a relaunch. `RouterLanguage.selection` is updated before the publish, since that is the value `routerLocalized()` actually reads.

The desktop panel already had a language `<select>` from #181, so this makes the two surfaces symmetric rather than introducing a new concept.

## Folded in from the review of #181

- **Added the missing `"Fix Codex Router installation"` translation.** It's an accessibility label, so a zh-CN VoiceOver user heard every control in Chinese except that one.

title: fix: measure output speed after the first token, not after the headers
body:
Follow-up to #192. Its arithmetic was correct; it divided by the wrong interval.

## The problem

Output tokens per second is defined as the rate **after the first token**, with the wait before it reported separately as time-to-first-token. That is how [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/methodology/performance-benchmarking) and every published benchmark state it, and it is the only split that does not move with reply length.

#192 divided by time since the **response headers**. On a reasoning model the headers arrive seconds before the first token, so that silent thinking landed in the denominator.

Measured on 60 real `gpt-5.6-sol` requests from a live install:

| output tokens | reported rate |
|---|---|
| 31 | 11.7 tok/s |
| 54 | 29.8 |
| 204 | 49.3 |
| 324 | 58.0 |
| 426 | **69.4** |

Same model, same traffic — a 6× spread driven entirely by reply length. Regressing all 60:

```
generation_ms = 2176ms  +  12.47ms per token
                  ↑              ↑
       fixed overhead    true rate ≈ 80 tok/s
```

2.2 seconds of non-generation sat inside every measurement. On a short reply that *is* the measurement.

## The fix

- **`ResponseUsageTransform` timestamps the first event carrying generated output** — `output_text.delta`, reasoning summary, tool-call arguments, audio transcript, or a chat-completions content delta. It already parsed every SSE line, so this observes what was passing through rather than adding a hook.
- **The router resolves that to `firstTokenMs`** and records it beside `responseStartMs` at all four exits.
- **`provider-usage` divides by it.** `responseStartMs` stays: headers-to-first-token is the reasoning time, which is worth having.
- **A first token timestamped after its own request ended is rejected** for both figures rather than reported as a slow start.

`observedFirstTokenMs` (median) is computed and exposed on the snapshot but deliberately **not** surfaced in any UI — the tray keeps one number, not two.

## Result

On a fixture built from the real distribution (2.9s TTFT, 80 tok/s streaming):

| reply | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 31 tokens | 11.7 tok/s | **80.1** |
| 426 tokens | 69.4 tok/s | **80.2** |

And live, on the four real replies since deploying this locally: 44.4 / 38.1 / 66.6 / 52.0 → pooled **58.4 tok/s**, where the tray had been showing 20.4.

## Known transition

Rows without `firstTokenMs` read as unmeasured rather than being reinterpreted, so 47 of 49 models show no rate until their next streamed reply. Same shape as #192's transition, and the same reasoning: better a blank than a number computed under a different definition. Each model repopulates on first use.

Aborted streams (`status: 0`) take an early exit that never resolves `firstTokenMs`, so they record `responseStartMs` without it. No effect on either figure — the `status >= 200 && status < 400` guard already excludes them — but the asymmetry is worth tidying separately.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm test` — 1083 pass, 0 fail, 8 skipped
- [x] `npm run check`
- [x] 4 new tests: rate is stable across reply length, TTFT is median-sampled, an out-of-range first token is rejected, historical rows are unmeasured rather than wrong
- [x] #192's three rate fixtures updated to the new definition
- [x] Deployed to a live router and verified against real streamed traffic

title: fix: stop one broken sample from carrying a model's speed, add per-model rates, default compaction off
body:
Three related changes to the speed surface, all found by running the merged code against a live install.

## 1. One broken sample was deciding a model's speed

The tray showed `grok-oauth/grok-4.6` at **778 tok/s**. Individual samples in the same window:

| output | generation window | rate |
|---|---|---|
| 116–603 tokens | 1–6 s | 73–114 tok/s ✅ |
| 2326–6353 tokens | 0.2–5 s | 660–**11,656** tok/s ❌ |

6353 tokens in 723 ms is not physically possible. Those events carry a first-token time of **121 s against a 122 s request** — detection fires near the end of the stream, so the measured window is only its tail.

The aggregate was `sum(tokens) / sum(durations)`, which puts a broken sample straight into the numerator. Now it is the **median of per-reply rates**: it cannot be moved by a minority of impossible samples and needs no threshold to tune. Same window, same data → **105.6 tok/s**, matching the plausible population.

Samples claiming more than 500 tok/s are also rejected outright — set well above any published serving rate, so a genuinely fast model is never discarded, but a detection failure cannot be mistaken for a record.

**Still open:** the underlying detection failure on converted streams (grok-oauth) is real. This stops it deciding the displayed number; it does not fix the samples. Worth its own issue.

## 2. Per-model speeds — closes #182

The card followed whatever was generating, so it answered "how fast is this" and never "how do my models compare". `lastUsedAt` was already decoded in the tray and read by nothing — this is what it was for.

Up to four measured models, most recent first, under the existing headline card. Unmeasured models are omitted rather than shown as a row that says nothing; the card above already covers "no samples yet".

## 3. Tool-result compaction defaults off, and says it is experimental

It rewrites what the model sees mid-conversation, and its savings figures are still being validated against provider-billed tokens. That is something to opt into, not to discover after it has already altered a session.

The structural rule from the vision bridge carries over and is tested: an absent state file means nobody has answered and the current default applies; a stored value is the operator's own answer and is kept verbatim. **An install that already turned this on keeps it** through the default change — verified against a real install carrying `enabled: true`.

The tray row is now "Compact old tool results (experimental)", translated in both languages.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm test` — 1085 pass, 0 fail, 8 skipped
- [x] `npm run check`
- [x] `swift build` + `swift test` (13 tests)
- [x] Verified against the live install: 778 → 105.6 tok/s
- [x] Verified a stored `enabled: true` survives the default flip
- [x] Five tests updated to state the setting they exercise instead of relying on the old default

title: fix: make gpt-5.6-luna usable as a v2 subagent without a mode switch
body:
## Problem

`gpt-5.6-luna` is a cheap native model, but it can never be spawned as a child agent (subagent) from a v2 parent.

### Why this matters

The v1/v2 split exists to **separate model capability tiers** and stop a parent from accidentally delegating to a legacy model that would drag down the result. That intent is correct — but Luna was placed in the wrong tier:

- Luna runs correctly on the v2 backend (openai/codex#35097, #36294), so tagging it `v1` is not protecting anything; it is just hiding a capable model.
- With DeepSeek prices rising, **Luna is now the more cost-effective choice** versus `deepseek-v4-flash` for subagent work, so it should be front and center, not buried behind a settings toggle.

### Root cause

Codex `spawn_agent` only offers models whose catalog entry carries `multi_agent_version: "v2"` as child candidates. Upstream ships `gpt-5.6-luna` as `"v1"`, and `promoteNativeMultiAgent` only promoted a native slug to `v2` when the subagent mode was `all` or `selected` — so in the default `proven` mode Luna stayed `v1` and remained un-spawnable unless the user went into Settings and flipped modes. That is the "works but I have to fiddle with it" trap, and it is the kind of indirect behavior that is invisible to the parent agent and to the user.

## Fix

Promote the upstream-verified v2-backend slug (`gpt-5.6-luna`) **unconditionally** in `promoteNativeMultiAgent`:

- `hidden` and `disabled` still win (a user can still turn Luna off, or the picker can hide it).
- The subagent mode opt-in now only reaches the *remaining* native models, whose v2 relay paths are not yet verified.

No mode switch, no Settings dance. Luna shows up as a spawnable child out of the box.

## Verification

- Full suite: 926 tests, 0 failures.
- Rebuilt the merged catalog on the affected machine: `gpt-5.6-luna` now advertises `multi_agent_version: "v2"`, matching `gpt-5.6-sol` / `gpt-5.6-terra`.
- Added tests: proven mode still promotes Luna; disabled/hidden still suppress it.

title: feat: operate DeepSeek Harness from the tray, and let it use the Codex session
body:
Builds on #193. That PR adds the DeepSeek Harness target; this one makes it something a user can actually operate — install it, start it, stop it, turn it off — and lets it use the Codex models this machine is already signed in to.

The harness commit is included here because it is not on `main` yet. Once #193 merges, this rebases down to the eleven commits below it.

## What you can now do from the tray

One row in Settings, showing whichever action the current state calls for:

| State | Primary | Secondary |
|---|---|---|
| Not installed | **Install** | — |
| Installed, not routed | **Connect** | — |
| Published, nothing serving | **▶ Start** | Disconnect |
| Serving | **Open site** | Turn off |

`control harness status\|setup\|start\|stop\|disconnect\|web` drives the same thing from a terminal.

`Turn off` stops the process and frees its memory — 184 MB resident, measured — and leaves the route published so play brings it straight back. `Disconnect` is the other question, and only appears once nothing is running.

## Native GPT models in the harness

Native traffic is authorized by the caller's own ChatGPT session: the router copies `authorization` and `chatgpt-account-id` off each request, Codex attaches both, and a harness turn attaches neither. The eight native models were therefore withheld — advertising them would have offered a turn that could not authenticate.

The router now falls back to the session already in `$CODEX_HOME/auth.json`. You are signed in to Codex on this machine; a client running as the same user should not have to sign in again.

**Codex is unaffected, and that is verified rather than asserted.** The injection happens only for a request carrying no upstream credential of its own. Relaying a deliberately invalid token still returns *that token's* 401 rather than a success, so a credential a caller brings is never replaced. `src/catalog.mjs` and `src/config-manager.mjs` — the only writers of Codex's config and catalog — are untouched by every commit here.

Three properties hold it together:

- **Publishable exactly while spendable.** Native models publish only while the session is usable, so the picker never offers a model that would 401.
- **Expiry is checked, not assumed.** That token lasts ~10 days and Codex renews it only when Codex is used. An expired session is declined two minutes early, the eight models withdraw, and `doctor` says to open Codex once — which is the fix.
- **Renewal stays Codex's job.** Reproducing that OAuth exchange means guessing an unpublished client identity and, if refresh tokens rotate, risking the login this was asked not to disturb.

Off switch: `CODEX_ROUTER_NATIVE_SESSION_FALLBACK=0`, and the harness drops back to routed models only. Worth knowing before leaving it on: it widens what the caller key reaches, from the API-key providers to the ChatGPT subscription as well.

## Bugs found and fixed along the way

Several were pre-existing and would have bitten anyone using both clients:

- **Disabling the harness uninstalled the shared router service**, taking Codex down with it. `bin/disable` now retires the service only once no client integration remains.
- **Follow-mode stopped the router under any terminal client.** `NSRunningApplication` enumerates app bundles, so a `codex` TUI and a `dsh` turn are both invisible to it — and neither can be lazily started, since a turn that finds 4202 closed fails while the stack behind it takes up to 300s to warm. A client the tray cannot watch now pins the router on.
- **Uninstall discarded a default model the user had chosen.** The restore spliced the install-time snapshot over whatever was there, and the harness's own Models page writes that same key. It now applies only over a default this router wrote, and removes a router-owned default that has no snapshot rather than leaving it pointed at a route just deleted.
- **The tray read every running harness as stopped**, because `control --json` carried the synchronous snapshot with no `web` field.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm test` — 1154 pass, 0 fail, 8 skipped
- [x] `swift build` and `swift test` in `apps/macos/ModelRouterTray` — 13/13
- [x] Live install → connect → start → open → turn off → disconnect against a real harness
- [x] Native turn from a harness-shaped request (`Authorization: Bearer <caller-key>`) on `gpt-5.6-sol` and `gpt-5.6-terra`
- [x] Codex regression: a caller-supplied token is relayed, not replaced, and its payload is not rewritten
- [x] Degradation: no session, expired session, and fallback disabled each publish 11 models and 0 native, with no errors
- [ ] Windows and Linux — unrun; file handling is platform-neutral and goes through `CODEX_HOME`
- [ ] The ten rejected native parameters were measured on one plan tier

title: fix: release the empty-completion hold when the upstream proves it is generating
body:
## The problem

`EmptyCompletionGuard` buffers every routed streaming response until it sees content, and reasoning deltas deliberately do not count as content. On a reasoning model the gap between the first reasoning delta and the first output token is seconds to minutes, so the guard held that entire gap. The client saw nothing until the turn closed or the 30s budget expired.

Measured against `opencode-go/deepseek-v4-pro`, two router processes sharing the same gateway, forwarder and provider, with only this behaviour varying and arms alternating so provider drift cancels:

| Model | Held | Released on liveness |
|---|---|---|
| `deepseek-v4-pro` | 30,638 / 30,531 ms | **517 / 526 ms** |
| `deepseek-v4-flash` | 29,409 / 29,577 ms | **536 / 503 ms** |

Both held arms park at `MAX_PRECONTENT_MS` — the hold budget, not the model, decided when the caller saw anything. `gpt-5.6-luna` showed no difference, because that upstream emits nothing until it emits text, so there was never a gap to hold.

Throughput is unaffected, which is why this never read as a slow turn — only a frozen one. It could not read as anything in telemetry either: `responseStartMs` stops at the response headers and `firstTokenMs` fires on reasoning deltas, and the guard kept holding past both. There was no field for the hold.

## What it cost, from 77,566 recorded turns

| | Count |
|---|---|
| Routed turns (guard applies) | 19,043 |
| Empty-completion retries fired | 168 |
| Retries that succeeded | **17** |

Every reasoning turn paid up to 30 seconds of dead air for a silent rescue on roughly one routed turn in a thousand. In the other 90% of empty turns the user got an error anyway, just 30 seconds later and after a second billed request.

## The change

The hold exists only to make the retry invisible. That is worth paying for when the upstream is silent — a silent upstream has no prologue worth waiting for — and not worth paying for when it is visibly generating.

- **`isLivenessEvent()`** — reasoning deltas, reasoning `.added`/`.done`, `output_item.added` carrying a reasoning item, and chat-completions `reasoning_content` / `reasoning`.
- Liveness **ends the hold without settling the verdict**. The guard relays and keeps parsing from behind the relay, so a turn that streams reasoning and then produces nothing is still classified empty.
- **`suppressedPrologue()`** — true only when every byte was still held at the moment the turn was declared empty. That is the precondition for an invisible retry, and it is what the router now branches on.
- A silent turn still holds every byte and still retries silently. Unchanged.
- When the attempt was already relayed, the router states the failure into the open stream via `writeStreamErrorEvent` rather than grafting a second response onto it.
- New `emptyCompletionUnrepairable` usage-event field. `recordUsageEvent` has an explicit field allowlist, so this had to be added there too or it is silently dropped.

One subtlety worth review: `#release()` no longer clears `#parseBuffer` on a liveness release. That buffer holds the partial SSE block straddling the release, and dropping it would corrupt the block the verdict may depend on.

## Why the visible error is not a regression

Verified against `codex-cli 0.145.0` with a stub upstream and an isolated `CODEX_HOME`, 3/3 reproducible:

| Stub response | Upstream turns | Answered | Codex retried |
|---|---|---|---|
| reasoning + text (control) | 1 | yes | — |
| reasoning + empty completion | 1 | **no** | **no** |
| reasoning + `event: error` | 2 | yes | yes |

The silent arm reproduces the original bug exactly: Codex prints the reasoning, reports tokens used, exits 0, and shows no answer and no error. The error arm makes Codex reissue the turn on its own ladder (`Reconnecting... 1/5`), so recovery is stronger than the single silent retry it replaces — up to five attempts instead of one — and visible instead of hidden.

Cosmetic wart: the reasoning summary renders twice in the error arm, once from the failed attempt and once from the retry. That is the visible seam that buys the 25 seconds.

## Test plan

- [x] `test/empty-completion-guard.test.mjs` + `test/empty-completion-router.test.mjs` — 52/52
- [x] `npm test` — 1161 pass, 0 fail, 8 skipped
- [x] `npm run check` — syntax checks pass
- [x] Live A/B against `opencode-go/deepseek-v4-pro` through the real provider: first byte 30,638 ms -> 1,159 ms
- [x] Live telemetry confirms the verdict survives the release: patched runs record `emptyCompletion` + `emptyCompletionUnrepairable` where the unpatched run recorded only `emptyCompletionGuardReleased` with no verdict at all
- [x] Codex client behaviour verified with a stub upstream, 3 modes, 3 reps

Fixture split for review: `SILENT_TURN` (no liveness — suppressed and retried) vs `EMPTY_TURN` (reasoning — relayed and stated). The byte/time-budget fixtures were repointed off reasoning, since liveness now releases long before the byte cap and they were about to exercise the wrong path.

## Base branch

Stacked on `feat/harness-lifecycle-and-native-session` (#198) because that branch also modifies `src/router.mjs`. Retarget to `main` once #198 merges.

title: feat: ship GLM-5.3, and split Z.ai's metered platform from its plan
body:
Z.ai shipped GLM-5.3 on 2026-08-14. This adds it on the three routes that actually serve it, and adds the metered Z.ai platform as its own provider.

## What is added

| Model ID | Route | Context | Efforts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `zai-coding/glm-5.3` | GLM Coding Plan | 200K | low/high/max |
| `zai-coding/glm-5.3-1m` | GLM Coding Plan, `glm-5.3[1m]` | 1M | low/high/max |
| `zai-api/glm-5.3` | Z.ai metered platform | 200K | low/high/max |
| `zai-api/glm-5.2` | Z.ai metered platform | 1M | high/max |
| `zai-api/glm-4.7` | Z.ai metered platform | 200K | — |
| `opencode-go/glm-5.3` | opencode Go subscription | 200K | high/max |

Command Code and Qwen Plan do not advertise GLM-5.3 yet — their live catalogs carry GLM-5, 5.1, 5.2 and (on Command Code) 5.2-Fast — so nothing was added there. Ollama Cloud and ClinePass could not be queried; no credential for either is stored on this machine.

## Why the plain entries are 200K, not 1M

Z.ai documents the one-million-token window for GLM-5.3 only behind the `[1m]` model suffix, together with a 1,000,000-token compaction window. That is a distinct upstream model name, so it is a distinct entry rather than an assumption folded into the plain one. The suffix-free entries stay at the 200K lineage default: under-declaring a context window compacts early, while over-declaring overruns the turn.

## Why `zai-api` is a separate provider

It is a separate product, not a second delivery mechanism for one credential. A Coding Plan key is not billable on `api.z.ai/api/paas/v4`, and a platform key buys no plan. So it gets its own key file (`zai-api-key.secret`), its own keychain service, and its own environment variable (`ZAI_PLATFORM_API_KEY`, never the plan's `ZAI_API_KEY`), and a `planNote` states the distinction wherever a key is connected.

Its account panel links the billing page rather than polling the plan's quota route: that route reports a Coding Plan's windows, Z.ai publishes no balance API, and spending a metered key to learn nothing is worse than saying usage lives on the dashboard.

## Effort ladders now follow the model

`glm-thinking` mapped every multi-tier GLM onto GLM-5.2's two rungs (high/max). GLM-5.3 adds a documented `low` tier, which that map would have silently rounded up to `high` — billing deeper thinking than the user asked for. The requested effort is now clamped onto the ladder each model's own registry entry declares. GLM-5.2's behavior is unchanged and is covered by the existing cases.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm run check`
- [x] `npm test` — 1087 passed, 0 failed, 8 skipped
- [x] `./bin/discover-models opencode-go` confirms `glm-5.3` in the live catalog
- [x] `./bin/providers` and `codex doctor` list `zai-api` with its own key path
- [x] New coverage: registry snapshot and credential isolation (separate key file, no shared environment variable), GLM-5.3 effort clamping (`minimal`/`low`/`medium` → `low`, `high` → `high`, `max` → `max`), GLM-4.7 never receiving `reasoning_effort`, and the metered platform degrading to the billing link without touching the plan quota route
- [ ] **Not live-tested against Z.ai** — no Z.ai credential is stored on this machine. Two things a live run would settle: that `glm-5.3[1m]` is accepted on the OpenAI-compatible coding endpoint (Z.ai documents that suffix for the Anthropic/Claude Code route), and that `glm-5.3` is billable on `paas/v4` today (Z.ai's launch post says the API is live; their pricing table has not been updated). `./bin/test-model 'zai-coding/glm-5.3' --live --yes` after storing a key settles both.

No `upgradeTo` modal is shipped for GLM-5.2 → GLM-5.3: that switches a user's default model, which should not happen on an unverified entry.

title: docs: say that native models publish, because they do now
body:
## Summary

#198 made native GPT models publishable to the DeepSeek Harness whenever this machine has a usable Codex session. | --- | --- |
| `src/dsh-catalog.mjs:9` | "Only routed models are published" — with `dshNativeModels` exported at :143 of the same file |
| `src/dsh-install.mjs:157` | "Native GPT models are never published" |

title: feat: give Model Router an app icon, and open it before Codex needs it
body:
## Why

Three separate ways the router was invisible or absent when it was needed.

**1. The app had no icon.** `Model Router.app` shipped without `CFBundleIconFile`, so it carried the generic macOS app icon and was effectively unfindable in Finder, Launchpad, and Spotlight.

**2. Opening the app did nothing visible.** It is `LSUIElement`, so there is no window and no Dock icon to appear. In follow mode with Codex closed, a double-click produced nothing at all — on exactly the launch that having an icon is for.

**3. Follow mode could not see a terminal Codex.** It asked `NSRunningApplication` for `com.openai.codex` and `com.openai.chat`. The npm CLI is a plain process with neither, so every CLI session read as "Codex is not running": the menu bar item was hidden immediately and the router was **stopped 30 seconds into the work it was needed for**.

## What changed

### App icon

`apps/macos/ModelRouterTray/Resources/AppIcon.svg` is the source; the `.icns` beside it is committed output of `scripts/build-app-icon.sh`. The script is not wired into the tray build on purpose — it needs `sips` and `iconutil`, and putting a rasterizer on the critical path of every build for one asset that changes almost never is a bad trade.

Each face is rendered from the vector rather than downsampled from 1024, so 16 px and 32 px keep their stroke weight. Two CoreSVG constraints are load-bearing and documented in `AGENTS.md`: `--` inside an XML comment is rejected outright, and SVG filter primitives are dropped silently (the glow is a radial gradient for this reason).

### Opening the app

A user launch reveals the surfaces for 20 seconds, starts the router, and pulses the status dot. Time-boxed rather than sticky, so follow mode resumes on its own instead of quietly leaving the user in always-on. It reads `effectivePresenceMode`, so it cannot undo the router's own pin.

`applicationShouldHandleReopen` handles double-clicking an already-running app, which is otherwise swallowed. launchd passes `--supervised` so a login start is distinguishable from a person opening the app and does not override follow mode every morning.

SwiftUI offers no supported way to open a `MenuBarExtra` window programmatically — the usual trick reaches into the private `NSStatusItem` behind it. A status dot that visibly reacts is worth more than a private API that breaks on the next macOS release.

### Seeing a terminal Codex

`routerPinsServiceOn` already keeps the router up *once such a client has connected*. This covers the window **before** the first connection, and makes the tray appear when Codex starts rather than when it first talks.

The scan is `sysctl`, not a spawned `pgrep`: it runs every five seconds for the life of the session, and 20 full scans measured 1.5 ms.

### The optional `codex` shim

Both the tray and launchd learn about a new Codex by polling, so a cold start races — the CLI can send its first request before the gateway accepts connections. A wrapper in front of Codex cannot race it.

```sh
model-router codex shim install | status | uninstall
```

Never installed automatically, because a file named `codex` on someone's PATH shadows a command the router was not asked to own. It:

- picks the writable directory **closest to** the real Codex but still **ahead of** it on PATH
- refuses to overwrite any `codex` not carrying its marker
- prints the `export PATH=...` line rather than editing shell startup files when nothing suitable is on PATH
- separates *installed* from *effective* in `status`, since a shim behind the real Codex is a silent no-op
- **always** execs Codex on every failure path — a stopped router, a deleted checkout, and a gateway that never comes up are recoverable; a `codex` that will not start is not

Fast path is one loopback connection and zero spawned processes. Cold path bounds the wait at `MODEL_ROUTER_SHIM_WAIT` (45s). `MODEL_ROUTER_SHIM=0` bypasses it.

## Not covered

Windows. `PATHEXT` makes shadowing a different problem, so the installer refuses rather than writing an unrunnable bash script. The tray's process scan is macOS-only.

## Test plan

- [x] `node --test test/*.test.mjs` — 1171 pass, 0 fail (11 new in `test/codex-shim.test.mjs`)
- [x] `swift test` — 18 pass, 0 fail (5 new in `HostProcessDetectionTests.swift`)
- [x] `npm run check` — syntax checks pass
- [x] `bin/model-router codex doctor` — core config, catalog, service, router health all OK
- [x] Icon verified end-to-end via `NSWorkspace.icon(forFile:)`, not just file presence
- [x] Shim exercised for: healthy router (no `control` spawned), dead router (bounded wait, warns, still runs Codex), missing checkout, recorded path gone (PATH re-resolution skipping itself), `MODEL_ROUTER_SHIM=0`, reinstall, and uninstall leaving a foreign wrapper intact
- [x] `codex --version` through the installed shim returns `codex-cli 0.145.0`
- [ ] Not verified: Linux tray path, and follow-mode hide/show across a full Codex desktop app quit cycle

title: fix: release the empty-completion hold when the upstream proves it is generating
body:
> Re-landing of #200, which was auto-closed on 2026-08-14 when its base branch `feat/harness-lifecycle-and-native-session` was deleted by the squash-merge of #198. The work was never reviewed down — it lost its base. This is the same commit, cherry-picked onto current `main` (clean, no conflicts) and re-tested: **1166 passed, 0 failed, 8 skipped**.

---

## The problem

`EmptyCompletionGuard` buffers every routed streaming response until it sees content, and reasoning deltas deliberately do not count as content. On a reasoning model the gap between the first reasoning delta and the first output token is seconds to minutes, so the guard held that entire gap. The client saw nothing until the turn closed or the 30s budget expired.

Measured against `opencode-go/deepseek-v4-pro`, two router processes sharing the same gateway, forwarder and provider, with only this behaviour varying and arms alternating so provider drift cancels:

| Model | Held | Released on liveness |
|---|---|---|
| `deepseek-v4-pro` | 30,638 / 30,531 ms | **517 / 526 ms** |
| `deepseek-v4-flash` | 29,409 / 29,577 ms | **536 / 503 ms** |

Both held arms park at `MAX_PRECONTENT_MS` — the hold budget, not the model, decided when the caller saw anything. `gpt-5.6-luna` showed no difference, because that upstream emits nothing until it emits text, so there was never a gap to hold.

Throughput is unaffected, which is why this never read as a slow turn — only a frozen one. It could not read as anything in telemetry either: `responseStartMs` stops at the response headers and `firstTokenMs` fires on reasoning deltas, and the guard kept holding past both. There was no field for the hold.

## What it cost, from 77,566 recorded turns

| | Count |
|---|---|
| Routed turns (guard applies) | 19,043 |
| Empty-completion retries fired | 168 |
| Retries that succeeded | **17** |

Every reasoning turn paid up to 30 seconds of dead air for a silent rescue on roughly one routed turn in a thousand. In the other 90% of empty turns the user got an error anyway, just 30 seconds later and after a second billed request.

## The change

The hold exists only to make the retry invisible. That is worth paying for when the upstream is silent — a silent upstream has no prologue worth waiting for — and not worth paying for when it is visibly generating.

- **`isLivenessEvent()`** — reasoning deltas, reasoning `.added`/`.done`, `output_item.added` carrying a reasoning item, and chat-completions `reasoning_content` / `reasoning`.
- Liveness **ends the hold without settling the verdict**. The guard relays and keeps parsing from behind the relay, so a turn that streams reasoning and then produces nothing is still classified empty.
- **`suppressedPrologue()`** — true only when every byte was still held at the moment the turn was declared empty. That is the precondition for an invisible retry, and it is what the router now branches on.
- A silent turn still holds every byte and still retries silently. Unchanged.
- When the attempt was already relayed, the router states the failure into the open stream via `writeStreamErrorEvent` rather than grafting a second response onto it.
- New `emptyCompletionUnrepairable` usage-event field. `recordUsageEvent` has an explicit field allowlist, so this had to be added there too or it is silently dropped.

One subtlety worth review: `#release()` no longer clears `#parseBuffer` on a liveness release. That buffer holds the partial SSE block straddling the release, and dropping it would corrupt the block the verdict may depend on.

## Why the visible error is not a regression

Verified against `codex-cli 0.145.0` with a stub upstream and an isolated `CODEX_HOME`, 3/3 reproducible:

| Stub response | Upstream turns | Answered | Codex retried |
|---|---|---|---|
| reasoning + text (control) | 1 | yes | — |
| reasoning + empty completion | 1 | **no** | **no** |
| reasoning + `event: error` | 2 | yes | yes |

The silent arm reproduces the original bug exactly: Codex prints the reasoning, reports tokens used, exits 0, and shows no answer and no error. The error arm makes Codex reissue the turn on its own ladder (`Reconnecting... 1/5`), so recovery is stronger than the single silent retry it replaces — up to five attempts instead of one — and visible instead of hidden.

Cosmetic wart: the reasoning summary renders twice in the error arm, once from the failed attempt and once from the retry. That is the visible seam that buys the 25 seconds.

## Test plan

- [x] `test/empty-completion-guard.test.mjs` + `test/empty-completion-router.test.mjs` — 52/52
- [x] `npm test` — 1161 pass, 0 fail, 8 skipped
- [x] `npm run check` — syntax checks pass
- [x] Live A/B against `opencode-go/deepseek-v4-pro` through the real provider: first byte 30,638 ms -> 1,159 ms
- [x] Live telemetry confirms the verdict survives the release: patched runs record `emptyCompletion` + `emptyCompletionUnrepairable` where the unpatched run recorded only `emptyCompletionGuardReleased` with no verdict at all
- [x] Codex client behaviour verified with a stub upstream, 3 modes, 3 reps

Fixture split for review: `SILENT_TURN` (no liveness — suppressed and retried) vs `EMPTY_TURN` (reasoning — relayed and stated). The byte/time-budget fixtures were repointed off reasoning, since liveness now releases long before the byte cap and they were about to exercise the wrong path.

## Base branch

Stacked on `feat/harness-lifecycle-and-native-session` (#198) because that branch also modifies `src/router.mjs`. Retarget to `main` once #198 merges.

title: [Bug]: Windows tray: every refresh fails with ESDIR on stat C, console windows flash, and tray status reports stopped
body:
## What happened

On Windows, every **Refresh** in the desktop companion fails. A refresh fires several `control` commands (snapshot, account, provider-usage, provider-setup, local-models), each spawning `node.exe <checkout>\src\control.mjs`. Every spawn dies at node startup before the script runs:

```
node:fs:2745
const out = binding.stat(base, false, undefined, true /* throwIfNoEntry */);
^
Error: ESDIR: illegal operation on a directory, stat 'C'
    at Object.realpathSync (node:fs:2745:25)
    at toRealPath (node:internal/modules/helpers:83:13)
    at Module._findPath (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:80:22)
    at resolveMainPath (node:internal/modules/run_main:35:21)
    ...
```

## Root cause

`resolve_source_root()` in `apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs` finishes with `candidate.canonicalize()`. On Windows, `std::fs::canonicalize` returns an extended-length `\\?\` path, e.g.:

```
\\?\C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\codex-router
```

`run_control()` then spawns `node \\?\C:\...\src\control.mjs`. Node cannot execute a `\\?\`-prefixed path as a script entry point — it strips the prefix, resolves the bare drive letter, and fails at startup. Reproduced with `node "\\?\C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\codex-router\src\control.mjs" --json`.

## Secondary issues

- **Console windows flash on every control call.** The tray is a GUI process with no console, but the node.exe spawns use a plain `std::process::Command` without `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` (`0x08000000`). Each control call flashes a new terminal window; with every spawn failing instantly, this shows up as a constant stream of popups.
- **Tray status always reports "stopped" on non-English Windows.** `taskRunning()` in `src/tray-service-windows.mjs` matches `\bRunning\b` against localized `schtasks` output (Spanish shows "En ejecución", for example), so `tray status` never sees a running task even while it runs.

## Expected behavior

Clicking Refresh loads the panel data; no console windows appear; tray status reflects the real task state.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Windows 10/11, install the router and the tray (`install.ps1 -WithTray`).
2. Open the tray panel and click **Refresh** (or wait for the 60-second auto-refresh).

## Fix (local patch; happy to open a PR)

- Strip the `\\?\` prefix before handing the script path to node.
- Set `creation_flags(0x08000000)` (CREATE_NO_WINDOW) on the spawn.
- Read the task state through `Get-ScheduledTask`'s locale-independent `State` enum in `taskRunning()`.

## Doctor output

All doctor checks pass (exit 0). This is desktop-companion specific and does not affect the headless router.

title: fix(desktop): make Windows tray control spawns and task status work
body:
Fixes #208

## What this fixes

On Windows, every refresh in the desktop companion app failed. A refresh fires several `control` commands, each spawning `node.exe <checkout>\src\control.mjs`, and every spawn died at node startup with:

```
node:fs:2745
const out = binding.stat(base, false, undefined, true /* throwIfNoEntry */);
^
Error: ESDIR: illegal operation on a directory, stat 'C'
```

This PR addresses three related Windows issues:

1. **`\\?\` extended-length paths break node spawns.** `resolve_source_root()` ends with `candidate.canonicalize()`, which on Windows returns a `\\?\C:\...` path. `run_control()` then spawns `node \\?\C:\...\src\control.mjs` — node cannot execute a `\\?\`-prefixed path as a script entry point and fails at startup (reproduced with `node "\\?\C:\...\src\control.mjs" --json`). The prefix is now stripped before the path is handed to node.

2. **Console windows flash on every control call.** The tray is a GUI process with no console, but the `node.exe` spawns did not set `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` (`0x08000000`), so every control call flashed a new terminal window.

3. **Tray task status always reported "stopped" on non-English Windows.** `taskRunning()` in `src/tray-service-windows.mjs` matched `\bRunning\b` against localized `schtasks` output (e.g. Spanish renders it "En ejecución"). It now reads the task state through `Get-ScheduledTask`'s locale-independent `State` enum, matching how `service-windows.mjs` already does it.

## Changes

- `apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs` — strip the `\\?\` prefix (`windows_readable_path`), set `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` on the spawn, add a regression test.
- `src/tray-service-windows.mjs` — locale-independent `taskRunning()`.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo check`, and `cargo test` pass (7 tests, including the new path-stripping test).
- `npm run check` and `npm test` pass; the 7 local failures are environmental (4 POSIX installer tests require `sh`, which is not on this session's PATH; 2 pre-existing `doctor-kimi` cleanup failures reproduce on clean `main`; 1 tray test expects a checkout with no compiled binary — the local checkout has one). title: force a stable HTTP/1.1 upstream transport
body:
## What changed

- install one process-wide Undici dispatcher before the router begins serving requests
- disable HTTP/2 while preserving the existing `fetch` call sites

## Root cause

A long-lived Node process could retain a destroyed HTTP/2 session. Once that happened, later upstream requests repeatedly failed with `ERR_HTTP2_INVALID_SESSION` and surfaced as local 502 responses until the service restarted. Forcing HTTP/1.1 avoids reusing the poisoned HTTP/2 session while keeping the existing request pipeline intact.

feat: group a vendor's providers, and let the tray restart itself
body:
Two tray changes.

## A vendor's providers are drawn together

The Providers list showed 13 rows for 5 vendors. `variantOf` already collapses the rows that share a credential — that is why Command Code and opencode Go each appear once despite carrying three protocol surfaces between them — but it cannot help the vendors whose providers are separate *accounts*:

| Vendor | Providers | Why they cannot merge |
|---|---|---|
| Z.ai | `zai-coding`, `zai-api` | different endpoints; a Coding Plan key is not billable on the metered one and vice versa |
| Kimi | `kimi-oauth`, `kimi-api`, `kimi-api-cn` | different regions and auth kinds |
| xAI | `grok-oauth`, `grok-api` | API key vs OAuth |

So they stay separately connectable and are only drawn together:

```
Z.ai                    2 accounts
    API
    GLM Coding Plan
```

The heading is derived from the display names rather than a new config field: `"Z.ai GLM Coding Plan"` and `"Z.ai API"` share their leading word, so the heading is `Z.ai` and the rows read `GLM Coding Plan` and `API`. Whole words only, so a group sharing a few letters cannot produce a heading that is half a word. A vendor with one provider renders exactly as before — a heading above a single row is noise, not structure.

`ownedBy` already existed on every provider and was already correct for all five vendors; it was only ever used for API metadata and error text. The only addition is passing it through `control`'s provider payload, and it is decoded as optional so an older router degrades to ungrouped rather than failing to decode.

## The grouped list is bound once per render

Reading the computed property inside its own `ForEach` regrouped and re-sorted the whole registry for every row. Measured at **89us per pass**, that is ~2.4ms of a render spent on nothing, and `body` re-runs on every store publish.

Bound once, the whole grouping costs **49us per render**, measured over 332 real renders with temporary instrumentation:

| | calls/render | cost/render |
|---|---|---|
| `providerVendorGroups` | 0.5 | 49us |
| `providerUsage(for:)` | 29.6 | 54us |
| `providerGroups(models:67)` | 0.5 | 8us |
| `providerName` | 4.8 | 1us |

~115us per render in total, so the remaining linear scans are deliberately left alone — hoisting them into the store would save a tenth of a millisecond and touch working code for it. The instrumentation was removed before this commit.

## Restarting the tray

Rebuilding the app replaces the bundle but leaves the running agent on the old binary, and quitting from the panel does not bring it back — `KeepAlive` is conditional on `SuccessfulExit: false`. A button beside **Refresh** closes that loop through the existing `control tray restart`.

It kills the process that asked for it, which is safe twice over: `launchctl kickstart -k` makes launchd commit to the relaunch *before* it signals the job, and an abnormal exit is exactly what `KeepAlive` covers. Only the failure path sets a message, because a success takes the window that would have shown it.

title: fix: close finished subagents instead of leaving them Working
body:
Work that was stranded on `feat/glm-5.3-and-zai-platform` — that branch's only PR (#201) merged for the GLM/Z.ai change, leaving these three commits pushed with nothing pointing at them.

## The problem

Codex 0.147 records a child's `FINAL_ANSWER` as `subAgentActivity: interacted` and maps that to **Working** until one of three things happens: the parent turn ends, the user clicks into the child, or the parent calls `interrupt_agent`. `close_agent` is not in the v2 toolset.

So a finished child sits there looking busy for the rest of a long parent turn, and a multi-agent run ends showing a row of children that all claim to still be working.

## The fix, in three parts

**1. Tell the parent to close them.** The managed `multi_agent_v2` block now ships a root usage hint instructing the parent to interrupt finished children, so new tasks settle the badge without a click.

**2. Close them anyway when it doesn't.** The hint alone is not enough — long San Francisco multi-agent parents often never call `interrupt_agent` despite it. The router scans request input for unfinished `FINAL_ANSWER` children and injects the missing `collaboration.interrupt_agent` calls into the parent response, on both the stream and non-stream paths, before `response.completed`.

**3. Do it for native parents too.** San Francisco multi-agent parents run through the router as **native GPT**, so a routed-only inject never fired for exactly the builds that needed it most. The close now queues on the native response path as well.

Model-authored interrupts are left alone; only missing closes are added.

title: fix: repair a nullable object root on every tool, not just namespaced ones
body:
Found while verifying #219. **That issue is already fixed on `main`** — confirmed live by deleting the sanitizer and reproducing the reporter's exact error — but probing the sanitizer with adversarial roots turned up one it lets through.

## The bug

A tool whose parameter root is `type: ["object", "null"]` is legal JSON Schema and is rejected **by name** by two independent upstreams. Both reproduced against the real backends:

| Upstream | Message |
|---|---|
| xAI | `tool parameter root must be an object type` |
| DeepSeek | `schema must be a JSON Schema of 'type: "object"', got 'type: ["object","null"]'` |

`hasObjectRoot` let it through because the root carried `properties`, so the declared type was never consulted.

## What changed

1. **`hasObjectRoot` reads a declared type literally** — only the exact string `"object"` passes. The `properties` fallback stays for schemas declaring no type at all, which xAI accepts (verified live).
2. **The shared relay repairs it too.** `providerToolSchema` is deliberately narrow because it runs on every namespace and MCP tool, and a schema that merely looks unusual must not be replaced with one accepting anything. A second upstream rejecting a nullable root *by name* is what promotes it from unusual to documented, alongside the union root already handled. A `type: ["string","null"]` root — no `"object"` member — is still left alone, since collapsing it would destroy the schema rather than fix it.
3. **Both repairs now reach plain function tools**, not only namespaced children. The rejections are the provider's, not the namespace's, so a client-declared tool with a union or nullable root failed on exactly the providers that object while the namespaced copy beside it was repaired. A tool needing nothing is passed through by identity, uncopied.
4. **A rewrite that merged no union keeps its own `additionalProperties`.** That `true` default exists because a merged object cannot say which branch a call belongs to; a nullable root becoming a plain object has no such ambiguity and should not be quietly widened.

The repair is lossless: properties, required and additionalProperties all survive, and only the root's own `null` alternative is dropped — a tool call whose entire argument object is null is not one any of these providers can dispatch.

## Measured live, before and after

|  | plain | nullable | union |
|---|---|---|---|
| `deepseek-v4-flash` | pass | **400 → pass** | pass |
| `deepseek-v4-pro` | pass | **400 → pass** | pass |
| `grok-4.6` | pass | **400 → pass** | pass |
| `glm-5.2` | pass | pass | pass |
| `minimax-m3` | pass | pass | pass |

Qwen could not be tested — the plan is out of quota. Kimi likewise (HTTP 403).

title: Feature request: zero-provider / no-credential-discovery install mode
body:
Codex Router currently expects at least one configured provider, and automatic setup may inspect existing macOS Keychain entries, CLI/OAuth sessions, and provider credential files. This makes it difficult to safely validate installation, service lifecycle, rollback, and uninstall behavior before trusting the router with real credentials. I would like to request an explicit credential-free installation mode, for example with flags such as `--no-provider` and `--no-discovery`.

When both flags are enabled, Codex Router should be installable without selecting or configuring any provider. It should not scan macOS Keychain, read existing CLI or OAuth sessions, inspect or import provider credential files, require provider credentials, create provider credential files, auto-discover providers, or automatically fall back to an existing provider. The existing native Codex configuration and authentication should remain unchanged. The router should be able to start in a deterministic idle state, bind only to loopback, preferably `127.0.0.1`, and should not route Codex traffic to any external provider or retry provider discovery in the background. Normal lifecycle operations such as `status`, `start`, `stop`, `doctor`, `uninstall`, and `rollback` should still work. If Codex traffic reaches the router while no provider is configured, it should return a clear local error instead of attempting discovery or external routing.

For network behavior, provider-related outbound connections should be `0`, credential-discovery-related outbound connections should be `0`, and the listener should be restricted to loopback only. If installation or update checks require GitHub, npm, PyPI, or another package registry, those connections should be explicitly documented and ideally suppressible for offline validation.

A possible validation flow would be:

```text
install --no-provider --no-discovery
service start
service status
doctor
service stop
uninstall
```

The complete lifecycle should work without configuring or reading any provider credentials.

## Acceptance criteria

- Keychain reads: `0`
- CLI/OAuth session reads: `0`
- Provider credential reads: `0`
- Provider credential writes: `0`
- Provider discovery attempts: `0`
- Provider external connections: `0`
- Listener: loopback only
- Original Codex config hash changed: `NO`
- Original Codex auth hash changed: `NO`
- Background provider retry/discovery: `NO`

After uninstall or rollback:

- Orphan router process: `0`
- LaunchAgent remaining: `NO`
- Proxy remaining: `NO`
- Router listening port: `NO`
- Routing override remaining: `NO`
- Native Codex launch: `PASS`
- Original config restored: `PASS`

This would allow users to verify Codex Router installation, lifecycle behavior, network behavior, rollback, and uninstall safety before granting it access to API keys, OAuth sessions, Keychain credentials, provider configuration, or production Codex traffic. The goal is not to change the normal user-friendly setup flow, but to provide an explicit, deterministic, credential-free lifecycle-validation mode for users who require stricter security controls. If an equivalent mode already exists through an undocumented flag, environment variable, or configuration option, documentation for that path would also solve this use case.

title: feat: research any enabled model for the v2 subagent role automatically
body:
Closes the gap #183 kept hitting: people want arbitrary models — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, whatever their provider serves — as native v2 subagents, but the only promotion path was a per-model registry change gated on a manual four-part probe. Six models ever made it through.

**Selection is now the assignment.** The operator toggles a model on as a subagent (tray or `control subagents set`); the router's job is answering whether that model *under that provider* can hold the child role:

1. **Auto probe on enable** — a detached worker (same shape as the vision-download worker, so the tray toggle never blocks) spends 2 live requests proving streaming + a forced tool call through the installed router. Snapshot shows `checking` → verdict → catalog republish.
2. **Experimental advertisement** — a passing model is offered to Codex as a v2 subagent, recorded in protected `multi-agent-proofs.json`.
3. **Proof by observation** — Codex marks child turns with `x-openai-subagent`; the router's request path records the first clean completion as the durable proof (`proven`), and a structural rejection (400/422) demotes back to v1 with the reason kept in the subagent snapshot. Transient failures (429/5xx/disconnects) prove nothing and leave the window open.
4. `control subagents verify [slug ...]` re-researches explicitly; no-arg sweeps the enabled list. Select-all and mode changes never probe — a sweep across every provider is quota the operator must ask for.

The AGENTS.md invariant survives intact: local settings still never manufacture a v2 claim. The only writers of promotion evidence are the probe worker and the router's own observation of real traffic; unreadable proofs promote nothing; hidden/disabled slugs stay v1 whatever evidence they carry. Registry v2 remains the path for repo-shipped defaults.

body:
Closes #224.

Adds an explicit, deterministic, credential-free install mode so the router's install, lifecycle, network, and uninstall behavior can be validated before it is trusted with API keys, OAuth sessions, Keychain credentials, or production Codex traffic.

## What's in here (7 commits, in dependency order)

1. **`fix:` retire the background service when the last managed config block is gone** — `installedTargets()` keyed "codex is installed" on the cached native catalog, a file uninstall deliberately retains, so the service, LaunchAgent, and listening ports survived every codex uninstall. The witness is now the managed block in `config.toml`. `bin/disable` of the last client retires the service too (matching the Windows wrapper), and `bin/enable` reinstalls it on the way back.
2. **`feat:` a `stop` subcommand** — `bin/stop`, `bin/model-router … stop`, and the Windows dispatcher, completing the install → start → status → doctor → stop → uninstall loop.
3. **`feat:` a persisted discovery kill-switch** — `src/discovery-mode.mjs` (`discovery-mode.json`, overridable with `CODEX_ROUTER_NO_DISCOVERY=1|0`), consulted by every credential reader: the credential resolver (env/file/Keychain/CLI-session), `configuredProviderIds()`, the Kimi/Grok OAuth status readers, the CLI-session reader, Codex's `auth.json` reader, and the `codex login status` probe (skipped with a distinct reason the catalog treats as deliberate signed-out).
4. **`feat:` local idle error instead of native forwarding** — with discovery disabled, `/responses` turns without a route and the native image/web-search endpoints return `503 router_idle_no_provider` before any upstream fetch. Hiding every provider *without* the flag keeps native passthrough exactly as today (regression-tested).
5. **`feat:` doctor idle mode** — an explicit empty selection plus the marker reports at warn, the merged catalog is held to the nothing-routable standard, the per-provider credential sweep (itself discovery) collapses to one row, and the config-load probe / session-refresh nudge — which make Codex read its real session file — are skipped. Doctor exits 0 on a healthy idle install; an empty selection without the marker still fails loudly.
6. **`feat:` the install flags** — `--no-provider` (empty explicit selection, no credential steps; conflicts with `--guided`/`--providers`/key flags) and `--no-discovery` (requires `--no-provider`), plumbed through `install.sh`, `install.ps1`, and `src/setup.mjs`. Setup writes the discovery marker on **every** run, so re-running without the flags is the exit path. `ensure-configured` now accepts an explicitly empty selection as idle — which also un-breaks `bin/update` for anyone who hid their last provider by hand.
7. **`docs:`** INSTALL.md section (flags, guarantees, lifecycle, uninstall-vs-rollback), SECURITY.md network-boundary claims (including the one remaining `codex debug models --bundled` static-list spawn), AGENTS.md invariant, README pointer, CHANGELOG.

- Keychain / CLI-OAuth-session / credential reads & writes: **0** — kill-switch at every reader; `test/provider-credentials.test.mjs` asserts `keychainProbeCount()` stays flat with a real credential file on disk.
- Provider discovery / external connections: **0** — `configuredProviderIds()` returns `[]`; `test/router-idle.test.mjs` points `CODEX_NATIVE_BASE_URL` at a recording server and asserts zero hits.
- Listener loopback-only: already the default everywhere; doctor now warns if `CODEX_ROUTER_HOST` is non-loopback while discovery is off.
- Codex config/auth unchanged: only the standard managed block is written; `auth.json` is never opened (reader guarded).
- Background retry/discovery: none exists (no timers in any server process); subagent verification has zero candidates with zero providers.
- Lifecycle: `status`/`start`/`stop`/`doctor`/`uninstall` all work idle; uninstall now actually removes the LaunchAgent/service (commit 1). `rollback` reverts the source checkout, not the install — documented.

title: fix(aging): prove the compaction pass ran even when it changes nothing
body:
## The bug

Reported from the field: an operator enabled `tool-result-aging`, ran a large repo-audit task on Qwen 3.8 Max, and afterwards saw `requests=0, resultsAged=0, bytesSaved=0` with `toolResultsAged=null` on every usage row. They reasonably asked whether the hook had loaded at all, or whether that task path bypassed it.

It had loaded. Every aging counter is written only when non-zero (`usage-events.mjs`, truthiness spreads), and `toolResultAgingTotals` only counts a request when `resultsAged` is truthy. So **a pass that ran and found nothing eligible was byte-identical to a pass that never ran** — there was no signal anywhere that could distinguish them.

The likely reason nothing qualified: only individual results over 32 KiB are eligible, and a repo audit produces many medium reads rather than a few huge ones. A session can reach 275K tokens without a single result crossing the floor.

## The fix

Record what the pass looked at, whether or not it changed anything:

- `toolResultsEvaluated` — tool results examined
- `toolResultBytesLargest` — largest one seen

Totalled as `evaluatedRequests` / `largestResultBytes`. A **disabled** pass still reports neither, so off stays distinguishable from on-and-idle. Observed on a synthetic session where nothing qualifies:

```
enabled:  {"toolResultsAged":0, ..., "toolResultsEvaluated":8, "toolResultBytesLargest":12000}
disabled: {"toolResultsAged":0, ...}
```

`12000` against the 32,768-byte floor is the answer to "why did nothing age". The tray shows that case as **"No result over 32 KB in N requests (largest 12 KB)"** instead of falling back to the "Off by default…" text, which read as though the toggle had done nothing.

## Deliberately not included

- **Lowering the 32 KiB floor.** Likely too high for repo-audit workloads, but these counters are what will tell us by how much, across real sessions rather than one report.
- **Lowering `autoCompact`.** Cannot help the reported case: that task opened at 246,688 input tokens on turn one, already past the 235,000 threshold, so it could never get back under it. Why a fresh task starts near 250K is the open question.

## Test plan
- [x] `npm run check`
- [x] `npm test`: 1,252 pass / 0 fail — includes a test reproducing the reported scenario and one asserting off stays distinguishable from on-and-idle
- [x] `swift build` + `swift test`: 20 pass

title: fix(qwen): correct qwen-plan context windows to the documented limits
body:
## What was wrong

All nine `qwen-plan` entries carried an identical **262,144 / 235,000** — across Qwen, DeepSeek, *and* GLM models from three different vendors. That uniformity is the tell: a placeholder, not nine researched values. Our own repo already declares the same underlying models at 1,000,000–1,048,576 through clinepass, commandcode, deepseek, opencode-go, ollama-cloud, and zai-api. qwen-plan was the lone outlier on every one.

## What the documentation actually says

Verified against Alibaba's Chinese model-studio reference pages (the English pages are stale — the `deepseek-v4-pro` EN page predates the 0813 release entirely):

| Model | Context | Max input | Was |
|---|---|---|---|
| qwen3.8-max | 1,000,000 | 991,808 | 262,144 |
| qwen3.7-max / 3.7-plus / 3.6-flash | 1,000,000 | 991,808 | 262,144 |
| deepseek-v4-pro / -0813 / -flash-0731 | 1,000,000 | 1,000,000 | 262,144 |
| glm-5.2 | 1,048,576 | 1,048,576 | 262,144 |

**No reseller cap is involved.** DeepSeek's output ceiling on DashScope is 393,216 = exactly 384×1024, and GLM's is 131,072 = exactly 128×1024 — both match the original vendors precisely, so Alibaba is passing these through at full size.

## Why it mattered

Codex compacts at the `auto_compact_token_limit` we advertise. A field report shows a legitimate repo-audit task opening at **246,688 input tokens** — already past the old 235,000 threshold on turn one. It compacted immediately, lost its working state, restarted its git preflight, regrew, and compacted again, never finishing. The same trace shows a **277,174-token request accepted with HTTP 200**, which the old 262,144 window says should have been impossible.

`autoCompact` moves to 900,000, the value every other million-token model in this repo already uses (the old 235,000 was also 89.6% of its window, against this repo's 85% convention).

## Known risk

These are standard Model Studio figures; we route through `token-plan.ap-southeast-1.maas.aliyuncs.com`. Subscription endpoints can enforce below published limits — a field report on Alibaba's *Coding Plan* endpoint measured 169,984 enforced for a model its own FAQ publishes at 1,000,000. Direct evidence for token-plan is "at least 277,174" (observed accepted). **Recommend confirming with an oversized-request probe before merge** — DashScope returns `400 InvalidParameter: "Range of input length should be [1, N]"` with the true N embedded. My own quota resets 2026-08-18.

## Follow-ups not in this PR

- **Delist `qwen3.8-max-preview`** — its upstream doc page 404s and it appears retired at GA. Left untouched here rather than given an invented number.
- **Learn limits at runtime** — parse `Range of input length should be [1, N]` from 400s and cache per model+endpoint. There is no metadata API on any DashScope host, so every tool in this ecosystem hardcodes and drifts; this bug will otherwise recur.

## Problem

#210 added LM Studio as a keyless local provider (`config/lmstudio/lmstudio.json`, OpenAI-compatible server at `http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1`). But the desktop/browser panel's local-model view (shipped in #202) is Ollama-centric:

- `localModelsSnapshot()` in `src/local-models.mjs` reads only `ollama list`, so models loaded in LM Studio never appear in the panel.
- The only way to publish an LM Studio model to the picker is `./bin/curate-models lmstudio` in an interactive terminal — the panel offers no path at all.
- The panel's Local Models header ("installed / enabled / usable as chat") silently under-reports when someone runs models through LM Studio instead of (or beside) Ollama.

The panel's local-model view should list models the LM Studio server is currently serving (read-only inventory — LM Studio owns download/removal), show whether each is published to the picker, and let the operator check/uncheck them the same way Ollama models are enabled, without needing an interactive terminal.

When the LM Studio server is not running, the section should say so instead of disappearing, mirroring how the Ollama runtime status is reported.

Noted as a follow-up during the #202 merge review.

title: feat: add official Xiaomi MiMo API provider
body:
# feat: add official Xiaomi MiMo API provider

## Problem

codex-router already routes MiMo through ClinePass, opencode Go, and Command Code, but there is no direct route for Xiaomi's official MiMo API (`https://api.xiaomimimo.com/v1`).

When a direct MiMo route was tried over the Responses gateway, Xiaomi rejected the standard Codex tool declarations:

```text
HTTP 400 responses_feature_not_supported
tool type 'web_search' is not supported by this gateway phase
tool type 'custom' is not supported by this gateway phase
```

Codex sends hosted-style tool declarations (`tools: [{type: "web_search"}]`, plus custom tools from the native template). Forwarding those untouched to `api.xiaomimimo.com/v1/responses` is rejected by Xiaomi's gateway. MiMo's official OpenAI-compatible API accepts chat completions with `web_search_options` instead.

## Changes

- Add `xiaomi-mimo` provider with `protocol: "openai"`, so LiteLLM generates `openai/<gatewayModel>` with `use_chat_completions_api: true` and requests never touch the Responses gateway.
- Add `xiaomi-mimo/mimo-v2.5` (text + image, Codex standalone web search, 1M context) and `xiaomi-mimo/mimo-v2.5-pro` (text only, 1M context).
- Allow routed model metadata to narrow tool capabilities inherited from the native template: `supports_parallel_tool_calls: false`, `experimental_supported_tools: []`, and `supports_apply_patch_tool: false` keep Codex from offering custom tools MiMo rejects.
- Validate the new `supportsParallelToolCalls` and `experimentalSupportedTools` registry fields.
- Add registry, catalog, and API-forwarder regression tests, including a chat-completions request that keeps `web_search_options` and strips `client_metadata`.
- Document the provider and credential setup in the README.

## Verification

- `npm run check` passes.
- `npm test`: 1294 passed, 0 failed, 13 skipped.
- Local end-to-end check: Xiaomi `/v1/chat/completions` accepts both a plain request and a request with `web_search_options` (HTTP 200); a router-gateway MiMo request carrying a `web_search` tool also returns 200 after the protocol change.

## Notes

- Credential environment variable: `MIMO_API_KEY`; protected key file: `xiaomi-mimo-api-key.secret`; keychain service: `codex-router-xiaomi-mimo-api`.
- Base URL override: `XIAOMI_MIMO_API_BASE_URL`.
- No API keys or credentials are included in this PR.

title: [Bug]: zai-coding GLM-5.3 1M entry sends glm-5.3[1m] to the OpenAI-compatible coding endpoint — Z.ai rejects it (error 1214, modelCode does not exist)
body:
## Summary

The `zai-coding/glm-5.3-1m` catalog entry (GLM-5.3 1M (Coding Plan)) routes the upstream model code `glm-5.3[1m]` to the OpenAI-compatible Coding Plan endpoint (`https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4`), but Z.ai rejects that code with HTTP 400, error `1214` (`modelCode: does not exist`). The entry is therefore unusable right now.

## Environment

- codex-router `v0.4.0-beta.4`, commit `397f455`, Linux, systemd user service
- Provider: `zai-coding` (GLM Coding Plan), default `baseUrl` unchanged (`https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4`)
- Verified right after a clean `bin/update` on 2026-08-15

## Reproduction

```
$ ./bin/test-model zai-coding/glm-5.3-1m --live --yes --quick --json
...
"markerReceived": false,
"error": "zai rejected the request for GLM-5.3 1M (Coding Plan). (HTTP 400: modelCode: does not exist)"
```

Baselines on the **same endpoint and credential** pass, so this is specific to the `[1m]` model code:

```
$ ./bin/test-model zai-coding/glm-5.3 --live --yes --quick --json   # 200, markerReceived: true
$ ./bin/test-model zai-coding/glm-5.2  --live --yes --quick --json  # 200, markerReceived: true
```

Router log (`~/.codex/codex-router/router.log`) for the failing request:

```
openai.BadRequestError: Error code: 400 - {'error': {'code': '1214', 'message': 'modelCode: does not exist'}}
litellm.exceptions.BadRequestError: litellm.BadRequestError: OpenAIException - modelCode: does not exist. Received Model Group=zai-coding-glm-5-3-1m
```

## Analysis

- `config/zai/coding/glm-5.3-1m.json` sets `"upstreamModel": "glm-5.3[1m]"`, and the api-forwarder passes it through verbatim (`src/api-forwarder.mjs:361`, `payload.model = model.upstreamModel`), so the bracketed code is what reaches Z.ai.
- Per Z.ai's docs (https://docs.z.ai/devpack/latest-model), the `[1m]` suffix is documented on the **Anthropic-compatible** endpoint (`https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic`, Claude Code examples with `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW=1000000`). The OpenAI-compatible coding endpoint does not recognize `glm-5.3[1m]` today — it returns error 1214 while plain `glm-5.3` and `glm-5.2` work fine on it.

## Suggestions

Any of these would resolve it:

1. Route the 1M entry through the Anthropic-compatible endpoint, where the docs actually place the `[1m]` code; or
2. Gate/hide the entry until Z.ai exposes a 1M model code on the OpenAI-compatible coding endpoint; or
3. At minimum, adjust the catalog description so users don't expect a working 1M route for GLM-5.3 yet.

Side note: `zai-coding/glm-5.2` already delivers a working native 1M context window (`contextWindow: 1048576`) on the coding endpoint, which is a viable 1M option for affected users in the meantime.

Thanks for the router — the model-catalog + auto-compact plumbing is a really nice design.
