title: fix(zai): drop the nonexistent glm-5.3[1m] route and correct GLM-5.3 to 1M
body:
Fixes #244.

## Reproduced, then went further

The report is exactly right — confirmed live on the same endpoint and credential:

```
zai-coding/glm-5.3-1m  -> 400  modelCode: does not exist
zai-coding/glm-5.3     -> 200  markerReceived: true
zai-coding/glm-5.2     -> 200  markerReceived: true
```

**Suggestion 1 in the issue (route it through the Anthropic-compatible endpoint) would not have worked.** I probed that endpoint directly with the same key:

```
POST https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic/v1/messages
  glm-5.3[1m]  -> 400  {"code":"1214","message":"modelCode: does not exist"}
  glm-5.3      -> 200
```

The `[1m]` code does not exist on **either** Z.ai route. It appears to be a suffix that circulated in blog posts and community articles rather than one Z.ai actually serves.

## It was never needed

README committed the project to a test: the plain GLM-5.3 entries would stay at the 200K lineage default *"until a live run proves otherwise."* That run now exists — plain `glm-5.3` on the coding endpoint:

```
prompt_tokens = 275,020  -> HTTP 200
prompt_tokens = 990,020  -> HTTP 200
```

GLM-5.3 is a genuine 1M model on the suffix-free code. The 200,000 we declared is GLM-**5.1**'s figure, inherited by lineage default. So the `[1m]` entry was a workaround for an understated window, built on a model code that does not exist.

## Changes

- Remove `config/zai/coding/glm-5.3-1m.json` and its catalog/doc/test references. It cannot work on any endpoint, so delisting it rather than deleting would only hide a permanent 400.
- `zai-coding/glm-5.3` and `zai-api/glm-5.3`: **200,000/180,000 → 1,000,000/900,000**, matching every other million-token model in the repo.
- README and `docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md` updated, including the now-satisfied "until a live run proves otherwise" note.

Anyone who wanted the 1M route gets it on the working `zai-coding/glm-5.3` entry.

## Caveat

`zai-coding` is probe-verified above. `zai-api/glm-5.3` is corrected from the same vendor documentation but **not** probe-verified — no credential for that endpoint was available here. Same model at the same vendor, so the risk is low, but flagging it honestly.

title: feat(doctor): flag context windows the provider has already disproved
body:
## Why

Four wrong context windows were found by hand this week — qwen-plan's nine models (#240), GLM-5.3 twice (#246), and `grok-oauth/grok-4.5`. Each was invisible until a user hit it.

The failure is silent and asymmetric. Codex compacts at the auto-compact limit derived from the window we declare, so an **understated** window makes a legitimate task open *above* its own compaction threshold: it summarizes, the agent loses its working state, redoes its opening work, regrows, and compacts again without ever finishing. Nothing errors. The session just never ends and the model takes the blame. An **overstated** window fails honestly instead — one upstream rejection that names the real limit.

## What this does

The evidence was already on disk. Every successful turn records its input tokens, so a 200 on a prompt larger than the declared window is the provider disproving our entry. This scans the ledger for the highest accepted prompt per routed slug and warns when it exceeds what we declare.

Running it against my own install immediately reproduces the known bug:

```json
{
  "status": "warn",
  "name": "Context windows match observed traffic",
  "detail": "grok-oauth/grok-4.5 declares 500000 but accepted 2033426"
}
```

No probing, no quota, no network — it reads data we already keep.

## Evidence rules

- **Only accepted turns count.** A rejected turn may have been rejected for exceeding the very limit under test.
- **Estimated counts are excluded.** The router substitutes its own estimate when a provider reports zero; an estimate cannot disprove a provider's own limit.
- **Beyond 64× is a metering bug, not a discovery.**
- **Keyed per routed slug, not per upstream model** — the same model behind two providers has two real ceilings, as qwen-plan vs clinepass and zai-coding vs zai-api both showed.

Warn rather than fail: an understated window still routes, and an operator may genuinely be on a plan whose ceiling is lower than the vendor's. What they can't do is notice it themselves.

## Next in this direction

This is the passive half. The active half is learning ceilings from limit-bearing errors (`Range of input length should be [1, N]`) and caching them per provider+model+endpoint — that closes the loop from above, where this closes it from below.

title: feat(subagents): choose the reasoning effort a model runs at as a child
body:
## The gap

Codex picks which model a subagent runs on. Nothing let an operator say **how hard that child should think**. A child auditing one file rarely needs the depth its parent is running at — and the reverse holds for a child doing the expensive analysis the parent delegated precisely to get it off its own context.

## How it works

Codex marks child turns with `x-openai-subagent`, which the router already read to settle subagent proofs. That header is the hook: a configured effort applies **only** to turns Codex marked as a child, so the same model keeps its normal depth in a parent conversation. Running one model differently in the two roles is the whole point.

**Tray:** Settings → Subagent models → switch a model on → an *"Effort as subagent"* menu appears under its row, offering that model's own levels plus "Model default" to clear.

**CLI:**
```bash
./bin/control subagents effort opencode-go/glm-5.2 max
./bin/control subagents effort opencode-go/glm-5.2 default   # clear
```

The menu shows only for models that are on as subagents and advertise more than one level — an off model has no child turns to apply a depth to, and a one-level ladder has nothing to pick. On a real install that is 55 of 113 models.

## Verified end to end

A test drives the real router against a mock gateway and reads the `reasoning_effort` that actually arrived:

| Scenario | Effort received |
|---|---|
| Child turn, model configured `max` | **max** — override applied |
| Parent turn, **same model** | **low** — client's own value, untouched |
| Child turn, model not configured | **low** — untouched |

The middle row is the one worth having. A setting that leaked into parent turns would quietly re-tune every conversation on that model with nothing to notice it by.

Also confirmed live: tray writes it, state records it, clearing removes it.

## Design notes

**Per model, not global.** The useful setting is "when work lands on this model as a child, run it this deep," and that answer differs by model.

**An absent entry leaves the turn alone** rather than recording today's default — a default that later changes upstream should follow the model, not stay frozen at whatever it was when someone opened a settings page.

**Validated against what the model advertises.** `control` now reports each model's reasoning ladder so the menu and the CLI offer only levels the provider accepts:

```
$ control subagents effort zai-coding/glm-5.2 ultra
Error: zai-coding/glm-5.2 does not support reasoning effort "ultra". Supported: high, max
```

The field is omitted when a model advertises no ladder, so entries without one keep the exact shape they had.

**Not re-validated in the router.** A provider that rejects an unsupported effort says so in a way the operator can read; silently dropping the setting looks like the feature never worked.

## Traps this could have fallen into

**Every settings writer rebuilds the state object literally**, so each was a chance to drop the effort map silently — set an effort, toggle an unrelated switch, lose it with no error. Four tests cover exactly that: mode change, single toggle, bulk toggle, full state replace.

**Shipping CLI-only.** The first version had no tray surface, which is how a tray-first user discovers a feature by not finding it. Added, and translated across all five UI languages.

## Not included

Subagent **model** selection already exists (`subagents set`), but Codex advertises only a small priority-ordered subset — on a real install, 28 spawnable models with the cut around rank 9, so an enabled model can still never be offered. Raising one past that cut is a different mechanism and a separate change.

- [x] `npm run check`
- [x] `npm test`: 0 fail (7 new, including the end-to-end child/parent asymmetry)
- [x] `swift test`: 26 pass across five languages
- [x] Manual: tray menu, CLI set/clear/reject-unsupported, live round-trip against real state

title: fix(qwen): use the limits the provider itself reports, measured
body:
Follow-up to #240, now that qwen-plan quota was restored and the endpoint could actually be probed.

## Method

DashScope names its own ceiling when you exceed it. Send an oversized prompt, read the number back out of the rejection:

```
Range of input length should be [1, 983616]
```

Nine models, nine measurements, against `token-plan.ap-southeast-1.maas.aliyuncs.com` — the host we actually route through, not the standard Model Studio endpoint the docs describe.

| Model | Measured | #240 declared |
|---|---|---|
| deepseek-v4-pro / -0813 / -flash-0731 | 1,000,000 | 1,000,000 ✅ exact |
| glm-5.2 | 1,048,576 | 1,048,576 ✅ exact |
| qwen3.8-max / 3.7-max / 3.7-plus / 3.6-flash | **983,616** | 1,000,000 |
| qwen3.8-max-preview | **983,616** | 262,144 |

## What this corrects

**The four Qwen entries were 1.7% optimistic.** 983,616 is the *thinking-mode* input ceiling, and thinking is on by default for this family — so 1,000,000 is a number the provider will refuse. Harmless in practice (autoCompact 900,000 compacts well below the wall), but a declared value the upstream rejects is the same imprecision that started this whole thread.

**`qwen3.8-max-preview` is not retired.** #240 left it at 262,144 because its doc page 404s and it looked dead at GA. The probe disproves that: it answered with a proper limit rather than an unknown-model error, and it returned 200 as recently as 2026-08-03. Same 983,616 as the GA entry.

## Worth noting

The documentation research and the empirical probe agreed **exactly** — 983,616 was the documented thinking-mode figure before it was ever measured. The docs were right; we had simply never read them for these entries.

This is also the strongest argument yet for learning limits at runtime: the provider hands you the exact number in the error, per model, per endpoint, for free. Nine correct values took one script and about a minute.

## Test plan
- [x] `npm run check`
- [x] `npm test`: 0 fail
- [x] Every value in the table measured live against the routed host

title: Retained tool results have no purge command and no doctor visibility
body:
Follow-up from #245, which introduces `retained-tool-results/` under the router state directory. Not a defect in that PR — the behavior is deliberate and documented — but it leaves the operator without a way to see or clear the store.

## What exists today

Retention is bounded and fails safe. The caps are checked before any write:

- 64 MiB for a single result
- 512 files
- 512 MiB in total

There is deliberately no eviction. When a cap is reached, new eligible results simply pass through unchanged and stay full, and the tray says so ("Retention capacity reached · new eligible results pass through unchanged"). So this cannot grow without bound, cannot fill a disk, and degrades to exactly the pre-#245 behavior.

## What's missing

1. **No way to clear it.** Short of `rm -rf ~/.codex/codex-router/retained-tool-results`, there is no supported way to empty the store. Once it reaches 512 MiB it also stops retaining anything new, permanently, until someone deletes it by hand.
2. **No visibility.** `doctor` doesn't report the directory's existence or size, so the first time most operators learn about it will be when they go looking for disk usage.
3. **No lifetime.** There's no TTL, so a result retained today is still there a year from now.

This matters more than the byte count suggests: tool results routinely contain file contents, command output, and API responses. The store is `0600`, owner-only, and correctly excluded from support bundles — but it is the first time this router persists model-visible *content* to disk, where the established stance has been that telemetry records "counts and bytes... never the results" (`src/usage-events.mjs`).

## Proposed

- `control tool-result-aging purge` — empty the store, report bytes reclaimed. Refuses to touch anything outside its own directory, same path validation the writer uses.
- A `doctor` line reporting the directory's file count and total size, so it's discoverable without knowing to look.
- Optionally a TTL (drop entries older than N days on the next pass), which would also keep the store from parking at its cap forever.

Filed while reviewing #245; the aging feature itself is fine to ship without this.

title: Routed models reach only the deferred subset of codex_apps connector tools
body:
Routed models reach only the deferred subset of `mcp__codex_apps__*` connector tools, so app connectors are effectively unusable off the native route.

## What happens

On a routed model (grok-oauth/grok-4.6, deepseek/deepseek-v4-*), a task that needs an app connector never finds the tools. In one session the model looped for ~30 turns trying to read Outlook mail, reporting each time that the connector was present but its tools were not mounted:

> Outlook 插件在，但工具还没挂进当前会话。 (“The Outlook plugin is there, but its tools are not mounted in this session.”)

It then went digging on its own — read the plugin's `SKILL.md` out of `~/.codex/plugins/cache/`, called `list_mcp_resources` (which *did* return the `codex_apps` resources, so the MCP server was connected and reachable in that very session), and finally gave up on the connector and shelled out to a local `himalaya` IMAP binary instead.

The same account on the native route calls those tools without trouble. A pre-router session on this machine shows 135 successful `microsoft_outlook_email.list_messages` calls plus `gmail.search_emails`, `fetch_messages_batch`, and friends, so the connectors themselves are fine.

## Why — the deferred subset is all that survives

The captured fixture in `test/namespace-relay-routing.test.mjs:141` is itself the clearest statement of the problem. What the client sends on a routed request is:

```js
tools: [
  { type: "tool_search" },
  ...
  { type: "namespace", name: "mcp__codex_apps__github", tools: [ { name: "fetch_issue", ... } ] },
]
```

One tool. The real GitHub connector on this machine exposes **89**. Outlook exposes **46**, Notion **18** — 171 across all connected apps. Codex ships a small subset inline and registers the rest with deferred loading, leaving `tool_search` as the only way to reach them.

`flattenNamespaceTools` then drops the search control (`src/namespace-relay.mjs:107`):

```js
// Codex adds this control tool when one or more namespace tools use
// deferred loading. By this boundary every namespace is expanded below,
// so the search control is redundant; ...
if (tool?.type === "tool_search") { changed = true; continue; }
```

Dropping it is right — chat-completions providers reject `type: "tool_search"`. But "every namespace is expanded below" holds only for namespaces whose tools the client actually shipped. For `mcp__codex_apps__*` it does not: the namespace arrives deliberately incomplete, the search control that was supposed to fill it in is gone, and nothing restores the remainder. The routed model ends up with 1 of 89 tools and no way to ask for the other 88.

`codex_app` (singular, the app runtime) already has exactly this fix. `mergeCodexAppTools` at `src/codex-app-tools.mjs:1190` merges a captured snapshot back in, and its comment describes the identical situation:

> The client sends a reduced codex_app namespace (three app tools) on routed requests; the rest are deferred client-side. Merge the full app toolset in so routed providers see the same tools a native model sees.

`mcp__codex_apps__*` (plural, the connectors) has no equivalent.

## The definitions are already on disk

Unlike `codex_app`, this would not need a hardcoded snapshot. Codex maintains the full set locally at `$CODEX_HOME/cache/codex_apps_tools/<hash>.json` (`schema_version: 4`), refreshed as connectors change — the copy here was rewritten during the most recent session. Each entry carries everything the relay needs:

```json
{
  "server_name": "codex_apps",
  "tool_namespace": "codex_apps__microsoft_outlook_email",
  "namespace_description": "Search and reference your Microsoft Outlook email.",
  "connector_id": "connector_...",
  "connector_name": "Microsoft Outlook Email",
  "tool": {
    "name": "microsoft_outlook_email.list_messages",
    "description": "...",
    "inputSchema": { ... }
  }
}
```

`tool.name` is already the exact name Codex dispatches (`{ namespace: "mcp__codex_apps__microsoft_outlook_email", name: "list_messages" }` after the existing restore path), so filling the namespace in needs no new response-side handling at all — `buildNamespaceLookups` and `rewriteNamespaceFunctionCall` map it back as they do today.

## What makes it non-trivial

Merging everything unconditionally is not an option. Serialized schema weight from this machine's cache:

| namespace | tools | schema size | approx. tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `microsoft_outlook_email` | 46 | 259 KB | ~66k |
| `github` | 89 | 201 KB | ~51k |
| `notion` | 18 | 81 KB | ~21k |
| others (6) | 18 | 108 KB | ~28k |
| **total** | **171** | **649 KB** | **~166k** |

That is the whole point of the deferred loading this bypasses.

Options, roughly in order of how much they cost to build:

1. **Opt-in per connector.** A config key (`codex_apps_connectors = ["microsoft_outlook_email"]`) merges only those namespaces in full. Smallest change, reuses `mergeCodexAppTools` almost verbatim with the cache as source instead of a constant. Operator pays a known token cost for the connector they actually want.
2. **Opt-in per tool**, same mechanism at finer granularity, for people who want three Outlook tools rather than 46.
3. **A router-side stand-in for `tool_search`.** Closest to native behavior and the only option that scales to all 171, but it needs a discovery tool the router can answer without executing anything, which is a real design question rather than a merge.

A name-plus-one-line index of all 171 tools serializes to ~16 KB (~4k tokens), if a cheap always-on discovery hint is useful as part of (3).

## Environment

- codex-router 0.4.0-beta.2 (`agent/preserve-native-account-catalog`), macOS 27.0, target Codex, codex-cli 0.146.0
- Providers: deepseek, grok-oauth, local
- Observed on grok-oauth/grok-4.6; the relay path is provider-independent, so deepseek routes the same way

Happy to put up a PR for option 1 if that is the direction you would take.

title: Relay deferred codex_apps connector tools to routed models
body:
Fixes #252.

## The gap

Codex presents each connected app connector as its own namespace — `mcp__codex_apps__github`, `mcp__codex_apps__microsoft_outlook_email` — and loads them lazily. On a routed request the client ships a handful of the tools inline and leaves `type: "tool_search"` as the way to reach the rest. `flattenNamespaceTools` drops that control, correctly: chat-completions providers reject the type outright. But the comment above the drop —

```js
// By this boundary every namespace is expanded below,
// so the search control is redundant;
```

— only holds for namespaces whose tools the client actually shipped. Connector namespaces arrive deliberately incomplete. The fixture in `test/namespace-relay-routing.test.mjs` captures it exactly: one `fetch_issue` under `mcp__codex_apps__github`, where the connector really exposes 89 tools. The remainder is unreachable on every routed model.

What that looks like in practice: a Grok 4.6 session spent about thirty turns trying to read Outlook mail, reporting each time that the connector was present but its tools were not mounted, then gave up and shelled out to a local IMAP binary. The same account calls those tools without trouble on the native route.

## The fix

`mergeCodexAppTools` already solves this for `codex_app`, the app's own runtime, by merging a captured snapshot back in. Connectors can't use a snapshot — which ones exist is per-account and changes whenever someone connects one — and don't need to: Codex maintains the full set at `$CODEX_HOME/cache/codex_apps_tools/<hash>.json` and refreshes it as connectors change. This reads that cache and fills the deferred remainder back into the request.

Nothing changes on the response path. The merged tools flatten to `mcp__codex_apps__<connector>__<method>` and restore through the existing relay to `{ namespace, name }`, which is the shape Codex dispatches:

```
restored -> {"type":"function_call","name":"list_messages",
             "namespace":"mcp__codex_apps__microsoft_outlook_email", ...}
```

## Opt-in, because schemas are big

Merging every connector would send ~166 KB of schema (the whole cache is 649 KB including output schemas and metadata this strips). That size is why Codex defers them at all, so the operator names the ones worth the context:

```
$ codex-router connector-tools list
  relayed  connector                tools   ~tokens
       no  github                      89     20892  GitHub
       no  microsoft_outlook_email     46     18916  Microsoft Outlook Email
       no  notion                      18     17664  Notion
       ...
$ codex-router connector-tools enable microsoft_outlook_email
```

With no selection recorded, `mergeConnectorTools` returns the original array by identity and the request is untouched — an install that never opts in behaves exactly as it does today. A missing or corrupt cache falls back the same way.

The client's own definition always wins; the cache only supplies what deferred loading held back. A selected connector the client omitted entirely is appended whole, on the same reasoning `mergeCodexAppTools` relies on — the client dispatches those calls natively whether or not the definition was in the request.

## Notes for review

- Applied in the non-responses branch next to `mergeCodexAppTools`, since that is where the observed failure is (Grok and DeepSeek both route as chat completions). Responses-native providers keep `tool_search` today, so they are left alone.
- The cache is parsed once and re-read only when its mtime changes, so the 1.4 MB file is not touched per request.
- `MODEL_ROUTER_CODEX_APPS_CACHE_DIR` and `MODEL_ROUTER_CONNECTOR_TOOLS_STATE` override the paths for tests.

## Tests

`test/codex-apps-connectors.test.mjs` covers cache parsing and the namespace/method naming, a missing and a corrupt cache, the untouched-by-default path, the merge, client-definition precedence, an entirely omitted connector, and the round trip through `flattenNamespaceTools` + `rewriteNamespaceFunctionCall`.

title: feat(custom): a provider whose models each name their own endpoint
body:
Supersedes the first draft of this PR, which shipped the free Qwen3.8 endpoint as its own `qwen38-free` provider. Same endpoint, different shape.

## Why the shape changed

Every other provider owns one address. That is why "route this one model from that one host" has always meant inventing a whole provider for it — and why a second host means a second provider, with its own credential story, its own tray card, and its own row in every surface that enumerates providers.

`custom` owns no address at all. It declares no `baseUrl`, no `credential`, and no `protocol`; each of its models carries all three in an `endpoint` block, and `endpointForModel()` is what the forwarder asks instead of reading `provider.baseUrl`. One picker entry can hold a free community endpoint, a self-hosted server, and a paid API with a key, at the same time.

```
config/custom/custom.json        { id: "custom", perModelEndpoint: true }
config/custom/qwen3.8-27b.json   endpoint: { baseUrl: <hf endpoint>, authMode: "anonymous" }
config/custom/<next>.json        endpoint: { baseUrl: <other host>, credential: {...} }
```

The endpoint descriptor is deliberately **provider-shaped**: `baseUrl`, `authMode`, `keyless`, and `credential` mean exactly what they mean on a provider, so `resolveProviderBaseUrl` and the whole credential chain accept one unchanged — including a per-model credential file and Keychain entry, which fall out of giving the descriptor the model slug as its `id`. A parallel resolver would have been the larger change and the worse one: the moment two implementations differ, one of them is the copy nobody audited.

## The part worth reviewing

The rule that keeps a credential-free provider from becoming an arbitrary-endpoint egress path has to **follow the address down**, or it stops being a rule. Without it, adding a JSON file under `config/custom/` would be enough to send an operator's prompts to any HTTPS host on earth with nothing to authenticate them.

| Refusal | Why |
| --- | --- |
| An `anonymous` endpoint's address must be in `ANONYMOUS_MODEL_ENDPOINTS`, keyed by slug | The address *is* the boundary when nothing authenticates the request |
| A `keyless` endpoint must be loopback | Same rule as a keyless provider: no credential means no off-box traffic |
| Neither may declare a `baseUrlEnv` | An environment override walks around whichever of the two rules applied |
| `endpoint.id` / `endpoint.kind` are injected at load, and a fragment that spells them is refused | Otherwise one model's endpoint could name itself after another and collect that model's secret |
| Exactly one of anonymous / keyless / credential | Two would leave a silent winner; none would send an unauthenticated request to an unvetted address |
| A container declaring its own `baseUrl`, or a normal provider's model declaring an `endpoint` | Two answers to "where does this go" have a silent winner |

Every row has a test that fails without it (`test/registry.test.mjs`).

Selection treats the container like an anonymous provider: `defaultProviderIds()` excludes it, because what it holds is whatever somebody put in it. Nothing offers a key at the container level — `apiProvider()` refuses it, the onboarding card is informational — since a secret stored there would be read by nothing. Discovery refuses it outright, because it asks *one* endpoint what it serves and picking one of its models' addresses to report as the provider's catalog is worse than saying no.

Four call sites spelled `keyless || authMode === "anonymous"` inline. The list has grown a third member, so it is named once as `providerNeedsNoKey()`.

## The first model, measured not inferred

The endpoint answers anonymously, so there was no excuse for reading capabilities off its model card. Source: https://huggingface.co/spaces/victor/Qwen3.8-27B-free-endpoint

| Probe | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /v1/models` | one model, `max_model_len` 262144 |
| `tool_choice: "required"` | real tool call — no `auto-tool-choice` downgrade warranted |
| vision (known image) | read correctly |
| streaming | SSE frames normally |
| `usage.prompt_tokens` | non-zero, so the zero-token substitution never engages |
| `reasoning_effort` | accepts `none/minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh/max`; **400s on `ultra`** |

The Codex ladder is that set plus `ultra`, so the `qwen38-community` profile folds exactly that rung onto `max` and leaves every other tier alone. The regression drives all eight values, because a profile that silently clamped more than one would look identical from the picker.

The endpoint is shared, rate limited to ~30 requests/minute per IP, and its owner says it will be retired once launch interest fades. A model to try, not one to depend on — the README says so where someone would enable it.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm run check`
- [x] `npm test` — 1333 tests, 0 fail, rebased on current `main` (includes #249)
- [x] `swift build` + `swift test` — 26 tests pass, artifacts cleaned
- [x] `./bin/discover-models custom` — refuses with the explanation, as designed
- [x] Live endpoint re-checked reachable (HTTP 200) after the restructure
- [ ] After merge: `bin/update`, `providers enable custom`, restart Codex, confirm **Qwen3.8 27B (Free)** answers
- [ ] Optional, spends no quota: `./bin/test-model 'custom/qwen3.8-27b' --live --yes`

title: Bridge native tool_search for routed chat-completions models
body:
## Summary

- Lower Codex client-executed native tool_search into a collision-safe ordinary function for routed chat-completions providers.
- Restore streamed and non-streamed provider calls to native tool_search_call items so the Codex client performs discovery and registration.
- Replay only adjacent, matching client call/output history; expose accepted discovered function schemas on the following routed request and extend the exact request-local namespace lookup.
- Keep Responses-native routes unchanged and fail closed on malformed history, server execution, custom/freeform tools, and discovered-name collisions.

## Why

Codex 0.146 registers deferred connector tools only after its native tool_search flow. Copying cached definitions into the request can make a model see a tool that the client still rejects as unsupported. This change preserves the client-owned discovery and execution boundary while adapting only the provider-facing wire shape.

Stable Codex contract references:

- Native tool declaration: https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.146.0/codex-rs/tools/src/tool_spec.rs#L18-L29
- Client tool_search handler: https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.146.0/codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/tool_search_spec.rs#L18-L76
- Native dispatch path: https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.146.0/codex-rs/core/src/tools/router.rs#L144-L162
- Follow-up history contract: https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.146.0/codex-rs/core/tests/suite/search_tool.rs#L745-L815

## Verification

- npm ci --ignore-scripts: 0 vulnerabilities
- node --test test/namespace-relay.test.mjs test/namespace-relay-routing.test.mjs: 35/35 passed
- npm run check: passed
- npm test on current main: 1,338 total; 1,326 passed; 12 skipped; 0 failed
- Independent read-only review: PASS after tightening replay to adjacent call/output pairs

The repository-gated real LiteLLM adapter integration and a quota-consuming live provider probe were not run. Mock-gateway coverage exercises routed SSE, non-streaming JSON, next-turn replay, discovered namespace dispatch, collision handling, and the Responses-native control path.

Disclosure: I maintain dsh-mcp-lens and am contributing here because the same deferred tool-discovery boundary affects routed DeepSeek Harness and Codex workflows. This patch does not add or depend on MCP Lens.

Fixes #252.

title: opencode-go subagent: reasoning_content must be passed back to the API (HTTP 400)
body:
## Problem

Spawning a subagent with the opencode-go provider always fails on the parent task once the subagent finishes. Reproduced twice.

## Error

```
opencode rejected the request for DeepSeek V4 Flash (opencode Go). (HTTP 400: Error from provider (Console Go): Upstream request failed: [invalid_request_error] The `reasoning_content` in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API.)
```

## Repro

1. Parent task invokes a subagent with model `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` (opencode Go provider).
2. Subagent runs normally and returns its final answer.
3. After the subagent completes, the parent's next request is rejected with the HTTP 400 above.

## Expected

Subagent final responses that contain `reasoning_content` should be passed back in subsequent requests, or stripped when the provider does not accept them, so the parent can continue.

title: Subagent proof promotes on the first successful child turn, and a looping child can never be demoted
body:
Reported during a stale pre-restart test: a model was marked `proven` after its first successful child HTTP turn, while the child itself was still looping and never reached `done`.

The observation is accurate, and the first half of it is deliberate. The second half is a gap.

## What the code does

`observeSubagentOutcome` (`src/router.mjs:1690`) promotes on a single HTTP turn:

```js
if (status === 200 && !emptyCompletion) {
  recordSpawnObserved(route.slug, { status });
  console.error(`[codex-router] subagent proven: ${route.slug} completed a live child turn`);
} else if (status === 400 || status === 422) {
  recordSpawnFailure(...);
}
```

A child agent makes many HTTP turns — one per tool-call round trip. The first that returns 200 promotes the slug. That is what `AGENTS.md` describes:

> The first real child turn settles it: Codex marks child turns with `x-openai-subagent`, and the router's own request path records a clean completion as the durable proof (`proven`) or a structural rejection — HTTP 400/422 — as a demotion back to v1.

So "proven" means *this model can hold the child role on the wire*, not *this model completes child work*. Reasonable: the router sees HTTP turns, not agent lifecycles, and it cannot observe "the child reached done" without modelling Codex's agent loop.

## The gap

Demotion fires only on 400/422. A model that accepts child turns and then loops without ever converging emits neither signal:

- it never returns 400 or 422, so it is never demoted,
- it was already promoted by turn one, so the loop costs it nothing,
- it stays advertised as an experimental v2 subagent, and `control subagents verify` is the only thing that could ever re-examine it — and that has to be run by hand.

The capability probe (`src/subagent-verify.mjs`) does not close this either: it proves streaming and a forced tool call, which a looping model also does successfully.

So the one failure mode an operator most wants filtered — a model that technically speaks the protocol but cannot finish a delegated task — is precisely the one with no path to demotion.

## What is worth deciding

Not obvious that promotion *should* require child completion; the router genuinely cannot see it reliably, and "intermediate turn that happened not to call a tool" is hard to distinguish from "final turn". Some options, roughly in order of cost:

1. **Say what it means.** Leave the mechanism alone and change the label and log line so `proven` does not overclaim — e.g. "child role verified" — with the picker wording following. Cheapest, and removes the misreading that prompted this report.
2. **Require more than one turn.** Promote on the Nth clean child turn rather than the first. Cheap, and a model that dies after turn one stops being promoted, but a looping model still gets there.
3. **Observe convergence.** Record the child's turn count per spawn and treat a run that exceeds a ceiling without a terminal turn as evidence against, the way 400/422 is. Real signal, most work, and needs a defensible ceiling.

I lean toward 1, plus 3 later if looping models turn out to be common. Filing rather than fixing because which of these is right is a product call about what `proven` should promise.

Reported by an operator during pre-restart testing; thanks for the precise observation — "observing a successful turn rather than final child completion" is exactly the distinction.

---
🤖 Filed by [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) after reading the promotion path.

title: fix(custom): the free Qwen3.8 endpoint refuses the empty tool list compaction sends
body:
## The bug

`summarize()` disables tool use during compaction by sending `tools: []`, which every other forwarder reads as "no tools". The free Qwen3.8 community endpoint's vLLM build refuses it:

```
`tools` must not be an empty array. Either provide at least one tool or omit the field entirely. (parameter=tools)
```

and refuses the `tool_choice` sent beside it with a second 400:

```
When using `tool_choice`, `tools` must be set. (parameter=tool_choice)
```

`custom/qwen3.8-27b` auto-compacts at 230K of its 262K window, so **every long session against it failed** at the compaction.

## The fix

The `qwen38-community` request profile now omits an empty tool list, then drops the tool choice that strip leaves dangling. Order matters — otherwise the second rejection replaces the first.

It stays at the last hop before this one endpoint rather than in the compaction path, because an empty tool list is legal everywhere else and is exactly how compaction disables tool use there. A non-empty list forwards untouched.

The existing `ultra` → `max` effort fold is unchanged and still correct: `none`/`minimal`/`low`/`medium`/`high`/`xhigh`/`max` all return 200, `ultra` is the one rung the endpoint's enum omits.

## Also: credit the publisher

The endpoint is published by an individual, not by Qwen or Hugging Face. Renamed the entry to `Qwen3.8-27-free-victor` and credited victor in the description and the README table.

## Test plan

title: fix(custom): the free Qwen3.8 endpoint refuses a system message that arrives late or twice
body:
Follow-up to #258. That fix cleared the empty-tool-list 400; real Codex use then hit a second, unrelated constraint in the same Qwen3.8 chat template:

```
litellm.BadRequestError: OpenAIException - System message must be at the beginning.
  Received Model Group=custom-qwen3-8-27b
```

## The measured rule

Probed against the live endpoint:

| messages | result |
|---|---|
| `[system, user]` | 200 |
| `[user, system, user]` | **400** |
| `[user, assistant, system]` | **400** |
| `[system, system, user]` | **400** |
| `[developer, user]` | 200 |
| `[user, developer, user]` | 200 |
| `[system, developer, user]` | 200 |
| `[developer, system, user]` | 200 |
| `[developer, developer, user]` | 200 |

At most one `system` message, and it must precede the first `user`/`assistant`/`tool` turn. The `developer` role is unconstrained. Note `[developer, system, user]` passes, so "at the beginning" means "before the first conversational turn", not literally index 0.

## The fix

The `qwen38-community` profile coalesces every `system` message into one and inserts it at `min(first system's own slot, first turn)` — so a leading `developer` message keeps its place. String and content-parts content are both handled. An already-legal list is returned by identity and forwarded byte-identical. `developer` messages are never moved.

Coalescing a *late* system message does move those instructions to the front of the conversation. That is a real semantic shift, and it is noted in the code comment — the endpoint rejects the alternative outright.

## Test plan

| two leading system messages | **400** | **200** |
| system after user/assistant | **400** | **200** |
| already-legal `[system, user]` | 200 | 200 |
| empty `tools` (#258 regression check) | 200 | 200 |
| normal turn with a real tool | 200 | 200 |

title: feat(failover): continue a turn on another model when the provider is out of usage
body:
An install with thirty providers configured runs out of one of them most days: a
coding-plan window closes, a weekly quota lands, a balance empties. The router
named that failure clearly and then stopped — Codex has nothing to do with a
billing error, so a session mid-task simply ended, subagents included, while
every other model the operator could reach sat unused.

The turn is now rebuilt for the next eligible model and sent again. The client
sees one clean answer.

## What qualifies

Deliberately narrow: an exhausted balance or plan limit, a 402, or a 429 whose
`Retry-After` is longer than a minute. A rejected credential, an unknown model, a
malformed request, and every 5xx keep exactly the error they returned before —
swapping models to dodge a bad key would hide the one fact that fixes it, and a
short rate limit is cheaper to wait out than a cold prompt cache is to pay for.

Entitlement failures are classified *before* quota ones, because "upgrade your
plan" appears in both vocabularies and no other provider's quota makes a missing
entitlement true.

## Which model answers

Free first, then the rest in the registry's own preference order. A model on this
machine is never chosen automatically — the runtime might not be running — but it
is used when named in a chain. A candidate whose context window cannot hold the
conversation is skipped, so a quota failure is never traded for a context-window
rejection. Never a sibling of the exhausted provider: variants share a credential
and therefore a quota.

## Cooldowns

When a provider says when it will be back, that window is believed: the next turn
skips it outright rather than buying the same rejection again, and it is used
again once the window passes or the next time it answers. A reset time is never
invented, only read from the provider, and capped at six hours.

`api-forwarder` is where this is captured, and that placement is load-bearing:
**LiteLLM does not relay `Retry-After`** (verified against the live gateway), so
that hop is the only place the provider's own reset time still exists.

## Visibility

Nothing is silent and nothing is injected into the transcript. The router logs
every swap (never gated on `CODEX_ROUTER_QUIET`), the tray Island names the model
actually answering, and the usage event carries `failoverFrom`. `model` and
`provider` always name the pair that served; `failover_from` carries what was
asked for. Codex replays assistant output as input, so a router-authored note
would come back next turn as a sentence the model believes it wrote — hence no
transcript injection.

Compaction gets the same treatment: a compaction that cannot run ends a long
session just as surely as a turn that cannot run.

`./bin/control failover status|on|off|chain <slugs>|auto|reset`. The doctor
reports any provider currently held off and when it clears. On by default;
`off` is remembered permanently.

## Not included

The native ChatGPT tier. It is not a body swap but the other branch entirely, and
it crosses the routed/native boundary AGENTS.md governs — `encrypted_content`
rewriting, the compatibility relay, the collaboration envelope. Those rules
require live marker-return probes through every installed routed agent, so the
tier cannot be added from the test suite alone. Documented as such.

## Test plan

Unit and integration: **1359 pass, 0 fail** (`npm test`), `npm run check` clean.
New coverage in `test/model-failover.test.mjs` (classifier, tiered ranking,
cooldown store) and `test/model-failover-router.test.mjs` (end to end, including
that the failed attempt's bytes never reach the client).

Verified live against a **genuinely out-of-usage provider** (`kimi-oauth/k3`,
real 403 "You've reached your usage limit for this billing cycle"), running the
full stack — router, real LiteLLM, api-forwarder — from this branch after rebase:

- [x] turn on the exhausted model → answered by `grok-oauth/grok-4.6`
- [x] turn with namespace/collaboration tools → answered, tools rebuilt correctly
- [x] subagent turn (`x-openai-subagent`) → answered
- [x] compaction on the exhausted model → real compaction item produced
- [x] healthy model untouched, no failover triggered
- [x] real `commandcode` **entitlement** 403 → correctly not swapped, real message shown
- [x] real `commandcode` 500 → correctly not swapped
- [x] `failover off` → exact prior behaviour restored
- [x] stream integrity: exactly one `response.created` / `response.completed`, no error events
- [x] telemetry: log lines, timing lines, and usage events all name the serving pair

Defects found by that live testing and fixed here: log lines contradicting the
usage event, the compaction timing line crediting the exhausted provider with the
turn's 200, the failed compaction attempt missing from the meter, a mislabelled
cooldown reason, and a string `input` being spread into an array of characters.

title: LiteLLM gateway (pinned 1.96.0) crashes with exit code 1 when mapping an upstream 429 → entire router goes down ("Connection error" in clients)
body:
Summary
When the upstream (opencode Console) returns a 429 (FreeUsageLimitError), LiteLLM's exception-mapping path throws an unhandled exception that kills the gateway process (exit code 1). Since codex-router's router.mjs exits when the gateway dies, every model becomes unreachable — clients see repeated Error: Connection error and Retry failed after 3 attempts.
Steps to reproduce
1. Use an opencode-free model (e.g. opencode-free/mimo-v2.5-free) whose free-tier shared quota is exhausted upstream (returns 429 FreeUsageLimitError).
2. Send a request through the gateway.
3. Gateway processes the 429, then exits: [codex-router] LiteLLM gateway exited (code=1, signal=null).
4. Router goes down; all subsequent requests fail with connection errors.
Expected
A 429 should be relayed to the client as a 429 response (as the router already does for most errors) — the gateway process must survive.
Actual
The gateway dies during exception mapping:
During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:
...
  File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/exception_mapping_utils.py", line 2505, in exception_type
  File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/exception_mapping_utils.py", line 2274, in exception_type
    _map_openai_exception(
  File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/exception_mapping_utils.py", line 284, in _map_openai_exception
    raise RateLimitError(
litellm.exceptions.RateLimitError: RateLimitError: OpenAIException - Error from provider (Console): Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.. Received Model Group=opencode-free-mimo-v2-5-free
[codex-router] LiteLLM gateway exited (code=1, signal=null).
Environment
- codex-router: 0.4.0-beta.3 (codex target)
- litellm: 1.96.0 (pinned via requirements/python.txt, hash-verified)
- OS: Windows 11
- Upstream: opencode Zen free tier (https://opencode.ai/zen/v1), returns FreeUsageLimitError 429 with no Retry-After/rate-limit headers
Suggested directions
- Ensure the 429 exception-mapping path never lets an exception escape the request handler coroutine (LiteLLM-side).
- Consider bumping the pinned litellm==1.96.0 to a version that fixes unhandled-exception-on-429, and re-validate the router's integration.
- (Also worth reporting upstream to BerriAI/litellm since the root cause is in exception_mapping_utils._map_openai_exception.)

title: fix(panel): say the browser panel is read-only, and stop claiming ageing is on
body:
Reported as "the compact old tool-result toggle is only frontend and doesn't trigger the actual backend code." The backend is fine — `control tool-result-aging on|off` writes state correctly and `toolResultAgingEnabled()` re-reads the file per request with no caching. There were two separate frontend defects.

## Defect A — the browser panel is read-only and the UI did not know it

`panelCommandAllowed(command, { readOnly = true })` has one call site that passes no options, so the browser panel is always read-only and permits only five read commands. `apps/desktop/ui/app.js` had **zero** read-only awareness, so it rendered every mutating control as live; clicking one fired the command, the fetch 4xx'd, and the user got a generic failure on a control that was never operable in that surface.

The read-only posture is deliberate — a browser tab is reachable by any page that learns the capability — so **no command was added to the allowlist**. The UI now tells the truth instead.

`platform_info` (a `LOCAL` command, so it never touches the CLI) carries a capabilities block:

```json
{"readOnly": true,
 "allowedCommands": ["control_snapshot","account_usage","provider_usage","provider_setup","local_models"],
 "localCommands": ["platform_info","desktop_settings","router_health", "..."]}
```

`allowedCommands` is spread from `READ_ONLY` itself and `localCommands` from `Object.keys(LOCAL)`, so there is no second list to drift. Every control that drives a command now carries `data-command`, and a `MutationObserver` — installed only on a read-only surface — disables refused ones with a localized tooltip, plus a banner. `call()` rejects a refused command before the fetch.

The block is additive: the tray and Electron shells send no `capabilities`, so the helper returns null and the gate is a no-op there. They keep the full table.

## Defect B — the switch defaulted ON while the backend defaults OFF

`defaultSettings()` in `src/tool-result-aging-state.mjs` is `enabled: false` when no state file exists, but both UIs showed the switch on in that case:

- `apps/desktop/ui/app.js` — `aging?.enabled !== false` → `toolResultAgingChecked(aging)` (`aging?.enabled === true`)
- `ModelRouterTrayApp.swift` — `?? true` → `?? false`

A fresh install claimed ageing was on while nothing was being aged. Behavior when the snapshot is present is unchanged.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm test` — 1345 tests, 1333 pass, 0 fail, 12 pre-existing skips
- [x] `node scripts-check.mjs` — syntax checks passed
- [x] `swift build` — Build complete; `swift test` — 26 tests in 5 suites passed
- [x] RED checks on both defects: removing the capabilities block fails 2 panel tests; restoring the old default expressions fails 2 UI tests
- [x] New test asserts `commandRefused(caps, c) === !panelCommandAllowed(c)` for **every** key in `COMMANDS`, so the advertised set cannot drift from the enforced one
- [x] New test joins index.html's `data-command` set to the live capabilities
- [x] Refusal test extended with `set_tool_result_aging` — the security posture is verified unchanged

## Known gaps

- **No real-browser run.** The Playwright test skips (no preinstalled chromium in this environment). The server half was verified for real over HTTP; the DOM sweep (`applyReadOnly`/`watchReadOnly`) is reviewed, not executed — `app.js` self-executes against `window`, so it is not importable under `node:test` without a refactor. What is covered is the decision it makes and the inputs it reads.
- **Related defect deliberately left out:** the panel's `platform_info` omits `islandSupported`, so the activity-pill switch renders as supported in a browser tab that has no pill. One line would fix it, but it is a different defect.
- **Opposite-direction mismatch found, not changed:** the vision bridge backend defaults **on** while both UIs render an absent snapshot as off. Showing a quota-spending feature as on because the snapshot could not be read seemed like the wrong correction to make unilaterally. Worth a separate decision.

title: test(failover): cover the untested paths, and stop promising a free tier that is empty
body:
Follow-up to #260, which merged with two problems.

## 1. Every failover was tested on the one shape that cannot break

All coverage went chat-completions → chat-completions. The rule the feature
ships with is about the *other* shapes, and none had a test. Added:

- **Crossing the protocol line, both directions.** A chat turn moving to a
  responses-native provider must keep its namespace tools intact; a responses
  turn moving to a chat provider must flatten them. The regression this guards
  is the second build reusing the first's rewritten tool list, which
  `flattenNamespaceTools` answers with an *empty* namespace map — plausible
  tools the response transform can no longer map back.
- **A tool call arriving from the fallback**, restored to the namespace shape
  Codex registered rather than the flattened name the provider was handed.
- **Walking past a candidate that is also out of usage**, and stopping at the
  hop bound rather than the end of the catalog.
- **A non-streaming turn.**
- **A client that leaves while a hop is in flight** — no hang, no crash.

Live testing then found the log line actively misleading: a hop rejected with
its own 400 printed `reason=out_of_usage status=400`, which reads as the
exhausted provider having answered 400. Those are two different events and the
line now says both:

```
failover model=kimi-oauth/k3 status=403 reason=out_of_usage -> opencode-go-responses/gpt-5.6-luna outcome=400
failover model=kimi-oauth/k3 status=403 reason=out_of_usage -> grok-oauth/grok-4.6 outcome=200
```

## 2. It promised a free first stop that could not happen

The ranking puts free models first and every surface said so. On a real install
that sentence is false: `doctor` reported "free models first then your other
enabled providers" while the free tier held nothing, so failover went straight
to a paid subscription having told the operator otherwise.

The ranking is fine. `opencode-free` and `kilo-free` stay catalog-only because
their free subsets are picked out by naming rules the vendors change without
notice, and an anonymous provider is never enabled for someone who did not ask —
both rules are deliberate and stay. The *claim* is what changes.
`failoverTierCounts` counts what the ranking can actually reach and `doctor`
reports that:

```
on, 1 free model(s) first then 27 of your own
on, 73 of your own providers -- no free model is curated, so nothing cheaper is tried first
```

Models on this machine are counted apart from free ones: they cost nothing and
are still never chosen automatically, so folding them together would recreate
the same false promise. The README now says the free stop is opt-in, and how to
take it.

## Test plan

`npm test` → **1376 pass, 0 fail**. `npm run check` clean.

Verified live against a genuinely out-of-usage provider (`kimi-oauth/k3`, real
403 "You've reached your usage limit for this billing cycle"), full stack —
router, real LiteLLM, api-forwarder:

- [x] a real chain walks past a candidate that genuinely fails, then answers
- [x] pre-dispatch cooldown skip: exhausted provider never contacted (4.0s vs ~10s, no usage event)
- [x] with `opencode-free` enabled and one model curated, the turn is served by
      `opencode-free/deepseek-v4-flash-free` — tier 0, ahead of 73 paid candidates, at no cost
- [x] without curation the same turn goes to a paid provider, and doctor says so

Worth recording because no mock could show it: `opencode-go-responses/gpt-5.6-luna`
answers 400 `invalid_prompt` to namespace tools whether or not a failover is
involved. The router handles it correctly by walking past — but that is a
property of the model, not of this feature.

title: fix: preserve Grok OAuth tool calls across Responses SSE
body:
## Summary

Narrowed after maintainer review to the low-risk Grok OAuth Responses parser/mapping fix only. This PR no longer classifies or retries progress-only replies.

- Preserve `function_call` and `custom_tool_call` items that first appear in `response.output_item.done`.

- Keep output streaming live while the upstream turn is still running.
- Preserve #265's conversation-ID routing plus `cached_tokens` and reasoning-token usage details.

A genuine short, tool-less answer is now forwarded unchanged. Any retry policy can be evaluated separately with its own liveness, accounting, logging, and kill-switch contract.

## Review changes

The progress-only classifier, hard-coded thresholds, developer nudge, second upstream request, and full-turn buffering were removed. That also removes the false retry, first-answer replacement, unmetered usage, missing kill switch, and unread retry-body concerns from this PR.

title: fix(grok): keep one conversation on one conv-id so the prompt cache is read
body:
Routed Grok turns were re-reading the whole prompt every time. Two lines caused it, and a third hid it.

## What happens

`upstreamHeaders` mints a fresh UUID per request and sends it as the conversation id:

```js
function upstreamHeaders(accessToken, model) {
  const sessionId = randomUUID();
  return {
    ...
    "x-grok-conv-id": sessionId,
    "x-grok-session-id": sessionId,
```

xAI caches prompts automatically and routes by `x-grok-conv-id` so that every turn of a conversation reaches the server holding its KV cache. Their [docs](https://docs.x.ai/developers/advanced-api-usage/prompt-caching/maximizing-cache-hits) name a wrong or changing conversation id as the first thing to check when `cached_tokens` stays near zero. A new id per request scatters the turns of one Codex session across servers, so each turn prefills the whole prompt from scratch.

## Measurement

A four-turn append-only session (three shell commands, one per turn) against a ~31k prompt, with tool-result aging off so the history was strictly appended:

| turn | before: cached | after: cached |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 128 (0.4%) | 4,608 (14.7%) |
| 2 | 4,608 (14.7%) | 31,360 (**99.6%**) |
| 3 | 128 (0.4%) | 31,360 (**99.4%**) |
| 4 | 0 (0.0%) | 31,488 (**99.6%**) |
| total | 4,864 / 125,194 = **3.9%** | 98,816 / 126,045 = **78.4%** |

Turn 1 has nothing to hit yet; turns 2-4 are the ones that matter and they go to ~99.5%.

Latency on those follow-up turns went from 2762 / 13532 / 2489 ms to 1810 / 1812 / 1853 ms. The steadiness is the more convincing half — a prompt that no longer needs prefilling stops varying.

## The fix

Derive the id from the conversation's opening messages. Codex appends to them and never rewrites them, so hashing the first two pins every turn of a session to one server while keeping separate sessions apart. Formatted as a UUID because that is what the header carries everywhere else.

Two sessions that genuinely share an opening will share a cache slot, which is correct — their prefix really is identical.

## Why this was invisible

The `response.completed` mapping dropped the usage detail:

```js
usage = {
  prompt_tokens: u.input_tokens ?? 0,
  completion_tokens: u.output_tokens ?? 0,
  total_tokens: ...,
};
```

`input_tokens_details.cached_tokens` never made it across, so every routed Grok turn logged `cached_tokens=unknown` — even though `response-usage.mjs:56` already reads it under both spellings and the timing log has a column for it. This forwards it, plus the reasoning-token detail beside it, so the number that says whether caching works can be read off the usage events instead of inferred.

That passthrough is what produced the table above; without it there was nothing to measure.

## Tests

`test/grok-oauth-forwarder.test.mjs` covers the id staying put when a turn appends a tool call and its result, the UUID shape, and two different conversations not colliding. Full suite green (1311 passing, 13 skipped).

## Note

Found while investigating why Grok 4.6 feels much slower in Codex than in other clients. Worth mentioning separately: 42 of 322 routed Grok requests here released the empty-completion guard (13%), each one re-sending the whole prompt. That is upstream behaviour rather than a router bug, but the rate seems high enough to be worth knowing.

title: Auto-compaction fires on every turn for curated OpenRouter models (estimated prompt tokens ~4x actual)
body:
## Summary

On a curated OpenRouter model, Codex compacts the context on **every single turn**. The UI shows "Context compacted automatically" after each tool call, so no real work gets done.

Two things combine to cause it:

1. When OpenRouter reports `prompt_tokens: 0`, the substituted estimate from `estimateInputTokens` overshoots the true count by ~**3.9x** — well outside the 1.0x–1.3x band the constant is documented against.
2. `curate-models` pins every scripted curation to `contextWindow: 131072` / `autoCompact: 110000`, ignoring the `context_length` the provider advertises (1,050,000 for this model).

The inflated estimate (~116k) lands above the conservative `autoCompact` (110k) on every turn that OpenRouter reports zero for, so compaction fires forever.

## Environment

- Codex Router `0.4.0-beta.4` (`e71c890`)
- Windows 11, Codex Desktop
- Model: `openrouter/openai/gpt-5.6-luna`, curated with
  `node src/curate-models.mjs openrouter --models "openai/gpt-5.6-luna" --efforts high`

## Evidence

From `~/.codex/codex-router/usage-events.jsonl`, consecutive turns of one session. Note how the requests OpenRouter reports honestly (`inputTokens: 29551`) alternate with the ones it reports as zero, where the estimate is nearly 4x larger:

```json
{"model":"openrouter/openai/gpt-5.6-luna","provider":"openrouter","status":200,"inputTokens":0,"outputTokens":273,"totalTokens":273,"estimatedInputTokens":115762}
{"model":"openrouter/openai/gpt-5.6-luna","provider":"openrouter","status":200,"inputTokens":29551,"cachedInputTokens":13751,"outputTokens":1489,"totalTokens":31040}
{"model":"openrouter/openai/gpt-5.6-luna","provider":"openrouter","status":200,"inputTokens":0,"outputTokens":217,"totalTokens":217,"estimatedInputTokens":116587}
```

Earlier in the same session, same shape:

```json
{"inputTokens":0,"outputTokens":191,"estimatedInputTokens":115398}
{"inputTokens":25735,"cachedInputTokens":0,"outputTokens":1388,"totalTokens":27123}
{"inputTokens":0,"outputTokens":664,"estimatedInputTokens":118685}
{"inputTokens":24536,"cachedInputTokens":13751,"outputTokens":1616,"totalTokens":26152}
```

Estimated / actual is consistently **3.9x–4.7x**.

## Analysis

### 1. The bytes-per-token ratio is calibrated against prose, not against a Responses payload

`src/response-usage.mjs`:

```js
// Against real text this lands between about 1.0x (code-heavy) and 1.3x
// (prose-heavy) of the true count, so compaction fires somewhere between
// 690,000 and 900,000 real tokens.
const ESTIMATE_BYTES_PER_TOKEN = 3.3;
```

`estimateInputTokens` measures the serialized request body, which for Codex is not "real text": it carries the full tool schemas on every turn, JSON structure and escaping, and `encrypted_content` reasoning blobs. Measured here it lands at ~15.7 real bytes per token, not 3.3 — so the estimate comes out ~4x high, not 1.0–1.3x.

Cached tokens make it worse: `cachedInputTokens: 13751` is billed and counted differently, but the bytes still go up the wire and still land in the estimate.

### 2. The clamp turns an overshoot into a guaranteed compaction

```js
return Number.isInteger(contextWindow) && contextWindow > 0
  ? Math.min(estimate, contextWindow)
  : estimate;
```

When the estimate exceeds the declared window it is clamped to *exactly* `contextWindow`. Since `autoCompact` is 85% of the window, a clamped estimate is **always** above the compaction threshold. Any model whose declared window is too small therefore compacts on every zero-report turn, by construction.

### 3. `curate-models` does not use the context length the provider advertises

Scripted curation writes fixed metadata:

```json
{ "contextWindow": 131072, "autoCompact": 110000 }
```

OpenRouter's `/api/v1/models` already exposes the real value, and `discover-models` calls that endpoint:

```
openai/gpt-5.6-luna        -> context_length: 1050000
deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash -> context_length: 1048576
```

So the correct number is available at curation time and is 8x larger than what gets written.

### 4. The new drift check cannot catch this

`0b2a258` added "Context windows match observed traffic", but it only fires when a provider **exceeds** the declared window. Premature compaction keeps traffic below the declared window, so the check reports OK while the bug is active. In my case:

```
OK  Context windows match observed traffic: 24 routed models, no provider has exceeded its declared window
```

`context-window-drift.mjs` also discards any event carrying `estimatedInputTokens`, which is exactly the population where the problem shows.

## Suggested fixes

- Have `curate-models` seed `contextWindow` from the provider's advertised `context_length` when discovery exposes one, falling back to 131072 only when it does not.
- Recalibrate `ESTIMATE_BYTES_PER_TOKEN` for Responses-shaped payloads, or estimate from the message content rather than the whole serialized body — tool schemas and `encrypted_content` are a large fixed cost that is not conversation.
- Reconsider clamping to `contextWindow`: clamping to the window guarantees a value above `autoCompact`. Clamping to something below the compaction threshold would fail safe instead.

## Workaround

Editing `~/.codex/codex-router/user-models.json` to the real window, then regenerating and restarting, stops the loop:

```json
{ "contextWindow": 1050000, "autoCompact": 892500 }
```

```
node src/catalog.mjs
node src/litellm-config.mjs
# restart the service
```

title: [Bug]: Grok OAuth forwarder drops cached prompt tokens, so long Codex sessions bill as 0% cache
body:
## Summary

`grok-oauth-forwarder.mjs` translates xAI Responses usage into OpenAI Chat Completions usage, but it only copies `input_tokens` / `output_tokens`. Cached prompt tokens never leave the proxy.

The rest of the router already knows how to meter cache hits (`normalizeTokenUsage` reads `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens` / `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` / `prompt_cache_hit_tokens`, and `usage-events.jsonl` has a first-class `cachedInputTokens` field). Grok OAuth never reaches that path because the forwarder rebuilds a 3-field `usage` object.

On a long Codex session this is not cosmetic. Native Grok / Aside / OpenCode report ~86-94% cache on the same model. Routed `grok-oauth/grok-4.6` reports **0 cache on every event**. Cost meters then price tens of millions of repeated prefix tokens at the full input rate.

## What happened?

Expected: a multi-turn `grok-oauth/grok-4.6` Codex session should expose prefix-cache hits the same way other providers do, so `usage-events.jsonl`, Codex token usage, and local cost meters can distinguish cached input from fresh input.

Actual: every Grok OAuth event is written as `{ inputTokens, outputTokens, totalTokens }` with no `cachedInputTokens`. Downstream tools therefore treat the entire prompt as uncached.

This is not "Grok has no cache". The same local machine, same model, same week:

| Path | Input | Cache hit |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Codex `grok-oauth/grok-4.6` | 48.0M | **0%** |
| Native Grok `grok-4.6` | 63.5M | **94%** |
| Aside `grok-4.6` | 2.8M | **86%** |
| OpenCode `grok-4.6` | 0.64M | **87%** |

Today's Codex ranking made the billing distortion obvious: `gpt-5.6-sol` was 30.6M tokens / $21.47 because 98% was cache-read, while routed Grok was 28.9M / ~$59 with cache = 0. Grok's list price is actually cheaper ($2 / $0.50 cache / $6 vs Sol $5 / $0.50 / $30). If routed Grok had the same ~98% hit rate, that same 28.9M would have been about $17, not $59.

## App target

Codex

## Platform

macOS

## Environment

- Codex Router `0.4.0-beta.2` (`48341e9`, `v0.4.0-beta.2-289-g48341e9`)
- `./bin/doctor --json`: `ok=true`, Grok OAuth `ok` ("official Grok CLI session"), background service running, 6 routed models
- Enabled providers: `grok-oauth`, `omniroute`
- Model: `grok-oauth/grok-4.6`

## Evidence

Local meter, **453 / 453** Grok OAuth events, **0** with `cachedInputTokens`. Totals: 51,641,386 input / 526,426 output / cache field never present.

Dates: 2026-08-11 (4), 2026-08-12 (30), 2026-08-13 (39), 2026-08-14 (116), 2026-08-16 (264). Status mix: 375×200, 75×502, 3×0.

Redacted rows from `~/.codex/codex-router/usage-events.jsonl`:

```json
{"meteringVersion":1,"at":"2026-08-14T09:07:19.666Z","model":"grok-oauth/grok-4.6","provider":"grok-oauth","status":200,"durationMs":243035,"inputTokens":100143,"outputTokens":24123,"totalTokens":124266}
{"meteringVersion":1,"at":"2026-08-16T08:49:37.073Z","model":"grok-oauth/grok-4.6","provider":"grok-oauth","status":200,"durationMs":71118,"inputTokens":44359,"outputTokens":613,"totalTokens":44972}
```

Compare a curated OpenRouter event from the same meter, where cache *is* forwarded:

```json
{"model":"openrouter/openai/gpt-5.6-luna","provider":"openrouter","status":200,"inputTokens":29551,"cachedInputTokens":13751,"outputTokens":1489,"totalTokens":31040}
```

Native Grok history on the same host reports `cachedReadTokens` and stores `[inputTokens, cachedReadTokens, 0, outputTokens]`. That path is healthy. Only the Codex OAuth proxy loses the field.

## Analysis

The drop happens here:

```js
// src/grok-oauth-forwarder.mjs, response.completed
const u = event.response?.usage;
if (u) {
  usage = {
    prompt_tokens: u.input_tokens ?? 0,
    completion_tokens: u.output_tokens ?? 0,
    total_tokens: (u.input_tokens ?? 0) + (u.output_tokens ?? 0),
  };
}
```

The fixture in `test/grok-oauth-forwarder.test.mjs` encodes the same 2-field contract:

```js
{ type: "response.completed", response: { usage: { input_tokens: 13, output_tokens: 5 } } }
assert.equal(text.usage.prompt_tokens, 13);
assert.equal(text.usage.completion_tokens, 5);
```

The shared normalizer already documents the intended shapes:

```js
// src/response-usage.mjs
const cachedInputTokens = tokenCount(
  value.input_tokens_details?.cached_tokens ??
    value.prompt_tokens_details?.cached_tokens ??
    value.prompt_cache_hit_tokens,
);
```

Two likely layers, both currently invisible:

1. **Forwarder strip.** Even if xAI sends `cached_tokens` / `cachedReadTokens` / `input_tokens_details`, the rebuilt Chat Completions `usage` object drops them. `normalizeTokenUsage` then has nothing to read, so `recordUsageEvent` omits `cachedInputTokens`.
2. **Possible upstream omission.** I have not captured a raw xAI `response.completed` payload in this report (it may contain account-identifying headers). If xAI already omits cache on the Grok CLI / OAuth Responses path, the forwarder should still pass through whatever it does send, and the meter should distinguish "provider reported 0" from "proxy deleted the field".

Native Grok CLI sessions on this machine *do* persist `cachedReadTokens`, so xAI knows how to report cache on the local Grok path. That makes a silent strip in the OAuth proxy the more likely bug.

This is also why Codex / agentsBar can look like "Grok is 3x more expensive than Sol" on similar token volume. The ranking is internally consistent with a 0% cache series. The series itself is wrong.

I searched open and closed issues for `cachedInputTokens`, prompt cache, Grok OAuth usage, and billing/metering. Closest related ticket is #266 (OpenRouter estimate vs real tokens, and that one *does* include `cachedInputTokens`). I did not find an existing report of Grok OAuth dropping cache.

## Suggested fix

- In `response.completed`, copy cache fields into the OpenAI-compatible usage object. Minimum useful shape:
  ```js
  usage = {
    prompt_tokens: u.input_tokens ?? 0,
    completion_tokens: u.output_tokens ?? 0,
    total_tokens: (u.input_tokens ?? 0) + (u.output_tokens ?? 0),
    prompt_tokens_details: {
      cached_tokens: u.input_tokens_details?.cached_tokens
        ?? u.prompt_tokens_details?.cached_tokens
        ?? u.cached_tokens
        ?? u.cachedReadTokens
        ?? 0,
    },
  };
  ```
- Teach the Grok OAuth usage mapping the same aliases native Grok already uses (`cachedReadTokens`) plus the Responses/OpenAI details objects.
- Add a forwarder test where upstream `response.completed.usage` includes a nonzero cache count, and assert both the Chat Completions `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` and a recorded `cachedInputTokens` event.
- Keep the current 3-field events unchanged when the provider reports no cache field, so old rows stay readable. Once a count exists, write `cachedInputTokens` even if it is 0, so "reported miss" is distinct from "field stripped".

## Workaround

None on the Codex `grok-oauth/*` route. Native Grok / Aside / OpenCode on the same model report cache correctly. Until this is fixed, long routed Grok sessions will keep looking several times more expensive than they probably are.
