title: Rebuild the Models page, and make subagent selection work again
body:
Two things: the Models page is rebuilt, and subagent selection works again.

## Subagent selection was inert

`applyMultiAgentSettings` only ever demoted. It read `disabled` and `hidden` and nothing else, so the three modes `.claude/skills/codex-subagents/SKILL.md` documents — `proven`, `selected`, `all` — did nothing, and every selection an operator had made was silently discarded.

On the install this was found on: `mode: selected` with twenty routes enabled, **four spawnable, one agent definition on disk**. The repo's own report answered the question exactly:

```
Mode:     selected
Catalog:  86 models, 4 spawnable as subagents
```

The modes work again as documented. An explicit `off` still beats every mode, hidden still demotes, and only an explicit choice promotes — a machine-local probe still promotes nothing on its own. Same install now:

```
Mode:     selected
Catalog:  86 models, 20 spawnable as subagents
~/.codex/agents/  →  17 definitions
```

Three tests asserted the broken behaviour (*"all mode never promotes"*, *"selected mode retains only registry-proven claims"*). They encoded the regression rather than a requirement, and now assert what the skill documents.

With that fixed the Subagents switch needs nothing behind it: flipping it selects the route, the router publishes it as v2, the agent definition is written. One click from off to spawnable.

## The Models page

The page asked the reader to learn a taxonomy before it would answer *"which models can I use"*. Two sections both changed what ended up in the picker, six words described three concepts, and the row you had just switched on jumped to a different group while you were looking at it.

One list now, ordered independently of the switches. Provider accounts collapse into a connections strip whose chips open the credential controls, and one **Add models** dialog searches every connected catalog instead of hiding one browser inside each provider. Rows are two lines rather than four columns, the switch states its own value, and the disclosure moved to the far left where it can no longer read as part of that switch.

On a real install this collapses 189 provider-qualified checkbox rows into 59 named models. Roughly 600 lines of dead CSS went with it.

The route list inside an expanded model is a real table: one header, one shared column definition, so cells cannot drift apart. Thinking effort has its own column — stacked under the switch it doubled every row's height and repeated the word down the list. Its menu is this page's own, because a native `<select>` popup is drawn shifted by the macOS checkmark gutter, which reads as misalignment inside a table.

The tray was brought in line: it lists every model and varies only the switch, with none of the `Proven v2` / `v1 only` / `Certification candidate` vocabulary the page had already dropped. Twenty dead translation entries across five languages went with it.

Ox Alpha, Fugu Ultra and Inkling — the only models in the registry with no maker to match — get one shared mark instead of wearing whichever provider served them.

## Wrong verdicts fixed

Each of these was reported to the operator as *"this model cannot run subagents"*:

- posting to `chat/completions`, which the caller endpoint does not serve — a 404 became a verdict about the model
- an HTTP 429 rate limit
- a client-side timeout, which never got an answer at all
- a rejected forcing mode (`Thinking mode does not support this tool_choice`) on a route that calls tools correctly when simply offered them
- Codex refusing to spawn a non-OpenAI child under a ChatGPT account
- asking the registry for a capability the catalog had already granted, so a route the app had just made spawnable was described as unusable

Statuses that answer about the account or the moment — 401, 402, 403, 408, 429, 5xx, aborts, timeouts — now record as **deferred** and clear their record so the switch stays retryable. **Only a reply the provider actually sent can refuse a route.**

## Certification, for the registry

The five-check runner from `v2_agent/README.md` is here as `subagents certify`, separate from the switch. A complete pass promotes the route locally and writes `v2_agent/<provider>/<model>/proof.json`, so evidence gathered once can be reviewed and shipped rather than re-measured on the next machine.

The gate is narrow by construction: all five checks passing in one run, the record's slug matching the route exactly, the current proof epoch, and the route neither hidden nor switched off. The cheap stream/tool probe is two of the five and still cannot stand in for native collaboration; the legacy `candidate`, `experimental` and `proven` statuses still promote nothing.

**Known limitation:** checks 3–5 cannot complete while Codex is signed in with a ChatGPT account — it refuses to spawn a non-OpenAI child and says so in the parent's own message. Checks 1–2 are verified live. Signed routing is not a way around it (`requires_openai_auth = true` is the same account). The untested path is `auth_mode: "apikey"`, which bills separately.

## Verification recorded, not repeated

`docs/SUBAGENT-CERTIFICATION.md` carries a table of every question this work paid provider quota to answer — the endpoint, the tool_choice rejection, the account refusal, signed routing, which routes hold a registry certification — each with its evidence, so the next reader can check a claim instead of re-running it. `AGENTS.md` records the rule change and points there.

## Finding models, and naming them

A provider chip sits beside the status one, built from the same trigger, menu and close handling. Selecting a provider keeps families with a route from it, composing with the search and status filters rather than replacing them; the results count and empty-state copy both widened so they stay truthful when it is the provider narrowing the list. It appears only above three distinct providers — below that the menu is slower than reading the provider each row already names.

Marks that were missing or wrong:

- **Kimi, Gemini and Claude** were monochrome silhouettes painted with one brand colour. That works for a wordmark and destroys these, because the colour is part of the mark — Gemini came out flat purple instead of its purple-to-cyan gradient, and Claude lost the orange entirely. All three are the official full-colour icons now, drawn as artwork rather than masked. Gemini uses the `gemini_sparkle_v002` SVG Google itself serves, so the gradient is the real one.
- **Antigravity** had no brand entry at all, so every Antigravity route fell back to a monogram built from its provider id. It gets the official press icon.
- **Ox Alpha, Fugu Ultra and Inkling** — the only models in the registry with no maker to match — share one mark instead of wearing whichever provider served them, and the user-defined **Custom** endpoint uses it too.

Every asset records in `SOURCES.md` the page it came from and, where it replaced something, what it replaced.

## A proxied provider read as a broken one

Fetching the Venice catalog from the app returned `fetch failed` while every sibling worked. Venice is only reachable through the proxy here, and the address and the permission to use it are separate answers: the app is launched by the desktop session, so it inherits `HTTP_PROXY` from the login environment but nothing telling Node it may use it. The discovery child dialled `api.venice.ai` directly and its connect timeout was reported as the provider failing.

The service definition already resolves this the same way, so children spawned by the app now read the opt-in the install manifest recorded, and only for the install that recorded it. Only the opt-in is restored, never an address — supplying a proxy the environment does not name is `inheritedProxyEnvironment`'s decision to defer, and `AGENTS.md` says not to widen that trigger.

Verified against a live install: `venice --json --refresh` returns `fetch failed` without the opt-in and a 113-model catalog with it. The other three providers asked about (Nous Research, OpenRouter, MiniMax Token Plan) already fetched — 372, 419 and 8 models — and needed no change.

## Checks

- Full suite **2496 pass, 0 fail**
- `npm run check` clean, `tsc --noEmit` clean, Swift builds clean
- `doctor`: **0 FAIL, 0 ERROR** on a live install (two pre-existing WARNs: vision-bridge pin, absent Antigravity credential)
- Toggle path exercised end to end on that install: 17 → 18 definitions and 20 → 21 spawnable on `set … on`, and back on `set … off`
- Both HTTP checks confirmed live against `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp`: a real SSE stream, and `codex_router_probe` returning `{"token": "ok"}`
- New tests pin the promotion gate (including the exact failure it prevents), the runner's endpoint and decision logic, the false pass where a parent repeats the marker from its own prompt, the parallel fan-out shape, the deferral rules, and the stable row ordering
- Driven by hand in the built app against a real 59-model install, light and dark

title: Fix false empty-completion limits on large stream prologues
body:
## Problem

PR #426 changed the empty-completion guard's 1 MiB pre-content budget from a conservative release into a hard failure. Some routed Responses streams send more than 1 MiB of valid, parseable response metadata before their first visible output delta. Those turns generated output, but the router retried them and eventually returned:

> The model produced no output before the router's safety limit.

This reproduced consistently with GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 through opencode Go. Failed usage rows sometimes already had a first-token timestamp or output-token count, confirming that the upstream model was not silent.

## Cause

Two guard conditions combined:

1. Crossing the byte budget always threw, even after complete JSON SSE events had established that the stream was well framed.
2. After a budget/liveness release, the guard checked the residual parse buffer even when parsing the same chunk had just recognized output and settled the stream.

The second condition could therefore turn an already recognized output delta into a false byte-limit error.

## Fix

- Relay a large prologue at the byte budget when at least one complete JSON SSE event has parsed, no terminal event has arrived, and the current partial event remains within the parser bound.
- Re-check settlement before applying the post-release residual-buffer limit.
- Keep malformed or oversized unterminated events fail-closed.

This restores the coherent-attempt behavior from the original empty-completion work in PR #145 without removing PR #426's bounds or retry/error semantics.

## Verification

- `node test/empty-completion-guard.test.mjs` — 36 passed
- `node test/empty-completion-router.test.mjs` — 25 passed
- `node test/pipe-response.test.mjs` — 8 passed
- `npm run check` — passed
- `git diff --check` — passed
- Live GLM-5.3 probe after restarting the narrowed build: exact `GLM_STREAM_OK`, HTTP 200, 4 output tokens; telemetry recorded `emptyCompletionPreludeLimit: "bytes"`, proving the repaired budget-release path was exercised.

The regression tests include both the valid large-prologue case and a negative control proving that an earlier valid event cannot excuse a later oversized unterminated event.

title: fix(start): restart the managed service and restore the installed proxy
body:
## Problem

`stop` unloads the background service, but `start` exec'd the *foreground* supervisor. The obvious `stop; start` pair was therefore asymmetric: the managed service went away and an unmanaged copy took its place, carrying the calling shell's environment rather than the installed one, and dying with the shell that started it.

A shell spawned by a desktop app has no proxy variables. So the replacement dialled every upstream directly and answered with **a 502 naming an opt-in that was already set** — set in the service definition it had just unloaded. The error surfaced far from its cause.

## Change

- `bin/start` restarts the managed service. The foreground supervisor stays reachable, but only behind an explicit `--foreground`.
- `inheritedProxyEnvironment()` restores the recorded proxy for any start path whose own environment is silent. Silence is the only trigger — `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=0` counts as the operator speaking, so a deliberately unproxied run stays unproxied.
- `src/start.mjs` applies it before anything reads the environment or spawns a child, and logs the restored host unconditionally (credential redacted). Nothing near the router previously said which network path it was using, which is the main reason the original failure took so long to find.

## Tests

21 passing, including `start and stop act on the same layer`, `the foreground supervisor is reachable, but only on purpose`, and `a declared proxy environment is left exactly as the operator set it`. Verified the live launchd service is untouched by the run.

## What

Adds `src/model-discovery-audit.mjs` (287 lines), which walks every anonymous catalog and every API-key catalog whose credential is configured, reporting new candidates, unavailable registered IDs, skips, and failures.

**The report is research input only.** It never invokes curation and never changes the registry, so a newly advertised slug still needs the normal live compatibility proof before it can become a listed model.

## Workflow paths

Three deliberately separate paths:

| Trigger | Behaviour | Secrets |
|---|---|---|
| Pull request | Fixture-backed discovery tests only | **None** |
| Weekly cron (Mon 04:17 UTC) | Live audit of all configured providers | Scoped to the audit step |
| Manual dispatch | `all`, one provider ID, or a comma-separated set | Scoped to the audit step |

Two safety properties worth reviewing:

- Scheduled and manual runs pin checkout to the repository's **default branch**, so a user cannot select a feature branch and expose the provider secrets to it.
- Credentials are declared on the audit step rather than the job, so checkout, setup, and npm lifecycle scripts never receive provider keys.

A targeted run fails when a requested provider's credential is absent; an `all` run records unconfigured providers as skipped, so one missing subscription does not hide the rest of the audit.

title: Groq models fail in Codex because routed requests exceed Groq's 128-tool limit
body:
## Summary

Groq models cannot be used through Codex Router because the routed request contains more than Groq's maximum supported 128 tools.

The failure occurs even in Codex CLI with all configured MCP servers disabled, so this does not appear to be caused by user MCP configuration or Codex Desktop-only app tools.

## Environment

- Windows
- Codex CLI: `0.149.1`
- Codex Router
- Model: `groq/openai/gpt-oss-120b`
- Groq provider configured with a valid API key
- Model discovery succeeds
- `openai/gpt-oss-120b` is registered / curated

## Error

```text
groq rejected the request for openai/gpt-oss-120b (curated).
(HTTP 400: 'tools' : maximum number of items is 128)
```

## Minimal reproduction

Configured MCP servers:

```text
node_repl
twlaw
```

Both were disabled for the test using one-shot Codex config overrides:

```powershell
codex `
  -c 'mcp_servers.twlaw.enabled=false' `
  -c 'mcp_servers.node_repl.enabled=false' `
  exec `
  --skip-git-repo-check `
  -m "groq/openai/gpt-oss-120b" `
  "只回覆 OK，不要使用任何工具。"
```

The request still fails with:

```text
HTTP 400: 'tools' : maximum number of items is 128
```

The same failure also occurs in Codex Desktop.

## Expected behavior

A Groq-routed model should receive a provider-compatible tool surface and be usable in Codex.

## Actual behavior

The request is rejected before inference because more than 128 tool definitions are sent to Groq.

## Notes

This does not appear to be model-specific prompt behavior because Groq rejects the request during request validation before the model runs.

Simply truncating `tools` to the first 128 would be unsafe because essential Codex tools could be silently removed.

A provider-aware solution may need to use Codex's deferred/tool-search exposure mechanism, or otherwise reduce the directly exposed tool set while preserving required core tools.

Additional observation: Codex first logs WebSocket `426 Upgrade Required` errors against the local router endpoint, but then falls back and reaches Groq; the blocking error is the Groq `tools` validation failure above.

title: [Bug]: opencode Go's Responses endpoint rejects the Codex-native tool shapes the Free endpoint accepts
body:
### What happened?

Every model on the `opencode-go-responses` provider (`grok-4.5`, `muse-spark-1.2-contributor`, `gpt-5.6-luna`) fails with HTTP 400 on the first turn from the Codex desktop app. Models on `opencode-go` (chat completions) are unaffected, which is what made this hard to see.

`buildRoutedRequest` keeps `type: "namespace"` and `type: "custom"` tools whenever `provider.protocol === "openai-responses"`, and `needsZenFreeToolCompatibility` is scoped to `opencode-free` / `opencode-free-responses`. The comment there says the Free pair's observed limits "do not establish a contract for paid Zen, Go, or any other free model" — reasonable without evidence. This is the evidence for Go: the Console Go Responses endpoint has the same limits, plus one more.

Three distinct rejections, all from Console Go, all on the real app path:

**1. `namespace` and `custom` discriminators**

```
[400] validation failed: tools[8]: unknown discriminator value: custom;
tools[10]: unknown discriminator value: namespace; ... tools[26]: unknown discriminator value: namespace
```

**2. `search_content_types`**

```
`tools[].search_content_types` is only supported for web_search_preview tools.
```

**3. a 64-character cap on function tool names**

```
tools[42]: function tool name must be at most 64 characters; tools[43]: ...; tools[121]: ...
`name` must be at most 64 characters, got 66
```

(3) only becomes visible once (1) is fixed, because the flattened `<namespace>__<tool>` names are what exceed the cap. App connector and MCP tools blow past it easily — `mcp__codex_apps__github__list_repository_pull_request_review_comments_for_branch` is 80 characters.

### Why the existing check does not catch it

`node src/compatibility-test.mjs opencode-go-responses/grok-4.5 --live --yes` passes all four checks (basic, streaming, tool calling, compaction) on all three models. Its payload carries no `namespace`, `custom`, or `web_search` entries, so it exercises a tool shape the client never sends. Four green checks while every real turn 400s.

### Local fix that works

Happy to turn this into a PR if the shape is right.

- New predicate `needsConsoleGoResponsesToolCompatibility(route)` — provider id `opencode-go-responses`.
- In the responses branch of `buildRoutedRequest`, flatten for that provider with `flattenNamespaceTools(tools, { bridgeToolSearch: false, maxNameLength: 64 })` and set `namespacesFlattened` so `flattenNamespacedHistory` runs. `bridgeToolSearch: false` keeps the request consistent with the history rewrite, since `flattenToolSearchHistory` stays gated on `chatCompletionsProvider`.
- Both `needsZenFreeToolCompatibility` gates accept the new predicate as well, which brings `stripSearchContentTypes` and `bridgeCustomTools` to Go.
- New `maxNameLength` option in `flattenNamespaceTools`: a flattened child over the cap becomes `<truncated>_<fnv1a-base36>`, recorded in a `NAME_ALIASES` WeakMap keyed by the namespaces `Map` — the same side-channel pattern as `CUSTOM_TOOL_RELAYS` — merged into `flatToNative` by `buildNamespaceLookups`, and used by `flattenNamespacedHistory` so the transcript cites the name that was actually sent. The native `{ namespace, name }` pair in the namespaces map is untouched, so restoration still resolves through the map rather than by splitting the name. Inactive unless a caller passes a limit, so every existing path emits identical names.

### Verification

- `node --test test/namespace-relay.test.mjs` — 47/47 pass.
- Offline: an 80-character flattened name becomes a 64-character alias, a 36-character sibling is left alone, `buildNamespaceLookups` resolves the alias back to `{ namespace, name }`, and `flattenNamespacedHistory` renames stored calls to the same alias.
- Live, posting to the local router endpoint with a payload carrying `namespace` + `custom` + `web_search` with `search_content_types` + an 80-character namespaced tool name: `200` on `opencode-go-responses/grok-4.5`, `opencode-go-responses/muse-spark-1.2-contributor`, `opencode-go-responses/gpt-5.6-luna` and `opencode-go/ox-alpha`. The same payloads returned `400` before the change.

### Which app do you route through?

Codex

### Platform

Windows

### Version

codex-router `0.4.0-beta.4`, commit `1878d9e`, Codex desktop app on Windows 11, opencode Go subscription.

title: feat(install): say whether the client is running when its config changes
body:
## Problem

The configuration an install rewrites is read **once, at client start**. A client that was already running keeps serving the previous routing, and the failure that follows — a connection error naming neither the install nor the client — reads as a network fault.

The installer already knew the remedy. It printed:

```
Fully quit and reopen Codex, then start a new task.
```

…unconditionally, as one line among ten, with no way for the reader to tell whether it applied to them *right now*. `grep` confirms none of the three "fully quit and reopen" sites check whether the app is actually running.

This is not hypothetical: it cost a real debugging session. Codex had been running ~6.5 hours; the reinstall rewrote its config at 00:45 and replaced the router process 22 seconds later. Every local check said healthy — router `HTTP 200`, 86 models, proxy up, secret unrotated — because the stale half was the client, which nothing looked at.

## Change

`clientRestartNotice` looks before it speaks.

**Running:**
```
Codex is running right now (PID 15809 and 13 other processes) and loaded its
routing configuration at startup. Fully quit and reopen it, then start a new
task -- until you do, it keeps using the previous configuration.
```

**Not running:**
```
Codex is not running; it reads this configuration the next time it starts.
```

**DeepSeek Harness:** nothing at all — it reloads `settings.yaml` on the next request, so a restart notice would be busywork. This matches the reasoning `targetRestartHint` already applies.

## Two properties that matter more than the wording

- **The probe excludes this checkout.** The router runs from paths with `codex` all over them, so a naive match makes the notice tell the user to quit the very thing printing it. There's a test for this.
- **A failed probe returns nothing, not a guess.** If `ps` is missing or errors, the installer falls back to the old unconditional advice. Failing to look must never be worse than never having looked — also tested.

Helper processes fold into their root via ppid, so a desktop client reports one actionable PID rather than fourteen.

## Tests

7 new tests, all passing. `npm run check` passes. `sh -n bin/install` passes.

One pre-existing quirk to note: `test/installer-scripts.test.mjs` reports `pass N-1, fail 0`. I verified this is **unchanged on unmodified `origin/main`** via a clean worktree — not introduced here.

## Not included

`bin/install` still prints "Installed the selected external model routes for Codex." on the `gemini` path too. That mislabel predates this change; the second line is now correct for Gemini, and I left the first alone to keep the diff focused.

title: [Bug]: opencode-go (Chat Completions) sessions report cached_tokens=0 and inflated input — LiteLLM drops Console Go's choice-bearing usage chunk; the existing Z.ai compat transform fixes it
body:
First: thank you for this project. It is the only thing that let me run MiMo-V2.5 on my opencode Go subscription from the Codex CLI at all — Go's `/v1/responses` returns 500 for mimo on any request and Codex 0.148 refuses `wire_api = "chat"`, so the LiteLLM bridge here is the whole story. Genuinely appreciated.

### What happened?

Every `opencode-go/*` session (Chat Completions provider) reports **`cached_input_tokens: 0`** to Codex and `cached_tokens=unknown` in `router.log`, and the `input_tokens` figure is inflated — even though Console Go is caching the prefix.

Same model, same day, direct to `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/chat/completions` (`stream: true`, `stream_options.include_usage`), repeated prefix:

| Call | prompt_tokens | prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 (cold) | 2,571 | 0 |
| 2 (same prefix) | 2,571 | **2,560** |

Through the router, a two-turn `opencode-go/mimo-v2.5` Codex session:

| Path | Turn 2 input_tokens | cached_input_tokens |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Routed, `main` as shipped | 54,218 | **0** |
| Routed, with the one-line change below | 37,609 | **36,416** (97%) |

The 54k vs 37k gap is LiteLLM substituting its own tokenizer estimate for the provider's count once it has dropped the upstream usage object — so cost meters and `ccusage codex` are wrong in both columns, not just the cache one.

**Root cause.** Console Go's Chat Completions stream puts `usage` on the `finish_reason` chunk while `choices` is still non-empty, then `[DONE]`. LiteLLM 1.96.0 discards upstream usage on that shape and falls back to a local estimate — BerriAI/litellm#36168 (open). The router already handles exactly this shape for Z.ai in `src/zai-cache-usage.mjs` (`ZaiCacheUsageCompatTransform` splits the terminal chunk into terminal + usage-only chunk and mirrors `cached_tokens` into `prompt_cache_hit_tokens`), but `zaiCacheUsageTransform()` is gated to `zai-api` / `zai-coding` only, so `opencode-go` never gets it. Same class as #267 (Grok OAuth), different provider.

**Fix.** Add `opencode-go` to the provider gate. That is the whole change; the transform needs no edits. Verified on Windows / Codex CLI 0.148 as in the second table; `node --test test/zai-cache-usage.test.mjs` passes with an added assertion. PR follows.

I did not add `opencode-go-messages` (Anthropic protocol, different stream) or `opencode-zen` — I only verified Go's Chat Completions endpoint.

### Which app do you route through?

Codex (CLI, `codex exec` and the interactive TUI)

### Platform

Windows 11, Node v24.11.0, codex-router v0.4.0-beta.4 (checkout install, `main` @ 7a191fa at the time), LiteLLM pinned 1.96.0.

### Doctor output or support bundle

```
OK    Codex binary: ...\OpenAI\Codex\bin\codex.exe
OK    Enabled providers: opencode-go, opencode-go-messages, opencode-go-responses, opencode-zen
OK    Merged catalog: 23 routed models
OK    Generated gateway config: ~/.codex/codex-router/litellm.yaml
OK    LiteLLM venv runtime: ...\codex-router\.venv\Scripts\litellm.exe exists
OK    Background service: running
OK    Router health: version 0.4.0-beta.4

router.log, before:
[codex-router] timing ... model=opencode-go/mimo-v2.5 provider=opencode-go status=200 out_tokens=113 cached_tokens=unknown est_input=54218
router.log, after the gate change:
[codex-router] timing ... model=opencode-go/mimo-v2.5 provider=opencode-go status=200 out_tokens=24 cached_tokens=36416
```

title: Apply the choice-bearing usage compat transform to opencode-go (cached_tokens=0 → real cache reads)
body:
Fixes #457.

One-line gate change: `zaiCacheUsageTransform()` now also covers `opencode-go`. Console Go's Chat Completions stream has the same choice-bearing terminal usage chunk as Z.ai, which LiteLLM 1.96.0 discards (BerriAI/litellm#36168), so routed `opencode-go/*` sessions reported `cached_input_tokens=0` and an inflated `input_tokens` to Codex.

| Two-turn `opencode-go/mimo-v2.5` session, turn 2 | input_tokens | cached_input_tokens |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| main | 54,218 | 0 |
| this branch | 37,609 | 36,416 |

`router.log` goes from `cached_tokens=unknown` to `cached_tokens=36416`; `ccusage codex session` shows the Cache Read column for the session.

Scope: `opencode-go` only — the provider whose stream I captured and verified. `opencode-go-messages` (Anthropic protocol) and `opencode-zen` were not tested and are left out. Test: added the gate assertion to `test/zai-cache-usage.test.mjs`; `node --test test/zai-cache-usage.test.mjs` passes (6/6).

And thank you for the router — it is what makes MiMo on the Go subscription usable from Codex in the first place.

title: fix: preserve custom provider identity in login-free mode
body:
## Summary

Preserve an already selected custom `model_provider` while login-free mode is active, so the Codex client keeps the same provider identity instead of remounting its chat surface. The router temporarily replaces that provider's complete table with an ownership-marked, auth-free Responses table, then restores the original table and root model exactly when the mode is disabled.

The built-in `openai` provider is intentionally different: Codex 0.141 requires authentication for its implicit definition, while current 0.150 Desktop builds reject an explicit `[model_providers.openai]` override. Root-OpenAI configurations therefore use the established `codex-router` provider fallback during login-free mode and restore the original root provider afterward.

## Safety and compatibility

- Keeps custom provider IDs unchanged and sets `requires_openai_auth = false` only in the temporary router-owned table.
- Snapshots every replaced provider section, including nested tables, in protected state and restores it only after an ownership check.
- Preserves ownership ID, model selection, and restore metadata across ordinary updates and native-catalog refreshes.
- Restores the prior transport after catalog publication failures and refuses restoration if the direct provider/model source changed concurrently.
- Journals login-free catalog refreshes before parking the transport. Recovery requires a private, non-symlink journal bound to the exact provider-state bytes, ownership ID, canonical route, and display alias; state plus inactive config alone remains fail-closed.
- Serializes the complete refresh with a cross-process lock. A second refresh waits instead of interleaving, and an abandoned stale lock permits the protected journal to resume.
- Only `bin/refresh-catalog` may resume or complete a pending refresh. Ordinary enable/disable/model changes, installation, and doctor repair refuse without mutating state until that recovery command completes.
- Migrates the draft root-OpenAI v3 state to the cross-version provider fallback without losing the original model restore record.
- Keeps the state writer transactional and restores the previous state if the Codex config write fails.

## Verification

- Real signed-out `codex app-server` Responses turns pass through both the root-OpenAI fallback and a preserved custom provider on installed `codex-cli 0.141.0` and bundled `0.150.0-alpha.8`.
- A real custom-provider refresh round trip proves: original table/secret → managed auth-free table under the same ID → failure restoration → successful refresh with identical state/model → byte-identical final provider restoration.
- Hard-exit regressions cover the crash window immediately after transport parking for both custom-provider v3 and root-OpenAI v1 state. Model, provider-table/secret, state-ownership, and recovery-route drift leave config, state, and journal untouched.
- Concurrency regressions cover two-process overlap, bounded lock contention, owner death, and abandoned-lock recovery.
- Pending-journal regressions prove that both explicit disable forms, ordinary enable/disable, and user model changes refuse byte-identically; an interrupted disable without a journal is never revived.
- POSIX and Windows installer/doctor ordering checks prove a pending refresh cannot publish a catalog or falsely report recovery. Malformed, non-private, and symlinked state/journal inputs refuse without mutation.
- Deterministic legacy-layout coverage reproduces the 0.141 configuration shape that lacks the modern agent feature table.
- Windows fixtures use the production private-state writer so ACL assertions exercise the same owner-only state contract as production.
- `npm run check` passes; the exact final full suite reports 2,632 passing, 0 failing, and 17 skipped tests (2,649 total). Repo-maintainer review covers all 108 current hunks with no findings.

The branch is linearly rebased onto current `main`; the original contributor commits are retained, followed by bounded maintainer repair commits.

title: Windows: router.mjs crashes with exit code 3221226505 (0xC0000409 STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN), suspect zstdDecompressSync
body:
## Summary

`router.mjs` (the main process listening on `CODEX_ROUTER_PORT`, e.g. 4202) intermittently crashes on Windows with exit code `3221226505` (`0xC0000409` / `STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN`), a native-level crash with no JS stack trace. When it happens, every child process (litellm gateway, oauth forwarders) dies with it and the whole router stays down until something restarts it — Task Scheduler's own `RestartCount`/`RestartInterval` on the installed task did not bring it back on its own in my testing.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 Home Single Language 10.0.26200
- Node: v22.22.2 (`C:\nvm4w\nodejs\node.exe`)
- codex-router: `0.4.0-beta.4` (confirmed the relevant code paths below are unchanged as of current `main` / `v0.5.0` — `router.mjs`'s `decodeBody()`/`zstdDecompressSync` and `antigravity-oauth-forwarder.mjs` have no diff between my checkout and `origin/main`)
- Router run via `start-codex-router.cmd` under a Task Scheduler task (logon trigger)

## Observed pattern

Reproduced 3 times over one day, always the same exit code, always at the end of a long session with a lot of traffic:

```
[codex-router] Codex router exited (code=3221226505, signal=null).
```

- The request immediately before the crash always completed normally (`status=200`) — no single "poison" request visible in the log.
- All 3 crashes happened after a sustained streak of successful `antigravity-oauth/gemini-3.7-flash` requests, in sessions where `cached_tokens` had climbed well into the 100k–200k range (i.e. long-running sessions with large accumulated context).
- No stack trace is logged, consistent with a native crash rather than an uncaught JS exception.

## Suspected cause (unconfirmed — no crash dump yet)

`decodeBody()` in `src/router.mjs` (around line 372) calls `zstdDecompressSync` from `node:zlib` to decompress the incoming request body:

```js
if (encoding === "zstd") decoded = zstdDecompressSync(decoded, options);
```

This runs unconditionally at the top of `handleResponses()` (the handler for every `/v1/responses` request, line ~2656), since Codex CLI zstd-compresses its request bodies by default. The buffer size grows with conversation length over a session, which fits the "crash only after heavy/long sessions" pattern. `zstdDecompressSync`/Node's native zstd support is comparatively new relative to gzip/deflate/brotli, so it's my best guess for where a native buffer-handling bug could live — but I have not captured a crash dump to confirm the actual native frame, so this is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis.

## What I've done so far

- Confirmed via `netstat`/Task Scheduler that when this happens, nothing is listening on any of the router's ports until manually restarted.
- Set up a local watchdog (polls the port, relaunches `start-codex-router.cmd` if down) as a workaround, since Task Scheduler's built-in restart-on-failure did not actually recover the process after a crash in my testing.
- Diffed my checkout against `origin/main`/`v0.5.0` — no changes to `decodeBody()`, `zstdDecompressSync` usage, or `antigravity-oauth-forwarder.mjs` since my version, and nothing in the CHANGELOG referencing this.

## Ask

- Has anyone else hit `0xC0000409` crashes on Windows? Any known issue with `zstdDecompressSync` under `node:zlib` on large/growing buffers?
- If useful, I can capture a proper crash dump (WER `LocalDumps`) next time it happens and attach it.

title: Native model compaction fails with 404 through codex-router (store:false forced on substituted callers)
body:
Title: Native model compaction fails with 404 through codex-router (`store:false` forced on substituted callers)

## Environment
- codex-router: v0.4.0-beta.4 (commit 866cb8b / b8d8e6e, `main`)
- Client: ChatGPT.app (Codex framework) on macOS
- Model: native OpenAI model selected via router catalog (e.g. `gpt-5.6-luna`, `gpt-5.6-terra`)

## Steps to reproduce
1. Make a native OpenAI model available through the codex-router catalog.
2. Start a session on that native model through the router, OR switch to it from another model inside an existing session.
3. Let the session grow until Codex triggers its remote compact task (or trigger it via a mid-session model switch, which forces one compaction).

## Expected
Compaction completes and the session continues on the native model.

## Actual
```
Error running remote compact task: unexpected status 404 Not Found: Item with id 'rs_f4f1bcd6-...' not found. Items are not persisted when `store` is set to false. Try again with `store` set to true, or remove this item from your input., url: http://127.0.0.1:4202/_codex-router/.../v1/responses
```

## Root cause analysis
In `src/router.mjs`, `normalizeNativeForSubstitutedCaller()` unconditionally sets:

```js
// Not optional upstream: `store` must be false, and anything else is a 400.
payload.store = false;
```

This is applied on the "substituted caller" path (the ChatGPT-app-via-router path). Forcing `store: false` on the OpenAI Responses API request means response objects (`rs_...`) are never persisted server-side. Codex's remote compact task then references those `rs_...` ids by id, and OpenAI returns 404 because they were not persisted.

Routed (LiteLLM / OpenCode Go / OpenRouter Free) models are unaffected because they do not rely on OpenAI-side `rs_` persistence.

## Workaround (verified)
Perform the compaction on a LiteLLM-backed model (OpenCode Go or OpenRouter Free) first, then switch to the native model. The switch triggers only a single compaction (openai/codex#29426 class) and succeeds. Alternatively, run the native model directly without the router (it does not need it) — a fresh native chat compacts correctly.

## Suggested fix
Do not force `store: false` for native Responses requests that Codex itself issues for compaction. Either honor Codex's own `store` value, or set `store: true` when the caller is Codex rather than a generic substituted client. Please clarify whether the native backend truly requires `store: false` — the public OpenAI Responses API permits `store: true`, and the compaction flow depends on persisted response items.

title: [Bug]: translated routed tool activity is split into repeated rows
[Bug]: Translated providers emit phantom assistant items between tool calls
body:
### What happened?

With codex-router enabled, native Responses models such as 5.6 Luna show one compact activity group for a multi-step task. Translated external routes such as Gemini and Ox Alpha/OpenCode can show repeated standalone “Ran command” rows for the same task.

This is observable in the translated /v1/responses stream: empty assistant message items are emitted before function-call items. Codex renders each empty assistant item as a separate activity boundary. These phantom items are produced only on translated routes; the native Responses route does not emit them.

The issue is not that the model makes multiple legitimate tool calls. The problem is that the adapter adds empty assistant lifecycle items in addition to those calls. Real assistant text, genuine separate turns, tool results, IDs, and indexes must remain intact.

Expected behavior:

- Empty bridge-only assistant items must not be emitted as visible activity events.
- Consecutive tool calls should have stable activity grouping.
- Real assistant content and genuine separate turns must never be removed or merged.
- Native Responses routes must remain unchanged.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Run codex-router 0.4.0-beta.4 on Windows 11 with Codex Desktop.
2. Select a translated external model.
3. Give it a repository task requiring several file edits and command calls.
4. Observe repeated standalone “Ran command” rows.
5. Compare the relayed /v1/responses stream with the same task using a native Responses model.
6. Count the empty assistant message items appearing before function-call items.

Proposed direction:

Normalize only assistant envelopes proven to be empty bridge messages before tool traffic. Keep the transformation protocol-scoped, bounded, and fail-open. Add conformance tests for multiple empty envelopes, retries, streaming and non-streaming responses, and tool-schema restoration. Do not claim full native-Luna lifecycle parity for upstream protocols that cannot provide it.

### Which app do you route through?

Codex

### Platform

Windows

### Doctor output or support bundle

_No response_

title: fix: support reviewed external skill coexistence
fix: avoid false Windows service liveness
body:
## Summary

Fix Windows background-service status/readiness incorrectly treating an unrelated manually started foreground router as the Task Scheduler-managed service.

The bug has two causes in `windowsScheduledTaskState()`:

- `[array]$task.GetInstances(0)` turns a null COM result into a one-element array, so zero real task instances can be reported as `instanceCount: 1`.
- launcher discovery accepted any process whose command line matched `*codex-router*src*start.mjs*`, so a manually started foreground router could satisfy `launcherAlive: true` even when the scheduled task itself was idle.

The fix normalizes null COM instances out and derives launcher liveness from the registered task action itself: it requires `wscript.exe` and the exact generated `start-codex-router-hidden.vbs` path from that task definition. A manual `src/start.mjs` process is deliberately not evidence that Task Scheduler is supervising the router.

## Reproduction

On a real Windows install with the scheduled task in `Ready` state, no `wscript`/CMD launcher process, and only a manually started foreground `src/start.mjs` running, current main reported:

```json
{"instanceCount":1,"lastTaskResult":267014,"launcherAlive":true}
```

With this patch, the same machine reports:

```json
{"instanceCount":0,"lastTaskResult":267014,"launcherAlive":false}
```

This tightens the live-launcher verification introduced by #432 rather than replacing its two-signal design.

## Verification

Rebased onto `0eac3ff`.

- regression test was RED before the implementation and GREEN after it
- focused service/readiness tests — pass
- post-rebase bounded suite covering Windows task state plus the new upstream GLM-5.3 Flash / registry / routing changes — **159 tests, 159 passed, 0 failed**
- `npm.cmd run check` — pass (`v2-agent applications valid (6)`, syntax checks passed)
- `git diff origin/main..HEAD --check` — clean
- GitHub CI — pass
- Provider model discovery workflow — pass
- no live provider/quota-consuming calls were used

### Live Windows verification — 2026-08-27

The exact Ready-task + manual-router case was exercised on a Windows 11 host after the review comment requesting native validation.

Positive control with the scheduler-managed service running:

```json
{"instanceCount":1,"lastTaskResult":267009,"launcherAlive":true}
```

Controlled negative case:

1. Stop the installed service from its canonical checkout and verify Task Scheduler is `Ready`, COM instance count is `0`, no generated VBS launcher is running, and no router root remains.
2. Manually launch the generated CMD wrapper outside Task Scheduler; one `node ...\\src\\start.mjs` router root is then live while Task Scheduler remains `Ready`, COM instance count remains `0`, and no `wscript.exe` launcher exists.
3. Run this branch's probe and service status.

Observed result:

```json
{"instanceCount":0,"lastTaskResult":267014,"launcherAlive":false}
```

```json
{"installed":true,"loaded":false,"state":"ready"}
```

The manual router was then stopped and the scheduler-managed service restored. Final positive control:

```json
{"instanceCount":1,"lastTaskResult":267009,"launcherAlive":true}
```

```json
{"installed":true,"loaded":true,"state":"running"}
```

No Codex Desktop process was restarted or terminated during this validation.

Codex

macOS

title: fix: record state ownership before installing the service
body:
## Why

Reinstalling over a state directory owned by a different checkout
(`foreign_state_owner`) deadlocked on every retry, and the only escape was
deleting the whole state directory -- every stored provider key with it.

The deadlock chain, as observed on a real install:

1. `bin/install` runs with `MODEL_ROUTER_ALLOW_FOREIGN_STATE=1`, so the
   installer itself writes the generated catalog and gateway config fine
   (`state-owner.mjs` documents `bin/install` as the sanctioned ownership
   transfer).
2. The background service it installs does **not** get that override. On
   every boot, `start.mjs` calls `writeLiteLlmConfig()`, which
   `assertStateOwnership` refuses while `install-manifest.json` still names
   another checkout -- so the service crash-loops forever.
3. `service.mjs install` contains the readiness wait (up to 300 s), and the
   manifest was recorded only *after* it returned. Ownership therefore
   never transferred: the service cannot boot until the record updates, and
   the record cannot update until the service is healthy. The installer
   looks hung for the full budget, then rolls back, and the next retry
   repeats the cycle.

The crash loop also had no fast signal on Linux: with `Restart=always`, the
unit cycles back to "active" after every crash, so a crash-looping service
and a slow cold start are indistinguishable for the whole 300-second wait.

Triggering this requires having installed from two different checkouts
(e.g. a development checkout once, then the managed `install.sh` checkout)
-- exactly the cross-checkout scenario the ownership guard exists to manage
safely, and whose documented recovery ("reinstall from here") deadlocked.

## What

- **`bin/install` / `install.ps1`: record the manifest before the service
  step.** The generated state is already written by this checkout at that
  point, so the record is truthful, and the service boots against its own
  ownership instead of a stale one. The `--prepare-only` path is unchanged
  and still does not record. An install that previously deadlocked recovers
  by re-running the installer; no state migration is needed, since the next
  install overwrites the manifest.
- **`service-readiness.mjs`: fail fast on a Linux crash loop.** When the
  caller supplies a restart counter, the wait polls it alongside health and
  aborts once the count climbs 3 restarts above the value observed at wait
  start, with an error naming `journalctl --user -u codex-router.service`
  and the router log. The comparison is relative to the wait's own
  baseline, so residue from before the install cannot trigger it, and a
  failed query is inconclusive -- the wait stays health-only, which is the
  shape macOS launchd has (Windows already has its task-state guard).
- **`service-linux.mjs` / `service.mjs`: feed the counter to the guard.**
  New `restart-count` verb reading systemd's `NRestarts`; `service.mjs`
  injects it only for the Linux script.

## Test

- `test/installer-scripts.test.mjs` extends the manifest-ordering test:
  the record must now precede `service.mjs install` on both installers,
  not only the health wait.
- `test/service-readiness.test.mjs` gains five cases: the crash loop
  rejects early (well inside the budget) with the journal hint; a steady
  count and a high-but-static count both keep the wait alive; a throwing
  counter cannot fail the wait; the threshold is measured against the
  wait's own baseline. A source-level test pins the `restart-count` verb
  and the `service.mjs` wiring.
- `npm run check` passes; `sh -n bin/install` passes.
- `npm test`: 2824/2854 pass. The 12 failures reproduce on the unmodified
  branch and are environmental: most disappear under `umask 077` (fixture
  directories created 0775), one file needs the not-installed `playwright`
  devDependency, and two are source-root-discovery / `rmSync` quirks of
  this machine. None of the failing files import the changed modules.

## Design notes

- **Transfer semantics are unchanged.** `bin/install` was already the
  sanctioned ownership transfer: it runs with the override and rewrites the
  generated state either way. This PR only reorders the steps inside that
  same run, so the record lands before the service that depends on it. The
  guard's behavior on the unattended paths -- service boot, non-override
  rewrites -- is untouched.
- **Output surface is unchanged.** The readiness error names the state
  directory path and the unit name, the same identifiers doctor already
  reports. The `restart-count` verb emits a single integer, and
  `install-manifest.mjs record` output stays suppressed on both platforms,
  as before.
- **systemctl is invoked the same way as the existing verbs**: fixed argv
  arrays, a constant unit name, no shell. Unparseable counter output
  degrades to "unknown".
- **The guard degrades to the previous behavior.** With no counter
  available -- no systemd session, a non-zero exit, unparseable output --
  the wait is health-only, which is what this platform did before. A query
  failure can never fail an install, matching the existing Task Scheduler
  precedent on Windows.
- **A record failure now stops earlier.** If recording the manifest fails,
  the install aborts before the service step, so no service is started into
  a state it cannot boot in.

Compatibility: `systemctl --value` needs systemd >= 236 (2018). Older
builds yield an empty value, which reads as "unknown" and only disables the
early abort.

title: fix: safely transfer cross-checkout state ownership
body:
Continues #497 from @mayrazing while preserving the contributor commit as this branch's direct parent.

The reported deadlock is real: the service performs a guarded gateway rewrite during boot, so recording the new checkout only after service installation makes cross-checkout installs wait on a service that cannot become healthy.

This maintainer continuation keeps that core ordering fix and adds the missing parity/safety boundaries found during review:

- Windows CheckoutInstall temporarily applies the same sanctioned foreign-state override as POSIX before guarded generated writes, then restores the caller's environment in finally.
- Prepare-only runs no longer receive an installer-created ownership override, because they do not record an ownership transfer.
- The separable Linux restart-counter add-on is removed for now: its synchronous unbounded systemctl polling can exceed the readiness deadline, and a reproduced health/counter race can reject an already healthy service.

Local verification: sh syntax; npm run check; installer/state-owner/readiness tests pass (50 applicable tests, 1 PowerShell-only skip on macOS). Exact-head CI is required before merge.

Contributor credit and original investigation remain in ancestry through #497.

fix: preserve Windows foreign-state override
body:
## Summary

Preserve the caller's `MODEL_ROUTER_ALLOW_FOREIGN_STATE` value across every Windows installer path, including `-PrepareOnly` and failures that occur before the full-install ownership override is set.

## Root cause

#497 initialized `$HadForeignStateOverride = $false` / `$SavedForeignStateOverride = $null`, then captured the real caller environment only inside `if (-not $PrepareOnly)` deep in the main `try`. The outer `finally` always restores/removes the variable.

That means:
- a successful `-PrepareOnly` run never captures the caller value, then `finally` removes it;
- any failure before the capture block does the same.

This violates the installer's stated contract that the caller environment is restored exactly as found.

## Fix

Snapshot both presence and value before `Push-Location` / the outer `try`. The full-install branch now only sets the temporary value to `1`; the existing `finally` restores the pre-run snapshot.

POSIX needs no matching change because its exported override exists only in the installer child shell and cannot mutate the caller environment.

## Verification

- red/green regression: the ownership test failed before the fix because the snapshot occurred after the outer `try`, then passed after moving the snapshot;
- focused installer group (`install.ps1` parse, rollback, manifest ordering, foreign-state override) — **4 passed, 0 failed**;
- `npm.cmd run check` — pass (`v2-agent applications valid (6)`, syntax checks passed);
- direct PowerShell parser check — pass;
- `git diff --check` / staged diff check — clean.

I also attempted the entire installer policy file with Git's POSIX shell manually added to this Windows PATH. One unrelated POSIX fixture test became active and failed because that artificial PATH changes its platform assumptions; the changed regression itself passed. I did not broaden this PR to that separate test issue (#500 already addresses the native-Windows shell portability regression).

opencode-go routes (mimo-v2.5, minimax-m2.5/m2.7, hy3) stuck at the 131072 context default; compact far too early
body:
## Summary

Several `opencode-go` routes carry the conservative `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` (131,072) / `DEFAULT_AUTO_COMPACT` (110,000) even though the underlying models document a much larger window. In a coding session this triggers auto-compaction very early and repeatedly, well before the model would actually run out of room.

This is the same class of staleness that was already corrected for `glm-5.3` (whose `config/opencode/go/glm-5.3.json` description notes *"the 200K figure it previously carried belongs to GLM-5.1"*). The models below appear to have been curated before curation started preferring the advertised `context_length`, and `opencode-go`'s catalog advertises no context length at all, so nothing has moved them off the default since.

## Affected routes

| Route (slug) | Current `contextWindow` | Documented context | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `opencode-go/mimo-v2.5` | 131,072 | **1,050,000** | [Xiaomi](https://mimo.xiaomi.com/mimo-v2-5/) · [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/xiaomi/mimo-v2.5) · [HF](https://huggingface.co/XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.5) |
| `opencode-go/mimo-v2.5-pro` | 131,072 | **1,050,000** | [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/xiaomi/mimo-v2.5-pro) |
| `opencode-go-messages/minimax-m2.7` | 131,072 | **204,800** (max output 196,608) | [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/minimax/minimax-m2.7) · [MiniMax docs](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/token-plan/best-practices) |
| `opencode-go-messages/minimax-m2.5` | 131,072 | **204,800** | [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/minimax-m2) · [cline/cline#10007](https://github.com/cline/cline/pull/10007) |
| `opencode-go/hy3` | 131,072 | **262,144** (256K) | [Tencent](https://www.tencent.com/tencent-unveils-hy3-preview-model-enhances-agent-capabilities-and-real-world-usability/) · [innFactory](https://innfactory.ai/en/ai-models/tencent-hunyuan/) |

For contrast, on the same install these `opencode-go` routes already carry the right figure: `glm-5.3` / `glm-5.3-flash` = 1,000,000, `glm-5.2` / `glm-5.1` / `deepseek-v4-*` = 1,048,576, `kimi-k2.x` / `kimi-k3` = 262,144, `minimax-m3` = 1,000,000.

## Root cause / evidence

`opencode-go` publishes no per-model context length:

```
$ ./bin/discover-models opencode-go --json
{
  "provider": "opencode-go",
  ...
  "contextLengths": {},
  "modelMetadata": [
    { "upstreamId": "mimo-v2.5",     "contextWindow": 131072 },
    { "upstreamId": "mimo-v2.5-pro", "contextWindow": 131072 },
    { "upstreamId": "minimax-m2.5",  "contextWindow": 131072 },
    { "upstreamId": "minimax-m2.7",  "contextWindow": 131072 },
    { "upstreamId": "hy3",           "contextWindow": 131072 },
    ...
  ]
}
```

With nothing advertised, `src/user-models.mjs` falls back:

```js
export const DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW = 131072;
export const DEFAULT_AUTO_COMPACT   = 110000;
```

and the merged catalog then ships that:

```
$ jq '.models[] | select(.slug|test("mimo-v2.5|minimax-m2|hy3")) | {slug, context_window, auto_compact_token_limit}' merged-models.json
{ "slug": "opencode-go/mimo-v2.5",             "context_window": 131072, "auto_compact_token_limit": 110000 }
{ "slug": "opencode-go/mimo-v2.5-pro",         "context_window": 131072, "auto_compact_token_limit": 110000 }
{ "slug": "opencode-go-messages/minimax-m2.7", "context_window": 131072, "auto_compact_token_limit": 110000 }
{ "slug": "opencode-go-messages/minimax-m2.5", "context_window": 131072, "auto_compact_token_limit": 110000 }
{ "slug": "opencode-go/hy3",                   "context_window": 131072, "auto_compact_token_limit": 110000 }
```

The route clearly accepts far more than 131K in practice — `router.log` on this install shows successful (`status=200`) `opencode-go/mimo-v2.5` turns with `cached_tokens` up to ~180,000, i.e. Codex was already sending prompts past the declared window and the provider served them.

## Impact

`auto_compact_token_limit = 110000` means a coding session on `mimo-v2.5` compacts at ~110K tokens and keeps compacting from there, even though the model has ~1M of headroom. It makes these routes noticeably worse for long agentic work than the `glm-5.3` / `deepseek-v4` routes on the same subscription.

## Suggested fix

Bump `contextWindow` (and `autoCompact` to ~85% of it) in the checked-in configs, same as the `glm-5.3` correction:

| File | `contextWindow` | `autoCompact` |
| --- | --- | --- |

title: Standard signed-in mode cannot disable Codex Responses WebSockets on routed openai_base_url
body:
## Summary

Codex Desktop `26.825.4187.0` bundles `codex-cli 0.150.0-alpha.12.2`. In the router's standard signed-in Codex mode, `config.toml` keeps the built-in `openai` provider selected and points root `openai_base_url` at the local router. Current Codex still defines that built-in provider with `supports_websockets = true`.

The router, however, deliberately does not implement Responses-over-WebSocket and rejects HTTP upgrades with `426 Upgrade Required`.

Result: Codex currently believes the active provider supports Responses WebSockets while its configured base URL points at an endpoint that intentionally does not. `codex doctor --json` reproduces this locally as:

- `network.websocket_reachability`: warning
- summary: `Responses WebSocket failed; HTTPS fallback may still work`
- handshake: HTTP 426

No capability-bearing router URL is included here.

## Why existing `supports_websockets = false` handling does not solve standard mode

`src/config-manager.mjs` already writes `supports_websockets = false` for the router-owned explicit provider tables used by the external/login-free/signed-provider paths.

Standard signed-in mode is intentionally different: it preserves the user's native `model_provider` / OpenAI login behavior and uses the root `openai_base_url` override. Codex's built-in provider IDs cannot be overridden through `model_providers`, so there is nowhere for the router to declare `supports_websockets = false` while retaining that architecture.

The older local branch `fix/external-provider-disable-websockets` addressed explicit external provider tables; current upstream already contains that flag on those paths and the old branch does not fix this standard-mode case.

## Why not switch standard mode to a custom provider

That would be a much broader behavior change. This repository explicitly preserves `model_provider` outside the user-enabled login-free mode. Taking it over merely to express `supports_websockets = false` would weaken an existing Codex safety/compatibility boundary and needs an intentional architecture decision, not a small compatibility patch.

## Upstream Codex evidence

Current OpenAI Codex source still creates the built-in `openai` provider with `supports_websockets: true`, including when `openai_base_url` supplies its base URL. Current Codex issues also document ordinary-turn stalls/retries when WebSocket transport fails and the built-in provider cannot be opted out of without switching to a custom provider (for example openai/codex#38638 and related reports).

In this local reproduction the router's 426 response is immediate, so I did not spend provider quota merely to measure the ordinary-turn delay. The compatibility mismatch itself is deterministic from the provider metadata plus the router's upgrade handler, and `codex doctor` reproduces the failed handshake without a model call.

## Possible resolutions

This likely needs one of these, in preference order:

1. **Upstream Codex:** when `openai_base_url` overrides the built-in OpenAI endpoint, provide a supported way to override/disable `supports_websockets`, or default an overridden endpoint to HTTP unless WebSocket support is explicitly known.
2. **Router:** implement Responses WebSocket transport/proxying with the same authentication, routing, failover, usage, retry, and protocol-safety boundaries as the HTTP path. This is substantial and should not be faked by returning a successful upgrade without full semantics.
3. **Router architecture change:** move standard signed-in operation to a router-owned provider with `requires_openai_auth = true` and `supports_websockets = false`, but only if all native/routed behavior and the existing `model_provider` preservation contract are deliberately reworked and tested.

## Acceptance criteria

- Standard signed-in router mode no longer advertises/causes a WebSocket attempt against an endpoint that cannot serve it; **or** the router fully supports that transport.
- Native ChatGPT authentication and native-model routing remain intact.
- Normal mode does not silently take over unrelated `model_provider`/`model` choices unless that architectural contract is explicitly changed.
- No capability-bearing managed URL is logged during connection/fallback diagnostics.
- Add regression coverage for the standard `openai_base_url` path, not only explicit router-owned provider tables.

title: Add a supported transactional rotation path for the local router caller capability
body:
## Problem

The router's caller key is a local capability and can be embedded into client-facing managed URLs. The repository correctly treats it as sensitive and keeps it out of normal status/support output, but there is currently no supported way to rotate it after suspected exposure.

`src/secret.mjs` exposes only `ensure|status`; `ensure` deliberately preserves an existing valid caller secret. The practical recovery path today would therefore require manual mutation/removal of the caller-secret file followed by regeneration, client republishing, and a service restart. That is too easy to perform incompletely and can strand running clients on the old capability.

This surfaced during Windows/Codex compatibility maintenance where an existing capability was found in historical local client session artifacts. The artifact contents and capability are intentionally not included here. The important repository-level gap is simply that exposure cannot be remediated through a supported transaction.

## Desired behavior

Provide an explicit operator action such as `model-router codex caller-key rotate` (exact naming flexible) that:

1. Generates a fresh caller capability without printing it.
2. Republishes every installed client target that embeds/references the caller capability (Codex, DSH, Gemini as applicable), preserving unrelated user configuration.
3. Rebuilds/restarts the managed router service so the new capability is authoritative.
4. Verifies health and that the old capability is rejected before reporting success.
5. Rolls back coherently if republishing/service activation fails, rather than leaving clients and service on different keys.
6. Preserves the internal service key unless that key is also explicitly being rotated.
7. Never writes either old or new capability to logs, command arguments, support bundles, or terminal output.
8. Clearly warns that already-running clients/tasks may need to be restarted/reopened because they can cache the previous managed URL.

## Why this should be explicit

Rotation is consequential and should not happen during ordinary install/update/doctor. A stable caller capability prevents needless client churn. But once an operator has reason to consider it exposed, there should be a first-class recovery operation instead of undocumented file deletion.

## Suggested coverage

- Successful rotation updates service + all installed client surfaces atomically enough that they agree on the new key.
- Old capability is rejected after success.
- New capability is accepted.
- Failure during client republish/service install restores the previous usable state.
- No capability appears in stdout/stderr or serialized diagnostics.
- Windows file ACL remains current-user-only after rotation.
- Running-client warning is emitted without terminating Codex automatically.

title: LiteLLM custom-tool streams can terminate before response.completed
body:
## Summary

A routed Responses stream can terminate after a native `custom_tool_call` has already been relayed, leaving Codex with:

```text
stream disconnected before completion: stream closed before response.completed
```

This is reproducible with the pinned LiteLLM 1.96 custom-tool bridge and was observed on `zai-coding/glm-5.3` with max reasoning effort. It is not an upstream 429/EOF failure: the gateway has already returned HTTP 200 and the router has started relaying bytes.

## Root cause

LiteLLM 1.96 converts Responses `type: "custom"` tools into Chat Completions functions with a required `content` string property. On the return stream it can reconstruct the output item as native `custom_tool_call`, but still emit legacy:

- `response.function_call_arguments.delta`
- `response.function_call_arguments.done`

whose JSON wrapper is `{"content":"..."}`.

`NamespaceToolCallTransform` correctly recognizes the already-native `custom_tool_call` opening, but currently decodes every later legacy function-argument event using codex-router's own custom-function wrapper contract, `{"input":"..."}`. The delta is therefore suppressed as undecodable and the terminal arguments fail with:

```text
ERR_NAMESPACE_RELAY_COMMITTED_STREAM
invalid custom tool arguments done
```

Because semantic output has already been committed, the router must fail closed rather than retry/fail over or pass inconsistent lifecycle bytes through. The client then sees EOF before `response.completed` and may retry the sampling request.

## Expected behavior

When the source opening itself is already native `custom_tool_call`, legacy function-argument events from the pinned LiteLLM bridge should decode the `content` property and be relayed as native `response.custom_tool_call_input.*` events. Router-bridged custom functions must continue using `input`, and streamed/final/close payload disagreement must continue to fail closed.

## Deterministic reproduction

A synthetic SSE sequence is sufficient; no provider quota is required:

1. `response.output_item.added` with a native `custom_tool_call`
2. `response.function_call_arguments.delta` carrying chunks of `{"content":"..."}`
3. `response.function_call_arguments.done` carrying the same JSON
4. `response.output_item.done` with the same raw custom input
5. `response.completed`

On current main, step 3 raises the exact committed-stream error above. A focused regression plus a full router fixture with a mock gateway can exercise the repair without live model calls.

body:
Commandcode advertises a 98% cache hit via its own CLI. Wondering if this is a good idea?

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
When using `codex-router` to bridge Codex with provider endpoints like Command Code, requests bypass the client-side harness optimizations offered by the `commandcode` CLI (such as AST context filtering, native tool-call repairs, and prompt caching). This leads to significantly higher token consumption against provider credit pools compared to running the CLI natively.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
An optional adapter or execution backend in `codex-router` that can shell out tasks directly to an installed local CLI binary (e.g., `commandcode`) for tool execution and context gathering, rather than acting strictly as a raw HTTP API proxy.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
- Running standard raw HTTP routing (works for billing, but loses all harness token savings).
- Manually invoking `commandcode` CLI via terminal calls within Codex custom skills.

**Additional context**
This would allow users to keep the Codex interface while benefiting from CLI-level harness optimizations and higher prompt cache hit rates on providers that utilize CLI-side context management.

title: fix(macOS): keep the tray panel anchored to the status item
body:
## Summary

- Follow-up to #75: the reserved-width status label shipped, but the panel still jumped between the top-left and bottom-right of the screen.
- Replace `MenuBarExtra(.window)` with one AppKit `NSStatusItem` and a fixed-size `NSPanel`.
- Place that panel from the status-item window's screen frame, then clamp it to `visibleFrame`.

## Root cause

`MenuBarExtra(.window)` still owns the status item. RouterStore publications redraw `StatusItemLabel`, SwiftUI remeasures the extra, and macOS re-anchors the panel from that rect. When the rect is invalid or screen-sized, AppKit clamps the window to opposite screen corners.

#75 reserved 180pt on the SwiftUI label. That does not set `NSStatusItem.length`, so the system anchor kept moving. The Dynamic Island and desktop panel use separate fixed-position windows and are not involved. Island mode was `off` in the reproduction.

## Validation

- `swift build -c release --package-path apps/macos/ModelRouterTray`
- Installed the release binary into `~/Applications/Model Router.app` and relaunched it
- Idle `ModelRouterTray` CPU dropped from ~45% to under 1%
- `node --test --test-name-pattern 'status item keeps native square' test/tray-rebuild.test.mjs`

`swift test` for `ModelRouterTrayTests` needs the Swift Testing module from Xcode; this checkout only has Command Line Tools, so those tests were not run here. `TrayPanelPlacementTests` covers left-edge clamp, dock lift, and the screen that contains the extra.

## Manual smoke test

1. Launch the tray and open the menu-bar panel (Settings is enough).
2. Keep it open while activity transitions between idle, one active request, concurrent requests, and idle.
3. Confirm the panel stays under the status item and that the left-side labels are not clipped against the screen edge.

title: Generic OpenAI-compatible providers miss the per-provider compat shims (web_search + tool_choice) — every turn 400s against a strict gateway (api.b.ai)
body:
## Summary

Runtime generic OpenAI-compatible providers (`providers generic add`, shipped in v0.5.1 via #496/#491) route end-to-end, but they do **not** receive the per-provider request/payload compatibility shims that checked-in named providers get in `src/api-forwarder.mjs` (the `provider.id === "fireworks"` / `"meta"` / `isGeminiProvider(provider)` branches in `normalizeBody`).

For a strict upstream this makes the generic route unusable rather than degraded. With `https://api.b.ai/v1` (an OpenAI-compatible aggregator) I hit two independent hard-400s, each on **every turn**:

### 1. Hosted web search → 400 on every turn

```
HTTP 400: The current model does not support web search. (request id: 2026...c955d5687TLT7vCK)
{'type': 'api_error', 'code': 'invalid_request'}
```

`src/config-manager.mjs` writes `supports_standalone_web_search = true` into the managed `[model_providers.codex-router]` block unconditionally, so Codex attaches the hosted search tool / `web_search_options` to every turn (same "declared whenever enabled, not only when the model searches" behavior as the Meta case in #286). `normalizeBody` only strips `web_search_options` for `provider.id === "fireworks"` and Gemini; a generic provider gets it forwarded and b.ai rejects the whole request.

The routed model's catalog entry already has `supports_search_tool: false` (identical to `opencode-go/glm-5.3-flash`), but that per-model gate does not prevent the tool being sent here.

### 2. `tool_choice` in "thinking mode" → 400

```
HTTP 400: The request is invalid: Thinking mode does not support this tool_choice. (code 400001)
HTTP 400: The tool_choice parameter does not support being set to required or object in thinking mode. (invalid_parameter_error)
```

Hit `bai/deepseek-v4-flash` and `bai/qwen3.8-flash` whenever Codex sends `tool_choice: "required"` (or an object). `src/api-forwarder.mjs` already has the exact repair for this under the `deepseek-thinking` and `qwen-plan` request profiles (`payload.tool_choice = "auto"`), but those profiles are not in `CURATABLE_REQUEST_PROFILES`, so a **generic** model cannot select them (`model-registry.mjs`: "generic model may use only an explicitly curatable requestProfile"). Only `auto-tool-choice` and `codex-encrypted-schema` are curatable.

## Repro

```sh
codex-router providers generic add bai --name "B.AI" --base-url https://api.b.ai/v1 --adapter openai-chat
codex-router providers generic credential bai set        # any api.b.ai key
codex-router curate-models bai --models glm-5.3-flash,deepseek-v4-flash --apply
# quit + reopen Codex, select bai/glm-5.3-flash, send any message
#   -> 400 "The current model does not support web search"
# select bai/deepseek-v4-flash, ask for something that forces a tool call
#   -> 400 "Thinking mode does not support this tool_choice"
```

## Local workarounds currently applied

- `user-models.json`: added `"requestProfile": "auto-tool-choice"` to each `bai/*` entry — fixes (2), verified (deepseek + qwen tool-calling PASS).
- `src/api-forwarder.mjs`: after the fireworks line, added
  ```js
  if (provider.generic === true) {
    delete payload.web_search_options;
    if (Array.isArray(payload.tools)) {
      payload.tools = payload.tools.filter(
        (t) => t?.type !== "web_search" && t?.type !== "web_search_preview",
      );
    }
  }
  ```
  — fixes (1), but this is a checked-in file so it's discarded on `update`.

## Suggested direction

- Honor the routed model's `supports_search_tool: false` by not forwarding `web_search_options` / the hosted `web_search` tool for that route (applies to any provider, not just generic).
- And/or a generic-provider-scoped payload shim hook in `normalizeBody`, or widening which request profiles are curatable for generic models (at least the tool_choice-softening ones), so operators of strict OpenAI-compatible gateways don't have to carry a source patch.

## Environment

- codex-router `v0.5.1` (`b370228`, git checkout, Windows install)
- Codex `v0.151.0`, provider `codex-router` (`http://127.0.0.1:4202/v1`, `wire_api = "responses"`)
- Node `22.23.2`, Windows 11

title: fix: avoid repeated routed compaction prefixes
body:
## Summary

- configure Codex to count only post-prefix growth toward automatic compaction while routing is enabled
- preserve an explicit user-owned `model_auto_compact_token_limit_scope` value
- probe the installed Codex binary before writing the newer scope key, so older builds keep loading normally
- remove the router-owned value again during the normal disable lifecycle

## Problem

A routed compaction does not begin with an empty context. Codex carries a large stable prefix into the next compaction window, including system/developer instructions, tool schemas, and the router's rendered checkpoint.

With Codex's default `total` scope, that carried prefix is charged against `model_auto_compact_token_limit` again. On models whose routed session already has a large fixed prefix, the next window can therefore reach the threshold after little or no meaningful new work. In practice this presents as an agent compacting after nearly every round and failing to make sustained progress.

Codex now exposes `model_auto_compact_token_limit_scope = "body_after_prefix"` for this window shape. Its context-window implementation snapshots the carried prefill and charges only subsequent growth against the configured automatic-compaction limit, while the full context-window safety check remains active:

- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/core/src/session/context_window.rs
- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/protocol/src/config_types.rs

## Implementation

When the router enables its managed Codex configuration, it now writes:

```toml
model_auto_compact_token_limit_scope = "body_after_prefix"
```

The setting lives inside the existing `codex-router-managed` root block, so the established enable/disable lifecycle owns it.

Two guardrails keep the change conservative:

1. If the user already configured any scope explicitly, the router leaves that value unchanged.
2. The config manager asks the installed Codex binary to parse a minimal probe config before adding the key. A build that reports a configuration-load error, cannot be probed, or is not installed does not receive the managed setting.

This PR does not change model context windows, per-model compaction limits, checkpoint contents, or provider request payloads.

## Verification

Focused config-manager tests (3 passed, 0 failed):

- managed installs add `body_after_prefix` and remove it on disable
- an explicit user-owned `total` scope survives enable and disable unchanged
- a simulated older Codex build that rejects the key does not receive it

Also checked:

- branch rebased onto current `main`
- `git diff --check`
- PR diff contains only `src/config-manager.mjs` and `test/config-manager.test.mjs`

Per the repository testing policy, no broad full-suite run was performed for this isolated config-manager change.
