title: fix: strip unsupported Console Go search options
body:
## Summary

- remove `web_search_options` from ordinary and compaction requests routed to the fixed `opencode-go` Chat Completions provider
- enforce the same provider boundary in the API forwarder before Console Go receives the upstream request
- preserve the option for providers that accept it and retain all other search/tool payload fields
- document the compatibility repair in the Unreleased changelog

## Reproduction

Selecting `opencode-go/glm-5.3` in Codex can fail before generation with:

```text
opencode rejected the request for GLM-5.3 (opencode Go).
HTTP 400: Error from provider (Console Go): Upstream request failed:
[invalid_request_error] Extra inputs are not permitted,
field: 'web_search_options'
```

Codex can attach `web_search_options` to a Responses request even when the selected routed model does not advertise hosted search. LiteLLM translates the routed request to Chat Completions, and Console Go forwards the unsupported OpenAI extension to its strict model backend instead of ignoring it. The backend rejects the complete turn.

## Relationship to #540

This branch is based on current `main` at `43deff5` and preserves #540's runtime-generic search-capability contract unchanged.

#540 strips unadvertised hosted-search artifacts for **runtime-generic** providers. OpenCode Go is a fixed registry provider (`provider.generic !== true`), so it intentionally bypasses that generic compatibility path. On current `main`, its `web_search_options` still reaches both the gateway request and the downstream API forwarder.

This PR adds the narrower fixed-provider repair at the two existing Fireworks compatibility boundaries rather than broadening or weakening #540.

## Implementation

At the outer router boundary, `rejectsWebSearchOptions(route)` identifies only:

- `fireworks` (existing behavior)
- `opencode-go` (new measured behavior)

The field is removed from both ordinary routed turns and `/responses/compact` requests before serialization. The latter matters because compaction re-enters the same provider with the caller payload and can otherwise fail on an option unrelated to summarization.

The API forwarder repeats the provider-scoped removal immediately before sending OpenCode Go Chat Completions upstream. This keeps direct/internal forwarder traffic safe and follows the existing Fireworks defense-in-depth pattern.

The repair deliberately does **not**:

- remove `web_search` function tools or tool results
- change standalone/client-side search capability
- alter `include`, `tools`, or `tool_choice`
- affect OpenCode Responses or Messages variants
- strip the option from compatible providers

## Verification

Red/green reproduction was established for both boundaries: before the production change, the focused router and API-forwarder tests received the original `{ search_context_size: "medium" }`; after the change, both receive no `web_search_options`.

Fresh verification on exact head `9ef8907`:

- `npm run check` — syntax and v2-agent application checks passed
- focused routing tests — 5 passed, 0 failed:
  - current-main generic capability enforcement from #540 remains intact
  - OpenCode Go API forwarder strips the unsupported option
  - OpenCode Go ordinary and compaction requests strip the option
  - Fireworks retains its existing repair
  - Xiaomi MiMo retains the option as a compatible-provider counterexample
- `git diff --check`

Per the repository testing policy, no broad full-suite run was performed for this isolated provider-compatibility change. No live provider/quota request was made; deterministic upstream fixtures reproduce the exact rejected field without spending account quota.

title: [Bug]: Codex picker sorts by colliding priority, so vendor grouping never appears
body:
## What happened?

Codex Desktop's model picker interleaves native GPT models with routed providers instead of keeping vendor groups together.

On a signed-in Codex install with `grok-oauth` and `deepseek` enabled, the published catalog already groups by vendor in array order (`native`, then `deepseek`, then `grok-oauth`). Codex does not use that array order. It sorts the visible picker by each entry's `priority`. Routed models reuse the same low integers as native GPT models, so they land in the middle of the GPT list.

Observed on `0.5.1` (`43deff51bf07454cd6afffc252a4d65a465a16b1`):

| slug | priority | display name |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `gpt-5.6-sol` | 1 | GPT-5.6-Sol |
| `grok-oauth/grok-4.6` | 1 | Grok 4.6 (OAuth) |
| `gpt-5.6-terra` | 2 | GPT-5.6-Terra |
| `grok-oauth/grok-4.5` | 2 | Grok 4.5 (OAuth) |
| `gpt-5.6-luna` | 3 | GPT-5.6-Luna |
| `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` | 6 | DeepSeek V4 Flash (API) |
| `gpt-5.5` | 7 | GPT-5.5 |
| `deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro` | 7 | DeepSeek V4 Pro (API) |

Expected: native GPT models stay together, then DeepSeek, then Grok, matching `pickerProviderGroup()` / `sortCatalogModels()` in `src/catalog.mjs`.

This is not a request to hide models, and it is not a request to set every routed model to `nativeMax + 1`. `routedPickerPriorities()` already documents why that would crowd certified native v2 spawn-agent overrides out of Codex's small priority-ordered window, and `test/catalog.test.mjs` locks that choice in: the merged array may be grouped, but each model's `priority` must stay as authored.

The current grouping therefore only reorders `merged-models.json`. The Codex picker still renders the colliding integers.

A durable fix would keep spawn-agent overrides in a small low-priority subset, while giving the picker contiguous vendor bands that Codex actually reads. One way is a dual numbering scheme: keep a handful of spawn-visible low priorities, and assign the remaining listed models to provider ranges that do not collide with native GPT. Hiding unused models locally is only a workaround.

## Which app do you route through?

Codex

## Platform

macOS

## Doctor output or support bundle

Not attached. This reproduces from the published catalog priorities on a current Git checkout (`codex-router update check` reports `updateAvailable: false`). No credentials, prompts, or managed base URL are included.

title: Responses WebSocket repeats successful native requests when internal 200 response is non-streaming
body:
## Summary

On current main, the authenticated Responses WebSocket adapter can reject successful native responses as:

```
unexpected status 502 Bad Gateway:
The internal Responses endpoint returned a non-streaming response.
```

Codex then retries the same paid/native request repeatedly. This also appears in tasks using routed external models because Codex makes a native Luna request for task-title generation.

## Environment

- Windows 11
- Codex desktop bundled CLI
- Codex Router source: `4d5ca178ffdf3a0e6def80cdc0957ab5c4da93a1`
- Router health/version: `0.5.1`
- Routing mode: standard signed-in mode; active provider `openai`
- Router, gateway, and provider health were ready
- Repository was clean and matched current `main`

## Controlled reproduction

Three fresh tasks were run sequentially while one unrelated task was also active.

### Native Sol task

Prompt:

```
Reply exactly SOL-WS-TEST
```

The usage log recorded the same native request **7 times**:

- model: `gpt-5.6-sol`
- provider: `openai`
- identical `inputTokens: 24402`
- identical `outputTokens: 9`
- all seven upstream statuses: `200`
- first event: `2026-08-31T14:06:27Z`
- last event: `2026-08-31T14:06:54Z`

The task eventually displayed the expected response after the reconnect cycle.

### Routed DeepSeek task

Prompt:

```
Reply exactly DS-WS-TEST
```

The external request ran once and succeeded:

- model: `genspark/deepseek-v4-flash`
- provider: `genspark`
- status: `200`
- duration: about 34 seconds

At the same time, the hidden native Luna/title request repeated seven times.

### Routed Gemini task

Prompt:

```
Reply exactly GEM-WS-TEST
```

The external request ran once and succeeded:

- model: `antigravity2api/gemini-3.7-flash`
- provider: `antigravity2api`
- status: `200`
- duration: about 12 seconds

Again, the native Luna/title request repeated during task creation.

Across the three fresh tasks, the same Luna title-generation shape (`inputTokens: 12017`, normally `outputTokens: 33`) was recorded 20 times, all with upstream status 200.

The unrelated active task overlapped with these trials, but the external DeepSeek and Gemini requests still completed on their first upstream attempt. This does not look concurrency-dependent.

## Code path

The displayed error is emitted by `src/responses-websocket.mjs` when the internal HTTP Responses hop returns `200 OK` without a `Content-Type` containing `text/event-stream`.

The adapter preserves `stream: true` while reconstructing `fullRequest`, so these are successful internal/native executions whose response media type fails the WebSocket adapter's strict check. The adapter drains and discards the body, returns a WebSocket 502, and Codex retries the entire request.

## Important observations

- This is not automatic compaction. In the longer observed task, compaction started only after the reconnect sequence had completed.
- It is not a provider rejection: the duplicated native usage events all report upstream status 200 and contain output usage.
- It is not a dead router: health remained ready.
- The WebSocket adapter was added after the v0.5.1 tag, while the affected checkout is current main.

## Expected behavior

A successful internal Responses result should not cause the entire inference to be repeated seven times solely because its response is non-SSE.

A safe fix could do one of the following:

1. normalize a valid bounded non-streaming Responses JSON result into the WebSocket event contract;
2. prevent accepting the WebSocket upgrade when the internal path cannot guarantee SSE, allowing Codex's HTTP fallback;
3. otherwise fail before inference is executed, so a protocol mismatch never duplicates a completed model request.

It would also help to record the rejected internal response media type (not its body) so this path is diagnosable without exposing prompt or response content.

title: [Bug]: Windows scheduled task exits 1 and reports existing start.mjs as MODULE_NOT_FOUND
body:
### What happened?

On a fresh Windows installation, the Control Center installed successfully but initially reported:

`Codex Router source root could not be located.`

Running the current `install.ps1` created the managed checkout, dependencies, state manifest, Codex integration, and the `Codex Router` scheduled task. The installation then failed at the background-service step because the scheduled task exited immediately with result `1`.

The generated task launched:

`wscript.exe //B //NoLogo C:\Users\<user>\.codex\codex-router\start-codex-router-hidden.vbs`

The router log repeatedly reported:

```text
Error: Cannot find module 'C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\codex-router\src\start.mjs'
code: 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND'
```

However, that file exists and can be read. Running the generated `start-codex-router.cmd` from an elevated interactive shell starts all four listeners successfully, and `http://127.0.0.1:4202/health` returns:

```json
{"ok":true,"service":"codex-router","version":"0.5.1","degraded":[]}
```

Changing only the scheduled-task action from the generated VBS wrapper to direct `cmd.exe /D /C ...start-codex-router.cmd` did not resolve it; the task still exited with result `1` and the same `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` message. The generated task principal used the current user, `Interactive` logon, and `Limited` run level.

### Expected behavior

The Windows installer should create a scheduled task that can read and execute the managed checkout under `%LOCALAPPDATA%` and bring the router healthy without requiring an elevated interactive launch.

If Windows permissions or task-token restrictions prevent that, the installer/doctor should identify the cause and provide a targeted recovery message instead of reporting that the existing module cannot be found.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install the Windows Control Center package.
2. Run the current `install.ps1` for the Codex target with the default managed checkout at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\codex-router`.
3. Observe that dependencies, generated state, and the scheduled task are created.
4. Observe installer failure: `Background-service installation failed.`
5. Query the `Codex Router` task and observe `LastTaskResult=1`.
6. Inspect `router.log` and observe `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for the existing `src\start.mjs`.
7. Run the generated launcher from an elevated interactive shell and observe that the router becomes healthy.

### Environment

- App target: Codex Desktop
- Platform: Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26100 (build 26100)
- Node.js: 24.14.0
- Control Center/router version shown by health endpoint: 0.5.1
- Managed checkout commit: `4d5ca17`
- Checkout: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\codex-router`
- State directory: `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\codex-router`

No provider credentials, managed capability URLs, or authentication material are included.

title: fix: preserve orphan Codex app tool outputs during routed replay
body:
## Problem

Codex app-server can persist a standalone native app-tool result without the originating call, for example a `function_call_output` in the `codex_app` namespace whose `call_id` is null.

When that history is replayed through a routed Responses provider, the strict provider adapter correctly rejects the unpaired result. The same history can be replayed during `/responses/compact`, so the rejection surfaces as `invalid_responses_request` (and may be wrapped by a gateway as `provider_api_proxy_error`), interrupting ordinary turns or automatic compaction.

## Fix

- Recover only named `codex_app` outputs that have a defined result and a missing or empty `call_id`.
- Preserve those results as tagged, readable history at the final provider boundary.
- Do not synthesize a `call_id` and do not relax strict Responses validation; unrelated malformed lifecycle items still fail closed.
- Leave well-formed `function_call` / `function_call_output` pairs unchanged.
- Normalize after compaction analysis so the original record remains classified as a tool result rather than a user requirement.

## Tests

- `node --test test/routing.test.mjs test/openai-adapters.test.mjs test/compaction-checkpoint.test.mjs` (144 passed)
- `npm run check`

The regression test covers both `/responses` and `/responses/compact`, verifies paired tool results remain unchanged, and verifies compaction evidence still classifies the orphan record as `tool_result`.

title: fix: preserve completed Responses WebSocket results
[Bug]: Windows model-router.ps1 adds an empty trailing argument for zero-argument subcommands
body:
## What happened?

On Windows, the convenience wrapper rejects otherwise valid zero-argument commands such as:

```powershell
.\model-router.ps1 codex start
```

with:

```text
Usage: codex-router.ps1 start [--foreground].
```

The direct launcher works:

```powershell
.\codex-router.ps1 start
```

## Root cause

`model-router.ps1` declares the remainder as:

```powershell
[Parameter(ValueFromRemainingArguments = $true)]
[string[]]$CommandArguments
```

When there are no remaining arguments, PowerShell binds `$CommandArguments` as `$null`. Splatting that null value into the child invocation:

```powershell
& (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "codex-router.ps1") $Command @CommandArguments
```

contributes one empty positional argument.

An isolated child-wrapper probe receives:

```text
ARG_COUNT=2
ARG_0=<start>
ARG_1=<>
```

instead of only `start`. `codex-router.ps1` correctly treats that extra argument as invalid because `start` accepts either zero arguments or exactly `--foreground`.

## Expected behavior

The wrapper should forward exactly the arguments supplied by the caller. With no remainder, the child should receive only the subcommand itself.

## Proposed fix

Normalize only the absent remainder before splatting:

```powershell
if ($null -eq $CommandArguments) { $CommandArguments = @() }
```

This preserves non-empty argument forwarding unchanged.

## Verification

A Windows regression fixture copies `model-router.ps1`, replaces the child with a harmless argument-reporting stub, and proves `codex start` reaches the child as exactly one argument. Existing one-argument and multi-argument wrapper tests remain green.

No router service, Codex Desktop process, credential, or provider request is needed to reproduce this.

Responses WebSocket continuation can orphan custom tool outputs after a successful call
body:
## Summary

The authenticated Responses WebSocket adapter can reconstruct the next turn with a `custom_tool_call_output` whose matching completed custom-tool call has been replaced by a conflicting/incomplete terminal snapshot item. The native Responses backend then rejects the next turn with:

```text
No tool call found for custom tool call output with call_id ...
```

This is distinct from #546's non-SSE/JSON 502 path, although both occur in `src/responses-websocket.mjs` and are fixed by #551.

## Observed behavior

Environment:

- Windows 11
- Codex Desktop `26.825.6671.0`
- bundled CLI `0.151.0-alpha.7.2`
- codex-router `0.5.1`
- native GPT-5.6 Luna turn through the OpenAI path

The persisted Codex transcript contained a valid sequence:

```text
custom_tool_call
  name = exec
  call_id = <same id>
  status = completed

custom_tool_call_output
  call_id = <same id>
```

The tool itself executed successfully. The following model request returned HTTP 400 saying no tool call existed for that output.

A scan of recent persisted sessions found no orphan stored tool outputs, so the persisted Codex history was not corrupted. The mismatch occurs in transient WebSocket continuation reconstruction.

## Root cause

The adapter collects authoritative completed items from `response.output_item.done`, but when `response.completed` arrives it previously preferred `response.completed.output` wholesale whenever that field was an array:

```js
const output = Array.isArray(completed.output) ? completed.output : outputItems;
```

If the stream emits a complete item such as:

```json
{"type":"custom_tool_call","call_id":"call_...","name":"exec","input":"..."}
```

while the terminal snapshot contains a conflicting/incomplete representation for the same call, such as:

```json
{"type":"function_call","call_id":"call_...","name":"exec"}
```

the adapter caches the terminal representation and discards the complete streamed one. On the incremental follow-up, the reconstructed request becomes effectively:

```text
function_call(call_...)
custom_tool_call_output(call_...)
```

which violates the Responses custom-tool pairing contract.

## Deterministic reproduction

A two-turn mock regression now reproduces this without provider usage:

1. first internal response streams a completed `custom_tool_call` in `response.output_item.done`;
2. its terminal `response.completed.output` contains a conflicting incomplete `function_call` with the same `call_id`;
3. second WebSocket request supplies the matching `custom_tool_call_output` using `previous_response_id`.

Before the fix, the second internal request contains the wrong `function_call` and the pairing assertion fails.

## Expected behavior

Continuation state should preserve the complete streamed output item when a terminal snapshot conflicts with or omits it. Terminal-only items should still be retained.

## Fix / verification

PR #551 reconciles streamed completed items with `response.completed.output` by stable `call_id`/item `id` instead of replacing the streamed set wholesale.

Verified locally on Windows:

- focused regression: RED before / GREEN after;
- `test/responses-websocket.test.mjs`: 32 passed;
- adjacent namespace/routing suites: 237 passed;
- `npm run check`: passed;
- router-only reload healthy;
- the originally failing Codex thread subsequently completed 9 additional custom-tool call/output pairs with zero repeated pairing/502 errors.

No provider inference was generated solely for the regression test.

title: fix: cool down a provider that named its reset in the body
body:
## Problem

Z.ai's GLM Coding Plan refuses an exhausted window with `429` code `1308`:

> Usage limit reached for 5 hour. Your limit will reset at 2026-09-01 21:32:15

It sends **no `Retry-After` header** — the window is stated in the body. Cooldowns
were derived from that header alone, so nothing was ever recorded and
`provider-cooldowns.json` stayed `{}`. Every turn re-attempted the exhausted
model, paid the 429, and failed over again.

Observed in one live router log: **225 quota refusals against a single window**,
one of them stalling a turn for **305 seconds** against a 4.7s upstream response.

## Change

`classifyRoutedFailure` now falls back to a reset time the provider stated in its
own refusal body when no `Retry-After` is present. This stays inside the AGENTS.md
rule that *"a cooldown is only ever a window the provider itself named"* — the
source is the provider's own sentence, not a guess.

### The zoneless stamp

The stamp names no timezone, and the two ways of getting that wrong are not
symmetric:

- **Waking early** costs one extra refusal, and the window is re-recorded.
- **Waking late** withholds a model the operator chose and is paying for.

Reading it as the host's local time does the second thing to every operator whose
clock does not match the plan's — most of a day out at the extremes, clamped to
the six-hour cap, against a reset that may be minutes away.

So the stamp resolves to the **earliest instant any real UTC offset allows that
has not already passed**. The true reset is always one of those candidates, so a
recorded window can never outlast it. This also makes the reading independent of
the host's timezone.

### Other guards

- `Retry-After` still wins when both are present.
- The match is narrow: only a wall-clock stamp directly after `reset at`, so
  prose merely mentioning a reset never becomes a window.
- A stamp no offset can place ahead records nothing.
- The same six-hour `MAX_COOLDOWN_MS` cap as every other source.

## Effect

The first 429 parks the provider until its stated reset; later turns skip
straight to the fallback. No repeated quota round trips, no multi-minute stall.

## Tests

Six cases in `test/model-failover.test.mjs`, including one asserting a zoneless
stamp can never strand a model across the offset spread. Verified identical under
`TZ=UTC`, `America/Los_Angeles`, `Asia/Shanghai`, `Pacific/Kiritimati` (+14) and
`Asia/Kathmandu` (+5:45).

The existing test asserting that exact Z.ai message produces *no* window is
updated — that was the behavior being fixed. Its stamp is nearly a week out, so
it now covers the cap.

Full suite: 3127 tests, 3107 pass, 0 fail. `npm run check` clean.

title: fix: decompress request bodies off the event loop and refuse oversize zstd frames early
body:
## Problem

#465 reports `router.mjs` intermittently dying on Windows with exit `0xC0000409`
(`STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN`) and no JavaScript stack — always late in a long
session with 100k–200k cached tokens, always immediately after a successful
turn. Every child (LiteLLM gateway, OAuth forwarders) dies with it and the
router stays down.

The reporter's hypothesis points at `decodeBody()`, which inflated every request
body through `zstdDecompressSync` on the event loop. Codex zstd-compresses every
request, and the body grows with the conversation.

## Change

1. **Refuse an oversize frame from its header.** A Zstandard frame declares its
   decompressed size when the encoder knew it (Node's one-shot encoder always
   does). `zstdFrameContentSize()` in `http-utils.mjs` reads only the header —
   it never decodes, so it is safe on untrusted input — and `decodeBody` answers
   413 before any native decoder runs if the declared size exceeds the cap.
2. **Inflate through the asynchronous decoder.** Everything else goes through
   promisified `zstdDecompress` under the same `maxOutputLength`, keeping a
   multi-megabyte inflate off the thread that serves every other request.

gzip, deflate, and brotli are untouched; they are not implicated.

## Honesty about scope

I could not reproduce the crash on macOS, so this is defensive hardening on the
implicated path rather than a confirmed root-cause fix. The issue stays open
pending the WER crash dump the reporter offered.

## Tests

- `test/http-utils-zstd-frame.test.mjs` — 5 cases covering every header layout
  the format allows (1/2/4/8-byte size widths, Single_Segment, dictionary-id
  offset, the 2-byte form's +256), a real encoder's frames at sizes spanning all
  widths, frames that omit the size, non-zstd bytes, every truncation point of a
  header, and the safe-integer clamp.
- `test/routing.test.mjs` — end-to-end: with the decode cap set to 4 KB, a real
  zstd body that inflates to ~200 KB gets **413 with zero upstream requests**, a
  body inside the cap still routes on the async path, and **the router that just
  refused the body is still serving** — which is the actual failure mode in #465.

Full suite: **3407 tests, 3382 pass, 0 real failures, 24 skipped.** The one
failing test (`5-level owner SIGINT cleanup`, a process-tree timing test from
#542) passes 3/3 in isolation and is untouched by this change. `npm run check`
clean.

title: [Bug]: Windows Control Center tray opens multiple PowerShell windows during status refreshes
body:
## What happened

On Windows, the current unified Electron Control Center/tray opens a burst of visible **Windows PowerShell** terminal windows during routine status refreshes. In my setup this is especially noticeable every time I send a message in Codex: several PowerShell windows appear at once, then close one by one.

The router itself remains healthy; this appears isolated to the Control Center/tray child-process path.

Tested on a clean upstream checkout at:

`44029b8729b8166f8a662f5b62883c192bbeb9df`

Working tree was clean and `origin` was `https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router.git`.

## Process trace

A `Win32_ProcessStartTrace` capture showed the visible PowerShell processes are direct children of Control Center command invocations launched by the tray process.

Representative chain:

```text
Codex Router.exe --tray-only
  -> Codex Router.exe <checkout>\src\control.mjs --json
    -> powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "& { & '<checkout>\bin\codex-router.ps1' service status --json }"
      -> node.exe <checkout>\src\service.mjs status --json
```

The same burst included commands for:

```text
codex-router.ps1 service status --json
codex-router.ps1 account status --json
codex-router.ps1 providers status --json
codex-router.ps1 presence status --json
codex-router.ps1 provider-usage --json
```

Eight `powershell.exe` processes were captured in one short burst. The parent/grandparent chain consistently pointed back to:

```text
Codex Router.exe --tray-only
```

No credentials were present in the captured command lines.

## Reproduction

1. Windows 10/11.
2. Use a clean current checkout with the Windows Control Center/tray installed and running.
3. Keep the router backend running normally.
4. Use Codex normally; in my case, sending a message reliably triggers the Control Center status/activity refresh.
5. Multiple visible Windows PowerShell / Windows Terminal windows open and then close.

## Isolation / workaround

I disabled and stopped **only** the `Codex Router Tray` scheduled task:

```text
schtasks.exe /Change /TN "\Codex Router Tray" /DISABLE
schtasks.exe /End /TN "\Codex Router Tray"
```

After that:

- no `Codex Router.exe --tray-only` process remained;
- the main router stayed healthy on `127.0.0.1:4202` (`TcpTestSucceeded: True`);
- Codex/Sol continued working normally;
- sending messages in Codex produced **no PowerShell popups**;
- the Git checkout remained clean.

Re-enabling the tray is therefore the condition associated with the popups; disabling only the tray removes them without affecting routing.

## Expected behavior

Background Control Center/tray status probes should run without creating visible console/terminal windows.

## Possibly related

This looks related in symptom to #208, which previously fixed Windows tray console flashes by using a no-window creation path. #208 is closed, but the current unified Electron Control Center appears to have another Windows child-process path that still launches PowerShell visibly.

It may be worth checking the Windows command runner path that invokes `codex-router.ps1` for Control Center status/account/providers/presence/provider-usage probes and ensuring its PowerShell child is created with the appropriate hidden/no-console flag.

title: [Bug]: Antigravity BYO OAuth client can never pass the live probe — cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com cannot be enabled on an operator's own project
body:
### What happened?

On `44029b8` (v0.5.1), the operator-owned ("BYO") Antigravity OAuth client that
README now *requires* cannot complete the live probe, because
`cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com` is a **private Google API that a normal Cloud
project is not allowed to enable**. The provider is unreachable for anyone
without an allowlisted project, and README does not mention this prerequisite.

Sign-in itself works. The probe fails:

```
$ providers login antigravity-oauth
Google Antigravity OAuth sign-in completed with the operator-owned OAuth client.
The route remains disabled until an explicit live compatibility test succeeds.

$ providers probe antigravity-oauth --live --yes
Antigravity project bootstrap failed (HTTP 403; HTTP 403).
```

The credential record is written correctly (`version: 3`, `managed_by:
codex-router`, client pair + refresh token present), so this is not the
"incompatible older record" path.

Calling `v1internal:loadCodeAssist` directly with the same access token shows
what the two 403s are:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": 403,
    "status": "PERMISSION_DENIED",
    "message": "Cloud Code Private API has not been used in project <PROJECT_NUMBER> before or it is disabled. Enable it by visiting https://console.developers.google.com/apis/api/cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com/overview?project=<PROJECT_NUMBER> then retry.",
    "details": [{ "reason": "SERVICE_DISABLED", "metadata": { "service": "cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com" } }]
  }
}
```

`loadCodeAssist` is billed to the project that owns the calling OAuth client.
With the bundled vendor client (0.5.1) that was Google's own allowlisted
project; with a BYO Desktop client it is the operator's project, which does not
have the private API enabled — and cannot enable it:

```
$ gcloud services enable cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com --project=<PROJECT_ID>
ERROR: (gcloud.services.enable) PERMISSION_DENIED: Permission denied to enable
service [cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com]
- '@type': type.googleapis.com/google.rpc.ErrorInfo
  domain: serviceusage.googleapis.com
  metadata:
    permission: servicemanagement.services.bind
    service: servicemanagement.googleapis.com
  reason: AUTH_PERMISSION_DENIED
```

`servicemanagement.services.bind` is a producer-side permission: only
allowlisted consumer projects may bind `cloudcode-pa`. This was run by the
project **owner**, through gcloud's own first-party client, so no IAM role the
operator can grant themselves changes the outcome. The Cloud Console route is
also a dead end — `cloudcode-pa` has no API Library entry, so
`/apis/api/cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com/overview?project=…` redirects to
`/apis/library/…` and fails to load.

### What I expected

Either:

1. README/INSTALL to state the prerequisite plainly — Antigravity OAuth needs a
   Google Cloud project that is allowlisted for `cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`,
   with instructions on how an operator obtains that (Gemini Code Assist
   licence? Antigravity onboarding? something else?) — and the probe to surface
   `SERVICE_DISABLED` as that specific, actionable message instead of
   `bootstrap failed (HTTP 403; HTTP 403)`; or
2. a documented supported path for operators whose project cannot be
   allowlisted.

Right now the documented flow (create a Desktop client you own → login → probe →
enable) terminates in an unactionable 403 for what I suspect is every user
without a pre-allowlisted project.

### Suggested small fix regardless of the answer

`loadAntigravityProject()` in `src/antigravity-project.mjs` collapses every
attempt into `HTTP <status>` strings, so the response body — which contains
Google's exact reason and the activation URL — is discarded. Surfacing
`error.status` / `error.details[].reason` (at least for 403 `SERVICE_DISABLED`)
would have turned an hour of guessing into one line.

### Which app do you route through?

Codex

### Platform

Windows

### Version

`44029b8` (package version 0.5.1), Node 22.23.2, Windows 11.

Reproduced with a fresh Google OAuth **Desktop app** client created per README
§Antigravity, consent screen in Testing with the account added as a test user
(the Google consent step itself succeeds — `Signed in`).

title: fix(grok-oauth): suppress repeated progress after stream abort
body:
## Why

After a Grok conversation has produced a progress-only stop, a later turn can emit another short progress prefix and then abort upstream. Because that prefix is already committed to the Codex stream, the chat can look stuck in a loop even though the terminal stream error is reported correctly.

This implements the evidence-gated buffering alternative discussed in #295: keep the first affected turn fully live, and change streaming behavior only after the same stable Grok conversation ID has exhibited the progress-only shape.

## What changed

- remember affected conversation IDs in a bounded in-memory set
- on later eligible user turns, buffer only the short visible prefix while keeping headers and preceding reasoning live
- release the prefix for healthy short answers, longer answers, and tool calls
- suppress that prefix when the upstream stream aborts, while preserving the terminal SSE error
- document the behavior and add regression coverage for both the healthy and aborted paths

## Verification

- `npm run check`
- `node --test test/grok-oauth-turn.test.mjs test/grok-oauth-forwarder.test.mjs` — 58 passed
- `npm audit --omit=dev` — 0 vulnerabilities
- autoreview on the final dirty patch — no P0/P1 findings; secret scan clean

The full `npm test` run reported 3,377 passed, 24 skipped, and 7 failures in `test/control-center-harness.test.mjs`. The same 7 failures reproduce on a clean worktree at `origin/main` (`44029b8`), so they are not introduced by this patch.

title: [Bug]: Qwen Plan v1 collaboration calls are returned as pre-flattened names and rejected by Codex Desktop
body:
### What happened?

# [Bug] Qwen Plan v1 collaboration calls are returned as pre-flattened names and rejected by Codex Desktop

## Summary

When Alibaba Model Studio Token Plan models are used through `codex-router`, normal responses, streaming, and ordinary tool calls work, but the affected models cannot spawn native Codex Desktop subagents.

The model returns a function call such as:

```json
{
  "type": "function_call",
  "name": "multi_agent_v1__spawn_agent",
  "namespace": null
}
```

Codex Desktop then rejects it:

```text
unsupported call: multi_agent_v1__spawn_agent
```

No native child task, child rollout, or `thread_spawn` relationship is created.

This does not appear to be an authentication, networking, or basic tool-calling failure. The same credentials and route can serve normal responses and execute ordinary tools. The evidence instead points to a tool-identity or namespace-restoration problem affecting legacy v1 collaboration tools on the Chat Completions bridge.

## Environment

- OS: Windows
- Codex Desktop / CLI: `0.151.0-alpha.7.2`
- Runtime reproduction: `codex-router 0.5.1` at commit `4d5ca178ffdf3a0e6def80cdc0957ab5c4da93a1`
- Current upstream source audit: `main` at commit [`44029b8729b8166f8a662f5b62883c192bbeb9df`](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/commit/44029b8729b8166f8a662f5b62883c192bbeb9df)
- Provider: `qwen-plan`
- Endpoint: `https://token-plan.cn-beijing.maas.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1`
- Credentials: valid; secrets are intentionally omitted

Affected models observed in the runtime reproduction:

- `qwen-plan/deepseek-v4-flash-0731`
- `qwen-plan/glm-5.2`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure `qwen-plan` with valid Alibaba Model Studio Token Plan credentials.
2. Select either affected model in Codex Desktop.
3. Start a new task and ask the model to spawn multiple native Codex Desktop subagents.
4. Inspect the resulting rollout.
5. Observe that the model calls `multi_agent_v1__spawn_agent` and that Codex Desktop rejects it as an unsupported call.

Example prompt:

```text
Spawn five native Codex Desktop subagents in parallel and assign one independent analysis task to each subagent.
```

## Actual behavior

The affected route produces a plain, pre-flattened function call with no namespace:

```json
{
  "name": "multi_agent_v1__spawn_agent",
  "namespace": null
}
```

Codex Desktop returns:

```text
unsupported call: multi_agent_v1__spawn_agent
```

During a separate run with `qwen-plan/glm-5.2`, the model attempted to fall back to:

```text
codex_app__create_thread
```

That call was rejected as well:

```text
unsupported call: codex_app__create_thread
```

Neither run produced any of the following native-subagent evidence:

- a child rollout
- `source.subagent.thread_spawn`
- a `thread_spawn_edges` record

## Control case

On the same machine, `zai-coding/glm-5.3` emits the native v2 tool identity:

```json
{
  "name": "spawn_agent",
  "namespace": "collaboration"
}
```

This successfully creates native Codex Desktop subagents, child rollouts, and `thread_spawn` relationships. That route is published with `multi_agent_version: "v2"`.

## Current upstream source audit

The issue was reproduced dynamically on commit `4d5ca178`, not on the latest upstream commit. No paid Qwen Plan request was made against the latest HEAD during this audit.

However, the source-level trigger remains present at upstream commit `44029b8`:

1. The affected Qwen Plan registry entries do not declare `multiAgentVersion`:
   - [`config/qwen/plan/deepseek-v4-flash-0731.json`](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/blob/44029b8729b8166f8a662f5b62883c192bbeb9df/config/qwen/plan/deepseek-v4-flash-0731.json#L4-L30)
   - [`config/qwen/plan/glm-5.2.json`](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/blob/44029b8729b8166f8a662f5b62883c192bbeb9df/config/qwen/plan/glm-5.2.json#L4-L30)
2. An omitted value still falls back to `multi_agent_version: "v1"` in [`src/catalog.mjs`](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/blob/44029b8729b8166f8a662f5b62883c192bbeb9df/src/catalog.mjs#L613-L616).
3. [`recoverPreflattenedMcpTools()`](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/blob/44029b8729b8166f8a662f5b62883c192bbeb9df/src/namespace-relay.mjs#L994-L1007) intentionally limits pre-flattened recovery to MCP tools and excludes app and collaboration tools.
4. The current local settings mechanism can explicitly promote selected routes to v2, but this is an operator opt-in rather than an upstream route certification. See [`src/multi-agent-state.mjs`](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/blob/44029b8729b8166f8a662f5b62883c192bbeb9df/src/multi-agent-state.mjs#L177-L200).
5. The current test suite contains generic namespace and catalog coverage, but no regression fixture was found for the exact `qwen-plan` plus `multi_agent_v1__spawn_agent` failure.

Current status should therefore be described as:

- Confirmed runtime failure on `4d5ca178`.
- Source-level trigger still present on `44029b8`.
- Latest-HEAD runtime reproduction not yet performed.

## Suspected failure chain

The following is a source-supported hypothesis, not yet a fully proven root cause because a sanitized request-side tool inventory has not been captured:

1. Codex sends a legacy v1 collaboration tool that is already represented as a pre-flattened plain function.
2. The Router treats that definition as an ordinary function and does not construct a collaboration reverse mapping.
3. The provider returns `multi_agent_v1__spawn_agent`.
4. The Router preserves the call as `namespace: null`.
5. Codex Desktop cannot dispatch that ordinary function and returns `unsupported call`.

An alternative possibility is that Codex `0.151` changed the executable legacy-v1 surface while the routed catalog still advertises v1. Capturing the sanitized request-side tool definitions and `x-codex-turn-metadata` would distinguish these cases.

## Expected behavior

Any of the following outcomes would be acceptable:

1. Restore the provider's pre-flattened call to the executable native identity:

   ```json
   {
     "name": "spawn_agent",
     "namespace": "collaboration"
   }
   ```

2. If legacy v1 collaboration is no longer compatible with current Codex Desktop releases, do not advertise an unusable subagent tool to routed models.
3. After a real native-subagent verification succeeds for the Qwen Plan route, publish the affected model with `multiAgentVersion: "v2"`.

A model should not be offered a tool that it can call but that Codex Desktop will always reject as unsupported.

## Suggested regression coverage

1. Create a routed-model fixture whose effective catalog entry uses `multi_agent_version: "v1"`.
2. Supply Codex `0.151`-style request metadata and pre-flattened tool definitions.
3. Make the simulated provider return:

   ```json
   {
     "name": "multi_agent_v1__spawn_agent"
   }
   ```

4. Assert that the client receives an executable native call rather than an ordinary function with `namespace: null`.
5. Add equivalent coverage for `codex_app__create_thread`.
6. Add collision-safety coverage so that an intentionally declared ordinary function with the same literal name is not incorrectly restored.
7. Add a full Qwen Plan native-subagent integration test covering:
   - spawn marker return
   - native child rollout creation
   - encrypted payload relay
   - same-thread follow-up

## Possible fix directions

- Safely recover known pre-flattened collaboration and app tools using the current turn metadata and effective `multi_agent_version`, with collision checks.
- Alternatively, suppress the legacy v1 subagent surface for routed models on Codex clients that cannot dispatch it.
- Only enable v2 by default for a Qwen Plan route after it passes a real native-subagent verification.

## Temporary workaround

Current upstream code allows an operator to explicitly select a Qwen model as a local v2 subagent, rebuild the catalog, and fully restart Codex. The upstream subagent guide recommends `selected` mode rather than `all` mode:

- [Spawning subagents through codex-router](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/blob/44029b8729b8166f8a662f5b62883c192bbeb9df/.claude/skills/codex-subagents/SKILL.md#L23-L65)

This is only a machine-local opt-in. It does not demonstrate that the Qwen Plan route has passed the upstream native-subagent certification requirements.

## Security and privacy

API keys, complete rollouts, local filesystem paths, and private prompts have been omitted. The snippets above contain only the minimum tool-call evidence required to reproduce and diagnose the problem.


### Which app do you route through?

Codex

### Platform

Windows

### Doctor output or support bundle

_No response_

title: fix: publish routed models in vendor bands so the Codex picker groups them
body:
## Problem

Codex renders its model picker by each entry's `priority`, **never** by catalog
array order. Routed models reuse the same low integers as native GPT entries, so
they interleave with them and the vendor grouping the published array already
carried never reaches the screen (#544):

| slug | priority |
| --- | ---: |
| `gpt-5.6-sol` | 1 |
| `grok-oauth/grok-4.6` | 1 |
| `gpt-5.6-terra` | 2 |
| `grok-oauth/grok-4.5` | 2 |

`routedPickerPriorities()` only reordered the array, which Codex ignores.

## Why the obvious fix was wrong

Setting every routed model to `nativeMax + 1` was explicitly rejected in the
code and locked by `test/catalog.test.mjs`, for a real reason: `priority` also
feeds Codex's `spawn_agent` override window (AGENTS.md step 5), which advertises
only a small priority-ordered subset. Renumbering a certified v2 spawn route
crowds it out of that window and breaks subagent routing.

## Change

Publish **two numberings**, which is the dual scheme the issue asks for:

- A **certified v2** route keeps the priority its registry entry authored — that
  low value is what keeps it inside the override window.
- Every **v1** routed model is published in a band above the highest *visible*
  native priority, in vendor-group order. Codex never offers a v1 route as a
  spawn override, so moving one can crowd nothing out.

The band ignores hidden native entries; their arbitrary numbers would otherwise
push every routed model far down the picker for no reason a user can see.

**Only the published entry is renumbered.** `model-failover`, `vision-bridge`,
and the DSH/Gemini/OpenClaw/Claude managers all read the registry's authored
`priority` and are untouched — I checked each consumer rather than assuming.

## Tests

The existing lock test is **unchanged and still passes**: its fixture inherits
`multiAgentVersion: "v2"`, so every routed model in it keeps its authored
priority — exactly the property that test exists to protect. I only extended its
comment to say why.

A new test covers the band: v1 routes land at 30–33 above a visible native max of
29 (not the hidden entry's 500), in vendor-group order; the v2 route keeps its
authored 2 and its certificate; natives are never renumbered; and the published
picker has **no duplicate priorities left to interleave on**.

Full suite: **3402 tests, 3378 pass, 0 fail.** `npm run check` clean.

Closes #544

title: fix: explain a Windows scheduled-task launch that cannot read its own checkout
body:
## Problem

#548 reports a Windows install where the scheduled task exits `1` and the router
log names an existing file as missing:

```
Error: Cannot find module 'C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\codex-router\src\start.mjs'
code: 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND'
```

The operator can read that file. Readiness reported only
`no running launcher process (LastTaskResult=0x1)`, leaving them to reconcile
two messages that each point somewhere else.

## Diagnosis

The reporter's own evidence rules out the launcher: swapping the generated VBS
wrapper for a direct `cmd.exe /D /C ...start-codex-router.cmd` action reproduced
the **identical** result and message, while running the same launcher from an
**elevated** interactive shell started the router normally. The task principal
ran at **Limited** level.

That points at the task token's access to the managed checkout, not at how the
task invokes it. Node surfaces an unreadable module and an absent one
identically, which is what made the log misleading.

## Change

`diagnoseWindowsLaunchFailure()` checks the one piece of local evidence that
separates the two cases — whether the path the loader named exists right now:

- **Exists** → a permission or token problem, with the likely cause (an elevated
  install leaving the checkout readable only to the elevated identity while the
  task runs Limited) and how to confirm it.
- **Absent** → an incomplete checkout; re-run the installer.
- **No module error in the log** → nothing added, original wording kept.

The log tail is read by seeking to a 64 KB window rather than loading a
long-lived log on a path that is already reporting an outage.

## Scope — please read

**This improves the diagnosis, not the underlying condition.** I could not
reproduce the ACL failure from macOS, so the fix makes the failure name itself
instead of guessing at a remedy I cannot verify. The issue should stay open for
the ACL work, and the `icacls` output the reporter can capture would confirm the
cause.

## Tests

`test/windows-launch-diagnosis.test.mjs` (5 cases): the exists/absent split, that
the **most recent** launch decides the verdict when an older failure sits in the
same log, that a log without a module error stays silent, and that the tail read
handles a missing, empty, oversized, and undersized log.

`test/service-readiness.test.mjs` (2 new): the diagnosis reaches the operator's
error **appended to** the original `LastTaskResult=0x1` verdict rather than
replacing it, and an uninformative log leaves that verdict untouched.

Full suite: **3495 tests, 3470 pass, 0 fail.** `npm run check` clean.

Refs #548

title: fix: hide the console windows Windows background PowerShell helpers create
body:
## Problem

#565 reports a burst of visible **Windows PowerShell** windows during routine
Control Center status refreshes — noticeable on every message sent — with a
`Win32_ProcessStartTrace` showing them as children of Control Center command
invocations launched by the tray.

A console process spawned by a parent that has **no console of its own** (the
Electron Control Center, the tray) gets its own window unless `windowsHide` is
set.

## Four call sites, not one

The reporter's trace pointed at the child-process path; auditing every
PowerShell launch in `src/` found four background helpers missing the flag:

| Call site | Why it fires |
| --- | --- |
| `file-security.mjs` ACL writer | **every private write** — this is the one that made it constant |
| `file-security.mjs` ACL verifier | same GUI-parented paths |
| `service-windows.mjs` task registration | GUI installer and Control Center |
| `service-windows.mjs` task-state poll | tray timer, so the window **returns on its own** |

`file-security`'s own *async* path already hid correctly, which is why this was
easy to miss.

## What is deliberately left visible

`setup.mjs`, `setup-shared.mjs`, `secret-prompt.mjs`, and the `doctor --fix`
repair all inherit stdio — they prompt or stream through a console the operator
is already looking at. Hiding those would ask for input through a window nobody
can see, so the rule is a **property of the call**, not an allowlist: a
PowerShell child whose stdio inherits is exempt; every other one must hide.

## Test

`test/windows-hidden-consoles.test.mjs` asserts that rule over `src/`. It scans
source because the failure is invisible on macOS and Linux and reproducing it
needs a Windows desktop session.

Three things keep it from passing vacuously:

- It resolves an options object **or** an stdio value held in a variable, so a
  hoisted `options` or a ternary `repairStdio` is read correctly rather than
  reported as a false positive.
- A second test asserts the population it inspects is non-empty and includes
  both `file-security.mjs` and at least one interactive call.
- I verified it fails — naming the exact file and line — when a `windowsHide`
  flag is deleted.

Full suite: **3490 tests, 3465 pass, 0 fail.** `npm run check` clean.

Closes #565

title: fix: name the Antigravity allowlist failure instead of reporting a bare 403
body:
## Problem

#566 shows the operator-owned Antigravity OAuth client completing sign-in and
then failing the live probe with:

```
Antigravity project bootstrap failed (HTTP 403; HTTP 403).
```

That reads as a credential problem, so the operator re-runs a sign-in that is
already working. Google was returning the actual reason and
`loadAntigravityProject()` discarded the body, pushing only `HTTP ${status}`.

## What is actually happening

The reporter established this thoroughly. `loadCodeAssist` is billed to the
project owning the calling OAuth client. With the bundled vendor client that was
Google's own allowlisted project; with an operator-owned client it is the
operator's, which is not allowlisted for `cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`.

That service is a **private API**. Binding it needs the producer-side
`servicemanagement.services.bind` permission, so `gcloud services enable` fails
even when run by the project owner through gcloud's own first-party client, and
the service has no API Library entry to enable through the console.

**There is no operator-side workaround**, so the message should not imply one.

## Change

`antigravityBootstrapFailure()` reads the structured error and, for
`SERVICE_DISABLED` on that specific service, explains that the project is not
allowlisted and that **sign-in succeeded** — the part that stops the operator
retrying the wrong thing.

Deliberate restraint in three places:

- **Only structured fields are read.** Google's free-text `message` embeds the
  caller's project number and a console URL built from it, and this string is
  printed and logged. A test asserts neither appears.
- **The allowlist explanation is specific to the private API.** A different
  disabled service reports its status, reason, and name without it, because an
  ordinary service really can be enabled and saying otherwise would misdirect.
- **Every unexpected body degrades to the bare status** — absent, empty, HTML,
  malformed, non-error JSON, or oversized.

README now states the prerequisite, including plainly that the provider cannot
currently be used without an allowlisted project.

## Scope

This makes the failure legible. It does **not** make the provider work — nothing
in this repository can, since the allowlist is Google's. #566 should stay open
for the question of whether a supported path exists at all.

## Tests

`test/antigravity-bootstrap-failure.test.mjs`, 6 cases, using the exact response
shape from the issue.

Full suite: **3494 tests, 3469 pass, 0 fail.** `npm run check` clean.

Refs #566

title: fix: honor a Retry-After that names a date instead of seconds
body:
## Why

`Retry-After` is the only reason `classifyRoutedFailure` ever learns a window for a burst rate limit, and RFC 9110 §10.2.3 lets a provider express it two ways: `delay-seconds` **or** an `HTTP-date`. The router reads it with `Number()`:

```js
retryAfterSeconds: Number(upstream.headers.get("retry-after")),
```

so `Retry-After: Sat, 25 Jul 2026 12:05:00 GMT` becomes `NaN`, and every consumer discards `NaN`:

- `classifyRoutedFailure` returns `{ swap: false }` for a 429, so the turn does **not** fail over — it dies on a provider that had just said when it would be back, with other credentialed models sitting right there.
- No `provider-cooldowns.json` entry is written, so the next turn asks the same limited provider again, and the one after that — for the whole window. That is the same shape as the "225 quota refusals against one window" the module's own comments describe.
- `translateGatewayError` loses the "Retry in about Ns." hint and falls back to "Wait a bit and retry."

The repo already has a parser that handles all of this: `resetAt()` in `src/rate-limit-headers.mjs` reads delay-seconds, an HTTP-date, and a Go-style duration, and `api-forwarder` had a private helper wrapping it. The router just never used either.

The same expression has a second, smaller defect: `headers.get()` answers `null` for a header that was never sent, and `Number(null)` is `0` — finite, so `Number.isFinite` accepts it and a 429 with no `Retry-After` at all told the operator to "Retry in about 0s.". Absence and a real zero are different answers, and neither one is worth quoting as a wait; the second commit separates them at the parser and settles the wording at the message.

## What changed

- add `retryAfterSeconds(headers, { now })` to `src/rate-limit-headers.mjs`, built on the existing `resetAt()`. It reports what the header said and nothing more: `undefined` only when the value is absent or unparseable, a number otherwise — including the `0` that RFC 9110's `delay-seconds` permits, and an already-elapsed date, which is the same zero wait. A sub-second value still ceils to 1 rather than rounding into the zero that means "no wait"
- quote a wait in the 429 message only when it is positive. `Retry in about 0s.` was the wording a *missing* header produced, and it is no better as advice when a provider really did send zero, so both cases read as `Wait a bit and retry.`
- use it at the four `Retry-After` reads in `src/router.mjs` (compaction failover, the failover hop, the primary failure classification, and the translated error)
- delete `api-forwarder`'s private `responseRetryAfterSeconds` in favor of the shared helper — same semantics, one definition
- regression coverage: a 429 whose window is an HTTP-date now fails over and records a `rate_limited` cooldown that the next turn honors; a 429 with no window no longer advises "in about 0s"; unit coverage for each accepted and rejected header form

No registry, catalog, or subagent surface is touched.

## Verification

- `npm run check` — passes
- `npm test` — 3,414 passed, 0 failed, 25 skipped. 66 tests in `test/control-center-electron.test.mjs` are `cancelledByParent` in this environment; they reproduce identically on the unmodified tree, so they are not from this patch.
- `node --test test/model-failover-router.test.mjs test/rate-limit-headers.test.mjs test/error-translation.test.mjs` — 70 passed
- `node --test test/provider-api-key-forwarder.test.mjs test/commandcode-forwarder.test.mjs test/rate-limit-quota.test.mjs test/model-failover.test.mjs` — 51 passed (the `api-forwarder` call sites)
- `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` — 0 vulnerabilities
- Both new integration tests were confirmed red before the fix: the HTTP-date turn returned 429 instead of failing over, and the zero-wait turn produced `Retry in about 0s.` — each half of that test was re-checked against a reverted tree so neither passes vacuously.

title: fix: keep a separately billed variant out of its parent's cooldown
body:
## Why

`opencode-zen` is declared `variantOf: "opencode-go"` because it shares Go's credential and selection toggle. It does not share Go's bill — it is a different endpoint (`/zen/v1` vs `/zen/go/v1`), and it is the only variant in the registry whose `baseUrl` differs from its parent's. `src/provider-cooldown.mjs` already names this exactly:

> opencode Zen is the exception: it shares a credential and selection toggle with Go, but it uses the separately billed /zen endpoint. Exhausting Go must not disable a route the operator can still pay for through Zen.

The live failover path never used that scope. `providerCooldown`, `recordProviderCooldown`, `clearProviderCooldown`, and `eligible()` all keyed windows by `canonicalProviderId`, which folds Zen into `opencode-go`. Both directions cost the operator a paid route:

- **Go's window withdraws Zen.** With `{"opencode-go": {...}}` in `provider-cooldowns.json`, a turn on a curated `opencode-zen/...` model is never sent. It is silently answered by a different provider — reproduced against the existing harness before the fix:

  ```
  [codex-router] failover model=opencode-zen/glm-5.3 status=not-sent
    reason=cooled_until_2026-09-02T19:00:19.932Z -> zai-api/glm-5.2 outcome=swapped
  ```

- **Zen's window withdraws Go.** An exhausted Zen balance is filed under `opencode-go`, so the whole Go subscription is skipped for up to six hours over a balance that has nothing to do with it.

Zen models are curated locally (nothing is checked in for that provider), so this hits any operator who curated one and then hit either limit.

## What changed

- `src/model-failover.mjs` keys windows by `cooldownScope` when recording, reading, clearing, and ranking candidates
- `src/router.mjs`'s vision-bridge engine selection uses the same scope: it pre-canonicalized before reading a window its own writer (a few lines above, `recordProviderCooldown(visionEngineProvider(engine), …)`) files by raw provider id, so after this change the two halves would otherwise disagree
- `src/api-forwarder.mjs` passes `normalized.provider.id` through unresolved, so the scope is decided in one place instead of being pre-collapsed at the call site
- regression coverage in both directions, unit and end-to-end

Deliberately unchanged: `eligible()` still refuses a candidate whose canonical provider is the one that just failed, so an exhausted Go plan does not automatically fail over onto separately billed Zen credits. Spending a second balance on the operator's behalf is a different decision from not withdrawing a route they chose. Usage-event attribution also keeps `canonicalProviderId` — usage rolls up to the account.

## Verification

- All four new tests confirmed red before the fix and green after:
  - `a closed Go plan window does not withdraw the separately billed Zen route` (also asserts a Go route *is* still skipped by the same window, so the test cannot pass by disabling cooldowns)
  - `an exhausted Zen balance cools Zen rather than the Go subscription`
  - `a separately billed variant keeps its own window`
  - `rankFailoverCandidates still offers a separately billed variant`
- The existing `a cooldown is recorded against the whole variant family` test passes unchanged — protocol variants still share one window.
- `npm run check` — passes
- `npm test` — 3,415 passed, 0 failed, 25 skipped. 67 tests are `cancelledByParent` in this environment (66 in `test/control-center-electron.test.mjs`, 1 in `test/search-sidecar.test.mjs`); both reproduce identically on a clean tree, so they are not from this patch.
- `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` — 0 vulnerabilities

Independent of #573 (both branch from `main`; no overlapping lines).

title: Provider circuit-breaker subsystem ships unreachable, and its telemetry key disagrees with the failover cooldown identity
body:
Two related findings from reading the cooldown paths while preparing #574. Neither is a user-visible failure today, which is why this is a question rather than a PR: the answer is a design decision, and the second finding only becomes a real bug once the first is resolved in one particular direction.

Everything below is against `main` at `a68418f`.

## 1. `src/provider-cooldown.mjs`'s circuit breaker and `src/subagent-availability-sync.mjs` are unreachable

`src/subagent-availability-sync.mjs` is the only module in the repository that nothing references. Searching every tracked file (not just `src/` and `test/`) for the name returns its own internal recursion and nothing else, so `startSubagentAvailabilitySync()` is never called:

```
$ grep -rn "subagent-availability-sync" . | grep -v '^\./\.git/'
(no matches outside the module itself)
```

The subsystem it drives is inert end to end:

| export in `provider-cooldown.mjs` | referenced from `src/` |
| --- | --- |
| `recordProviderCooldown` | — (the identically named live function is `model-failover.mjs`'s) |
| `activeProviderCooldown` | — |
| `cooldownErrorPayload` | — (not referenced by its own test either) |
| `temporarilyUnavailableSubagentSlugs` | — |
| `quotaResetAt` | — |
| `cooldownScope` | — |
| `nextQuotaCooldownExpiry` | `subagent-availability-sync.mjs` only |

And the one production link is closed at the other end too. `nextQuotaCooldownExpiry` selects snapshots by `snapshot?.reason !== "quota"`, but the only production writer of `rate-limits.json` is `api-forwarder.mjs:1108`, which stores `parseRateLimitHeaders()` output — a document that never carries `reason`. The sole writer of `reason: "quota"` is `provider-cooldown.mjs`'s own `recordProviderCooldown`, which nothing calls. So the predicate cannot be true on a real install regardless of the missing wiring.

What this means in practice: no quota circuit is ever opened, `cooldownErrorPayload`'s two operator-facing sentences are never rendered, no subagent is ever temporarily withdrawn, and the catalog is never rebuilt when a window expires. `test/provider-cooldown.test.mjs` passes and reads like a live contract ("opens a durable provider circuit", "temporarily remove subagent models"), which is what makes this easy to miss. `docs/OPENCODEX_IMPLEMENTATION_ROADMAP.md` also cites the file as implemented provider-cooldown support.

Both files entered in `350971d` and were never wired; `model-failover.mjs` (`9731681`, five days earlier) already owned the "skip a provider that said it was empty" job, so the plausible reading is that this is a second design that was superseded before it was connected. **Wiring it or removing it is your call** — the two mechanisms would otherwise maintain two cooldown stores with different scoping and different bounds (`MAX_COOLDOWN_MS` is 6h in one and 24h in the other).

## 2. Header telemetry is keyed by canonical id, not by billing scope

`api-forwarder.mjs:1108` files header-derived quota under `canonicalProviderId(...)`:

```js
// Variant-routed responses meter the same upstream subscription, so quota
// headers land under the family's canonical provider id.
if (rateLimit) recordRateLimitSnapshot(canonicalProviderId(normalized.provider.id), rateLimit);
```

That premise holds for protocol variants but not for `opencode-zen`, which is `variantOf: "opencode-go"` for credential and selection purposes while being billed at its own `/zen/v1` endpoint — the case #574 is about, and the one `cooldownScope` already exists to name. Driving one Zen request through the forwarder against a stub upstream that answers `x-ratelimit-remaining-requests: 7` stores it as the Go plan's window:

```json
{
  "opencode-go": {
    "requests": { "limit": 100, "remaining": 7 },
    "observedAt": "2026-09-02T19:14:08.104Z"
  }
}
```

I could not find a way for this to reach an operator today, and I would rather say so than dress it up:

- `provider-cooldown.mjs` reads snapshots through `cooldownScope`, so it would disagree with this key — but per finding 1 that reader never runs.
- `provider-account-usage.mjs`'s `headerQuota()` is the live reader, and `opencode-go` never reaches it: `opencodeGoAccount()` queries `/usage` and its failure path returns `status: "unavailable"` rather than falling back to headers.
- `providerAccountUsageSnapshot()` only queries providers without `variantOf`, so there is no Zen card that could show the wrong numbers either.

So this is latent rather than broken. It stops being latent the moment finding 1 is resolved by wiring: `activeProviderCooldown("opencode-zen")` would then read a window recorded from Go traffic, and a quota card fallback for a variant would attribute one bill's remaining requests to the other. If the answer to finding 1 is removal, the one-line change to `cooldownScope` here is still worth making so the two identities cannot drift back apart — happy to send it either way once the direction is decided.

## Not included

No PR attached on purpose. Deleting a subsystem you wrote, or connecting one that changes routing behaviour on every turn, is not a call I should make from the outside — and the second finding's fix depends on which way the first one goes.

title: ci: fix CodeQL runner death by excluding Swift from analysis
body: ## Problem The CodeQL / Analyze (swift) (dynamic) job is failing on `main` with runner death after ~52 minutes: > The hosted runner lost communication with the server. Anything in your workflow that terminates the runner process, starves it for CPU/Memory, or blocks its network access can cause this error. **Evidence:** - Failed run: https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/33653043718/job/100324612945 - Head SHA: `a68418fc6142ab97324042f6910e395db769c3e0` (main, merge of #571) - Other CodeQL languages (javascript-typescript, python, ruby, actions) succeeded - Native macOS CI (test / Electron / native macOS) is **green** on the same SHA — Swift compilation works fine **Root cause:** The GitHub default CodeQL setup is running Swift analysis against `apps/macos/ModelRouterTray` (Swift Package Manager) and `apps/macos/RouterUsageWidget` (xcodeproj), exhausting the GitHub-hosted macOS runner's CPU/memory. ## Solution This PR adds an **advanced CodeQL workflow** (`.github/workflows/codeql.yml`) that: 1. ✅ Keeps security scanning for `javascript-typescript`, `python`, `ruby`, and `actions` 2. ❌ **Excludes Swift** to prevent runner resource exhaustion 3. 📝 Documents why Swift is excluded (native macOS CI already builds/tests it) ## Expected PR Check Failures **The advanced CodeQL jobs on this PR will fail until the Settings switch is made.** This is expected behavior: ``` Code Scanning could not process the submitted SARIF file: CodeQL analyses from advanced configurations cannot be processed when the default setup is enabled ``` Both default and advanced CodeQL setups **cannot run simultaneously**. The advanced workflow in this PR is correct and ready—it's blocked only by the Settings toggle that must be switched after merge. Evidence: run 33682236782 shows all four advanced jobs failed with this exact error, while default setup (including Swift) continued to run. ## Required Settings Change **After merging this PR**, a repository administrator must switch from default to advanced setup: 1. Navigate to: **Settings** → **Code security and analysis** 2. Locate the **"CodeQL analysis"** row 3. Click the `⋯` (three dots) menu 4. Select **"Switch to advanced"** 5. In the confirmation dialog, click **"Disable CodeQL"** This disables the default setup and activates the advanced workflow file committed in this PR. **Why this must be done after merge:** GitHub default setup is a repository Settings toggle, not controlled by workflow files. The default setup will continue running (and failing on Swift) until manually switched to advanced. Only advanced setup reads the committed `.github/workflows/codeql.yml` file. ## Verification Once switched to advanced setup: - ✅ CodeQL will analyze JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Ruby, and GitHub Actions - ✅ No Swift analysis = no runner death - ✅ Swift security remains covered by native macOS CI (builds + tests) - ✅ No product behavior changes (this is pure CI configuration) ## References - GitHub Docs: [Configuring advanced setup for code scanning](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/code-scanning/creating-an-advanced-setup-for-code-scanning) - GitHub Docs: [About setup types](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/code-scanning/setup-types) - GitHub Docs: [Upload rejected because default setup enabled](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/code-scanning/sarif-files/troubleshoot-sarif-uploads/default-setup-enabled)

title: fix: grant Users read access to checkout so Limited task can start
body: ## Issue Fixes #548 Windows scheduled tasks run at Limited level, but an elevated installer creates the checkout directory with ACLs that only allow the elevated account to read it. This made the task's attempt to load `src/start.mjs` fail with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` even though the file exists. ## Analysis The problem occurs when: 1. The installer runs in an elevated shell 2. The checkout directory and files are created with restrictive ACLs (only readable by the elevated account) 3. The scheduled task is created with `-RunLevel Limited` (line 208 in `src/service-windows.mjs`) 4. The Limited-level task cannot read files owned by the elevated account 5. Node.js reports this as `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, which is indistinguishable from a truly missing file Commit 1476c60 improved the diagnostic message to explain this ACL problem and suggest running `icacls` manually, but did not fix the underlying cause. ## Solution This PR makes service installation automatically grant `BUILTIN\Users` ReadAndExecute access to the checkout directory. This allows the Limited-level scheduled task to traverse directories and read source files. The fix preserves the security boundary: - **STATE_DIR files remain owner-only protected** (credentials, secrets, private state) - **Only the checkout tree becomes readable by all users** (contains no secrets) - This matches the installer's documented advice to either grant the task's account access or run the installer non-elevated ## Changes 1. **Added `ensureCheckoutReadable()` to `src/file-security.mjs`** - Grants BUILTIN\Users (S-1-5-32-545) ReadAndExecute permission on the checkout directory - Uses inheritance flags so permissions apply recursively - Best-effort operation: warns but doesn't fail if ACL modification fails - Only runs on Windows 2. **Updated `src/service-windows.mjs`** - Calls `ensureCheckoutReadable(SOURCE_ROOT)` during service installation - Ensures the checkout is readable before writing launchers and installing the task 3. **Added test coverage in `test/file-security.test.mjs`** - Verifies that `ensureCheckoutReadable()` grants Users ReadAndExecute access - Skipped on non-Windows platforms ## Testing Note **This agent runs on Linux and cannot live-test the Windows scheduled task.** The implementation: - Uses the same PowerShell ACL pattern as existing `protectPrivateFile` code - Adds a test that verifies the ACL is correctly set (Windows-only) - Follows the documented SID for BUILTIN\Users (S-1-5-32-545) - Uses `DirectorySecurity` rather than `FileSecurity` for directory ACLs A Windows maintainer should verify that: 1. An elevated `install.ps1` followed by scheduled task start succeeds 2. The task can read `src/start.mjs` and start the router 3. Private files in STATE_DIR remain owner-only protected ## Verification The fix should allow the exact failure scenario from #548 to succeed: 1. Run `install.ps1` from an elevated PowerShell 2. The service installs and grants Users read access to the checkout 3. The scheduled task (running at Limited level) can now read `src\start.mjs` 4. The router starts successfully instead of failing with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`

title: Surface Antigravity 403 SERVICE_DISABLED body and document allowlist requirement
body: Fixes #566 ## Problem Antigravity BYO OAuth sign-in with an operator-owned Desktop OAuth client succeeds and writes credential record v3, but the live probe fails with a bare `HTTP 403` error message. The actual Google response body contains `SERVICE_DISABLED` for `cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`, which is the actionable information that explains the project is not allowlisted for this private API. Additionally, README/INSTALL/AGENTS documentation currently **require** a BYO Desktop client but do not mention the private-API allowlist prerequisite upfront, so the documented happy path dead-ends for non-allowlisted projects. ## Solution The code already correctly calls `antigravityBootstrapFailure()` which parses the error body and surfaces the structured Google error. No code changes were needed. This PR adds: 1. **Test**: Added regression test in `test/antigravity-project.test.mjs` verifying that a 403 response with `SERVICE_DISABLED` body appears in the operator-visible error message with the allowlist explanation 2. **AGENTS.md**: Updated Antigravity OAuth setup section to state upfront that the OAuth client's Google Cloud project must be allowlisted for `cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`, clarify that operators cannot enable this private API themselves, and note that the live probe will fail with `SERVICE_DISABLED` if not allowlisted 3. **INSTALL.md**: Added warning before Antigravity setup instructions stating the allowlist requirement and that sign-in will succeed but probe will fail if project is not allowlisted ## Testing - ✅ New test `a 403 SERVICE_DISABLED body appears in the operator-visible error (issue #566)` passes - ✅ All existing `antigravity-bootstrap-failure.test.mjs` tests pass - ✅ All existing `antigravity-project.test.mjs` tests pass ## Documentation Changes Documentation now honestly states that BYO Desktop client OAuth requires a project already allowlisted for the private `cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com` API, which ordinary project owners cannot enable themselves (requires producer-side `servicemanagement.services.bind` permission). No invented unofficial allowlist signup URL - this is a Google allowlist that operators cannot self-service.

title: Fix namespace restoration for Qwen Plan collaboration calls (#568)
body: ## Summary Fixes Qwen Plan (Alibaba Model Studio Token Plan) collaboration calls being rejected by Codex Desktop due to flattened namespace identity. ## Problem Qwen Plan returns Codex v1 collaboration calls with flattened names: ```json {"type":"function_call","name":"multi_agent_v1__spawn_agent","namespace":null} ``` Codex Desktop rejects these with: `unsupported call: multi_agent_v1__spawn_agent` The root cause is that the Chat Completions → Responses adapter was flattening namespace tools but not restoring them on the way back to Desktop. ## Solution Added namespace restoration in the Responses protocol adapter (`src/openai-adapters.mjs`): 1. **`buildNamespaceLookupsFromTools(tools)`** - Builds a lookup map from flattened tool names back to their native namespaced form, but only for: - Tools that came from actual `type: "namespace"` entries in the request - Known collaboration namespaces (`multi_agent_v1`, `collaboration`) 2. **Restoration transforms** - Both SSE (`createResponsesStreamTransform`) and JSON (`createResponsesJsonTransform`) transforms now apply these lookups to restore `response.output_item.added` and `output[].function_call` items. 3. **Safe by design** - MCP-style names like `mcp__node_repl__js` are left unchanged unless they originated from a real namespace tool, preventing false positives. ## Testing ### New focused regression tests (`test/qwen-plan-namespace-restoration.test.mjs`) All 10 tests passing: ✅ `buildNamespaceLookupsFromTools` extracts flattened collaboration tool names ✅ `buildNamespaceLookupsFromTools` handles Chat Completions format ✅ `buildNamespaceLookupsFromTools` handles namespace tools with nested names ✅ `createResponsesStreamTransform` restores namespaced function calls (SSE) ✅ `createResponsesJsonTransform` restores namespaced function calls (JSON) ✅ Transforms preserve non-flattened function calls ✅ Transforms work with empty lookups ✅ `buildNamespaceLookupsFromTools` ignores MCP-style names without namespace tools ✅ `buildNamespaceLookupsFromTools` restores tools from namespace entries ✅ MCP-style names are left unchanged in responses without namespace tools ### Existing test coverage - `test/namespace-relay.test.mjs` - Existing namespace flattening/restoration logic ✅ - `test/openai-adapters.test.mjs` - Responses protocol adapters ✅ ## Changes - Modified `src/openai-adapters.mjs`: - Added `COLLABORATION_NAMESPACES` whitelist - Added `buildNamespaceLookupsFromTools()` function - Added `restoreNamespacedFunctionCall()` helper - Updated `normalizeResponsesEvent()` to restore namespaced calls in SSE - Updated `normalizeResponseBody()` to restore namespaced calls in JSON - Updated `createResponsesStreamTransform()` and `createResponsesJsonTransform()` to accept `flatToNative` parameter - Modified `src/api-forwarder.mjs`: - Added call to `buildNamespaceLookupsFromTools()` for Responses protocol requests - Passed `flatToNative` lookups to stream/JSON transforms - Added `test/qwen-plan-namespace-restoration.test.mjs` - Focused regression tests - Added CHANGELOG Unreleased note ## Verification **Live verification note**: A live Qwen Plan ping would require Alibaba Model Studio credentials. The fix is proven by: 1. Focused unit tests covering both SSE and JSON restoration paths 2. Tests ensuring MCP tools are not mis-restored 3. Existing namespace-relay tests still passing 4. The fix applies the same restoration contract used successfully for other providers ## Related Fixes #568
