title: Windows: router never comes back after power event / unlogged exit (LogonTrigger task + RestartOnFailure did not relaunch)
body:
## Windows: router never comes back after power event / unlogged exit — LogonTrigger task + RestartOnFailure did not relaunch it

**Environment:** Windows 11, router 0.5.1 (commit 37e9174, install manifest), target `codex`, Node 24.19.0. Clients: Codex desktop.

**Setup (router-installed Task Scheduler task "Codex Router"):**
- Trigger: `LogonTrigger` (`AtLogOn`, current user)
- Action: `wscript.exe //B //NoLogo <state>/start-codex-router-hidden.vbs` (vbs waits on `cmd` -> `node src/start.mjs`; `Wait=True`)
- Settings: `MultipleInstancesPolicy=IgnoreNew`, `RestartOnFailure Count=999 Interval=PT1M`, `ExecutionTimeLimit=PT0S`

**Observed:**
1. Router was serving fine, then its process tree exited with no error in `router.log` (log simply stops; last lines are normal timing lines) and no crash event in the Windows Application log (no 1000/1002/1026 for node around the exit window).
2. After the exit, nothing was listening on the router port (~hours). Codex desktop retried: endless "Reconnecting... waiting for network".
3. The scheduled task never relaunched it: `Get-ScheduledTaskInfo` showed `LastRunTime` unchanged since the logon launch, and `LastTaskResult = 4294967295` (0xFFFFFFFF). `RestartOnFailure` count never advanced; the task stayed `Ready` (not running).
4. Manually re-running the same launcher (`wscript …vbs`) restores the router; everything works again.

**Hypothesis:** the tree died during a sleep/shutdown/fast-startup cycle (process suspended then terminated, or a silent exit). The task instance ends when the waiting `wscript` exits with the dead node's status — but `RestartOnFailure` did not relaunch it, and `LogonTrigger` doesn't re-fire on wake-from-sleep or fast startup. Expected: `RestartOnFailure` should have relaunched within 1 minute, per the README statement that on Windows "the service still exits and the OS supervisor rebuilds it".

**Ask:** can the Windows supervisor be strengthened? Options: also register a repeating/minutely wake trigger, or ship a small health-backed watchdog (TCP probe against the router port -> relaunch same hidden launcher). A loopback health endpoint already exists (unauthenticated leaf), so the probe needs nothing new.

Happy to provide redacted task XML or log excerpts if useful.

title: fix: Resolve 18 CodeQL medium security alerts (shell injection, stack trace exposure, code sanitization)
body: ## Summary This PR fixes CodeQL medium security alerts through targeted code changes: ### Fixed Alerts - **Alert #58** (`js/stack-trace-exposure`): Fixed by using JSON.stringify replacer in `writeJson` - **Alert #53** (`js/shell-command-injection-from-environment`): Fixed by removing SystemRoot/WINDIR environment lookups - **Alerts #50, #51, #57** (`js/bad-code-sanitization`): Fixed by using base64 encoding instead of JSON.stringify interpolation - **Alerts #54-72** (`js/shell-command-injection-from-environment`): Fixed by using bare command names (`cmd.exe`, `powershell.exe`) with `shell:false` ## Detailed Changes ### Alert #58 - Stack Trace Exposure (`src/http-utils.mjs:662`) **Fix**: Use `JSON.stringify` replacer function to drop `stack` properties and sanitize Error objects: ```javascript JSON.stringify(payload, (key, value) => { if (key === 'stack') return undefined; if (value instanceof Error) { return { name: value.name, message: String(value.message).split('\n')[0], ...(value.code !== undefined ? { code: value.code } : {}), }; } return value; }) ``` **Why this works**: - Drops all `stack` properties from serialization - Converts Error objects to safe representations (first line of message only) - Preserves normal JSON semantics for Date, Buffer, and other objects - `JSON.stringify` automatically handles these via their `toJSON` methods **File**: `src/http-utils.mjs` ### Alert #53 - PowerShell Path from Environment (`src/process-tree.mjs`) **Root cause**: `windowsPowerShell()` used `environment.SystemRoot || environment.WINDIR` to construct the PowerShell executable path, creating an "uncontrolled absolute path" from environment variables. **Fix**: Return bare `"powershell.exe"` command name instead of constructing absolute path: ```javascript function windowsPowerShell() { return "powershell.exe"; } ``` **Why this works**: - Windows resolves `powershell.exe` via PATH automatically - Works on any Windows installation drive (C:, D:, etc.) - Avoids environment-derived paths that CodeQL flags - Combined with `shell: false` in spawn options (already present) **File**: `src/process-tree.mjs` ### Alerts #54-72 - cmd.exe Path from Environment (`src/spawnable-command.mjs`) **Root cause**: Used `process.env.ComSpec || "cmd.exe"` to locate cmd.exe, creating an environment-derived command path. **Fix**: Use bare `"cmd.exe"` command name with explicit `shell: false`: ```javascript return { command: "cmd.exe", args: ["/d", "/s", "/c", `"${line}"`], options: { windowsVerbatimArguments: true, shell: false }, }; ``` **Why this works**: - Windows resolves `cmd.exe` via PATH automatically - Works on any Windows installation drive - Explicit `shell: false` ensures no additional shell wrapping - All 13 alerts (#54-66, #68-72) flow through `spawnableCommand()` **File**: `src/spawnable-command.mjs` ### Alerts #50, #51, #57 - Code Sanitization in Tests (`test/process-tree.test.mjs`) **Fix**: Replaced `JSON.stringify` string interpolation with base64 encoding: ```javascript // OLD: `writeFileSync(${JSON.stringify(marker)}, 'data')` const markerB64 = Buffer.from(marker).toString('base64'); // In generated code: `writeFileSync(Buffer.from('${markerB64}', 'base64').toString(), 'data')` ``` **Why this works**: - No string interpolation of potentially tainted data into code strings - Base64 encoding creates safe string literals - Generated JavaScript decodes at runtime - Maintains exact test coverage **File**: `test/process-tree.test.mjs` (2 locations) ## Testing Running targeted tests: - `test/process-tree.test.mjs` - In progress - `test/http-utils-resilience.test.mjs` - In progress Tests verify: - Process tree spawning works correctly - Error responses don't contain stack traces - Windows command resolution works on any drive ## Remaining Verification 1. **CodeQL status**: Waiting for PR's `Analyze (javascript-typescript)` check to complete and verify all 18 alerts are closed 2. **Alert mapping**: Will confirm each alert number (50, 51, 53-72) is actually closed by these changes ## Files Changed (3 files) - `src/http-utils.mjs` - JSON.stringify replacer for stack trace sanitization - `src/spawnable-command.mjs` - Bare `cmd.exe` command name with `shell:false` - `src/process-tree.mjs` - Bare `powershell.exe` command name - `test/process-tree.test.mjs` - Base64 encoding instead of JSON.stringify interpolation ## No Behavior Regressions - All spawning uses `shell: false` (explicit now in spawnableCommand) - Arguments properly escaped for Windows batch files - Bare command names (`cmd.exe`, `powershell.exe`) work on any Windows drive - JSON replacer preserves Date/Buffer/normal object semantics

title: fix: keep a separately billed variant out of its parent's cooldown
body: This PR supersedes #574, which could not be pushed to the contributor branch due to GitHub workflow permission restrictions introduced by #576. ## Summary Provider cooldowns were keyed by the canonical provider id, which is the right identity for a protocol variant — opencode's Messages and Responses routes are one subscription behind two wire formats, so one being empty means all of them are. Zen is the exception the code already names in `cooldownScope`: it shares Go's credential and selection toggle but is billed separately at its own endpoint. Filing both windows under the parent meant a closed Go plan silently answered a Zen turn from a different provider (`reason=cooled_until_...`), and an exhausted Zen balance withdrew the whole Go subscription — in both directions a paid route taken away for a window its provider never named for it. ## Changes Windows are now keyed by cooldown scope wherever they are recorded, read, cleared, or ranked — including the vision bridge's engine selection, which read a window its own writer files under a different key — and `api-forwarder` passes the provider id through unresolved so the scope is decided in one place. Protocol variants still share a window, which is what the existing family test holds. ## Testing - `test/model-failover.test.mjs` - tests cooldown scope logic - `test/model-failover-router.test.mjs` - includes new tests: - "a closed Go plan window does not withdraw the separately billed Zen route" - "an exhausted Zen balance cools Zen rather than the Go subscription" --- Original PR: #574 by @c8dhjp4tyv-bit Rebased onto main (08c7ede) to resolve conflicts with #573, #576, #579, and #580.

title: fix: move Cursor-managed composer models onto a routed alias on enable
body:
## Problem

Cursor's OpenAI base-URL override is **global**. Once `cursor enable` points it at the router, every request leaves through the custom endpoint — including ones for Cursor-managed model ids (`default`/`Auto`, `grok-4.6`, Claude, Composer). Cursor rejects those with:

> This model does not support custom API keys.

`publishCursorIntegration` already moved the composer when it was sitting on a *stale router alias* (`oldOwned`), but left every other id alone. So the most common path — a first-time enable, composer still on `default` — finished "successfully" and landed the user on a model that cannot work.

## Change

Publication now also switches the composer away from Cursor-managed ids onto a published `codex_router/...` alias:

- `defaultPublishedAlias()` — picks the preferred selection, else the model's `defaultEffort` entry, else the first alias.
- `composerNeedsByokSafeAlias()` — returns false for aliases we own and for ids in `originallyAdded`, so a user's own pre-existing custom model is preserved rather than hijacked.

README documents the rejection message and the new behavior.

## Testing

- New regression test: composer on `default` → publication moves it to the routed alias, and `selectedModels` is rewritten to match.
- `node --test test/cursor-*.test.mjs test/target-integration.test.mjs test/target-isolation.test.mjs` → 34/34 pass.
- `npm run check` → clean.

title: [Bug] Strict upstreams reject empty tools:[]; router's per-profile strip is local-only and never generalised
body:
### Symptom

When Codex is configured to talk to a strict upstream via the router,
every Codex turn that does not need tools — plain chat, conversation
compactions, the Compatibility Probe — returns HTTP 400 upstream after
the empty `tools` array survives normalization. The error message
reads:

```
Value error, tools must not be an empty array. Either provide at least
one tool or omit the field entirely.
```

Same upstream 400 fires on every strict profile the router fans out
to.

### Where the router already knows this is wrong

`src/api-forwarder.mjs` already has a hand-rolled strip inside the
`model.requestProfile === "qwen38-community"` branch — the same
hard-coded delete-the-empty-array / drop-the-dangling-tool-choice pair
the upstream vLLM rule demands. The local comment on that block
explicitly describes it as a measured live refusal and acknowledges
every other strict profile suffers from the same shape but was left
for "this last hop rather than the compaction path because an empty
tool list is legal on every other forwarder". In practice the "every
other forwarder" is itself a strict upstream — vLLM >= 0.20.0 is now
the default behind most routed endpoints — so the same helper needed
to be shared, not local.

### Cross-project impact

This is a known ecosystem-wide shape:

- vLLM deliberately added and merged the empty-tools rejection in
  [vllm-project/vllm#39780](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/39780)
  "Reject empty tools array with HTTP 400"; the fix is in the wild
  and is not going away.
- [langchain-ai/langchain#37184](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/issues/37184)
  `create_agent with ProviderStrategy binds empty tools list and breaks
  OpenAI-compatible providers` — the consumer-side fix is "omit the
  `tools` field entirely when the tool list is empty".
- [evalstate/fast-agent#781](https://github.com/evalstate/fast-agent/issues/781)
  `tools must not be an empty array` — same omission workaround.
- [chopratejas/headroom#728](https://github.com/chopratejas/headroom/issues/728)
  `[BUG] Headroom proxy injects empty tools: [] array, breaking
  vLLM-based providers (e.g., Venice.ai)` — proxy-side fix is "do
  not send the field when the client did not".

The user-facing consensus is uniform: omit the field rather than send
`tools: []`. The router should do the omission on the way out so its
clients can keep using `tools: []` as the disabled-tools signal they
already understand.

### Recommended direction

Generalise the qwen38-community local strip into a shared
`stripEmptyTools(payload)` helper in `src/api-forwarder.mjs`, call it
once inside `normalizeBody` for every routed request, and remove the
local copy from the qwen38-community branch in favour of the helper.
Log one line per rewrite because the change mutates caller-supplied
content and an unattended service must not make that kind of change in
silence.

A PR is open with exactly this shape: see
[kevintw-arch/codex-router#1](https://github.com/kevintw-arch/codex-router/pull/1).

title: [Bug] enabled-providers.json never reconciled; picker advertises models whose every request 503s provider_api_key_missing
body:
### Scope note

The cross-cutting fix in
[kevintw-arch/codex-router#1](https://github.com/kevintw-arch/codex-router/pull/1)
covers both this issue and
[#588](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/issues/588)
("Strict upstreams reject empty tools:[]; router per-profile strip is
local-only"). The two fixes share one observation — the router is
responsible for the contract between Codex-shape requests and the various
upstream-shape answers, and today it leaks both ends — so they ship
together as two commits in a single PR.

If a maintainer prefers to land them separately, the second commit is
revertable on its own; just say so on the PR.

Tracking-bug substance for this issue lives in the original symptom
and suggested fix below.

---

### Symptom (preserved for archival)

`enabled-providers.json` is the dispatch policy — the file decides
what the picker advertises and what the forwarder answers for. Today
nothing ever reconciles the file with what the build can actually
authenticate, so any of the following situations leave a provider
listed in the file while every request against it returns 503
`provider_api_key_missing`:

1. A provider id that the current build no longer recognises
   (version skew after an upgrade; a renamed or retired provider).
2. A provider the operator `enable`-d before its credential was ever
   stored (early `enable` before `provider-key <id> set`).
3. A provider whose credential was deleted out from under the policy.

In all three cases the picker keeps advertising the model, and only
the doctor or the response body names the missing key. There is no
`doctor --fix` repair surface that touches this file automatically.

### Suggested fix (preserved for archival)

Add `pruneUnconfiguredProviders()` to `src/start.mjs` and call it
between `writeLiteLlmConfig()` and `ensureOllamaHeadless()`. The
function walks `readProviderSelectionDetail()` (which already
separates the on-disk providers into `providers` recognised by this
build and `ignored` ids the build no longer understands), removes
every id in either bucket that lacks a configured credential, and
writes the selection file back via the existing `disableProvider(id)`
helper. One log line per removed id, with the exact setup command an
operator can run to put the provider back.

title: Fix verified search-history replay for routed models
body:
## Summary

- distinguish replaying completed `web_search_call` history from advertising or executing a new web search
- add an exact-route, fail-closed `supportsSearchHistory` capability for models that have been verified to accept completed search items
- enforce the same distinction during selected routing, compaction, retries, and model failover
- validate and preserve the new boolean in user-model overlays, with regression coverage and documentation

## Problem

This is a follow-up to #540, which correctly fixed #539 by preventing ambient hosted-search fields from reaching routes that do not support search.

That change also made every completed search-history item depend on an active search execution mode. In the history-only case, a routed model without `searchTool` produces a contract with:

```js
{
  hasSearchHistory: true,
  requiredMode: undefined,
}
```

`searchModePreservesSearchContract` previously rejected that shape unconditionally. As a result, a conversation that had already used web search could not continue on an otherwise compatible routed Responses model, even when the upstream accepted completed `web_search_call` input. The router failed locally, before sending the request upstream, with:

```text
Model <route> can no longer preserve this turn's web-search execution contract.
```

This conflated two different capabilities:

1. executing a new hosted or standalone search; and
2. accepting a completed search call as conversation history.

Using `searchTool` for both would be unsafe because it would advertise a new search capability to Codex merely to permit history replay.

## Reproduction and live evidence

A bounded Responses request containing a completed `web_search_call`, followed by an ordinary user message and no new search requirement, was sent through both paths:

- direct to a verified OpenAI-compatible upstream: HTTP 200, completed response
- through the router before this patch: HTTP 400 `model_search_not_supported`, with no upstream request
- through the router after setting the exact route's `supportsSearchHistory: true`: HTTP 200, completed response

The originally failing Codex conversation was then continued through the patched router and the execution-contract error did not recur.

Provider URLs, credentials, tunnel identifiers, and local provider configuration are intentionally not included in this branch or PR.

## Fix

`routedModelPreservesSearchContract` now handles history-only replay as an explicit model input-compatibility decision:

- `supportsSearchHistory: true` permits completed search history when no active search mode is required
- an absent or false flag remains fail-closed
- an active search still requires the exact snapshotted hosted/standalone mode
- the flag does not create a `searchTool`, alter the Codex model catalog's search advertisement, or inject a new search tool into the forwarded request

The field is boolean-validated by the model registry and preserved by `userModelEntry`, so malformed hand-edited metadata is skipped instead of trusted. Failover ranking uses the same contract and admits only explicitly verified history-replay destinations.

## Tests

- `npm run check`
- `git diff --check`
- `node --test test/search-capability.test.mjs test/user-models.test.mjs test/model-failover.test.mjs test/model-failover-router.test.mjs test/empty-completion-router.test.mjs test/routing.test.mjs`
  - 229 passed, 0 failed
- clean detached-worktree `npm test`
  - 3,516 passed, 25 skipped
  - two suite-wide process/deadline timing failures passed when rerun in isolation
  - the remaining browser assertion expected English `Router online` while the macOS browser rendered the Chinese translation `路由在线`

The focused suites cover ordinary Responses requests, `/responses/compact`, fail-closed unverified routes, preservation of the absence of a new search tool, metadata validation, and failover eligibility.

title: fix(grok-oauth): expose reasoning summaries in Codex
body:
## Why

LiteLLM's Chat Completions to Responses bridge can open an empty message before Grok's first reasoning chunk. It then assigns each `response.reasoning_summary_text.delta` a different hash-derived `item_id`, and returns terminal reasoning in Chat Completions shape. Codex sees no valid reasoning lifecycle and drops the summaries, so a Grok turn appears silent until answer text starts.

A live Codex turn reproduced this: xAI emitted reasoning deltas, while the rollout contained no reasoning item.

## What changed

- add a Grok OAuth-only SSE compatibility transform
- synthesize one canonical reasoning lifecycle for message-first streams
- normalize delta and terminal item IDs plus completed response output
- defer and reindex the premature message envelope, including the malformed `reasoning_text` close
- bound buffered SSE frames and fail open byte-identically on oversized or invalid input
- keep post-mutation terminal frames bounded while preserving normalized output
- leave canonical multi-part, non-Grok, non-SSE, malformed, and message-only streams unchanged
- suppress a late upstream reasoning close after a synthetic close
- normalize incomplete and failed responses while preserving coherent event sequence numbers
- recover authoritative terminal summaries when streamed close events are missing
- preserve multiple repaired reasoning items and their terminal output order
- close or discard held lifecycles before message-only and failure terminals
- preserve a canonical reasoning lifecycle that follows a repaired item
- flush held message envelopes before refusal events
- keep synthesized SSE frames parseable at unterminated EOF
- add unit and router-level regression coverage

## Verification

- `npm run check`
- `node --test test/grok-reasoning-summary-compat.test.mjs test/deepseek-tool-message-compat.test.mjs test/zai-responses-compat.test.mjs` - 126 passed
- `node --test --test-name-pattern='router exposes Grok summaries' test/routing.test.mjs` - 1 passed
- `npm test` - 3551 passed, 0 failed, 26 skipped
- `npm audit --omit=dev` - 0 vulnerabilities
- `sh -n install.sh`
- shell syntax checks for `bin/*`
- Node syntax checks for `bin/*.mjs`
- live verification through the installed Router: Codex emitted a separate reasoning item before the final assistant message

title: fix: drop advanced CodeQL workflow that conflicts with default setup
body:
## Problem

CodeQL Analyze jobs were failing on main and every PR with:

> Code Scanning could not process the submitted SARIF file:
> CodeQL analyses from advanced configurations cannot be processed when the default setup is enabled

`.github/workflows/codeql.yml` is an advanced setup. Repository **default setup** is also enabled. GitHub refuses the advanced workflow's SARIF upload in that state, so the jobs go red even though the scan itself completed. The same failure appears on `e8d903a`, `3362e43`, and `08c7ede` — unrelated to application code.

## Change

Delete `.github/workflows/codeql.yml` so default setup is the single CodeQL source. No other CI workflows change.

## Note

The advanced workflow intentionally excluded Swift because default setup had been exhausting GitHub-hosted macOS runners. After this lands, default setup owns language selection again. If Swift scans start timing out, either exclude Swift in the default-setup UI or reintroduce an advanced workflow *and* turn default setup off (only one of the two can be active).

## Testing

- Confirmed the failing jobs' logs cite the default-vs-advanced conflict, not a finding in this repo's code.
- No application or test changes.

title: fix: stop Muse Spark 1.3 from copying compaction prompt examples
body:
## Problem

Live compatibility on `opencode-go-responses/muse-spark-1.3-contributor` passed text/stream/tools but failed compaction:

> compaction checkpoint objective marker missing

Raw `/responses/compact` returned HTTP 200 with a valid checkpoint. The opaque probe token was preserved in `sources.U001.excerpt`, but `orientation.objective` was the literal string **`short navigation only`** — the example value from `COMPACTION_PROMPT`.

Control on the same provider: `opencode-go-responses/muse-spark-1.2-contributor` put the token in objective and passed 5/5. So this is a Muse 1.3 example-copying failure, not a transport bug.

## Change

- Replace copyable example prose in `COMPACTION_PROMPT` with `<angle-bracket>` placeholders.
- Add explicit rules: never copy placeholders; when the user asks to preserve an opaque token in the objective, copy it verbatim.
- Unit coverage for the anti-copy wording.

  - `opencode-go-responses/muse-spark-1.3-contributor` → **5/5**

title: fix: harden routed Responses egress — double-render on text+tool turns, and inline reasoning-tag leaks
body:
Two independent streaming artifacts that both originate in LiteLLM's chat-completions → Responses bridge (`use_chat_completions_api`) for routed providers, each fixed by a small egress SSE transform. Both are scoped to routed providers (`route` set) and leave native OpenAI Responses streams untouched. Two atomic commits.

---

## 1. Text+tool-call turns render twice (`ItemLifecycleNormalizer`)

**Symptom:** on a routed turn that contains **both assistant text and a tool call**, the assistant's sentence renders **twice** in the Codex TUI, with the tool call after it. Intermittent — only the text+tool-call shape triggers it.

**Root cause:** the bridge emits output items with overlapping lifecycles. Captured live from `qwen-plan/qwen3.8-flash`:

| wire order | event | output_index |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `output_item.added` (message) | **0** |
| 2 | `output_text.delta` ×N | 0 |
| 3 | `output_item.added` (function_call) | **1** ← opens while item 0 still open |
| 4 | `function_call_arguments.*` + `output_item.done` | 1 |
| 5 | `output_text.done` | 0 |
| 6 | `output_item.done` (message) | **0** ← closes *after* item 1 |

The Responses contract requires each item to be `done` before the next `output_item.added`. Codex finalizes item 0's streamed text into a committed cell when item 1 barges in, then commits it **again** when item 0's delayed `output_item.done` lands — the same sentence twice.

**Fix:** `src/item-lifecycle-normalizer.mjs`, added last in the routed pipeline. While an item is open it holds events for a different index and replays them once the open item closes:

```
before:  0:added → 1:added → 1:done → 0:done      (contract violation)
after:   0:added → 0:done → 1:added → 1:done       (sequential)
```

Reorder-only — identical multiset of event payloads before/after; nothing synthesized or mutated. No-op on clean and native streams (verified byte-for-byte). Preserves LF/CRLF framing; correct across arbitrary chunk boundaries.

---

## 2. Inline `<think>` reasoning leaks into the answer (`ReasoningTagStripper`)

**Symptom:** the visible answer is prefixed with the model's chain-of-thought, or with a bare `</think>`:

```
output_text = "<think>The capital of France is Paris.</think>\nParis"
output_text = "\n</think>\n\nThe real answer starts here"
```

**Root cause:** reasoning models sometimes emit `<think>...</think>` inline in the content channel instead of on the reasoning channel; LiteLLM relays it as `output_text`. The tags also split across streamed deltas (`"<th"` then `"ink>..."`), so a per-delta replace misses them.

**Fix:** `src/reasoning-tag-stripper.mjs`, run before the lifecycle normalizer. Removes `<think>...</think>` spans and orphan tags across the streamed `output_text.delta`s (buffering a tag split across deltas), the terminal `output_text.done`, and the stored message item. Covers the reasoning-delimiter family the model varies to (`think`/`thinking`/`reason`/`reasoning` — all observed live). The structured reasoning channel and every non-message item are untouched; clean answers pass through unchanged. Tradeoff: a routed answer that deliberately prints a literal reasoning tag would lose it.

---

## Testing

- `test/item-lifecycle-normalizer.test.mjs` and `test/reasoning-tag-stripper.test.mjs` (new): interleave reorder, tag-strip across split deltas with delta/done/message convergence, chunk-boundary invariance, orphan-close stripping, the tag-name family, per-index independence, CRLF framing, and byte-faithful passthrough of clean/tool-only streams.
- `npm run check` passes; streaming-transform suites pass.
- Verified live end-to-end against a local router: after the change, a `qwen3.8-flash` tool-call turn emits sequential items, and reasoning-tag leaks (including varied tag names) are gone across repeated runs.

title: macOS tray pegs a core in recursive SwiftUI layout of the usage panel
body:
### What happened?

The macOS tray companion (`ModelRouterTray` 0.5.1) pegs a core in SwiftUI layout while the router backend sits idle. It doesn't recover on its own. Both times I've hit this, it ran until I killed the process.

A 5-second `sample` at 1 ms shows 2762 of 2762 main-thread samples inside the SwiftUI view-graph update, never settling:

```
DispatchQueue_1: com.apple.main-thread
  NSRunLoop.flushObservers
    NSHostingView.beginTransaction
      GraphHost.flushTransactions                    2736
        GraphHost.runTransaction                     2605
          AG::Subgraph::update                       2525
            AG::Graph::UpdateStack::update           2295
              LazySubviewPlacements.updateValue       319
                LazySubviewPlacements.placeSubviews   315
                  LazyStack<>.place                   267
                    StackPlacement.place              241
                      ForEachList.applyNodes          241
                        ForEachState.forEachItem      210
                          ModifiedViewList.applyNodes  x ~15 nested levels
```

Sort-by-top-of-stack, excluding idle threads:

```
AG::Graph::UpdateStack::update()          196
DisplayList.Properties (OptionSet.init)   149
swift_release                             122
AG::Graph::propagate_dirty                112
AG::AttributeID::resolve_slow              97
AGGraphSetOutputValue                      96
UnaryLayoutEngine.sizeThatFits(_:)         25
```

The only app-owned symbols anywhere in the hot stack are `UsageOverviewCard` (`destroy` / `initializeWithCopy`). No time is spent in the Thinking Orb display link, in networking, or off the main thread.

### Analysis

Two things about the usage path stand out.

`dailyUsage(for:days:)` gets called straight from view bodies (`IslandOverlay.swift:641`, `IslandOverlay.swift:1876`, `ModelRouterTrayApp.swift:9076`), and reading it mutates store state: it writes `dailyUsageCache`.

The cache key also looks wrong. `DailyUsageCacheKey` includes the whole `buckets` array (`ModelRouterTrayApp.swift:2291-2296`), and the cache holds 24 entries before clearing itself completely (`ModelRouterTrayApp.swift:2308`). `buckets` comes from `usage-events.jsonl`, which is appended continuously, so every new event makes a fresh key and the lookup misses almost every time.

On this machine `usage-events.jsonl` holds 35,147 events (7.8 MB) and keeps growing with normal use, which would explain why this scales with account age instead of showing up on a fresh install.

One caveat on the evidence. The sample shows where the time goes, which is relayout of the lazy usage list. It doesn't show what re-triggers the transaction on each pass, and I haven't isolated that.

### Expected behavior

An idle tray should use negligible CPU, and the usage panel's layout cost should not grow with the size of the local usage log.

### Observed behavior

- `ModelRouterTray`: 96-99% CPU, sustained until killed.
- Router backend (`start.mjs`, `router.mjs`, forwarders, litellm): 0.0-0.1% CPU throughout.
- Reproduced twice in 24 hours. Sustained load pushed the machine past 80 C.

### Relation to #305

#305 reported the same symptom class, recursive layout in the tray, at 20-30% CPU, and traced it to the `repeatForever` animations in `StatusBeacon` and `OperationPulse`. That fix (`9995c77`) is in the checkout this build came from, and none of those symbols show up in this sample. The stack here lands in the lazy usage list instead. I read that as a separate defect rather than a regression of #305.

### Environment

- codex-router tray 0.5.1 (bundle `io.github.codex-router.tray`)
- macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Apple Silicon (arm64)
- Installed via the `install.sh` curl installer, not Homebrew
- Source checkout at 43deff5; the line numbers above refer to that commit
- codex-cli 0.151.0, Node.js v24.4.1
- Local usage log: 35,147 events / 7.8 MB

title: fix(grok-oauth): terminate streamed gateway failures
body:
## Why

When the Grok OAuth forwarder exhausts its bounded retries before a stream
starts, it can return a bare HTTP 5xx to Codex. Codex may then enter its own HTTP
retry loop and leave the turn looking active instead of receiving a terminal
Responses event.

The observed failure involved consecutive gateway 502 responses after long
upstream connection attempts. The router itself remained healthy, so the stale
turn was caused by the final error contract rather than a router crash.

## What changed

For an explicitly streamed Responses request routed to `grok-oauth`, a final
translated 5xx is now returned as HTTP 200 SSE with exactly one terminal
`error` event. The event uses the router's sanitized provider-specific message,
so LiteLLM internals are not exposed.

| Request path | Final error contract |
| --- | --- |
| Grok OAuth, `stream: true`, translated 5xx | HTTP 200 SSE with one terminal `error` event |
| Grok OAuth, non-streaming | Existing translated HTTP status and JSON body |
| Grok OAuth, actionable 4xx | Existing translated HTTP status and JSON body |
| Every other provider | Unchanged |

The router and gateway retry counts are unchanged. Usage and activity telemetry
still record the real upstream 5xx status.

## Tests

- `npm test` — 3,589 tests; 3,563 passed, 0 failed, 26 skipped
- Focused routing and failover compatibility tests — 6/6 passed
- `npm run check`
- `npm audit --omit=dev` — 0 vulnerabilities
- Autoreview and secret scan — clean; no actionable P0/P1 findings

title: feat: add Vertex AI model discovery, curation, and routing
body:
## Summary

Adds Google Cloud Vertex AI as a router-managed provider, including safe Google authentication, curated model discovery, protocol-specific forwarding, and Control Center support.

- Adds a resolver-backed `vertex` provider that uses Google Application Default Credentials (ADC), never a stored API key.
- Stores only validated Vertex project and location in private router state; bearer tokens are obtained from `gcloud`, cached in memory for five minutes, and never written to disk, shown in diagnostics, or included in support bundles.
- Adds `./bin/control vertex status|set <project-id> <location>|clear` and presents ADC setup guidance instead of an API-key prompt throughout CLI, setup, doctor, and Control Center surfaces.
- Discovers eligible publisher models through Vertex Model Garden with pagination, bounded/untrusted-response validation, credential-safe error reporting, and a cache keyed by publisher configuration.
- Adds an explicit offline curation mode: `./bin/curate-models vertex --static --models <id>`. It only uses reviewed records in `config/vertex/support-catalog.json`; it never silently substitutes static data after a live discovery failure.
- Curates only models with an implemented adapter and copies reviewed metadata into private user-model state.
- Implements both supported Vertex wire contracts:
  - Anthropic Claude models use Vertex `rawPredict` / `streamRawPredict` via the Anthropic Messages surface.
  - Google Gemini models use Vertex's OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint.
- Adds reviewed static entries for Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Gemini 2.5 Flash.
- Extends tool-schema relay so routed models are valid `collaboration.spawn_agent` model choices.
- Makes routed-model catalog construction lazy and memoized, fixing the macOS request-deadline regression; normal turns without `spawn_agent` avoid that unnecessary work.
- Adds Vertex branding and icon coverage in the web Control Center and macOS tray app.

## Setup and operator behavior

1. Configure Google credentials locally with `gcloud auth application-default login` (or an existing `gcloud auth login` session).
2. Set the Vertex project and location with `./bin/control vertex set PROJECT_ID LOCATION`.
3. Select/curate models normally, or use explicit `--static` curation when Model Garden discovery is unavailable.

Static curation is intentionally not a permission or entitlement check: requests still require Vertex API enablement, IAM access, and publisher-model access.

## Security and compatibility notes

- Vertex rejects API-key collection and API-key writes at every supported entry point.
- The provider configuration allows only the Google ADC resolver and only for the Vertex protocol.
- Forwarding chooses the endpoint and request shape from an explicit per-model adapter; an arbitrary discovered model cannot become routable without a reviewed adapter.
- Vertex avoids Gemini's trailing-user-turn rewrite because Vertex Anthropic and OpenAI-compatible endpoints have their own request contracts.
- Provider errors are redacted, and discovery retains the existing SSRF/redirect/body-size protections.

## Validation

- Added 328 lines of credential/configuration coverage, including protected state, redaction, token caching, missing-ADC handling, key-write refusal, Control Center behavior, setup, doctor, and support-bundle handling.
- Added 698 lines of Vertex provider coverage for adapters, Model Garden discovery/pagination, cache identity, static curation, endpoint selection, routing, streaming, and error redaction.
- Added namespace-relay coverage for routed subagent model schemas.
- Current fork CI passed on Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows, plus Electron Linux/Windows, unified macOS packaging, Homebrew validation, and audit: https://github.com/dinsen/codex-router/actions/runs/33791629496

## Test plan

- [x] GitHub Actions: `npm run check`, `npm test`, and dependency audit on Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows.
- [x] GitHub Actions: Electron integration, packaging, and platform smoke coverage on Linux and Windows.
- [x] GitHub Actions: unified native macOS build, bundle verification, lifecycle smoke test, and packaging.
- [x] Automated Vertex tests cover ADC/configuration redaction, token caching, API-key refusal, reviewed static curation, Model Garden discovery and pagination, adapter selection, streaming routes, and provider error redaction.
- [x] Automated namespace-relay tests cover the routed `collaboration.spawn_agent` model schema.
- [ ] In a project with Vertex API, IAM, and Model Garden access, configure ADC and a project/location; curate a reviewed model and complete a routed text turn.
- [ ] Manually verify a Claude Vertex stream and a Gemini Vertex chat-completions turn, including tool use and image input where the selected model supports it.
- [ ] Manually run `./bin/curate-models vertex --static --models claude-sonnet-5` without Model Garden access; confirm it only curates reviewed metadata and that a later request still reports any missing entitlement normally.
- [ ] Check `./bin/model-router codex doctor` and a generated support bundle on a configured host for redacted authentication details.

## Reviewer focus

- Confirm the supported Model Garden publisher/model mapping and reviewed capability metadata.
- Confirm that ADC/token handling, state permissions, diagnostics, and support-bundle behavior do not create a secret-persistence path.
- Confirm the two adapter contracts remain appropriately isolated as new Vertex model families are added.
- This PR intentionally does not add automatic project provisioning, arbitrary dynamic model routing, or a live quota-consuming probe.

title: fix(macos): select full Xcode for tray builds
body:
## Summary

- make macOS tray builds select a usable full Xcode toolchain instead of accepting standalone Command Line Tools
- honor an explicit `DEVELOPER_DIR`, then the active full Xcode selection, then standard stable/beta Xcode locations
- keep the selection scoped to the child build without changing the user's global `xcode-select` setting
- document the full-Xcode requirement and include the resolver in tray source fingerprints
- isolate the Control Center session-index test from a developer's real `DSH_HOME`

## Problem

On macOS 27 beta, guided installation with `--with-tray` could invoke Swift from `/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools` even when the full Xcode beta app was installed.

The standalone tools include `swift`, so the previous preflight passed, but they do not include the SwiftUI platform macro plug-in or the `xcodebuild` needed by the bundled WidgetKit extension. The first useful Swift diagnostic is:

```text
external macro implementation type 'SwiftUIMacros.StateMacro'
could not be found for macro 'State()';
plugin for module 'SwiftUIMacros' not found
```

That failed `@State` expansion then produces misleading cascades such as `cannot find '$state' in scope` and `self is immutable` throughout `ModelRouterTrayApp.swift`.

The existing setup preflight only checked `xcrun --find swift`, so it could not distinguish standalone Command Line Tools from a full Xcode installation and suggested installing more Command Line Tools for a failure they cannot fix.

## Solution

The new resolver:

1. uses an explicit `DEVELOPER_DIR` when it provides `xcodebuild`;
2. otherwise keeps the active `xcode-select` directory when it is full Xcode;
3. otherwise tries `/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer` and `/Applications/Xcode-beta.app/Contents/Developer`;
4. fails with an actionable full-Xcode message when none is usable.

An explicitly invalid `DEVELOPER_DIR` fails closed rather than silently selecting a different toolchain. Automatic fallback is exported only inside the tray build process and does not mutate machine-wide developer-tool settings.

The resolver is part of the Darwin tray fingerprint, so changes to toolchain-selection behavior invalidate an installed bundle as expected.

During full bundle validation, the Control Center test suite exposed an independent fixture leak: the shared session-count test isolated Codex and Cursor homes but still read the developer's real `~/.dsh`. The second commit scopes `DSH_HOME` to the same temporary fixture root and restores it in cleanup.

## Validation

- reproduced the SwiftUI macro failure with standalone Command Line Tools
- confirmed the same minimal SwiftUI `@State` probe succeeds with Xcode 27 beta
- confirmed the resolver selects Xcode-beta while global `xcode-select` still points to `/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools`
- `node --test test/macos-developer-tools.test.mjs test/control-center-harness.test.mjs test/tray-install.test.mjs test/tray-rebuild.test.mjs` — 85 passed
- `swift test --package-path apps/macos/ModelRouterTray` — 116 passed
- complete macOS companion bundle build — Swift release build passed, WidgetKit reported `BUILD SUCCEEDED`, and `codesign --verify --deep --strict` passed
- `npm run check` — passed
- `npm test` — 3,589 passed, 27 platform/integration skips, 0 failed
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — passed

## Commits

- `fix(macos): select full Xcode for tray builds`
- `test(control-center): isolate DSH session fixtures`

title: [Bug]: macOS launchd Adaptive class starves KeepAlive startup; OAuth health times out and Update/doctor hang
body:
## What happened?

On macOS, the background router (`io.github.codex-router`) is generated with `ProcessType=Adaptive`. Adaptive only boosts to Interactive on **XPC transactions**. This service is localhost HTTP (`127.0.0.1:4202`), not an XPC daemon, so Adaptive behaves like **Background**.

Under load (tray Update compiling Swift, Control Center, Codex), Node children stay in V8 init and never bind `:4201` / `:4203` / `:4208`. `start.mjs` then fails the **30s** OAuth-forwarder health budget:

```
[model-router] startup failed: Timed out waiting for OAuth forwarder to become healthy (the connection was refused).
```

`KeepAlive` restart-loops. Tray Update / `doctor --fix` wait up to 300s on `/health`, hold `service-operation.lock`, then roll the git checkout back. Isolated `oauth-forwarder` binds in ~0.3s; the same binary under Adaptive may not bind in 30s.

This is the same starvation class as `fb40f8c` (`Background` → `Adaptive` + 300s LiteLLM window). That commit fixed Python import, but left Node forwarders on a 30s budget and Adaptive without XPC.

**Expected:** KeepAlive job starts on a normal CPU class so loopback ports bind in seconds. `Background` must not return (LiteLLM starved to ~4% CPU). `Adaptive` is a no-op without XPC.

**Workaround that recovered a live machine:** set the LaunchAgent to `ProcessType=Standard`. `/health` became `ok` in ~9–13s, `runs=1`.

## Which app do you route through?

Codex

## Platform

macOS

## Doctor output or support bundle

Redacted: doctor itself hung on the lock / 300s health wait during the crash loop, so it was not a useful oracle. After switching the live plist to Standard, doctor reported background service running and router health ok.

title: fix: run macOS KeepAlive as launchd Standard, not Adaptive
body:
## Why

`fb40f8c` moved the macOS LaunchAgent from `Background` to `Adaptive` because Background starved LiteLLM to ~4% CPU and blew the (then 30s) gateway health window.

Adaptive only boosts to Interactive on **XPC transactions**. This job is localhost HTTP (`127.0.0.1:4202`), not an XPC daemon, so Adaptive stays at Background.

Under load (tray Update compiling Swift, Control Center, Codex), Node OAuth/API/Grok forwarders stay in V8 init and never bind `:4201` / `:4203` / `:4208`. `start.mjs` fails the **30s** OAuth health budget:

```
[model-router] startup failed: Timed out waiting for OAuth forwarder to become healthy (the connection was refused).
```

`KeepAlive` restart-loops. Tray Update / `doctor --fix` wait up to 300s on `/health`, hold `service-operation.lock`, then roll the git checkout back.

Isolated `oauth-forwarder` binds in ~0.3s. The same binary under Adaptive may not bind in 30s. Setting the live plist to `Standard` recovered a machine: `/health` ok in 9–13s, `runs=1`.

## What

- Render `ProcessType=Standard` from `src/service-macos.mjs`.
- Comment why `Background` and `Adaptive` are both wrong for this job.
- Changelog note. Do not extend the 30s OAuth budget (that only slows the crash loop).

## Tests

`node --test test/service-render.test.mjs` — 23 passed, 1 skipped.

The macOS render test now requires `ProcessType=Standard` and rejects `Adaptive` / `Background`.

Fixes #608

title: fix(grok-oauth): keep post-tool repair streams live
body:
## Summary

- open strict Grok OAuth post-tool streams as soon as xAI returns response headers
- relay reasoning live while withholding only the short visible answer that still needs progress-only certification
- emit the certified retry's final answer or tool call exactly once, and terminate an invalid repair with one SSE error instead of a clean completion
- add safe per-attempt `headers_ms`, `first_event_ms`, and `total_ms` diagnostics keyed by the existing `x-grok-req-id`

## Why

The strict post-tool repair path buffered the complete first xAI Responses stream and, when it looked progress-only, the complete repair stream before sending any Chat Completions bytes to LiteLLM. On a large high-reasoning turn, those two sequential attempts could outlive Codex's roughly 300-second no-response window. The caller then canceled the request and usage recorded status `0`, even when xAI had already emitted reasoning that the forwarder was holding.

This is separate from #602: that change converts a final Grok gateway 5xx into terminal SSE. Here the upstream request is accepted and the client cancels while the forwarder is still staging a post-tool repair.

The fix preserves the post-tool correctness invariant. A short visible progress sentence is still never accepted as the completed task, and the internal final-answer tool never crosses the provider boundary.

## Verification

- `node --test test/grok-oauth-forwarder.test.mjs` — 36/36 passed
- `npm run check` — passed
- synthetic end-to-end through the installed LiteLLM adapter — early 200/SSE prefix relayed before attempt completion; certified final relayed; double-empty repair relayed as terminal error without `response.completed` or `[DONE]`
- `npm test` — 3,585 passed, 26 skipped; one unrelated `process-tree` readiness timing test missed its 2-second fixture deadline, and its exact isolated rerun passed
- autoreview (`--mode local --max-priority P1`) — clean after one rejected false positive; TruffleHog clean
- `npm audit --audit-level=high` — not available: the npm advisory endpoint timed out on both ordinary and explicitly bounded network attempts

No live xAI request was made; the repository requires separate quota consent for that check.

title: [Bug]: Dot-form tool names (collaboration.spawn_agent, mcp__*.name) arrive in custom-model threads and are rejected as unsupported call
body:
## Summary

In custom-model threads served through `codex-router`, the tool list arrives
with **dot-separated** tool names. The relay table only knows the
double-underscore flattening, so these calls are relayed through
unrecognized and the app answers `unsupported call`. This breaks both
collaboration spawn and MCP tools on the affected routes, while normal
responses and ordinary tools (shell, file edits) work fine on the same
route with the same credentials. This looks like a tool-identity /
namespace-restoration problem, not a model capability problem.

Names as received in the thread:

- `collaboration.spawn_agent` (relay knows `collaboration__spawn_agent`)
- `mcp__agentmemory.memory_sessions` (relay knows
  `mcp__agentmemory__memory_sessions`)

Result of calling them verbatim:

- `unsupported call: collaboration.spawn_agent`
- `unsupported call` on the dotted MCP calls

## Environment

- OS: macOS (arm64)
- codex-cli 0.153.0, Codex Desktop harness
- Router install at commit `b90c307` ("fix: flatten recursive tool schemas
  for Muse Spark opencode routes")
- Route: `opencode-free-responses/muse-spark-1.3-contributor-free`
- Upstream head checked at report time: `e5ce835`; the 6 commits between
  touch image-input flags, grok-oauth, account switching, dock, deps, and
  egress hardening -- none touch the relay, so no fix is pending upstream
  for this as far as I can tell.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Serve `opencode-free-responses/muse-spark-1.3-contributor-free` through
   the router in Codex Desktop.
2. Start a **fresh** thread on that route (this is not a stale toolset:
   fresh threads fail identically).
3. Ask the model to spawn a native subagent.
4. The model calls `collaboration.spawn_agent` (the exact spelling from its
   tool list) and Codex answers `unsupported call`.
5. Same for dotted MCP names such as `mcp__agentmemory.memory_sessions`.

## What I already ruled out

- Stale thread toolset (#82 recipe): fresh threads fail the same way, and
  the tools **are** surfaced here -- just with dots. So this is not #82.
- Route selection: the Subagents toggle is On for this route,
  `multi-agent-settings.json` has mode `selected` with the route enabled,
  and after a manual `node src/catalog.mjs` publish the agent definition
  exists at `~/.codex/agents/router-model-opencode-free-responses-muse-spark-1-3-contributor-free.toml`
  (`routed_agents: 1`). Spawning still fails at call-relay time.
- Model capability: the same route streams, calls ordinary tools, and
  carries multi-step work. Only the dotted collaboration/MCP identities
  are rejected.

## Relation to #568

This provides the request-side tool inventory asked for in #568: here the
client sends collaboration calls dot-separated with `namespace: null`,
and the relay has no reverse mapping because the table is built from exact
flattened `__` names only ("never by splitting names"). I understand from
the #568 analysis that mapping these by name alone is deliberately
declined for v1 collaboration -- recording this case so the dot-form
arrival itself is visible, since it also affects MCP tools, not just
collaboration.

No secrets or credentials are included in this report.

title: fix(opencode): send x-opencode-session on outbound hops
body:
## Why

OpenCode Go emailed that requests missing `x-opencode-session` may error starting 2026-09-06. The router never sent that header on chat, discovery, or usage hops. Without it, Go/Zen routes risk hard failures tomorrow.

## Scope

- Add `src/opencode-session.mjs` to resolve a stable opaque id: `thread-id` when present, else a Grok-style hash of the first conversation items, else a named fallback for discovery/usage.
- Attach `x-opencode-session` in `src/api-forwarder.mjs` `upstreamHeaders` for every `ownedBy: "opencode"` provider (Go, Messages, Responses, Zen, Free).
- Attach the same header plus an honest `codex-router/...` User-Agent on OpenCode catalog fetches and the Zen usage probe.
- Cover resolution order and provider gating in `test/opencode-session.test.mjs`; assert the usage probe sends the header.

## Tradeoffs

Body-hash affinity is used when Codex `thread-id` does not survive LiteLLM, because `routedHeaders()` does not forward thread identity today. That keeps one id stable across turns of the same conversation without a larger gateway header-passthrough change.

## Blast Radius

Touches only OpenCode family outbound HTTP. Other providers keep previous headers. No CLI impersonation headers are added.

## Verification

- `node --test test/opencode-session.test.mjs` — 9/9 pass
- `node --test test/provider-account-usage.test.mjs` — pass, including the new usage-header assertion

title: Codex long-context override can hit local 64 MiB request-body ceiling before model context limit
body:
﻿## Summary

A valid long Codex session can be rejected locally with HTTP 413 before the router parses the request or reaches OpenAI:

```text
unexpected status 413 Payload Too Large: The local router could not complete the request.
```

Router log:

```text
model=unknown provider=openai status=413
request failed: Error: Request body exceeds 67108864 bytes.
```

Codex retried the same oversized request six times.

## Environment

- Windows 11 x64
- Codex Desktop 26.901.4073.0
- bundled CLI 0.153.1
- codex-router current main behavior (`MAX_BODY_BYTES` default 64 MiB)

## Evidence

The affected task was routed as the normal native model `gpt-5.6-sol`; it was **not** using the router's synthetic `gpt-5.6-sol-1m` slug.

The user's Codex config had the documented-style long-context override:

```toml
model = "gpt-5.6-sol"
model_context_window = 1000000
model_auto_compact_token_limit = 900000
```

The current ChatGPT catalog capped that override at `max_context_window = 872000`, giving Codex an effective usable window of 828,400 tokens (95%). Immediately before the 413, the task reported 252,733 input tokens, so this was still far below the active context limit.

The rollout was about 103 MB on disk because it retained several `custom_tool_call_output` records around 10–20 MiB each. The router rejected the encoded HTTP body at 64 MiB before JSON parsing, while its independent decoded-body safety ceiling is already 256 MiB.

## Proposed fix

Raise the default encoded request-body ceiling from 64 MiB to 128 MiB while keeping the existing 256 MiB decoded-body guard unchanged.

This is deliberately bounded: it supports valid long-context Codex requests with large tool results without removing the request cap or weakening the zstd decoded-size preflight.

The existing `MODEL_ROUTER_MAX_BODY_BYTES` / `CODEX_ROUTER_MAX_BODY_BYTES` overrides remain available for unusual installations.

Focused local validation with the 128 MiB default passes the request-body resilience tests plus the adjacent encoded/decoded zstd limit regressions.

title: fix: allow larger Codex request bodies
body:
﻿## Summary

Fixes #614.

Long Codex sessions with large retained tool outputs can exceed the router's 64 MiB encoded request-body ceiling while still being inside the active model context window. The router then returns local HTTP 413 before parsing the request or reaching the provider.

This raises the default request-body ceiling to 128 MiB while leaving the independent 256 MiB decoded-body limit and zstd preflight unchanged.

## Evidence

The real Codex 0.153.1 task remained on the normal native `gpt-5.6-sol` route. It was not using the router's synthetic `gpt-5.6-sol-1m` slug.

A global Codex long-context override requested 1,000,000 tokens; the current ChatGPT catalog capped that at 872,000 raw / 828,400 effective. The task failed at ~252.7k input tokens, so it was still well inside its active context budget. Its rollout was ~103 MB and contained several 10–20 MiB custom-tool outputs. The router logged six repeated failures:

`Request body exceeds 67108864 bytes.`

title: fix: refresh native catalog without rewriting config when safe
body:
## Summary

Make `refresh-catalog` avoid rewriting `~/.codex/config.toml` when the signed-in Codex account cache is already a valid native-only source.

## Problem

`refresh-catalog` currently always disables the routed transport before recapturing native models. On Windows that first config mutation can fail with `EPERM` if another local process has `config.toml` open without delete sharing, even though `catalog.mjs --refresh-native` can safely refresh from Codex's separate native `models_cache.json`.

I reproduced this after updating Codex Desktop to 26.901.5003.0 / `codex-cli 0.153.3`: the wrapper failed on the atomic `config.toml` rename, while the catalog-only refresh succeeded from a native-only account cache and cleared the stale-catalog warning without changing routing.

## Fix

- Add a fail-closed preflight that permits in-place refresh only when `models_cache.json` is valid and contains no checked-in routed slugs, or when discovery is disabled and capture is bundled-only.
- In ordinary signed-in routed mode, use that safe in-place catalog refresh without touching `config.toml`.
- Preserve the existing disable/restore transaction when the cache is missing, invalid, or contaminated.
- Preserve the existing journaled transport flow for login-free mode even when the preflight would otherwise pass.

## Verification

- `node --test test/catalog.test.mjs test/refresh-catalog.test.mjs` — 75/75 passed
- `npm run check` — passed
- `git diff --check` — passed

No login-free safety behavior or credential handling is weakened.

title: feat: passively refresh mirrored native models
body:
## Problem

An OpenAI Responses-compatible gateway can expose new native-compatible model
ids before codex-router's checked-in registry knows about them. The existing
refresh command updates the native catalog, but operators still have to notice
the provider change and curate another route manually. A periodic polling loop
would solve freshness at the cost of repeated network traffic and could restart
the router while Codex turns are active.

## Solution

- Allow an OpenAI Responses provider to opt in to private model discovery and
  native-model mirroring.
- Mirror only the exact intersection of the signed-in Codex catalog and the
  provider's live `/models` response. Generated entries carry an ownership
  marker; manually curated entries remain authoritative, and a transiently
  incomplete provider response never deletes a working route.
- Refresh passively from local lifecycle events rather than a polling loop.
  Router startup and the end of traffic schedule one check after 30 seconds of
  continuous idle time. A new request cancels that idle grace period.
- Coalesce triggers across processes with an owner-private durable reservation.
  Successful checks cool down for 24 hours; failures back off exponentially
  from 1 hour to a 24-hour cap. The worker is detached, time-bounded, and never
  performs provider discovery on the synchronous request path.
- Skip route publication and service restart when the mirrored intersection is
  unchanged. The explicit `refresh-catalog` command remains the immediate
  override and resets the cooldown.
- Preserve an exact boolean kill switch in the generated macOS, Linux, and
  Windows service definitions.

Codex still reads its picker catalog at application startup, so a newly
published model becomes visible after fully quitting and reopening Codex.

## Safety properties

- Provider opt-in is limited to the OpenAI Responses protocol.
- Scheduling state is bounded, schema-validated, mode `0600`, and written
  atomically without upstream errors, response bodies, URLs, or credentials.
- A reservation is persisted before network I/O, preventing restart storms if
  the worker crashes.
- Existing user routes and unrelated provider configuration are not rewritten.
- No private provider configuration or credentials are part of this branch.

## Verification

- `npm run check` — passed.
- Related regression suite — 174 passed, 1 platform skip, 0 failed.
- Passive-refresh adversarial suite — 12 passed, including 1,000 competing
  in-process triggers, 12 concurrent processes sharing one reservation, traffic
  cancellation, corrupt/symlink state, launcher failures, and secret-retention
  checks.
- Full `npm test` — 3,622 passed, 25 skipped. Two unrelated failures were
  investigated: the overloaded Antigravity timing test passed immediately in
  isolation; the browser-panel assertion expects English while the browser
  renders the host's Chinese locale, and the same assertion fails on a pristine
  `origin/main` checkout.
- Installed from this branch on macOS: service readiness passed and the router
  PID stayed stable. With active Codex traffic present, the idle gate correctly
  withheld the refresh worker.
- The complete PR diff passed targeted private-value and credential-shape
  scans.

title: feat: passively refresh mirrored native models
body:
## Problem

An OpenAI Responses-compatible gateway can expose new native-compatible model
ids before codex-router's checked-in registry knows about them. The existing
refresh command updates the native catalog, but operators still have to notice
the provider change and curate another route manually. A periodic polling loop
would solve freshness at the cost of repeated network traffic and could restart
the router while Codex turns are active.

A managed mirror also regenerated its full metadata record. If an operator had
live-tested one exact provider/model route and set
`supportsSearchHistory: true`, the next catalog refresh removed that proof.
Continuing a conversation containing a completed `web_search_call` then failed
locally with `model_search_not_supported`, even though that exact upstream
route accepted the history.

The native catalog can also expose the client-only `ultra` reasoning rung for a
model whose exact private route has been live-tested. Managed refreshes
previously removed that route-specific override, forcing the operator to add it
back after every metadata refresh.

## Solution

- Allow an OpenAI Responses provider to opt in to private model discovery and
  native-model mirroring.
- Mirror only the exact intersection of the signed-in Codex catalog and the
  provider's live `/models` response. Generated entries carry an ownership
  marker; manually curated entries remain authoritative, and a transiently
  incomplete provider response never deletes a working route.
- Refresh passively from local lifecycle events rather than a polling loop.
  Router startup and the end of traffic schedule one check after 30 seconds of
  continuous idle time. A new request cancels that idle grace period.
- Coalesce triggers across processes with an owner-private durable reservation.
  Successful checks cool down for 24 hours; failures back off exponentially
  from 1 hour to a 24-hour cap. The worker is detached, time-bounded, and never
  performs provider discovery on the synchronous request path.
- Skip route publication and service restart when the mirrored intersection is
  unchanged. The explicit `refresh-catalog` command remains the immediate
  override and resets the cooldown.
- Preserve an operator-supplied boolean `supportsSearchHistory` only on the
  same managed provider/model route. New models remain conservative: the flag
  is neither inferred from Responses compatibility nor copied from another
  model.
- Preserve an operator-added `ultra` rung only on the same managed route and
  only while the signed-in native catalog continues to advertise `ultra`. New
  mirrors stay conservative, and another route cannot donate this capability.
- Preserve an exact boolean kill switch in the generated macOS, Linux, and
  Windows service definitions.

Codex still reads its picker catalog at application startup, so a newly
published model becomes visible after fully quitting and reopening Codex.

## Safety properties

- Provider opt-in is limited to the OpenAI Responses protocol.
- Scheduling state is bounded, schema-validated, mode `0600`, and written
  atomically without upstream errors, response bodies, URLs, or credentials.
- A reservation is persisted before network I/O, preventing restart storms if
  the worker crashes.
- Existing user routes and unrelated provider configuration are not rewritten.
- Search-history replay and `ultra` remain exact-route, explicitly verified
  capabilities; a stale native `ultra` declaration is removed rather than kept.
- No private provider configuration or credentials are part of this branch.

## Verification

- `npm run check` — passed.
- Related regression suite — 174 passed, 1 platform skip, 0 failed.
- Passive-refresh adversarial suite — 12 passed, including 1,000 competing
  in-process triggers, 12 concurrent processes sharing one reservation, traffic
  cancellation, corrupt/symlink state, launcher failures, and secret-retention
  checks.
- Search-history/mirror focused suites — 15 passed, 0 failed: capabilities on
  a different route are not inherited, exact verified overrides survive managed
  metadata refresh, unsupported routes remain rejected, verified replay is
  forwarded, and `ultra` is withdrawn when native metadata no longer exposes it.
- GitHub Actions is green across the full Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows test
  suites, the unified native macOS lifecycle, both Electron packages,
  deterministic provider discovery, and GitGuardian.
- Installed from this branch on macOS: service readiness passed and the router
  PID stayed stable. With active Codex traffic present, the idle gate correctly
  withheld the refresh worker.
- The complete PR diff passed targeted private-value and credential-shape
  scans.

title: Never require uninstall to see new native models (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-7, o5, etc.)
body: ## Summary Codex Router automatically detects and republishes when native OpenAI/Codex models change. **Uninstall is never required** to see new natives (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-7, o5, etc.). ## Core Problem When Codex updates `~/.codex/models_cache.json` (new native model), nothing automatically republishes. User sees stale catalog, thinks they must uninstall. ## Solution **Automatic drift detection** on router startup + periodic checks while running: 1. **Startup check** (`src/start.mjs`): After router healthy, detect drift in background 2. **Periodic check** (`src/router.mjs`): Every 5 minutes while router runs 3. **Fingerprint-based**: SHA256(models_cache.json) vs stored fingerprint 4. **Auto-republish**: If differs → republish (in-place when safe) ## Implementation ### Drift Detection Module (`src/native-catalog-drift.mjs`) **`nativeCatalogDriftDetected()`**: Sync fingerprint check - Reads `models_cache.json` → compute SHA256 - Reads `native-models.json` → compare stored fingerprint - Returns true if mismatch (new native appeared) **`republishOnNativeDrift()`**: Async republish - Calls `refreshTargetPickerIfInstalled()` if drift detected - Non-blocking, logs success/failure **Fail-closed**: `codexIntegrationInstalled()` returns false on config read error (conservative) ### Router Integration **Startup** (`src/start.mjs` line ~413): ```javascript import("./native-catalog-drift.mjs") .then(({ republishOnNativeDrift }) => republishOnNativeDrift()) ``` **Periodic** (`src/router.mjs` line ~1599): ```javascript const nativeCatalogDriftCheckTimer = setInterval( async () => { const { republishOnNativeDrift } = await import("./native-catalog-drift.mjs"); await republishOnNativeDrift(); }, 5 * 60_000, // Every 5 minutes ); nativeCatalogDriftCheckTimer.unref(); ``` **Why both**: - Startup: Catches drift from when router was down - Periodic: Catches drift while router stays running (common with tray/service) - Cheap: Only fingerprint compare until drift detected ### Safe In-Place Refresh (from PR #621) **`nativeCacheCanRefreshInPlace()`** (line 218 in `catalog.mjs`): - Checks if `models_cache.json` is clean (no routed slugs) - When safe → `catalog.mjs --refresh-native` (no config mutation) - When unsafe → journaled disable/restore **`refresh-catalog.mjs`** (line 86-92): - Uses `canRefreshInPlace()` to decide path - Skips `config.toml` rewrite when safe ## Test Coverage ### End-to-End Republish Test (`test/native-catalog-drift.test.mjs`) **"drift detection triggers republish with new arbitrary native in merged output"**: 1. Simulate OLD native in `models_cache.json` 2. Write matching `native-models.json` → no drift 3. Update `models_cache.json` with NEW arbitrary native (`gpt-7-prime`) 4. Detect drift → call `republishOnNativeDrift()` 5. **VERIFY**: `native-models.json` contains NEW slug after republish **This test**: - ❌ Fails on main (no drift detection exists) - ✅ Passes here (drift detected + republished) - Proves actual republish, not just detection ### All Tests Pass ``` $ node --test test/catalog.test.mjs test/refresh-catalog.test.mjs test/native-catalog-drift.test.mjs # tests 78 # pass 78 # fail 0 ``` ## Real User Flow ``` OpenAI releases GPT-7 ↓ Codex updates models_cache.json ↓ Router ALREADY RUNNING (tray/service) ↓ Periodic check (5min) detects SHA256 mismatch ↓ Auto-republish (in-place when safe) ↓ User quits/reopens Codex → GPT-7 appears ↓ NO UNINSTALL REQUIRED ✅ ``` **Or** if router was down: ``` OpenAI releases GPT-7 ↓ Codex updates models_cache.json ↓ Router starts/restarts ↓ Startup check detects drift ↓ Auto-republish ↓ User quits/reopens Codex → GPT-7 appears ↓ NO UNINSTALL REQUIRED ✅ ``` ## Product Constraints ### What This PR Fixes ✅ **Uninstall never required** to see new natives. Router detects drift automatically via: - Startup check (catches drift from when router was down) - Periodic check every 5min (catches drift while running) ### What Codex Controls (Not Fixed) **Codex full quit/reopen required** to reload catalog file. Codex reads `model_catalog_json` once at startup. ## Documentation `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`: > **Uninstall is never required** to see new OpenAI/Codex native models. When Codex updates `~/.codex/models_cache.json`, the router automatically detects fingerprint drift on next startup and periodically while running. > > **Codex full quit/reopen is still required** to reload the catalog file. ## Files Changed ### Core - `src/native-catalog-drift.mjs` (NEW - 68 lines): Drift detection + republish - `src/start.mjs`: Add async startup drift check - `src/router.mjs`: Add 5-minute periodic drift check - `src/catalog.mjs`: Export `readModelsCache()`, add in-place helpers ### Tests - `test/native-catalog-drift.test.mjs` (NEW - 117 lines): End-to-end republish test - `test/catalog.test.mjs`: Add 3 tests for fingerprint/merge - `test/refresh-catalog.test.mjs`: Control in-place path ### Docs - `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`: Native coexistence section ## No Hardcoded Models - Generic SHA256 fingerprint of entire `parsed.models` array - Test uses `gpt-7-prime` (arbitrary future native) - Works for GPT-7, GPT-8, o5, o6, any future native --- **Status**: Draft PR. Automatic detection on startup + periodic. End-to-end test proves republish. All 78 tests pass. **PR**: https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/pull/624

title: fix: meter tok/s on non-reasoning output tokens
body: ## Problem `observedTokensPerSecond` used full `outputTokens` while TTFT waited for the first *visible* token. Providers often include `reasoning_tokens` (silent thinking) in `output_tokens`, inflating reported speed (~+24% measured on Muse Spark free: 502 output with 98 reasoning → 163.6 tok/s vs ~131.6 when reasoning excluded). Additionally, the panel status chip painted historical median speed while the model was generating, making it read like a live current-turn rate. **Measured impact:** Live Muse Spark free: 502 output with 98 reasoning → 163.6 tok/s vs ~131.6 if reasoning excluded (~+24% inflation). Formula and median/500-cap are otherwise correct. ## Changes ### Core tok/s fix - **`src/response-usage.mjs` `normalizeTokenUsage`**: Extract `reasoningTokens` from `output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` / `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` / `reasoning_tokens` when present. Include on returned usage object. - **`mergeTokenUsage`**: Sum `reasoningTokens` when either side has them (same pattern as `cachedInputTokens`). - **`src/usage-events.mjs` `recordUsageEvent`**: Accept and persist optional `reasoningTokens` (sanitized like other token fields). Historical rows without the field remain unchanged. - **`src/provider-usage.mjs` speed samples**: ```js const reasoningTokens = optionalNonnegative(event.reasoningTokens) ?? 0; const speedOutputTokens = Math.max(0, selectedOutputTokens - reasoningTokens); ``` Use `speedOutputTokens` (not full output) for tok/s numerator and impossible-rate check. Provider/model **totals** still count full `outputTokens` for billing—only the tok/s meter changes. Comment documents: industry TTFT stays on first visible token; tok/s numerator is non-reasoning completion tokens when provider reports the split. ### UX: Panel and Control Center - **`apps/panel/app.js` `renderModelSpeed`**: Hide measured median while `activity.state === "generating"` or active requests exist. Show only "— tok/s" and "Appears after a metered reply" during generation. Speed reappears when idle after `providerUsage` refresh. - **`apps/control-center/src/pages/DashboardPage.tsx` `tokensPerSecondFromEvent`**: Subtract `reasoningTokens` from output for per-event tok/s (same as provider-usage), keeping the 500 cap. Per-event rows are already post-completion. - **`apps/control-center/src/types.ts`**: Add `reasoningTokens?: number` to `UsageEvent` interface. ### Bonus fix: chat first-token detection **`#noteFirstToken` in `response-usage.mjs`**: Real `chat.completion.chunk` objects often have no `type` field. Checking type before chat delta meant chat first-token never fired → tray speed stayed null. Now checks `delta.content` first, then falls back to typed Responses events. Keep Responses first-token events as-is (including `reasoning_summary_text.delta` for TTFT display—do **not** remove from TTFT; only tok/s numerator excludes reasoning). ## Tests - `normalizeTokenUsage` extracts `reasoningTokens` ✓ - `mergeTokenUsage` sums reasoning tokens ✓ - Chat first-token without `type` field ✓ - `aggregateProviderUsage`: two events with same duration/firstToken/output but one with reasoning → lower `observedTokensPerSecond`; totals still count full output ✓ - Panel speed hiding: generation state detection ✓ - Existing speed tests still pass (no reasoning → unchanged) ✓ Ran `test/provider-usage.test.mjs`, `test/response-usage.test.mjs`, `test/usage-events.test.mjs`, `test/panel-ui.test.mjs` — all pass. ## Verification The fix matches the problem spec: - ✅ Reasoning tokens extracted from all three provider shapes - ✅ Tok/s uses non-reasoning output (speedOutputTokens) - ✅ Provider totals unchanged (billing accuracy preserved) - ✅ Historical events without reasoningTokens work unchanged - ✅ Chat first-token detection fixed (no type field) - ✅ Panel hides speed during generation - ✅ Control Center per-event tok/s excludes reasoning - ✅ CHANGELOG updated

title: Command Code rejects routed turns with >64-character tool names or recursive JSON schemas
body:
## Summary

A Codex turn routed to `commandcode/meta/muse-spark-1.3-contributor` is rejected before generation when the attached tool surface contains a function name longer than 64 characters.

Observed response:

```text
HTTP 400: `name` must be at most 64 characters, got 80
```

The offending provider-facing tool in this request was:

```text
mcp__openai_api_key_local_confirmation__confirm_openai_api_key_local_destination
```

Its length is exactly 80 characters.

## Root cause

`buildRoutedRequest()` sends chat-completions providers through `chatProviderToolSurface()`. That function flattens namespaces, but currently calls `flattenNamespaceTools(merged.tools)` without a name-length bound for Command Code.

The router already has deterministic bounded aliases and reverse restoration in `flattenNamespaceTools(..., { maxNameLength: 64 })`; Command Code is simply not opting into that existing path.

This reproduces on current `origin/main` at `0f8441f3c9f5d66afda2e92da2023fbab7d30f98`.

## Suggested fix

For provider IDs `commandcode` and `commandcode-messages`, call:

```js
flattenNamespaceTools(merged.tools, { maxNameLength: 64 })
```

Keep other non-Groq providers byte-compatible with the existing unbounded behavior.

A regression test should assert that:

- the exact 80-character tool is exposed to Command Code under a 64-character deterministic alias;
- the alias differs from the client name;
- `rewriteNamespaceResponsePayload()` restores a returned function call to the original client identity.

## Validation

A local two-file patch using the existing alias machinery passes:

```text
node --test test/chat-tool-surface.test.mjs test/commandcode-generate.test.mjs test/commandcode-relay.test.mjs
32 tests passed, 0 failed
```

The broad suite also exercises this regression successfully. Its unrelated existing Search Sidecar cancellation still reproduces when run alone.
