title: ci: cache the binaries electron-builder downloads
body:
## Why

The three packaging jobs download the Electron binary and electron-builder's own helper binaries on every run, so a bad response from those hosts fails the job outright. Three died that way inside one day:

| when | job | error |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 14 Sep 14:50 | [Electron control center (Windows)](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/34857987861/job/104022418711) | `Response code 504 (Gateway Time-out)`, right after `downloaded label=nsis-3.0.4.1.7z` |
| 14 Sep 14:53 | [Unified native macOS app](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/34857987861/job/104022418939) | `Response code 504`, right after `downloaded label=electron` |
| 14 Sep 01:16 | [Electron control center (Linux)](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/34795374753) | `Response code 500 (Internal Server Error)` |
| 14 Sep 15:36 | [Electron control center (Windows)](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/34863045029/job/104039870191) | `Response code 500`, again right after `downloaded label=nsis-3.0.4.1.7z` — **this PR's own first run** |

Both 504s are `HTTPError` thrown out of `got` inside `apps/control-center/node_modules`, three minutes apart on two different runners — the download host, not the build. All three cleared on a re-run.

That last one is this branch's own first CI run, and it is worth being plain about: **a cold cache does not protect anything**, so the first run was exposed exactly like any other. It did, however, demonstrate the second half of the problem — see below.

## What changed

`actions/cache/restore` + `actions/cache/save` around the two directories electron-builder already keeps, on all three packaging jobs, keyed on `apps/control-center/package-lock.json` so an Electron bump misses and everything else hits.

**Restore and save are separate steps on purpose.** I first wrote this as a single `actions/cache@v6`, and its post step came back `skipped` on the failing run:

```
9   failure  Package the native beta
...
24  skipped  Post Cache electron-builder downloads
```

The job had already fetched Electron and NSIS successfully before the 500. Discarding those leaves the next run starting cold, so a bad window repeats instead of closing itself. `actions/cache/save` with `if: !cancelled()` keeps what was downloaded even when packaging failed; the save is skipped on an exact-key hit, so a healthy run does not re-upload.

The directories come from `envPaths("electron"|"electron-builder", { suffix: "" }).cache` — read from `node_modules/env-paths/index.js` rather than assumed:

| | Electron binary | helper binaries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux | `~/.cache/electron` | `~/.cache/electron-builder` |
| macOS | `~/Library/Caches/electron` | `~/Library/Caches/electron-builder` |
| Windows | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\electron\Cache` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\electron-builder\Cache` |

## Verification

Measured locally on Linux against a cleared cache, with the same `--linux` flag CI uses:

- **Cold**: writes 120 MB to `~/.cache/electron` (`electron-v43.4.0-linux-x64.zip`) and 14 MB to `~/.cache/electron-builder` (`appimage-12.0.1.7z`, `7zip-linux-x64.tar.gz` — the same class of helper binary whose sibling NSIS immediately preceded the 504 on Windows). So both directories are the ones that carry the failing downloads.
- **Warm**: the whole packaging run takes 16 seconds and re-downloads nothing. I set the cached zip's mtime to 2020-01-01 before the run and it was still 2020-01-01 afterwards, so the file was read rather than refetched. The `appimage`/`7zip` download lines disappear from the log entirely.

What I could not verify is GitHub's own cache save/restore, or the macOS and Windows paths — I have no runner for either, and the paths above are read from `env-paths`' source rather than observed. If you would rather see it prove itself first, the safest read is the next few runs' "Cache restored from key" lines.

## One thing worth knowing

`ELECTRON_CACHE` and `ELECTRON_BUILDER_CACHE` — the usual advice for this — **do not move the Electron download here**. I set both to absolute, existing directories and the zip still landed in `~/.cache/electron` while both stayed empty. `@electron/get`'s `Cache.js` defaults its root to `envPaths('electron', { suffix: '' }).cache` and reads no environment variable at all, so the override never applies. I mention it because it is the first thing most suggestions reach for, and it would have been a silent no-op.

## Scope

CI only; no source or test change, and no CHANGELOG entry, matching the other workflow-only commits. It reduces exposure rather than removing it — a cold cache still downloads, so an Electron bump landing during an outage can still fail. If you want that closed too, a retry around the packaging step would do it, and I am happy to add one.

title: Windows install: `start-codex-router.cmd` reported installed but missing from disk; background-service registration fails with `fetch failed
body:
## Summary

On Windows, the installer reports `"installed":true` for `start-codex-router.cmd` but the file does not exist on disk. The background-service (Task Scheduler) registration step fails with `fetch failed`, and the install exits with status 1.

## Environment

- **OS:** Windows 11 (PowerShell 7, FullLanguage mode confirmed)
- **Node:** v26.1.0
- **Codex Router version:** 0.5.1
- **Elevated (admin) PowerShell:** Yes
- **Proxy variables (`HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`):** Not set
- **Windows Defender / Firewall:** Not the cause (tested)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run the Codex Router installer on a clean Windows 11 machine (admin PowerShell).
2. Accept all prompts.
3. Observe the install output.

## Actual behavior

```
{"installed":true,"path":"C:\\Users\\<user>\\.codex\\codex-router\\start-codex-router.cmd"}
fetch failed
Background-service installation failed.
At C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\codex-router\install.ps1:533 char:30
+ ... STEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Background-service installation failed." }
```

- `C:\Users\<user>\.codex\codex-router\start-codex-router.cmd` does **not** exist after install.
- Re-running the installer or `codex-router.ps1 doctor --fix` produces the same failure.
- The "Codex Router" scheduled task is never created.
- `codex-router.ps1 start` then fails because `schtasks /Change /TN "Codex Router" /ENABLE` targets a non-existent task.

## Expected behavior

- `start-codex-router.cmd` is written to disk.
- The "Codex Router" scheduled task is registered.
- `codex-router.ps1 start` / `stop` work.

## Workaround

```powershell
# 1. Create the missing .cmd
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.codex\codex-router"
@"
@echo off
node "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\codex-router\src\start.mjs"
"@ | Out-File -FilePath "$env:USERPROFILE\.codex\codex-router\start-codex-router.cmd" -Encoding ascii

# 2. Create the scheduled task
schtasks /Create /TN "Codex Router" /TR "$env:USERPROFILE\.codex\codex-router\start-codex-router.cmd" /SC ONLOGON /RL LIMITED /F
```

After these steps, `codex-router.ps1 start` and the router itself work correctly.

## Additional notes

- All other artifacts (merged-models.json, litellm.yaml, config) are written correctly.
- The `fetch failed` appears to be a Node `fetch()` call to `http://127.0.0.1:4202/v1` (the router's own health endpoint) made *before* the router is running, so the connection is refused.
- The `"installed":true` status is misleading — the file is not on disk despite the report.

title: fix(win): verify the service launchers exist before reporting an install
body:
A latent defect found while investigating #760. **It is not what happened to that reporter** — see "Relationship to #760" below, which corrects an earlier version of this description.

## Problem

`service-windows.mjs install` reported the launcher path without ever checking that the file was written:

```js
process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify({ installed: taskExists(), path: wrapperPath })}\n`);
```

`writeLaunchers()` runs inside the `try` whose `catch {}` was written for a restricted Task Scheduler, and that catch's own comment states an assumption it cannot guarantee — *"The launchers are still written, so the install is reported as success"*. That is false exactly when `writeLaunchers()` is what threw:

- `writeAtomic` -> `protectPrivateFile` -> `protectPrivateFilesWin32` (`src/file-security.mjs:167-193`) shells out to **`powershell.exe` — Windows PowerShell 5.1, not `pwsh`** — and constructs `[System.Security.AccessControl.FileSecurity]::new()`. Under ConstrainedLanguage, AppLocker or WDAC that throws, the temporary is discarded (`src/service-windows.mjs:161`), and nothing exists at `path`.
- `mkdirSync` EPERM, a `renameSync` sharing violation, or a denied write into an earlier elevated install's ACLs end the same way.

The exception was swallowed with no message and no effect on the exit code, so install would exit 0 having named a file that was not there, and the operator's first sign of trouble would come ~300 seconds later from the readiness wait's bare `fetch failed` (`src/service-readiness.mjs:80-82` strips the URL). A symptom reported in place of a cause.

## Change

- Read both launcher paths back after the write attempt and report a `launchers` boolean.
- `installed` now requires `launchers && taskExists()` — a task whose action does not exist is not an installed service.
- Print the swallowed exception instead of discarding it.
- Exit non-zero when no launcher reached disk, so `install.ps1` stops on this step rather than on the health probe.

Scoped deliberately: a **written** launcher with no registered task is still the survivable partial install the catch exists for, and still exits 0. Only a missing launcher — where nothing the task could run exists — fails. `process.exitCode` rather than `process.exit()`, because `process.stdout` is asynchronous for a Windows console and exiting would truncate the JSON line above it. The `status` command's output is untouched, so `caller-key.mjs` and `control.mjs` readers are unaffected.

## Relationship to #760 — correcting this PR's original description

This was first published as "the confirmed half of #760", asserting that the reporter's `installed:true` and "the task is never created" could not both be true. **That was wrong, and so was the different-admin-account hypothesis built on it.** Both of their observations are true and consistent, and the code path is fully determined:

1. `install.ps1:531` sets `$ServiceInstalled = $true` **before** calling `service.mjs install`.
2. `service-windows install` genuinely wrote the launchers and created the task. `installed:true` was **accurate at that moment**.
3. `service.mjs` then runs `waitForServiceReadiness` (`READINESS_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000`) — a step that `service-windows.mjs install` does not contain, which is why the `fetch failed` arrives after the JSON line rather than before it.
4. The router does not answer inside the budget, so `service.mjs` exits non-zero and `install.ps1:533` throws `Background-service installation failed.`
5. The catch at `install.ps1:599` runs `node src/service.mjs uninstall`, which deletes the task **and unlinks `launcherPath` and `wrapperPath`**.

So the missing `start-codex-router.cmd` was deleted by the installer's own rollback, seconds after being written correctly. `service.mjs:25-28` anticipates precisely this:

> A shorter wait reports failure while the service is still booting, and the installer's rollback then uninstalls the service and reverts the app config out from under a router that goes on to come up healthy seconds later.

It also explains why the reporter's manual workaround succeeds: by then the LiteLLM gateway is warm. **The real defect in #760 is a rollback that destroys a healthy install when a cold start overruns the readiness budget** — tracked separately; this PR does not fix it.

What remains true is that the swallowed exception above is a genuine latent bug: had it fired, it would have produced the same misleading report with no cause anywhere. That is what this PR fixes.

## Verification

```
node --test test/service-render.test.mjs test/service-write-guard.test.mjs \
  test/service-lifecycle.test.mjs test/windows-operations.test.mjs
tests 56  pass 52  fail 0  skipped 4   (Windows-only suites)
```

The new test makes `writeLaunchers()` throw by pointing `MODEL_ROUTER_STATE_DIR` beneath a regular file, then asserts a non-zero exit, `launchers:false`, `installed:false`, that `path` does not exist, a named cause on stderr, and that no task was registered. With the pre-fix source restored, both new assertions fail and nothing else does.

**Authored on macOS.** The Windows-specific cause cannot be reproduced here — the test covers the *report*, not the ACL failure. Four Windows-only suites skip on this host.

title: fix(support-bundle): report gitCommit only for the router's own checkout
body:
Found while triaging #761, and the reason that triage was expensive.

## Problem

`src/support-bundle.mjs` identified the installed tree by running `git -C SOURCE_ROOT rev-parse HEAD`. On a Homebrew install `SOURCE_ROOT` is `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/codex-router/<version>/libexec` — and **the Homebrew prefix is itself a Git checkout of `homebrew/brew`**, so `rev-parse` walks up out of the keg and answers with brew's HEAD.

Confirmed on a real machine:

```
$ git -C /opt/homebrew/Cellar rev-parse --show-toplevel
/opt/homebrew
```

That is why #761's bundle reported `gitCommit: b3625f73…`, a SHA that does not exist in this repository (`gh api …/commits/b3625f73… -> 422 No commit found`). The one field meant to identify the install was naming an unrelated project's commit, and a maintainer reading it has no way to tell.

## Change

Require the Git toplevel to **be** `SOURCE_ROOT`, compared through `realpath` so a symlinked root (macOS `/var`, `/tmp`) still matches. Keg and tarball installs now report `gitCommit: null` and leave `packageVersion` as the honest identifier; a Git checkout is unaffected.

A null is strictly better than a confident wrong answer here: the bundle exists to tell us what is running.

## Verification

```
node --test test/support-bundle.test.mjs
✔ gitCommit reports only a commit that describes the installed tree
tests 14  pass 14  fail 0
```

The new test builds a nested checkout whose parent is a Git repository and the child is not, mirroring the keg layout, and asserts the parent's HEAD is not reported. Existing redaction and log-omission coverage is unchanged.

title: fix(cursor): preflight and async-inflate the last synchronous zstd path
body:
Relates to #465. **This does not fix that crash**, and does not claim to.

## Context

PR #564 hardened `decodeBody` on `/v1/responses`: the Zstandard frame header is read for its declared content size and answered with 413 *before any native decoder sees the body*, and the inflate uses the promisified async `zstdDecompress` so a multi-megabyte frame does not run on the event loop.

`src/cursor-surface.mjs` was missed. It still called the one-shot synchronous `zstdDecompressSync` with no preflight, and it is imported by `src/router.mjs:33`. `git log -S zstdDecompressSync -- src/cursor-surface.mjs` returns exactly one commit — the one that introduced it — so the #564 hardening never reached this file.

It runs only for `/cursor/...` requests, so it cannot account for #465's `/v1/responses` crashes (Windows `0xC0000409` / `STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN`). That root cause remains unconfirmed and blocked on a crash dump. This is simply the last synchronous zstd inflate in the router, and it gets the same defensive treatment for the same reasons — as noted in the issue thread.

## Change

- `decodedRequestBody` is now `async`. Its zstd branch calls `zstdFrameContentSize` from `src/http-utils.mjs` — the existing parser, not a copy — and refuses a frame declaring more than `MAX_CURSOR_BODY_BYTES` before the native decoder is handed anything.
- The inflate is `promisify(zstdDecompress)` under the same `maxOutputLength`. The cap value (32 MiB) is unchanged.
- The three call sites (`handleCursorApp`, plus `RunSSE` and `BidiAppend` in `handleCursorCli`) gain `await`; all three were already `async`.
- gzip, deflate and br are untouched. No synchronous zstd inflate remains anywhere in `src/`.

## Status code

The oversize rejection is a `status`-carrying error, like the 400/404/415 this surface already raises. All three call sites sit outside the local `try`, so it reaches the server-level catch in `router.mjs` and `httpErrorStatus` returns 413 — the same status the equivalent rejection returns on `/v1/responses`.

Deliberately **not** ported: `decodeBody`'s `ERR_BUFFER_TOO_LARGE` -> 413 wrap. Here it would also change the gzip/deflate/br overflow status. A frame that omits its declared size and overflows the cap still returns 502, exactly as before. Porting that is a separate, broader call.

## Verification

```
node --test test/cursor-surface.test.mjs test/http-utils-zstd-frame.test.mjs
tests 14  pass 14  fail 0
```

One regression test, using the file's existing HTTP fixture: a real `zstdCompressSync` body still round-trips and routes, then a hand-built header declaring 64 MiB — followed by bytes that are deliberately *not* a decodable frame body — returns 413 with the upstream call count unmoved. The garbage tail is the point: if the preflight ever stops firing, the decoder fails the inflate instead and the status drops to 500. Verified by disabling the preflight, which produces exactly that failure.

title: fix(zai): GLM-5.3-Flash reads images natively on the Coding Plan, API and OpenRouter routes
body:
Fixes #756.

## Problem

`config/zai/coding/glm-5.3-flash.json` declared `inputModalities: ["text"]`. That field is what `bridgeVisionInput()` reads (`src/router.mjs:2237` -> `supportsImageInput`, `src/vision-bridge.mjs:189-191`) to decide whether an image reaches the model or is handed to a vision engine and replaced with a transcript. It is also published to Codex as `input_modalities` (`src/catalog.mjs:669`), which gates the paste.

So every screenshot on this route spent a **second provider's** quota to come back as prose, for a model that reads images natively.

Six routes point at this same upstream model, and they disagreed:

| route | before |
|---|---|
| `opencode-go/glm-5.3-flash` | text+image |
| `ollama-cloud/glm-5.3-flash` | text+image |
| `commandcode/glm-5.3-flash` | text+image |
| `openrouter/glm-5.3-flash` | **text** |
| `zai-api/glm-5.3-flash` | **text** |
| `zai-coding/glm-5.3-flash` | **text** |

## The text-only value was never a measurement

`config/zai/coding/glm-5.3-flash.json` has exactly one commit — `129a0be9`, part of the Ox Alpha cleanup — which took the conservative default with no rationale. The preset it replaced carried `["text","image"]`, and `docs/provider-catalog-audits/2026-08-26.json` still records three provider catalogs publishing this model under its preview name `stealth/ox-alpha` with `inputModalities: ["image","text","video"]`. The same audit records `z-ai/glm-5.3` (full size) as text-only, which is the Flash/full split AGENTS.md already documents.

The exact-route certification these routes passed covered basic, streaming, forced-tool, stateless tool-result and compact requests — never an image.

## Verified live, not just from docs

One real image turn per enabled route, through the installed router with this branch's config (so `bridgeVisionInput` passed the input through untouched and the image reached the provider **natively**). The test image is four coloured quadrants; naming all four in the right positions cannot be faked without seeing it.

```
=== zai-coding/glm-5.3-flash ===
HTTP        : 200
answer      : Top-left: red, top-right: green, bottom-left: blue, bottom-right: yellow.
colours hit : red,green,blue,yellow (4/4)   VERDICT: SAW THE IMAGE

=== openrouter/glm-5.3-flash ===
HTTP        : 200
answer      : Top-left: red, top-right: green, bottom-left: blue, bottom-right: yellow.
colours hit : red,green,blue,yellow (4/4)   VERDICT: SAW THE IMAGE
```

`zai-api` is not enabled on this machine and was **not** probed. It rests on Z.ai's documentation — [docs.z.ai/guides/vlm/glm-5.3-flash](https://docs.z.ai/guides/vlm/glm-5.3-flash) files GLM-5.3-Flash under the vision-language guides, gives its input modality as "Video / Image / Text / File", and documents the `image_url` block against that API — plus the fact that it is the same upstream model now measured on two other endpoints.

Two Coding-Plan signals that look like counter-evidence and are not: the [Vision MCP Server](https://docs.z.ai/devpack/mcp/vision-mcp-server) page says a pasted image bypasses it because the client "will by default transcode the image and call the model interface directly" — normal behavior, not a missing modality; and the `Uncheck Support Images` line in the Cline guide is written against `glm-5.2`, which is text-only, and never mentions Flash.

## Changes

- `zai-coding`, `zai-api` and `openrouter` GLM-5.3-Flash routes declare `["text", "image"]`, descriptions updated, `compHash` bumped on each so the catalog republishes.
- `test/glm-5.3-flash.test.mjs` asserts image input for every route in the Flash inventory as a shared constant rather than a per-slug ternary, so a new Flash route cannot quietly ship the old default — plus a counterpart test keeping the full-size GLM-5.3 routes text-only.
- `AGENTS.md` records the sourcing and why the two Coding-Plan signals are not counter-evidence.
- `README.md` gains the `zai-coding/glm-5.3-flash` row, which was missing from the Z.ai table.

Operators will need to rebuild the catalog and fully quit and reopen Codex, since `compHash` changed.

## Verification

```
node --test test/glm-5.3-flash.test.mjs test/registry.test.mjs test/vision-bridge.test.mjs
tests 118  pass 118  fail 0
```

title: fix: hold Command Code's GLM-5.3-Flash to the model's own compaction threshold and effort ladder
body:
`commandcode/glm-5.3-flash` shipped with two of its neighbours' defaults instead of the model's own values. Both were written in the same bulk catalog pin (fb0d3077), and neither has a commit message, comment, or research note behind it.

## 1. It compacted at 900K against a 400K rule

The other five checked-in GLM-5.3-Flash routes compact at 400,000. That threshold belongs to the model: large live multimodal Flash histories repeatedly returned empty completions before the advertised limit, which is why AGENTS.md records the rule and why `nousresearch/glm-5.3-flash` was dropped in 923578bf for "compacting at 943K … contradicted the 400K GLM-5.3-Flash rule". Codex ran this route 500,000 tokens past the point where the model has been seen to go blank.

900K was not a measurement — it is the Command Code house value, carried by every one of that provider's 1M-window entries (two dozen of them). The same file previously existed at 400,000 (1526183d), was deleted in db3f725e, and was re-created from scratch in a commit that documents the context window and says nothing about compaction. Same failure mode 448a593a describes for `inputModalities`.

The route was also missing from the `ROUTES` inventory in `test/glm-5.3-flash.test.mjs`, so none of that file's shared assertions covered it — while `test/gemini-3.8-muse-1.3-fable-5.1.test.mjs` pinned the outlier at `900_000`, giving the wrong value a green test. The inventory is now derived from the registry, so the next Flash route cannot be omitted silently.

## 2. It sent an effort rung the model refuses by name

The entry declares the model's `low`/`high`/`max` ladder and carried no `requestProfile`. The profile chain in `src/api-forwarder.mjs` is one if/else keyed entirely on that field, so the effort went upstream verbatim — and a Codex older than 0.143 has no `max` in its enum, so `clampModelEfforts` rewrites the default down to `xhigh`, which this model answers with `400 — [1210] This model always engages in thinking and cannot be disabled; please use low, high, or max`. The route now carries the same `ox-alpha` clamp the OpenCode Go and OpenRouter Flash routes use.

The new test in `test/commandcode-forwarder.test.mjs` drives the real forwarder against a mock Provider API across all seven rungs and the absent case; it fails without the profile with `xhigh` on the wire, so the exposure is measured rather than argued.

The clamp asserts nothing about Command Code's own validation, which the provider does not document — Command Code publishes no effort vocabulary at all, which is why `commandcode/muse-spark-1.3` ships `high` alone. It only guarantees the router sends a rung the entry itself advertises. The `/alpha/generate` plan fallback is unaffected: `toGenerateRequest` builds its own schema-strict params and carries no effort field, so on a coding-plan account those three picker rungs reach nothing either way.

## Left alone, deliberately

Nine sibling Command Code entries — `glm-5.3`, `glm-5.2`, the DeepSeek V4 routes, the GPT-5.x routes, and the `commandcode-messages` Claude routes — publish `max` or `xhigh` rungs with no clamp and are in the same unproven position. AGENTS.md now says so; each needs its own decision. No live request was sent to any provider for this change.

## Verification

`compHash` → `commandcode-glm-5-3-flash-v3`, so rebuild the catalog and fully quit and reopen Codex. `npm run check` passes; 329 tests across the registry, catalog, capabilities, routing and all five Command Code files pass, at both commits.

title: fix: keep a slow-starting service instead of rolling it back (#760)
body:
Fixes the cause of #760. #762 fixed a latent defect found in the same area; this is what actually happened to that reporter.

## What happened

Every symptom in the report follows from one path, with no contradiction between them and no misconfiguration:

1. `install.ps1` sets `$ServiceInstalled = $true` **before** calling `service.mjs install`.
2. `service-windows install` wrote both launchers and registered the task. **`installed:true` was accurate.**
3. `service.mjs` then runs `waitForServiceReadiness` (`READINESS_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000`) — a step `service-windows.mjs install` does not itself contain, which is why the `fetch failed` lands *after* the JSON line rather than before it. The router did not answer; `service-readiness.mjs:80-82` strips the URL, leaving the bare message.
4. Non-zero exit → `install.ps1` throws `Background-service installation failed.`
5. The catch runs `node src/service.mjs uninstall`, which deletes the task **and unlinks `launcherPath` and `wrapperPath`**.

So `start-codex-router.cmd` was deleted by the installer's own rollback, seconds after being written correctly. The operator then finds a log claiming `installed:true`, no file, and no task — all three true, in that order.

`service.mjs:25-28` already anticipates this exactly:

> A shorter wait reports failure while the service is still booting, and the installer's rollback then uninstalls the service and reverts the app config out from under a router that goes on to come up healthy seconds later.

The guard added for it gates the teardown on `service_was_installed` / `$ServiceWasInstalled`, which protects a **reinstall over a working router**. A first install on a clean machine has no prior state to compare against, so it was torn out regardless — and a first install is precisely when a LiteLLM cold start with a large model set is slowest. It also explains why the reporter's manual workaround succeeds where the installer failed: by then the gateway is warm.

## Change

- `waitForServiceReadiness` tags health-wait exhaustion as `readinessTimeout`. The crash-loop and dead-launcher throws are deliberately **left untagged** — those are broken rather than slow, and a rollback is still right for them, or a task that relaunches a failing router at every logon survives the install.
- `service.mjs` converts only the tagged failure into exit **75** (`EX_TEMPFAIL`) and says the service is installed and still starting. Everything else keeps exiting 1.
- Both installers branch on 75 and skip the teardown for **service and client config alike** — a router that comes up moments later needs its config still pointing at it — then stop before `wait-health.mjs`, which would only spend a second full budget failing the same way on the same cold start.

The install still fails, loudly, with a non-zero status. What changes is that it no longer destroys what it correctly built.

## Verification

```
node --test test/installer-scripts.test.mjs test/service-readiness.test.mjs \
  test/service-lifecycle.test.mjs test/service-render.test.mjs
tests 99  pass 95  fail 0  skipped 4   (Windows/PowerShell-only)
```

New coverage: a health wait that runs out is tagged retryable; a crash loop and a dead launcher are **not**; `service.mjs` converts only the tagged case; and both installers branch on 75, initialise the flag before the rollback reads it (under `set -u` an unset variable would abort the trap itself), guard ahead of the teardown, and decide before the second health wait. None of the four markers the new assertions match exists on `main`, so every one of them fails pre-fix.

**Authored on macOS.** `pwsh` is not available on this host, so the PowerShell edit rests on the installer-script assertions plus CI's Windows job rather than a local parse — worth a reviewer's eye on the bare `throw` rethrow in the catch.

## What this does not cover

Why that machine's router needed more than 300 seconds is still unknown, and this PR does not shorten it — it only stops the installer from reacting destructively. If cold starts routinely overrun the budget, the budget itself is the next question.

title: fix: drop past reasoning on off-contract Chat routes (#755)
body:
Fixes #755.

## The chain

**1. Command Code now gets the reasoning-lifecycle repair.** #708 widened it from `grok-oauth` to every provider whose protocol is `openai`. `config/commandcode/commandcode.json` declares no `protocol`, so it defaults in and qualifies. That is the *point* of #708 — it is why reasoning reaches Codex on these routes instead of being dropped as orphan `rs_` deltas — and Codex consequently **stores a reasoning item** for those turns.

**2. Most Command Code thinking models are outside the native-reasoning contract.** `commandcode/qwen3.8-flash` resolves to upstream `Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash`, which matches no family, so `usesNativeChatReasoning` returns false. So do all three `qwen3.7-*`, both `qwen3.8-max*`, `minimax-m2.7`, `kimi-k2.7-*`, `step-3.7-flash`, `mimo-v2.5-pro`, `nemotron-3-ultra` and `inkling*`.

**3. An uncovered route replayed that stored reasoning as visible text.** `carryReasoningThroughInput` received `nativeThinking: false`, and `assistantTextItem` then emits `{ type: "output_text" }` — the model meets its own past thinking as prose it apparently said aloud, moves new thinking into the answer channel, and loops on its last progress note. That is the documented trigger, measured on Hy4 at 2, 4, 5, 8 and 16 copies of one sentence per message.

Steps 1 and 3 are individually correct and only interact badly in the gap between them. Before #708 this was self-limiting here: no reasoning item was stored, so there was nothing to carry.

## The live probe that settled it

The issue was filed with an explicit hedge — `src/reasoning-tag-stripper.mjs` documents Qwen leaking chain-of-thought *inline* as `<think>…</think>` on this bridge, and if that were what happened the stripper would remove it, no reasoning item would be created, and this path would stay inert.

**That hedge is closed.** Two turns through the installed router, turn 2 replaying turn 1's own output items the way Codex does:

| | `qwen3.8-flash` | `hy4-preview` |
|---|---|---|
| in contract | **no** (`family=undefined`) | yes (`hunyuan`) |
| reasoning item stored, turn 1 | **YES** | YES |
| reasoning item stored, turn 2 | **YES** | YES |
| reasoning tokens (t1 / t2) | 89 / 69 | 2451 / 3260 |

Turn 1 on qwen returned `["reasoning","message"]` with a populated `summary`, and turn 2's `input_tokens` rose 81 → 419, so the replay genuinely carried. The route returns structured reasoning; the path is reached in practice.

## Change

Off-contract Chat Completions routes **drop** the reasoning from the carry instead of converting it to `output_text`. Three channels, not two:

- Chat route **inside** the contract → carried as `thinking` parts for the forwarder to restore as `reasoning_content`. Unchanged.
- Chat route **outside** it → dropped.
- Native Responses provider → existing item semantics, untouched.

This is the shape the issue proposed, and it is deliberately the conservative one: `AGENTS.md` requires vendor evidence plus a live echo-back probe before a family may be added, and dropping asserts nothing about any vendor's `reasoning_content` handling, so it needs neither. Adding a family remains the better outcome where that evidence exists — dropping keeps the model coherent, but it does lose the thinking.

## Not to be confused with #757

#757 moves in the opposite direction on a different path, and both are right. It converts reasoning to visible assistant text for the **native** backend, because that backend rejects a foreign reasoning item outright (`array_above_max_length`, a 404 on an unknown `rs_` id, `invalid_encrypted_content`) and never *reads* a reasoning `summary` — visible text is the only replay that survives there. The ChatGPT backend is not an interleaved-thinking model looping on its own progress notes. AGENTS.md now says so explicitly, so the two do not get reconciled into a single house style by a later reader.

## Verification

```
node --test test/routing.test.mjs test/chat-reasoning.test.mjs \
  test/deepseek-responses-routing.test.mjs
tests 153  pass 152  fail 0  skipped 1   (pinned-LiteLLM, needs MODEL_ROUTER_TEST_LITELLM_PYTHON)

node --test test/fold-intervening-assistant-messages.test.mjs \
  test/commandcode-generate.test.mjs test/empty-completion-guard.test.mjs \
  test/glm-5.3-flash.test.mjs
tests 71  pass 71  fail 0
```

Two new end-to-end tests through the router to a mock gateway. The off-contract one asserts the thought reaches the provider in **no** channel — not as prose, and not as a surviving `reasoning` item for the Chat translation to mishandle — while the assistant's actual answer and the turn structure survive. With `src/router.mjs` restored from `main` it fails and nothing else does. The in-contract counterpart asserts `hy4-preview` still carries its reasoning as a `thinking` part and never as `output_text`; it passes either way by design, as a guard that this fix does not silently delete the history #703's HTTP 400 requires back.

## Scope

Only routes that actually produce reasoning items change behaviour — for a non-thinking model there is nothing in the input to drop, so it is a no-op. The lost context is real and named in the issue: a conversation that switched models mid-thread no longer shows the newer model the older one's thinking on these routes. That is the trade the issue proposed, and it removes the loop trigger entirely rather than one vendor at a time.

title: chore: release v0.6.0
body:
Cuts **v0.6.0**. The motivating issue is #761: `Formula/codex-router.rb` still pins the **v0.5.1** tarball from **28 August**, so every Homebrew user is running code that predates the `x-opencode-session` header (#612, 5 September). opencode Go began requiring that header shortly after, which rejects all six opencode provider ids on that build. There is no workaround on v0.5.1 — the header has to be attached on the outbound hop — so a tag is the only fix that reaches those users.

**532 commits** since v0.5.1.

## What is in this commit

Only the version move and a fresh `## Unreleased` section. `.github/workflows/release.yml` does the rest on tag push: it verifies the tag commit is exactly `origin/main`, that `package.json` matches the tag, and that a **successful push-event CI run exists for that SHA**; then it builds the source archives and the unsigned Linux/Windows tester apps, publishes the release with attestations, and **rewrites `Formula/codex-router.rb` itself** and pushes it to main. Nothing about the formula belongs in this PR.

Four version fields move together because `control-center-electron.test.mjs` asserts it — the root `package.json`, the control center's `package.json`, and the `version` plus `packages[""].version` of both lockfiles.

## Note on the CHANGELOG

`## Unreleased` becomes `## 0.6.0`. Worth knowing: there is **no `## 0.5.1` section** in this file — that release shipped without one — so this block spans 0.5.0 → now rather than 0.5.1 → now. I have not tried to retroactively split it; doing so would mean re-attributing hundreds of entries on a guess.

## Verification

`npm run check` passes (v2-agent applications valid, syntax checks passed), and the version-consistency test passes.

**CI on this PR is the gate.** An earlier version of this description flagged 9 local full-suite failures as something to resolve before tagging. That was a false alarm, and the correction is worth recording: a full run of **untouched `origin/main`** on the same machine failed **97** tests, against 9 on this branch — two trees that differ only by six version strings and a CHANGELOG heading. Every one of them passes when its suite runs in isolation. The local environment is what is failing, not either tree, and the count swings between runs, so local whole-suite results carry no signal here.

## After merge

A push-event CI run on the merge commit must go green before the tag, or the release preflight refuses it — `main`'s current HEAD has no `ci.yml` push run at all, so this ordering is forced rather than optional. Tagging is a separate, deliberate step.

title: Codex picker order + Ollama-served context for generic providers
body:
# Codex picker order + Ollama-served context for generic providers

## Why

Two operator-facing gaps in one install:

1. Codex renders its picker by `priority`, and routed models always publish in a band after the highest visible native GPT entry. An operator whose everyday models are external cannot put them first.
2. Ollama's OpenAI-compatible `/v1/models` lists ids only, so a curated Ollama model keeps the 131072-token conservative default (#266) and text-only input even when the server runs it at 1M with vision.

## What

- `model-picker.json` gains `order`: `native-first` (unchanged default) or `routed-first`. Under `routed-first` every routed model, certified v2 spawn routes included, publishes at 1..N in the existing vendor-group order and the natives shift after them, so nothing interleaves. Visibility writers preserve the choice; an older file or unrecognized value keeps the default. New CLI: `./bin/model-router codex picker-order status|native-first|routed-first` (republishes the catalog).
- Generic discovery asks an OpenAI-chat provider rooted at `/v1` for each listed model's `/api/show`, proves the answer is Ollama-shaped (`capabilities` or `model_info`), and fills in only the fields the list left blank. The probe reuses `fetchUntrustedModelCatalog` (which can now POST a JSON body and return raw JSON under the same origin, redirect, and size guards), stops on 404/405/501 or after three leading refusals, and skips a model the server cannot describe. Discovery reports served modalities as a separate `inputModalities` map so curation never mistakes the merged text-only default for an advertised one; curation stores the advertised window and image input.

## Tests

- `test/model-picker-state.test.mjs`: default absent from file, round-trip, survives every visibility writer, rejects unknown values.
- `test/catalog.test.mjs`: routed-first ordering and native shift (hidden natives shift too), login-free path accepts the option.
- `test/generic-providers.test.mjs`: origin/record derivation, live local-server enrichment, non-Ollama origin asks once, per-model refusal does not end the probe.
- Full suite: only `test/desktop-panel.test.mjs` fails, identically on `main` in this environment (Electron control center).

## Docs

`docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md` picker paragraph; `CHANGELOG.md` Unreleased.

title: Routed agent definition: carry the configured per-model subagent effort
body:
Codex agent role files accept `model_reasoning_effort`, but the generated routed-agent definition only carried `name` / `description` / `model_provider` / `model`. A spawned subagent therefore inherited the **parent turn's** effort: with a low-effort orchestrator, every DeepSeek worker came up at low, even when the router's subagent settings had `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash: max`.

Observed on a live install: a parent running `gpt-6-astra-1m` at `low` spawned three DeepSeek workers; each child thread recorded `reasoning_effort = low` while the generated file carried no effort field at all.

## What

- `routedAgentDefinition(model, { effort })` now writes `model_reasoning_effort = "<effort>"` when an effort is supplied.
- `syncRoutedCodexAgents` passes `subagentEffort(model.slug)` from the multi-agent settings, so the operator's per-model subagent depth lands in the file.
- When no effort is configured the field is omitted, so a model's own default is never frozen into the file (matching `subagentEfforts()`'s "leave the turn alone" rule).

## Tests

- New unit test: the field is present with a configured effort, and absent without one.
- `node --test test/codex-agent-catalog.test.mjs` — 10/10; together with `agent-check` and `agent-bridges`, 16/16 on this branch.
- Live check on the affected install: after regeneration the preset now contains `model_reasoning_effort = "max"`, and the next spawned worker recorded `max` in its thread settings.

title: Poe generic provider on Windows: Codex tool compatibility results and setup notes
body:
Thanks for building this. I wanted to share a Windows field report on using Poe as an operator-defined generic provider with Codex Router.

## Scope

This is a compatibility report from one setup, not a general guarantee for all Poe models or accounts.

- Windows 11
- Codex Desktop / CLI `0.154.0-alpha.6.2` during initial testing
- Codex Router `0.5.1`
- Checkout: `14b2ce6aaf5370eda0dc897b31480681e8e73219`
- Poe generic provider at `https://api.poe.com/v1`

## Bottom line

Poe models could be used through Codex Router while retaining Codex agent tools.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8 both completed:

- terminal/tool use
- file creation/readback/deletion
- Codex in-app browser workflows
- real Codex Chrome-extension workflows
- read-only workflows against an already authenticated browser session

Claude Opus 4.8 was substantially more expensive, but also performed extremely well.

Observed path:

`Codex Desktop -> Codex Router -> Poe API -> model -> Codex tools`

## Provider adapter

I initially tried `openai-responses`:

```powershell
.\codex-router.ps1 providers generic add poe --name "Poe" --base-url https://api.poe.com/v1 --adapter openai-responses --no-apply
````

I stored the key through Router's protected generic credential command:

```powershell
.\codex-router.ps1 providers generic credential poe set
```

Several Poe models returned errors resembling:

```text
Model does not support responses method
```

Changing the generic provider to `openai-chat` was the key compatibility change:

```powershell
.\codex-router.ps1 providers generic edit poe --adapter openai-chat
```

After switching to `openai-chat`, multiple models could run through Codex successfully.

## Model observations

These are only my observed results through Poe + Router, not claims about the models themselves.

| Model               | Result                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash | Excellent / working. Terminal, files, in-app browser, real Chrome extension, and authenticated-browser workflow all succeeded. |
| Claude Opus 4.8     | Excellent / working. Same full workflow; expensive, but extremely capable.                                                     |
| GLM 5.3 Flash       | Basic terminal/tool use worked; a richer Chrome/files workflow later returned upstream HTTP 400.                               |
| Gemini 3.8 Flash    | Poe reported that the model did not support tool calling in this path.                                                         |
| Grok 4.6            | Basic inference worked; Codex tool use was unreliable in my testing.                                                           |
| Kimi K2.7 Code      | Rejected the Codex tool schema before execution; the failure looked similar to #175.                                           |

## Context-window and compaction behavior

The generic curation defaults I initially saw were:

```text
contextWindow: 131072
autoCompact:   110000
```

With my Codex tool/plugin surface, some tasks fell into a pattern like:

```text
automatic compaction
-> repeat same tool
-> automatic compaction
-> repeat same tool
-> ...
```

Even a trivial one-command terminal test could repeat several times.

Manually increasing the Router-side `contextWindow` / `autoCompact` metadata for the models I was testing eliminated the immediate compaction loop in my DeepSeek and GLM tests.

For DeepSeek, one setting I tested was:

```text
contextWindow: 1000000
autoCompact:   900000
```

After that, a fresh task behaved normally:

```text
one terminal call
-> result
-> final answer
```

I am reporting that as an observed workaround, not claiming those values are necessarily the ideal upstream limits.

Potentially useful improvements might include:

* generic-provider context metadata discovery
* better curation UX around context size
* documentation explaining that conservative context defaults can cause premature compaction with a large Codex tool surface

## Fresh tasks after model switches

Switching from one routed model to another inside an existing Codex task was less reliable in this setup.

I saw unnecessary compaction/repetition after changing models mid-thread.

Starting a brand-new task after changing routed models was consistently more reliable.

For now, I am treating:

```text
new routed model = new Codex task
```

as a practical rule.

## Windows install observation

My first Router installation was launched from inside Codex.

The resulting scheduled task failed with Node reporting:

```text
MODULE_NOT_FOUND
```

for `src\start.mjs`, even though the file existed.

During diagnosis, subprocesses launched from the Codex execution environment were also receiving `EPERM`.

I then ran the same Router installation from a normal, non-elevated external PowerShell window and it installed successfully.

So on my machine:

```text
Installing from normal Windows PowerShell worked.
Attempting the installation from Codex's restricted execution environment did not.
```

This may be worth mentioning explicitly in the Windows installation documentation.

## Generic-provider `doctor` observation

After Poe was configured and enabled with a valid protected credential and four curated model routes, `doctor` still reported:

```text
FAIL Enabled providers: none
```

At the same time, the same doctor output reported:

```text
OK Poe generic provider: bound credential is available; 4 curated model route(s)
OK Merged catalog: 4 routed models
OK Background service: running
OK Router health: version 0.5.1
OK Codex model catalog: 4 routed entries visible
```

And:

```powershell
.\codex-router.ps1 providers generic list --json
```

showed the Poe provider as:

```json
{
  "id": "poe",
  "adapter": "openai-chat",
  "enabled": true
}
```

The routed models worked despite `doctor` exiting with status 1.

It looks like generic providers may not be counted by the top-level `Enabled providers` doctor check.

## Curation UX

Interactive curation was a little awkward for me in PowerShell.

The deterministic/noninteractive form worked much better:

```powershell
node .\src\curate-models.mjs poe --models deepseek-v4.1-flash,claude-opus-4.8 --apply
```

That was much easier than using the interactive selector.

## Chrome-extension result

One of the most interesting results was that a Poe-routed model could retain the Codex Chrome-extension workflow.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash successfully:

* connected to the real Codex Chrome extension
* used an already logged-in browser session
* navigated account-specific pages
* read data from the authenticated session
* created a temporary file
* read it back
* deleted it
* completed the workflow without modifying the website

Claude Opus 4.8 also completed the same kind of end-to-end workflow successfully.

That makes the generic-provider path much more useful than simply adding alternate models to the picker.

## Summary

The combination that worked best for me so far is:

* Poe as a generic provider
* `openai-chat` adapter
* fresh Codex task when switching routed models
* adjusted context/compaction metadata for models with larger usable contexts
* DeepSeek V4.1 Flash as a practical lower-cost agent
* Claude Opus 4.8 as a premium/high-capability agent

Hopefully this is useful for documentation and compatibility work.

title: [Bug]: Windows Control Center still flashes a console window — the entry re-exec's `stdio: "inherit"` is exempt from the hidden-console rule
body:
## What happened

Related to #565 (closed by #571), #731, and #751 — this is the remaining path I could still reproduce on Windows 11 after #571 is present.

With the `Codex Router Tray` task running, a **visible console window flashes on every Control Center refresh cycle** (roughly every 40 s, plus the 5-minute snapshot/usage timers). Disabling only the tray task removes it; the router service itself is unaffected. That matches #565's isolation, but #571 does not cover this call site.

## Root cause

`src/control.mjs` re-execs every ordinary invocation through the process tree:

```js
const result = await runOperationProcessTree(process.execPath, [SELF, ...args], {
  cwd: REPO_ROOT,
  env: process.env,
  childEnvironment: {
    CODEX_ROUTER_OPERATION_CHILD: "1",
  },
  deadline,
  stdio: "inherit",
});
process.exit(result.status ?? 1);
```

and `src/process-tree.mjs` maps that to an unhidden console:

```js
const effectiveWindowsHide = stdio === "inherit" ? false : windowsHide;
```

That contract is correct for the case it was written for — a command attached to a terminal the caller is looking at. It is not correct for the Control Center, which runs `control.mjs` with the **packaged Electron binary**: a GUI image that owns **no console**. With no console to inherit, Windows allocates a **new console for the child**, and if that console has a window, the default terminal host shows it and it flashes.

So the failure is exactly the one #571's maintainer described — "a console process spawned by a parent that has no console of its own gets its own window unless `windowsHide` is set" — but the guard #571 added cannot catch it. `test/windows-hidden-consoles.test.mjs` classifies any call whose options match `stdio:[^\n]*inherit` as `interactive` and skips it:

```js
interactive: /stdio:[^\n]*inherit/.test(options),
hidden: /windowsHide\s*:\s*true/.test(options),
```

`inherit` is a fine proxy for "a human is watching a console" when the caller has a console. The Control Center is the counter-example: it inherits stdin/stdout for plumbing (its own pipes), not for a terminal.

## Evidence (redacted)

Processes created within 1 s of a visible window appearing; paths replaced with `<checkout>`, PIDs with `N`. Visible window was `WindowsTerminal.exe` / `OpenConsole.exe -Embedding`, class `CASCADIA_HOSTING_WINDOW_CLASS`, `IsWindowVisible = true`, lifetime ~1 s.

```text
t+0.000  Codex Router.exe  <checkout>\src\control.mjs chatgpt-account-pool status   (spawned by the tray)
t+0.186  powershell.exe  -NoLogo -NoProfile -NonInteractive -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass
                        -File <checkout>\src\windows-process-tree.ps1 <base64 payload: windowsHide=false>
t+0.206  OpenConsole.exe -Embedding        <-- the window
t+0.352  codex.exe app-server
```

The same wrapper shape is used for `--json`, `providers`, `presence status`, `account`, `provider-usage` — one visible window per re-exec.

### Controlled experiment

From a parent with no console of its own (Node started `detached: true, windowsHide: true`), spawning one child at a time and watching for visible console windows:

| Child spawn | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 3 × `windowsHide: true` (powershell wrapper, wrapper without `-WindowStyle Hidden`, `where.exe`) | 0 visible windows |
| 2 × `windowsHide: false` (same wrapper) | 2 visible windows, one per spawn |

So `-WindowStyle Hidden` and the job-wrapper plumbing are not the variable; asking for a hidden console is. (An earlier attempt on this machine added `-WindowStyle Hidden` and rebuilt the Control Center — it does not help, because the window is created and then hidden.)

### After the patch

- Tray active and refreshing normally: 7 job wrappers and 9 `Codex Router.exe` child processes observed across one 5-minute window.
- Visible console windows across 3+ minutes of watching: **0**.
- Output preserved: an ordinary subcommand and a provider-list subcommand both returned exit 0 with their JSON relayed intact.

## Proposed patch

Against `main`. Keeps the inherited terminal for a real terminal, and relays captured streams for a caller that has none.

```diff
--- a/src/control.mjs
+++ b/src/control.mjs
@@ -121,10 +121,29 @@
   const deadline = operationDeadlineFromEnvironment(process.env, {
     timeoutMs: maximumControlOperationMs,
     maximumMs: maximumControlOperationMs,
   });
+  // An inherited terminal is only meaningful when this process owns one. The
+  // Control Center runs this file with the packaged Electron binary, which is a
+  // GUI image: it has no console, so asking its child to inherit stdio makes
+  // Windows allocate a brand-new *visible* console -- the black window that
+  // flashes on every tray refresh. Keep the inherited terminal for a real
+  // terminal, and relay the captured streams for a windowless caller.
+  const callerOwnsConsole = process.stdin?.isTTY === true || process.stdout?.isTTY === true;
   const result = await runOperationProcessTree(process.execPath, [SELF, ...args], {
     cwd: REPO_ROOT,
     env: process.env,
     childEnvironment: {
       CODEX_ROUTER_OPERATION_CHILD: "1",
     },
     deadline,
-    stdio: "inherit",
+    stdio: callerOwnsConsole ? "inherit" : "capture",
   });
+  if (!callerOwnsConsole) {
+    for (const [stream, captured] of [
+      [process.stdout, result.stdout],
+      [process.stderr, result.stderr],
+    ]) {
+      if (!captured) continue;
+      await new Promise((resolve) => {
+        stream.write(captured, () => resolve());
+      });
+    }
+  }
   process.exit(result.status ?? 1);
 }
```

An alternative would be to make `process-tree.mjs` honour an explicit `windowsHide: true` even when `stdio` is `inherit`, and pass it from here. I did not take that route because the current mapping is deliberate and locked by `test/process-tree.test.mjs`, and because "inherit" from a terminal caller must stay a real console process.

Interactive callers are untouched: `setup`, `secret-prompt`, `doctor --fix`, and anything else running under a real terminal keeps `stdio: "inherit"`.

### Verification on the patched checkout

- `node --test test/process-tree.test.mjs` → 13 pass, 0 fail, 6 skipped
- `node --test test/control-center-electron.test.mjs` → 64 pass, 0 fail, 6 skipped

## Environment

- Windows 11, per-user scheduled tasks for the router service and the tray
- Checkout at `38a9fd7` (0.5.x era), so #571's four `windowsHide` fixes are already present
- Confirmed by reading `origin/main` (`b1ead7b`) that both the `stdio: "inherit"` call site and the `inherit ? false : windowsHide` mapping are still there

## Note

I could not open a PR for this: the account I have connected has read-only access to this repository (`push: false`), and there is no fork available from here. The patch above is complete and applies cleanly to `main`; happy to rework it if you would prefer the `process-tree.mjs` variant, a different flag name, or a test alongside it.

title: opencode Zen protocol variants + omit-tool-choice for Qwen behind Go Messages
body:
# opencode Zen protocol variants + omit-tool-choice for Qwen behind Go Messages

Follow-up to #772, rebased on v0.6.0.

## Zen Messages / Responses variants

Zen serves Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI and Meta models over their native wire protocols, exactly as Go does, but only the Go family had the `-messages` / `-responses` provider variants. Every curated Zen model from those families answered HTTP 500 through the chat route (probed live: 22 of 70 Zen models worked, all 48 failures were those families). This adds `opencode-zen-messages` and `opencode-zen-responses`, mirroring the Go variants (same credential, `baseUrl` `zen/v1`, `variantOf: opencode-go` because a variant may not be a variant of a variant). After curating under the right variant, Claude, GPT, Grok and Muse on Zen answer; Gemini on Zen does not on any route (Google-native protocol, no adapter here) and is left out.

## omit-tool-choice

opencode Go's Messages route now answers HTTP 400 (body is only the model id) for every Qwen model when the request carries `tool_choice` in any form, `auto` and `none` included, and calls the listed tools when the field is absent. MiniMax on the same route still accepts the field, so this is per model. `auto-tool-choice` no longer keeps these routes alive: Codex sends `tool_choice` on every tool turn, so every such turn failed. New request profile `omit-tool-choice` deletes the field and keeps the tools; applied to the five Qwen `opencode-go-messages` entries (hashes bumped) and exposed as a curatable profile for resellers with the same quirk. Verified live on all five after the change.

## Tests

`test/opencode-go-messages-qwen-tool-choice.test.mjs` (profile applied, profile known and curatable); registry loads with the new variants; related suites green.

title: [Bug]: opencode-go-responses rejects history after a custom tool call — bridged custom_tool_call_output keeps its ctco_ id
body:
### What happened?

On `opencode-go-responses` (Console Go), any conversation that calls a custom tool (`apply_patch`, `exec`) and then continues fails with HTTP 400. Console Go requires an `fc` prefix on function-shaped item ids, but the custom→function bridge rewrites the item `type` and keeps the item `id`, so a `custom_tool_call_output` still carries `ctco_...`.

```
Invalid 'input[8].id': 'ctco_...'. Expected an ID that begins with 'fc'.
```

Repro: route a turn to `opencode-go-responses/gpt-5.6-luna`, let it call `apply_patch` (that succeeds — the file is written), then send any follow-up turn. It 400s, and keeps failing every turn because the item stays in history. Resending the identical request reproduces the same id at the same index, so this is deterministic, not transient. The failing item is the *output*; the call item carries an `fc_` id and passes. My `router.log` has 44 rejected `ctco_` ids behind this (no raw logs attached).

Root cause (code path):

- `src/router.mjs:3323` — this provider bridges tools with `{ maxNameLength: 64, bridgeAll: true }`.
- `src/namespace-relay.mjs:452` (call) and `:480` (output) rebuild the type via `...rest` / `{ ...item, type }`, so `id` survives untouched.

Suggested fix: omit a non-`fc` `id` on the bridged items (keep `call_id`, which pairs them), or mint `fco_`. The native-direction fix #697 covers `fc`/`ctc`/`msg` but not `custom_tool_call_output`, and only runs toward the native endpoint, so it doesn't cover this direction.

Related: #450 brought this bridge to Console Go; #554/#551 is a distinct pairing bug. codex-router `0.5.1`, Windows 11, Codex desktop.

### Which app do you route through?

Codex

### Platform

Windows

title: [Bug]: DashScope reasoning effort is never delivered on generic-provider routes (curated models can only show one level)
body:
## What happens

Curated DashScope models (`dashscope/qwen3.8-max`, `-flash`, `glm-5.3`, `deepseek-v4.1-flash`) can only declare a single `high` reasoning level, so the picker offers no choice. I then measured whether a choice would even matter: through the router, `reasoning.effort` has **no effect at all** on these routes — six rungs, same reasoning-token count.

## Why

1. `bin/curate-models` falls back to the single-`high` default because DashScope's `/models` returns no effort metadata. That half is the documented policy (#86), so it is correct given what curation knows.
2. The request never carries the field DashScope reads. On `/compatible-mode/v1/chat/completions` DashScope **ignores the nested `reasoning.effort`** that Codex sends and honours the **flat `reasoning_effort`** instead, and no profile translates between them for a generic provider. There is no DashScope profile in `REQUEST_PROFILES`; `qwen-plan` is the closest thing and it deliberately drops the parameter (#13, #118).

## Documentation (Alibaba Model Studio)

- Thinking ladder: <https://docs.bailian.console.aliyun.com/zh/model-studio/deep-thinking>
- OpenAI-Responses-compatible surface: <https://docs.bailian.console.aliyun.com/zh/model-studio/qwen-api-via-openai-responses> — "思考强度控制：通过 `reasoning.effort` 参数控制模型的思考强度"

| family | documented ladder | default | doc's fold for other rungs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8 series | none / low / medium / xhigh | xhigh | minimal→low, high/max→xhigh |
| `glm-5.3` | low / high / max | max | minimal→low, medium→high, xhigh→max |
| `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`, `deepseek-v4-flash` | none / high / max | high | minimal/low/medium→high, xhigh→max |
| `deepseek-v4-flash-0731`, `deepseek-v4-pro-0813` | none / low / high / max | high | minimal→low, medium→high, xhigh→max |

## Measurements

Small prompts; `reasoning_tokens` read from `usage.output_tokens_details`.

`/compatible-mode/v1/chat/completions`, direct:
```
flat   reasoning_effort=none  -> 0 reasoning tokens, no reasoning_content   (x2)
flat   reasoning_effort=xhigh -> 92 / 98
nested reasoning.effort=none  -> 125 / 154   (ignored, thinking still on)
nested reasoning.effort=xhigh -> 102 / 85    (ignored)
```

Through the router, before any change, all six rungs on `dashscope/qwen3.8-max`:
```
none / minimal / low / high / xhigh / max -> 85..132 reasoning tokens; no rung turns thinking off
```

`/compatible-mode/v1/responses` exists (HTTP 200) and honours the nested spelling:
```
effort=none   -> 0 reasoning tokens, output items [message]        (x2)
effort=low    -> 195 / 205, [reasoning, message]
effort=medium -> 270 / 210
effort=xhigh  -> 98 / 84
```

Forced tool choice, both surfaces (same thinking-mode restriction `qwen-plan` already guards):
```
qwen3.8-max    tool_choice=required -> 400 "The tool_choice parameter does not support being set to required or object in thinking mode"
qwen3.8-flash  tool_choice=required -> 400 (same)
glm-5.3 / deepseek-v4.1-flash / kimi-k3 -> 200 with a function_call
```

An unsupported rung is a 400, not a silent fold: `glm-5.3` with `reasoning.effort: "none"` answers `400 Bad Request`. So the rungs have to be mapped, not forwarded verbatim.

## Suggested fix (what I did locally; works)

1. Switch the generic provider to the Responses surface: `bin/model-router codex providers generic edit dashscope --adapter openai-responses`.
2. Add a curatable `dashscope-reasoning` profile that folds Codex's rung onto the family ladder above, writes the nested spelling on a Responses surface and the flat one on chat completions, and downgrades a forced `tool_choice` for the Qwen3.8 family. `minimal` maps onto DashScope's `none`: Codex's ladder has no `none`, and thinking-off is the one rung a user can observe from outside.
3. Curate the four documented models with their ladders (metadata is written on add, so the entries have to be removed and re-added).

End-to-end after that change:
```
dashscope/qwen3.8-max         minimal -> 0 tokens, [message]   low -> 190/206   xhigh -> 83/86
dashscope/glm-5.3             low -> 0/0                       max -> 211/299
dashscope/deepseek-v4.1-flash minimal -> 0/0                   high -> 111/50
bin/test-model --live --yes: 5/5 (basic, streaming, tool calling, stateless tool-result replay, compaction) on all five curated models
```

## Notes

- `kimi-k3` is sold by DashScope but has no row in the ladder table, so it keeps the single `high` default rather than an invented ladder.
- The fix is local-only right now (an unmanaged checkout), so `bin/update` will overwrite it. Happy to open a PR with tests in the `test/routing.test.mjs` style if this shape is acceptable to maintainers.

title: fix(api-forwarder): fold DashScope's documented reasoning ladder for curated routes
body:
Fixes #785.

## Why

Curated DashScope routes could only publish a single `high` rung, and measuring whether a rung would change anything showed it would not: through the router, all six Codex rungs produced the same turn.

Two causes:

1. DashScope's `/models` publishes no effort metadata, so curation falls back to the conservative single-`high` default. That half is the documented policy (#86) and stays correct given what curation knows.
2. Nothing translated the effort into the field DashScope reads. Model Studio documents `reasoning.effort` with a ladder per upstream family, and its OpenAI-Responses-compatible surface honours that nested spelling, but `/compatible-mode/v1/chat/completions` ignores it and reads the flat `reasoning_effort` instead. A generic provider had no profile at all, and the closest existing one, `qwen-plan`, deliberately drops the parameter (#13, #118).

Documentation:
- thinking ladder: <https://docs.bailian.console.aliyun.com/zh/model-studio/deep-thinking>
- Responses surface: <https://docs.bailian.console.aliyun.com/zh/model-studio/qwen-api-via-openai-responses>

| family | documented ladder | default | doc's fold for other rungs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8 series | none / low / medium / xhigh | xhigh | minimal→low, high/max→xhigh |
| `glm-5.3` | low / high / max | max | minimal→low, medium→high, xhigh→max |
| `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`, `deepseek-v4-flash` | none / high / max | high | minimal/low/medium→high, xhigh→max |
| `deepseek-v4-flash-0731`, `deepseek-v4-pro-0813` | none / low / high / max | high | minimal→low, medium→high, xhigh→max |

## What

- `src/request-profiles.mjs` and `src/curate-models.mjs`: a new curatable `dashscope-reasoning` profile plus the prompt text curation needs for it.
- `src/api-forwarder.mjs`: the family fold table and the branch. It folds the requested rung onto the family ladder, writes the nested spelling on a Responses surface and the flat one on chat completions, maps Codex's `minimal` onto DashScope's `none` because Codex ships no thinking-off rung and that is the one rung a user can observe from outside, and downgrades the forced `tool_choice` for the Qwen3.8 family.
- `test/generic-routing.test.mjs`: a forwarder-level case over a mock upstream covering all three documented families plus one without a documented row.
- `AGENTS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`.

## Measurements

Live, small prompts, `reasoning_tokens` from `usage.output_tokens_details`.

`/compatible-mode/v1/chat/completions`, direct:
```
flat   reasoning_effort=none  -> 0 reasoning tokens, no reasoning_content   (x2)
flat   reasoning_effort=xhigh -> 92 / 98
nested reasoning.effort=none  -> 125 / 154   (ignored, thinking still on)
nested reasoning.effort=xhigh -> 102 / 85    (ignored)
```

Through the router, before this change, all six rungs on `dashscope/qwen3.8-max`:
```
none / minimal / low / high / xhigh / max -> 85..132 reasoning tokens; no rung turns thinking off
```

`/compatible-mode/v1/responses` exists (HTTP 200) and honours the nested spelling:
```
effort=none   -> 0 reasoning tokens, output items [message]        (x2)
effort=low    -> 195 / 205, [reasoning, message]
effort=medium -> 270 / 210
effort=xhigh  -> 98 / 84
```

Forced tool choice, both surfaces (the restriction `qwen-plan` already guards for Qwen):
```
qwen3.8-max    tool_choice=required -> 400 "The tool_choice parameter does not support being set to required or object in thinking mode"
qwen3.8-flash  tool_choice=required -> 400 (same)
glm-5.3 / deepseek-v4.1-flash / kimi-k3 -> 200 with a function_call
```

An unsupported rung is a 400, not a silent fold: `glm-5.3` with `reasoning.effort: "none"` answers `400 Bad Request`. That is why the profile maps rather than forwards.

## Verification

- `node --test test/generic-routing.test.mjs` — 4/4 on this branch. The new case is RED on the parent commit (`AssertionError`, 3 pass / 1 fail) with the test unchanged, and GREEN here.
- `node --test test/routing.test.mjs` — 143/143.
- `node --test test/curate-models.test.mjs test/generic-providers.test.mjs` — 66/66.
- Live through the installed router, generic provider on `--adapter openai-responses`:
  - `bin/test-model --live --yes` 5/5 (basic, streaming, forced tool calling, stateless tool-result replay, compaction) on `dashscope/qwen3.8-max`, `qwen3.8-flash`, `glm-5.3`, `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, `kimi-k3`.
  - effort sweep: `qwen3.8-max` minimal → 0 reasoning tokens / `low` 190, 206 / `xhigh` 83, 86; `glm-5.3` low 0, 0 / max 211, 299; `deepseek-v4.1-flash` minimal 0, 0 / high 111, 50.

## Notes

- A curated entry still has to be removed and re-added to pick up a ladder (`--efforts` is written on add only, as #118 documented for `--request-profile`).
- The nested spelling needs the generic provider on the `openai-responses` adapter; the profile also writes the flat one, so a chat-completions DashScope provider is covered too.
- `kimi-k3` is sold by DashScope with no row in the ladder table, so it keeps the single `high` default rather than an invented ladder. If a row for it appears in the documentation, it needs its own entry in the table.
- `ponytail:` comment in the table names the ceiling: only the three families the curated routes use are encoded, and the next family needs the documentation's own fold values before it is curated.

title: feat: quota-aware external fallback for Codex auto-review
body:
### Problem

When Codex Router is used with **Use Router with ChatGPT** enabled, an external model can handle the main agent turn while Codex's **Approve for me / auto-review** still uses the native `codex-auto-review` model.

This works while ChatGPT/Codex quota is available. Once the ChatGPT usage limit is exhausted, however, automatic approval requests fail even though the selected external provider still has usable quota.

As a result, a routed external-model session can continue reasoning and generating commands but becomes unable to execute commands requiring automatic approval.

This is particularly noticeable with commands such as `gh`, network access, or other sandbox escalations.

### Desired behavior

Add an optional **quota-aware fallback model for automatic approval review**.

Desired flow:

```text
approval required
      ↓
codex-auto-review / ChatGPT
      ↓
  success?
   ├─ yes → use native review decision
   └─ no, specifically usage/quota exhausted
            ↓
      configured external reviewer
            ↓
      use external review decision
```

When the native quota becomes available again, reviews should automatically return to `codex-auto-review`.

### Important safety behavior

The fallback should happen only when the **reviewer request itself cannot run because of quota/rate-limit exhaustion**.

It should **not** retry through an external model when:

- `codex-auto-review` returned `deny`
- a policy/safety rejection occurred
- the native reviewer produced a valid decision
- the failure is ambiguous or malformed

A native denial must never be interpreted as provider failure and bypassed through the fallback.

Ideally Codex-Router could cache the reported quota reset/retry time so it does not send a known-to-fail native reviewer request for every subsequent approval.

### Acceptance criteria

1. With ChatGPT quota available, `Approve for me` continues using the native Codex reviewer.
2. When that reviewer fails specifically because its usage limit is exhausted, the configured external reviewer is used.
3. Main-agent model selection remains independent of reviewer selection.
4. Native `deny` decisions never trigger fallback.
5. After the native quota resets, the native reviewer becomes primary again automatically.
6. The active reviewer/fallback state is observable to the user.
