title: fix: keep every line ending a Gemini .env arrived with
body:
## Why

`gemini-env.mjs` states its contract three times — "treats every other byte as somebody else's work", "removing the block restores the document exactly", "byte-identical rather than merely equivalent" — and then breaks it on any document that mixes line endings.

`newline()` picks one ending for the whole file (CRLF if the text contains one anywhere, LF otherwise), `splitLines()` splits on both, and the result is rejoined on that single choice. A `.env` touched by two editors has its untouched lines rewritten:

```js
const original = "A=1\r\nB=2\nC=3\r\n";
removeGeminiEnvBlock(spliceGeminiEnvBlock(original, values))
// main         -> "A=1\r\nB=2\r\nC=3\r\n"   <- B=2 gained a \r the router never wrote
// this branch  -> "A=1\r\nB=2\nC=3\r\n"     <- unchanged
```

Removing the block does not undo it — `removeGeminiEnvBlock` runs the same join — so the rewrite outlives the integration that caused it.

It is not destructive to `dotenv`, which reads both endings. It is a file the user owns being edited in a way they did not ask for, by the one module in the repository that makes a point of not doing that. The other managed-document writers already get this right: `toml-structure.mjs` and `yaml-structure.mjs` both split on `"\n"` alone, so a `\r` stays attached to its line and survives the rejoin. This module is the only one that strips it.

## What changed

`splitLinesWithEndings()` returns each line with the terminator that actually followed it, and `joinLines()` rebuilds from those. `spliceGeminiEnvBlock` and `removeGeminiEnvBlock` use them; the rendered block takes the document's prevailing ending, which is what keeps a republish byte-identical.

Nothing else moves: `locateBlock`, `conflictingAssignments` and `geminiManagedBlockPresent` still work off plain `splitLines`, since they only read.

## The one difference that remains

A document that ends without a newline gains exactly one, because the block has to start on its own line. That was already true, is already noted in `spliceGeminiEnvBlock`, and cannot be undone from the text alone — nothing records that the terminator was not there to begin with. `removeGeminiEnvBlock`'s doc comment claimed to restore the document exactly; it now says what actually holds.

## Verification

- Three new cases in `test/gemini-env.test.mjs`. Two fail on `main` (`a document that mixes CRLF and LF keeps every line's own ending`, `an LF document with a CRLF value line is not normalised either`) and pass here. The third pins the trailing-newline exception and passes on `main` too — it documents the behaviour rather than evidencing the fix.
- Property run over 30,000 generated documents (random mixes of CRLF/LF, comments, `export` forms, quoted values, with and without a trailing terminator): publish-twice was byte-identical in every one, and the only publish/remove differences were the trailing newline above — 6,404 of those, zero unexplained.
- Confirmed the before/after directly by importing `main`'s copy of the module alongside this one, rather than trusting a stash.
- `node --test test/gemini-env.test.mjs test/gemini-config-manager.test.mjs test/gemini-surface.test.mjs test/gemini-shape.test.mjs test/gemini-trailing-turns.test.mjs` — 85/85.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Two things I looked at and did not change

While chasing this I checked whether the same shape existed elsewhere, since the TOML equivalent was worth fixing (#737):

- **`findFrameEnd` is copied into five SSE transforms and has drifted.** `early-tool-item-done.mjs` recognises any CR/LF/CRLF pair as a frame separator; `item-lifecycle-normalizer`, `leaked-tool-call-recovery`, `message-phase` and `reasoning-tag-stripper` recognise only `\n\n` and `\r\n\r\n`. They are chained in one pipeline (`router.mjs:4479-4550`), so they can disagree about where a frame ends. I could not produce a stream where it bites — the separators they all agree on are the only ones anything emits here — so this is a note, not a change.
- **`eventBlock` reads only the first `data:` line** in `reasoning-tag-stripper` and `leaked-tool-call-recovery`, while `message-phase` joins every `data:` line and `early-tool-item-done` refuses a second one outright. SSE allows several. All three behaviours fail safe (the block passes through unrewritten), so again: a note.

Happy to open either as an issue if you want them tracked.

title: [Bug]: Direct Meta routes (muse-spark-1.3-contributor) fail with 400 on recursive Codex tool schemas
body:
### What happened?

Selecting **Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor (Meta)** (`meta-muse-spark-1-3-contributor`) in the Codex model picker fails on turns that carry Codex tool definitions. The turn dies before inference with:

> `meta rejected the request for Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor (Meta). (HTTP 400: {"error":{"code":null,"message":"Recursive JSON schemas are not currently supported","param":"parameters","type":"invalid_request_error"}})`

Router log (`router.log`) confirms the rejection happens downstream of LiteLLM:

> `litellm.BadRequestError ... Received Model Group=meta-muse-spark-1-3-contributor`
> `Available Model Group Fallbacks=None`

So the 400 surfaces 1:1 to the user with no fallback.

### Why it happens (from the 0.6.0 sources)

Codex attaches tool definitions whose JSON Schema contains a self-referencing `$ref` cycle. The router already knows Meta's endpoint refuses those with a bare 400 and has a repair (`flattenRecursiveToolSchemas` in `src/api-forwarder.mjs`, via `nonRecursiveToolSchema` which blanks only the cycle-closing edge). But the repair is gated behind the per-model flag `model.toolSchemaRecursion === "flatten"`, and per the code comment only locally curated Moonshot models opt in (`src/opencode-curation.mjs`); the direct `meta/*` routes don't have the flag, so the recursive schema passes through untouched and Meta rejects the whole turn.

Related prior art: #626 (same error class, fixed for the `commandcode` / `commandcode-messages` tool surface) and the changelog entry "Muse Spark 1.2 Contributor no longer fails on recursive Codex tool schemas through OpenCode Go" — the 1.3 direct-Meta route was never covered.

### Expected behavior

`meta/muse-spark-1.3-contributor` (and ideally all direct `meta/*` routes, same restriction presumably applies to 1.1/1.2/1.3) gets the same cycle-closing-edge flattening as the OpenCode Go Muse route, instead of losing the turn with a bare 400.

### Repro

1. Route Codex through codex-router with the `meta` provider enabled.
2. Pick `Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor (Meta)`.
3. Send a message in a thread where Codex includes its namespaced tools (any normal agentic turn with tools attached).
4. Turn fails with the HTTP 400 above.

### Environment

- codex-router 0.6.0 (`6d2d9cb`), target Codex, macOS
- Doctor: catalog healthy, `openai_authenticated: true`; only the Meta direct route fails. Native GPT models and other providers route the same turns fine, so this is not a credential or catalog problem.

### Workaround used meanwhile

Native GPT model or the OpenRouter Muse Spark variant for tool-heavy turns.

title: fix: flatten recursive tool schemas for direct Meta Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor
body:
## Root cause

Codex attaches tool definitions whose JSON Schema contains a self-referencing `$ref` cycle. Meta direct Responses endpoint answers those with HTTP 400 `Recursive JSON schemas are not currently supported` before inference, and the turn is lost downstream of the gateway (surfaces as `litellm.BadRequestError`, no fallback).

The router already has the repair for exactly this validator (`flattenRecursiveToolSchemas` via `nonRecursiveToolSchema`, gated on the per-model `toolSchemaRecursion === "flatten"`), but only the OpenCode-routed Muse entries opted in (checked-in Go-Responses configs + free curation docs). The direct `meta/*` routes added in #790-era work never got the flag, so the recursive schema passed through untouched. Verified against current HEAD: none of the five `config/meta/*.json` models carry the flag.

## Why this scope

- Declarative one-line opt-in on the verified route only (`meta/muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, the exact route from the #792 report). No new provider branch, no shared-logic change, no wire change for any other provider.
- Follows the `opencode-go-responses/muse-spark-1.3-contributor` precedent, which ships the forwarder flag without a router-level gate (the 400 comes from Meta downstream of LiteLLM, so the forwarder hop is the correct layer).
- Sibling Meta routes (1.1, 1.2, 1.2-contributor, plain 1.3) keep their payloads per the house rule that other Responses models retain recursive schemas until their own endpoint proves the same restriction. No `compHash` bump, matching the earlier Muse flatten commit.
- Also refreshes the now-stale gate comment in `api-forwarder.mjs` (it still claimed only curated Moonshot models opt in) plus a CHANGELOG entry.

## Before / after

- Before: `responses/meta-muse-spark-1-3-contributor` with a Codex-style recursive tool schema forwards the `$ref` cycle untouched to Meta, which 400s the turn.
- After: only the cycle-closing edge is blanked (`$defs.Node.properties.child` `{}`); definitions, acyclic `$ref`s, sibling constraints, and declared types are preserved. Same-provider `meta/muse-spark-1.3` control route is byte-identical.

## Regression tests

- `test/generic-routing.test.mjs`: strict mock upstream; asserts the verified route is flattened, acyclic info survives, the control route is untouched, both requests are routable (`/v1/responses`, correct upstream ids) and return 200. Fails before the fix (upstream receives the raw `$ref` cycle), passes after.
- `test/registry.test.mjs`: pins `toolSchemaRecursion: "flatten"` on `meta/muse-spark-1.3-contributor`. Fails before, passes after.

## Validation

- `node --test` on generic-routing, registry, tool-schema-root, namespace-relay-routing, namespace-relay, chat-tool-surface: 295/295 pass.
- `node --test test/routing.test.mjs`: 144/144 pass.
- `npm run check`: pass. `git diff --check`: clean.
- Full `npm test`: 3901 pass / 13 fail on this diff; every failure is in untouched areas (POSIX `sh -n` checks, Homebrew/macOS-only paths, Electron browser cascade, 600s-timeout files needing external CLIs/network/display, Antigravity OAuth, Linux packager, live Codex app-server, port-bind flakes). The fast subset (both POSIX-shell checks, Homebrew) was re-run on clean main and fails identically there, proving pre-existing/environment-specific.

## Live-testing limitation

No live Meta turn was run (no credentials in this environment, and it would spend quota). Verification is the mock-upstream forwarder proof above; the repair itself (`nonRecursiveToolSchema`) is unchanged shared code with existing unit coverage.

Fixes #792

title: fix: repair empty namespace descriptions for strict generic Responses endpoints
body:
From a real strict generic Responses deployment (Azure OpenAI /openai/v1 through codex-router's generic-provider system with adapter openai-responses): model discovery and plain inference worked, but any Codex turn carrying the large native tool surface was rejected before model inference.

Reproduction is now provider-independent and fixture-backed. test/generic-routing.test.mjs spins a strict mock upstream that enforces the public Responses contract documented in openai/codex#37422 and openai/codex#37952: every type: namespace tool requires a non-empty description (minLength 1). The mock 400s with the exact Azure shapes (empty_string / missing required parameter). The client-side fixture is a realistic current Codex inventory: image_gen/imagegen namespace, collaboration namespace, codex_app namespace, an MCP namespace, a shell function, and an ordinary function.

Root cause on pristine current main: the generic openai-responses forwarder path forwarded Codex's namespace tools verbatim. Codex itself emits namespaces with description: empty string (dynamic grouping and Responses Lite both serialize that shape), which OpenAI accepts leniently but strict validators reject. Pristine main therefore sent image_gen with an empty description and the strict mock rejected the whole turn (Outcome B, reproduced before the fix).

Why this solution is generic, not an Azure hack: the repair satisfies Azure's public OpenAI-compatible Responses contract via a general standards-compliant normalization. No hostname, resource-name, model-name, or provider-id checks; no new request profile; no blanket tool deletion. Empty or missing namespace descriptions become 'Tools in the {name} namespace.' Scoped to operator-configured generic Responses endpoints (provider.generic, alongside the existing withoutInputMessagePhase boundary); built-in Responses providers keep their current wire shape. Already-valid requests are forwarded byte-identical.

Exact tools/capabilities preserved (asserted in the test): image_gen keeps its name and inner imagegen function with the same parameters (repaired description only, never deleted); collaboration spawn_agent, codex_app create_thread, MCP js, shell exec_command, and ordinary get_weather are preserved verbatim; tool count unchanged; namespace identity restoration unaffected (identity is the name). No credential leakage (no Authorization forwarded, no cred_ or caller key in the body).

Tests run:
- node --test test/generic-routing.test.mjs (6/6 pass, including the new strict-validator case)
- node --test test/openai-adapters.test.mjs (12/12)
- node --test test/generic-providers.test.mjs test/generic-runtime-registry.test.mjs test/generic-doctor.test.mjs (22/22)
- node --test test/namespace-relay.test.mjs + namespace-relay-routing (174/175 pass, 1 flaky timeout that passes in isolation and is unrelated)
- npm run check (pass)
- git diff --check (pass)
- Full npm test was run on the pristine tree during this session (pre-existing unrelated failures in antigravity/chatgpt/browser/electron areas); targeted suites above pass with the fix.

Live Azure verification: not performed. Verification is fixture-backed only; no credentials were read, printed, committed, or included. No live endpoint or secret appears anywhere in the diff.

title: diagnose: name Windows fatal NTSTATUS exits and point at credential-safe capture
body:
Related to #465. Does not fix the crash — the native root cause is still unconfirmed, and this PR deliberately changes no decoding, supervision, or restart behavior.

## What I verified on current main

- Both zstd hardenings are in: #564 (async `zstdDecompress` + declared-size preflight + caps on `/v1/responses`) and #764 (same treatment for the last sync zstd path in `cursor-surface.mjs`).
- No `zstdDecompressSync` remains anywhere in `src/`. Encoded bodies are capped at 128 MiB (`MAX_BODY_BYTES`), decoded bodies at 256 MiB (`MAX_DECODED_BODY_BYTES`). The `an oversize zstd body is refused with 413 before decoding and the router stays up` regression test exists.
- Crash recovery half is closed: #581 moved relaunch to the minute heartbeat trigger (`src/service-windows.mjs`); the gateway supervisor intentionally still does not cover the router/forwarders (a crash in our own code is a bug report).
- Upstream: no public Node issue ties `node:zlib`'s zstd decoder to `STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN`. The closer match remains `nodejs/node#62260` (fast-fail on Windows build 26200 — the reporter's build), where commenters report the identical workload clean on Node 22.23.2. `0xC0000409` is the generic `__fastfail` envelope; parameter 0 names the reason.
- Remaining gap: when a child dies this way, the service log keeps only `exited (code=3221226505, signal=null)` — a number that identifies no subsystem and asks for an artifact (WER dump) that `__fastfail` bypasses, so it is never written.

## Change

- New `src/fatal-exit.mjs`: `describeChildExit()` names five high-confidence Windows fatal statuses (access violation, illegal instruction, heap corruption, stack-buffer overrun, stack overflow) in the supervisor exit fragment; unknown NTSTATUS-range codes gain hex but no invented name; signed spellings (`-1073740791`) classify the same death. `fatalExitFollowUp()` appends a capture pointer **only** for process-level native aborts: Event Viewer + WinDbg `!analyze -v` with parameter 0, Node report flags with `--report-exclude-env --report-exclude-network`, and an explicit ban on uploading raw reports/dumps (credential-bearing). Ordinary and signalled exits render byte-identical; crash lines stay ungated on `CODEX_ROUTER_QUIET`.
- Wired into the `start.mjs` service-exit line and the `gateway-supervisor.mjs` restart lines.
- New `test/fatal-exit.test.mjs` (8 tests): naming, signed/unsigned, unknown-code hex, non-integer safety, pointer gating/content, and a fatal-abort supervisor run proving the death is named and the gateway is still restarted.

## Validation (Windows 11, Node v22.23.2 — the reporter's retest runtime)

- `test/fatal-exit.test.mjs`: 8/8 pass.
- Related suites green: `gateway-supervisor`, `gateway-restart`, `startup-cleanup`, `http-utils-zstd-frame`, `cursor-surface`, `service-lifecycle`, `service-process`, `client-restart-notice`, `python-lock`, plus the #465 routing regression (`oversize zstd → 413`, router stays up).
- `npm run check` passes; `git diff --check` clean.
- Bounded local probe (uncommitted): valid 8 MB zstd body decodes async in ~29 ms; a header-tampered 512 MiB-declared frame is refused from the header in 0 ms without reaching the decoder; handed to the decoder it fails bounded (`Frame requires too much memory for decoding`); 20× large decodes leave the process healthy. No crash reproduced — expected for an intermittent native abort; no crash-prevention claim is made.
- Full suite: 3859 pass / 19 fail — triaged against pristine-main baseline, all pre-existing/environmental: `bin/codex-router is valid POSIX shell` fails on clean main (no POSIX `sh` here); `control-center-electron` shows the identical cancel profile branch-vs-baseline when run cleanly; the Antigravity pair passes identically in isolation on both; remaining full-run failures pass in isolation on both (parallel-load flakes).

## What remains unknown

The faulting native frame. If `0xC0000409` recurs, the next useful packet is what this PR's pointer asks for: sanitized Node report frames or WinDbg `!analyze -v` with exception parameter 0, the surrounding exit lines, and `Content-Encoding` + compressed/decoded byte counts for the final requests.

title: [Bug]: A local tool-argument conversion failure is reported as a provider rejection, and failover retries other providers
body:
### What happened

A Codex thread whose history contains an assistant `function_call` with
**invalid JSON arguments** is rejected with an HTTP 400 that names a provider:

```
opencode rejected the request for Union Alpha Free (opencode Go). (HTTP 400:
Failed to parse tool call arguments for tool 'exec_command' (Anthropic tool
invoke). Error: Unterminated string starting at: line 1 column 8 (char 7).
[redacted argument body]
```

That error is raised **locally**, before any provider request is sent. The
pinned LiteLLM (1.96.0) converts the Responses request to Anthropic Messages and
parses every assistant tool call's `arguments` to fill `tool_use.input`:

```
litellm/llms/anthropic/chat/transformation.py:1870  transform_request
 -> litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py:2741  anthropic_messages_pt
 -> prompt_templates/factory.py:1775  convert_to_anthropic_tool_invoke
 -> prompt_templates/common_utils.py:1688  parse_tool_call_arguments -> ValueError
 -> transformation.py:1876  raise AnthropicError
```

`context="Anthropic tool invoke"` is that function's hardcoded label, so the
parenthetical in the message is ours, not the provider's.

### Impact

* The message points at the provider. The real cause - a call already sitting in
  history - is invisible, and there is no way to tell which call is at fault.
* Because it is surfaced as a provider 400, failover retries other providers for
  a request that cannot succeed. Observed 2026-09-16: after a local conversion
  400 for `opencode-go-messages/union-alpha`, the same turn hit
  `openrouter/stealth/union-alpha` for a generic provider 400.
* Retained evidence: `router.log` frames 39171-39200 (Zen, 22:04:35 UTC) and
  39341+ (Go, 22:07:08 and 22:12:05 UTC); 20 error lines / 10
  `convert_to_anthropic_tool_invoke` frames.

### Expected behavior

Distinguish a local request-conversion failure from a provider rejection: say
which conversion failed and which call it was (tool name, call id, position), so
the offending history entry is identifiable, and do not attribute it to the
provider.

### Not claimed

Why the response carried unterminated arguments is unresolved - provider-side
early completion and a local bridge/relay tail loss are both open, and no raw
frames were retained. This report is only about misattribution.

title: [Bug]: A completed function_call with unterminated JSON arguments is relayed and permanently breaks the thread's history
body:
### What happened

A provider response was relayed to the client as a **completed** turn whose
`function_call` carried **unterminated JSON arguments**. The client stored the
call, could not execute it (`failed to parse function arguments: EOF while
parsing a string at line 1 column 1116`), replayed it in the next request, and
every later turn on that thread then failed - on the Go/Zen Messages routes with
the local conversion error of the linked issue, and on OpenAI-compatible routes
as a generic provider 400.

Retained examples (Codex rollouts, 2026-09-16):

* `exec_command` call with 1114 argument chars, cut inside a JSON string
  (Go, `opencode-go-messages/union-alpha`)
* `exec_command` call with 143 argument chars, cut mid-word
  (Go, `opencode-go-messages/union-alpha`)

Nothing on our side repairs it: the pinned LiteLLM's `_attempt_json_repair`
(`common_utils.py:1575`) only closes unmatched brackets, and refuses a string
that was never terminated - correctly, since closing it would invent bytes.

### Impact

One unusable provider response permanently breaks a thread; today the only
recovery is abandoning or rebuilding that history. `src/namespace-relay.mjs:2450
jsonArgumentsAreUnambiguous` gates only *rewriting*, and
`#unsafeSseFrame` (line 3151) then passes the frame through, so no layer refuses
the unusable call.

### Options (needs a decision; no implementation proposed here)

* Fail the turn when a completed `function_call` has non-empty arguments that do
  not parse as JSON, instead of relaying an item the client can never execute.
* At minimum adopt the attribution fix in the linked issue.
* Permissive JSON repair is not the answer: it would invent command bytes.

### Not claimed

The cause of the truncation is unresolved: the provider (or its gateway)
completing the tool call early and a local Responses-bridge / relay tail loss
are both consistent with what was retained. The stop/finish reason for those
responses was never recorded (the usage rows carry counts only), so it cannot be
checked. A structural capture would settle it without content: per upstream
request, event types with byte lengths and item ids, the terminal event type, the
upstream stop/finish reason when present, and per tool-call item a cumulative
arguments byte count plus a parsed-JSON boolean - no headers, prompts, schemas or
argument bodies.

title: Publish the real GPT-5.6 effort ladder for kiro-prism
body:
## The problem

The three GPT-5.6 tiers carried a single rung:

```json
"reasoningLevels": [{ "effort": "medium", "description": "Gateway default reasoning" }]
```

So no client routed through codex-router could select an effort for `gpt-5.6-sol`, `-terra`, or `-luna`, even though Prism advertises the full scale.

## Why it was wrong

That single-rung entry was recorded when Prism itself reported an **empty** effort ladder for these models. Prism's `effort_levels()` read only `output_config.effort` — the Claude container — while GPT-5.6 carries effort in `reasoning.effort` ([Kiro docs](https://kiro.dev/docs/models/effort/)). Prism now resolves both containers and reports the real ladder:

```
gpt-5.6-sol     effort_levels=['none','low','medium','high','xhigh','max']
gpt-5.6-luna    effort_levels=['none','low','medium','high','xhigh','max']
gpt-5.6-terra   effort_levels=['none','low','medium','high','xhigh','max']
```

## The change

Publishes the five **rankable** rungs. `none` is deliberately omitted: it is not on this repository's `EFFORT_LADDER` (`minimal..ultra`) and is an off-state rather than a depth the picker should rank. `clampEffort` passes off-ladder values through unchanged, so carrying it would put an unrankable entry in the picker.

`defaultEffort` stays `medium`, matching Prism's own per-family default for these tiers.

Claude entries are untouched — their effort has always lived in `output_config`, so they already advertised the correct ladder.

## Verified

After `refresh-catalog`, the merged catalog Codex actually reads:

```
kiro-prism/gpt-5.6-sol      default=medium  levels=['low','medium','high','xhigh','max']
kiro-prism/gpt-5.6-luna     default=medium  levels=['low','medium','high','xhigh','max']
kiro-prism/gpt-5.6-terra    default=medium  levels=['low','medium','high','xhigh','max']
kiro-prism/claude-opus-5    default=medium  levels=['low','medium','high','xhigh','max']
```

Cherry-picked onto `origin/custom/v0.5.1` in a temporary worktree so unrelated uncommitted work in the main checkout was never touched.

title: fix: move opencode tool-result images onto a user turn
body:
`opencode-go/glm-5.3-flash` loses the whole conversation the moment Codex's
`view_image` returns a screenshot:

```
POST /v1/responses -> 400
Error from provider (Console Go): Upstream request failed:
[invalid_request_error] messages[25]: tool content: part type "image_url"
is not supported; only text is
```

That route advertises image input (`config/opencode/go/glm-5.3-flash.json:30-33`)
and its user turns really do read images, so nothing is misdeclared: the
conversation is legal right up to the hop that sends it. LiteLLM turns the
Responses `function_call_output` carrying the screenshot into a Chat Completions
`{role:"tool", content:[{type:"text"},{type:"image_url"}]}` message
(`litellm/responses/litellm_completion_transformation/transformation.py:955-995`),
`sanitizeChatToolHistory` forwards it untouched because the only image sanitizer
in the forwarder is gated on `isGeminiProvider` (`src/api-forwarder.mjs:547-555`),
and opencode's chat surface refuses image parts anywhere but a user turn.

## Measured, 17 September 2026, `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/chat/completions`, `glm-5.3-flash`

| history | result |
| --- | --- |
| `[user, assistant(tool_calls), tool(text + image_url)]` | 400, the error above (422 `Input should be a valid string`, param `messages.2.tool.content.str`, when `tools` is omitted) |
| `[user(text + image_url)]` | 200, pixel described correctly |
| same history, tool result reduced to text, image on a following user turn | 200, image still read ("the result shows a solid red image") |
| hoisted user turn sitting mid-history, ahead of further assistant and user turns | 200 |
| one hoisted user turn carrying two images for a two-result tool batch | 200 |

The refusal is intermittent, and that matters for how this is fixed. Console Go
answers the same payload differently across attempts: the string-only validation
was observed three times (twice in the reporting session's live traffic, once on
a 1x1 PNG probe, once more as the 422 variant on a 900x900 PNG with
`stream: false`), while later attempts at the identical tool-placement payload
returned 200 four times out of four. So a route that "works today" is one
backend rotation away from losing every turn that reads an image, which is why
this normalizes the request rather than waiting for a reproducible failure.

## What this does

Where the provider is opencode and the model reads images, each tool result is
reduced to text and its images move to one user turn placed immediately after
the contiguous run of tool messages:

- Images move rather than being replaced with a placeholder. The model called
  `view_image` on purpose; a placeholder costs it the screenshot it asked for,
  and the vision bridge cannot read one here — this forwarder sits downstream of
  the gateway, as the existing strip path just below already explains.
- One hoisted turn per contiguous tool run, not one per message, so a parallel
  tool batch keeps every result adjacent to the assistant turn that called them.
- The hoisted turn is labelled as tool output and as untrusted data. Moving an
  image to `user` is the one thing the model can otherwise misread: text inside
  a screenshot must not become an instruction it attributes to the user.
- Tool content collapses back to a plain string, which is the shape this
  endpoint validates against (the 422 above names `.tool.content.str`). Parts
  the split does not recognize keep the list shape instead of being dropped.
- Gated on `supportsImageInput(model)`: a text-only route's images are already
  replaced with a spelled-out reason by the strip path in `normalizeBody`, and
  hoisting first would move them into a user turn just to have them replaced
  there.

Six catalog routes declare `image` on an opencode Chat Completions provider and
are affected: `opencode-go/glm-5.3-flash`, `opencode-go/kimi-k2.5`,
`opencode-go/kimi-k3`, `opencode-go/qwen3.5-plus`,
`opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash`, `opencode-go/deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp`.
The Messages and Responses variants do not reach this path.

## Verification

- New `test/opencode-tool-image-hoist.test.mjs` spawns the forwarder against a
  mock upstream and holds what a provider change cannot tell us: the tool result
  comes out text-only, both images of a two-call batch survive on one user turn
  behind the run, the labels name their `tool_call_id`, no image part remains
  outside a user turn, a text-only opencode route still goes through the strip
  path, and another vendor's multimodal chat route is forwarded byte-identical.
- Reverting only `src/api-forwarder.mjs` fails that test; restoring it passes.
- `test/gemini-trailing-turns.test.mjs`, `test/chat-reasoning.test.mjs` and
  `test/provider-api-key-forwarder.test.mjs` (the other tests on this code path)
  still pass.
- Live: with the patch loaded, the same illegal history sent through the running
  forwarder returns 200 and the model answers about the image. Captured upstream
  body shows the tool result as a string ending
  "1 image(s) from this tool result follow in the next message." and the image
  intact on the user turn that follows.

title: feature:  Support Custom Router Models as Codex Subagents
body:
I would like Codex to support using custom Router models as delegated subagents while keeping the primary Codex session on a different
  model.

  For example, the main session could continue running on gpt-6-astra with medium reasoning, while a delegated subagent runs on deepseek/
  deepseek-v4.1-flash with high reasoning for implementation, testing, or code review tasks.

  The requested capability should allow:

  - Selecting an available Router model as a subagent model.
  - Configuring the subagent’s reasoning effort independently from the parent session.
  - Running the subagent with the parent session’s workspace, tools, permissions, and task context.
  - Returning the subagent’s changes, findings, verification results, and status to the parent Codex session.
  - Preserving clear task and usage attribution between the parent and delegated model.
  - Providing a clear explanation when a model requires additional compatibility or collaboration certification.

  I am not asking Codex to silently treat an uncertified model as a native v2 subagent. I would like a supported, controlled delegation path
  for available custom models, with explicit compatibility checks and transparent failure reasons when a route cannot be used.

title: fix(devin): ask for the model-list method Devin 3000.x serves (#770)
body:
Fixes #770.

## What was wrong

`devin-cli` listed models with `GetCascadeModelConfigs`. That is the **IDE's**
method. The shipped `devin` CLI — whose session this provider reuses — moved to
`GetCliModelConfigs` in the 3000.x series.

Both methods are still declared on `exa.api_server_pb.ApiServerService`, which
is why a CLI-credentialed account got Connect `invalid_argument` rather than
`unimplemented`. That reads as "our bytes are wrong", and the reporter and I
both started there. It was the wrong place to look.

## The encoding was never wrong

The report itself contains the disproof, and it is worth stating because it is
the reusable part:

```
PASS  request encoding: 11 field(s) written, 498 bytes, all on their declared wire types
FAIL  model list: the upstream refused the request: an internal error occurred
      observed: http=400 connect-code=invalid_argument known=true retriable=false
```

**A refused call whose encoding audits clean is evidence about the method, not
about the bytes.**

I re-read every field the router writes against Devin **3000.10.31 (b98cc431)**
and all of them are unchanged:

| message | verdict |
|---|---|
| `GetCascadeModelConfigsRequest` / `GetCliModelConfigsRequest` | identical — `metadata` at 1 |
| `Metadata` | unchanged (`ide_name` 1, `api_key` 3, `f` 31, …) |
| `ClientModelConfig` | unchanged (`label` 1, `disabled` 4, `model_uid` 22, `description` 27, …) |
| `GetChatMessageRequest` / `Response` | unchanged (`chat_model_uid` 21, `delta_tool_calls` 6, `actual_model_uid` 23, …) |
| `ChatMessagePrompt`, `ChatToolCall`, `ChatToolDefinition`, `CompletionConfiguration`, `ImageData`, `ModelUsageStats` | unchanged |
| `GetChatMessage` method | unchanged |

So the method name was the entire drift, and the turn path was never affected —
only the model list, which is exactly what the reporter observed.

## Where the descriptor lives now

AGENTS.md said to transcribe from "the descriptor set embedded in the shipped
`devin` binary". That is no longer possible: 3000.10.31 is **stripped** of one
(`api_server.proto`, `GetChatMessageRequest` and friends return zero hits).

The readable source is now the desktop client's generated protobuf-es field
lists in `Devin.app/.../node_modules/@exa/chat-client`, which declare each
`no:` literally for the same messages:

```js
nw.typeName = "exa.api_server_pb.GetCliModelConfigsRequest",
nw.fields = proto3.util.newFieldList(() => [{ no: 1, name: "metadata", kind: "message", T: m.Metadata }]);

nb.typeName = "exa.api_server_pb.GetCliModelConfigsResponse",
nb.fields = proto3.util.newFieldList(() => [
  { no: 1, name: "client_model_configs", kind: "message", T: m.ClientModelConfig, repeated: true },
  { no: 3, name: "default_override_model_config", kind: "message", T: m.DefaultOverrideModelConfig, opt: true },
  { no: 4, name: "subagent_default_model_uid", kind: "scalar", T: 9 }]);
```

and the CLI binary's own Connect paths confirm which one it calls:

```
/exa.api_server_pb.ApiServerService/GetCliModelConfigs      20 occurrences
/exa.api_server_pb.ApiServerService/GetCascadeModelConfigs   0 occurrences
/exa.api_server_pb.ApiServerService/GetChatMessage           present
```

AGENTS.md now records both the moved source and what a clean-encoding refusal
means, so the next person does not repeat the field-by-field pass to learn it.

## Also in here

- **`MODEL_INFO` removed.** Nothing read it, and its numbers had drifted anyway
  (`model_name` is 8 and `max_output_tokens` is 13 today, not 1 and 8). An
  unused table with wrong numbers is a trap for the next transcription, not
  documentation.
- **The probe says what it saw.** An `invalid_argument` behind a passing
  request-shape check now names the method it asked for, so the next drift of
  this shape is diagnosable from the report alone rather than from a debugging
  session.

## Coverage

`test/devin-proto.test.mjs` is new. It pins the method names and the
depended-on field numbers **as literals** — a test that reads the constant it
guards passes straight through a rename, which is how this reached a user — and
drives the discovery path against a stub transport to assert the URL that
actually goes on the wire. It also asserts the response's two new members
decode to nothing rather than failing.

Both new assertions were checked against the old name and fail:

```
✖ the model list asks for the method the shipped CLI calls
✖ the discovery model list reaches GetCliModelConfigs on the wire
ℹ pass 3   ℹ fail 2
```

`npm run check` is clean; `test/devin-*`, `protobuf-wire`, `protobuf-audit`,
and `connect-stream-audit` are 143/143.

## What this does not claim

**The provider stays unverified.** No maintainer has run a live turn, the
registry still ships no models, and nothing here is evidence that Cascade
accepts the request — only that the router now asks the method the installed
CLI asks. Per AGENTS.md that still needs `bin/devin-probe --live --tools`
against a real account. @nsgreenw, if you are willing to re-run the probe on
this branch, that is the missing half.

title: fix(win): refuse start/restart when the scheduled task is absent (#760)
body:
Addresses the last open bullet of #760.

The other two are already on `main`:

- the rollback that deleted `start-codex-router.cmd` and the task — #767
- `"installed":true` reported for a launcher that was never written — #762

This is the third:

> `codex-router.ps1 start` then fails because `schtasks /Change /TN "Codex Router" /ENABLE` targets a non-existent task.

## What was wrong

`stop` has guarded on the task's existence since it shipped:

```js
if (taskExists()) {
  setTaskEnabled(false);
  endTask();
}
```

`start` and `restart` did not:

```js
} else {
  if (command === "restart") endTask();
  setTaskEnabled(true);          // schtasks /Change ... /ENABLE
  schtasks(["/Run", "/TN", taskName], ...);
  process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify({ state: "running" })}\n`);
}
```

With no task registered, the operator got schtasks.exe's own error — which
names neither the task nor anything to do about it — and the verb had already
committed to printing `{"state":"running"}`.

## Why the state is reachable

It is not only the rollback #767 removed. A restricted Task Scheduler leaves
`install` reporting `installed: false` with both launchers written, which is a
supported outcome the installer tolerates on purpose. Either way the operator
has a working checkout whose `start` cannot say what is wrong.

## Why it refuses rather than repairs

Nothing here can recover a task that was never registered. `/Run` fails the
same way one call later, and re-registering behind a `start` would make a
lifecycle verb quietly perform an install — the asymmetry that AGENTS.md's
"`stop` and `start` act on the same layer" rule exists to prevent.

So both verbs now name the task, say it is not registered, and point at the two
commands that do register it:

```
The "Codex Router" scheduled task is not registered, so there is nothing to start.
Register it with `node src/service.mjs install`, or repair the whole installation
with `./model-router.ps1 codex doctor --fix`.
```

Exit 1, no stdout, and nothing mutated: the test asserts `/Change`, `/Run`,
`/End`, `/Create`, and `/Delete` are all unreached, because an `/End` on the
way out would stop a task the operator may still have.

## Coverage

No new harness. `service-render.test.mjs` already puts stub `schtasks.exe` and
`powershell.exe` first on PATH and can fail one call on demand, so a `/Query`
that fails *is* what an unregistered task looks like to schtasks.exe — the
whole path is observable off Windows.

Both new cases fail against the previous code:

```
✖ start      ✖ restart      ℹ pass 0   ℹ fail 3
```

and pass with the change. `service-render`, `service-lifecycle`,
`service-readiness`, `service-write-guard`, and `installer-scripts` are
113/113 (5 skipped on this platform). `npm run check` is clean.

## Note for @Owie6789

This does not change the install path you hit — #767 already did that, and your
workaround remains correct. What it changes is that after *any* state where the
task is missing, `start` now tells you so and what to run.

The maintainer's question on the issue is still open and still the useful one:
how long the install sat before printing `fetch failed`, and whether the router
eventually comes up on that machine once the task exists. If it needed
materially more than 300 seconds on a cold start, that is a separate problem
from either of these.

title: [Bug]: opencode Go DeepSeek V4.1 Flash fails stateless tool-result replay with missing reasoning_content
body:
## What happened?

`opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash` passes the basic, streaming, initial tool-calling, and compaction compatibility checks, but fails the **stateless tool-result replay** check with HTTP 400 from OpenCode Go:

```text
FAIL stateless tool result: opencode rejected the request for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (opencode Go). (HTTP 400: Error from provider (Console Go): Upstream request failed: [invalid_request_error] The `reasoning_content` in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API.)
```

This reproduces on the current `main` checkout, not an older release.

## Environment

- Platform: Windows 11
- Codex CLI: `0.154.0`
- codex-router checkout: `08dc3b6b2c30f2fa11dd433a6db3f40f761b51d4`
- `git log -1 --oneline`: `08dc3b6 Merge pull request #806 from duolahypercho/chore/playwright-1.63.0`
- Router service reports version: `0.6.0`
- Model: `opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash`
- OpenCode Go credential stored in the router protected local store
- Router update check: `updateAvailable: false`

`doctor --fix` completes successfully. Relevant checks are green, including:

```text
OK Codex sign-in probe: authenticated
OK Codex config loads: Codex parses its configuration
OK Enabled providers: opencode-go, opencode-go-messages, opencode-go-responses, opencode-zen
OK Catalog matches gateway routes: 33 routed models
OK opencode Go/Zen key: protected file
OK opencode Messages key: protected file
OK opencode Responses key: protected file
OK Background service: running
OK Router health: version 0.6.0
```

## Reproduction

From the current `main` checkout:

```powershell
cd "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\codex-router"
.\codex-router.ps1 test-model "opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash" --live --yes
```

Observed:

```text
PASS basic response: live response marker verified
PASS streaming: stream text and completion event verified
PASS tool calling: function call and JSON arguments verified
FAIL stateless tool result: opencode rejected the request for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (opencode Go). (HTTP 400: Error from provider (Console Go): Upstream request failed: [invalid_request_error] The `reasoning_content` in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API.)
PASS compaction: compaction checkpoint objective verified
src\compatibility-test.mjs exited with status 1.
```

## Expected behavior

The stateless tool-result continuation should preserve or translate the prior assistant reasoning state in the form OpenCode Go expects, so the follow-up after a tool result is accepted.

Ideally the compatibility test should report:

```text
PASS basic response
PASS streaming
PASS tool calling
PASS stateless tool result
PASS compaction
```

## Additional context

The OpenCode Go account/key itself appears healthy:

1. A direct request to OpenCode Go's `/v1/responses` endpoint using `model=deepseek-v4.1-flash` succeeds.
2. Codex can also run this model through a direct custom provider profile using OpenCode Go's Responses endpoint, and the model can execute a simple shell tool call (`pwd`).

That suggests the failure is specific to the router's continuation/replay path rather than authentication, quota, or general model availability.

This looks related to #292, but #292 was for `opencode-go/deepseek-v4-flash` on an older build and was closed after #275 fixed that reproduction. This report is for **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash**, current `main`, and specifically the current `test-model` stateless tool-result replay.

No credentials, managed caller URLs, account identifiers, or private prompts are included.

title: feat: fall back to a routed reviewer when ChatGPT approval quota runs out (#787)
body:
Implements #787.

## The split neither surface makes obvious

Codex runs **Approve for me** on its own hidden native model,
`codex-auto-review` (it is in the native capture as `visibility: "hide"`). With
**Use Router with ChatGPT** on, the session and its approvals therefore spend
*different quotas*. An external provider answers the turn; every automatic
review still bills ChatGPT. Exhaust that plan and the session keeps reasoning
and proposing commands while being unable to run the ones that need review.

## Why a native slug may be singled out here

`native-redirect.mjs` is deliberately all-or-nothing, and its own comment says
why:

> the native turns carry no reliable marker separating background work from a
> deliberately picked GPT model

The reviewer is the exception to that sentence. It arrives under its **own
slug**, so scoping to it cannot touch a GPT model the operator chose on
purpose. That is the whole licence this change takes, and AGENTS.md now records
it as such.

## What may engage it

```
./bin/control auto-review-fallback set kimi-oauth/k3
./bin/control auto-review-fallback status
./bin/control auto-review-fallback clear
```

The verdict is **`classifyRoutedFailure`** — the routed path's existing
classifier, not a new one. It already:

- puts an entitlement refusal *ahead* of a quota one (the two vocabularies
  overlap, and "upgrade your plan" is not an exhausted balance),
- ignores every 5xx and every deterministic 4xx,
- reads a reset window only where the upstream stated one, in a header or in
  its own refusal body.

Introducing a second definition of "out of quota" would be one more than this
repository can keep correct, so there isn't one.

| reviewer answer | fallback? |
|---|---|
| `deny` (HTTP 200) | **no** — it is a decision |
| policy rejection (403) | no |
| missing entitlement (403) | no |
| 400 / 401 | no |
| 500 / 504 | no |
| malformed 429 body | no |
| 429, `Retry-After: 5` | no — a burst, not exhaustion |
| 429 / 402 with a stated window | **yes** |

A `deny` is HTTP 200 and so can never reach the classifier at all. There is a
test for it regardless, because asking a second model to re-review a command
the first refused is the one outcome the issue names as unacceptable.

## Returning to native

Any native answer clears the window — the rule `clearProviderCooldown` already
follows, and for the same reason: a quota that refilled early, a limit the
operator raised, or a reset time ChatGPT got wrong all end with a real answer,
and that outranks anything on disk. The window also expires by itself, capped
at six hours like a provider cooldown. A refusal that named nothing gets sixty
seconds: long enough that a burst of approvals does not each pay for the same
rejection (the issue's "ideally" paragraph), short enough that a returning
quota is noticed almost immediately.

## The one thing this does not do

**The first failing review is not rescued.** Its refusal is relayed
byte-for-byte and the window is recorded; the *next* approval goes to the
configured reviewer.

Rescuing the failing turn would mean rebuilding a native request as a routed
one mid-flight — the crossing AGENTS.md explicitly declines to make from the
test suite alone:

> It is not a body swap but the other branch entirely, and it crosses the
> routed/native boundary this file governs elsewhere […] Add it with those
> proofs or not at all.

So the fallback is decided **pre-flight**, at the exact point
`native-redirect` already performs that crossing safely. That keeps acceptance
criterion 2 satisfied from the second review onward rather than the first. I
can add the same-turn rescue as a follow-up, but it wants a live
quota-exhausted account to prove, not a mock.

Against the acceptance criteria: 1 ✅, 2 ⚠️ (second review onward, above),
3 ✅, 4 ✅, 5 ✅, 6 ✅.

## Observability

- an unquieted log line naming the status, reason, window and reviewer,
- `autoReviewFallback: true` on the usage row, so a switched review is
  distinguishable in the ledger from one that never had to switch,
- `status` reports the configured reviewer, the window, **and** `reviewer` —
  which reviewer the next approval will actually use, so the three fields do
  not have to be combined by the reader.

## Safety detail worth flagging in review

Native error bodies are relayed to Codex verbatim on purpose ("OpenAI errors
are already clear"). The classifier therefore reads `upstream.clone()`, only on
an already-failed response, and only for this one slug — so the tee buffers an
error body and never a turn. Any failure to read is reported as no body: a
missed window costs one extra round trip, while breaking the relay would cost
the operator the error itself.

## Testing

`test/auto-review-fallback.test.mjs` — 12 cases: slug recognition, unconfigured
defaults, the routed-slug requirement, protected state, window arithmetic and
the six-hour cap, the unnamed-window floor, clear-on-answer, the damaged-document
path, and the full classifier boundary table above.

`test/routing.test.mjs` — two end-to-end cases through the real router with mock
native and gateway servers:

- a 429 with `Retry-After` is relayed as 429, then the next two approvals reach
  the gateway as `kimi-oauth-k3` **and the native reviewer is never asked
  again** while the window is open;
- a native `deny` reaches Codex verbatim, the gateway is never called, and the
  window is gone from state afterwards.

Both router cases fail with the router hooks reverted:

```
✖ an exhausted native reviewer moves later approvals to the configured reviewer (#787)
✖ a native reviewer that answers keeps every approval native, deny included (#787)
ℹ pass 0   ℹ fail 2
```

`routing` + `native-redirect` + `auto-review-fallback` + `model-failover` +
`model-failover-router` are **247/247**. `npm run check` is clean. The CLI was
driven by hand through set / status / clear, including a simulated open window,
to confirm `reviewer` flips and back.

title: feat: explain why a route cannot be delegated to as a subagent (#804)
body:
Addresses #804.

## What already exists

Most of the request is shipped, which is worth saying plainly because it was
not discoverable:

| Ask | Today |
|---|---|
| Select a Router model as a subagent | `subagents set <provider>/<model> on`, or the Control Center's Subagents column |
| Subagent reasoning effort independent of the parent | `subagents effort <provider>/<model> <level>` — written into the agent definition as `model_reasoning_effort` |
| Parent's workspace, tools, permissions, task context | Codex's own delegation; the router does not mediate it |
| Returning changes, findings, status to the parent | likewise |
| Task and usage attribution | usage rows carry the child route; `observeSubagentOutcome` meters it |

## What was actually missing

The last bullet, and the one the issue closes on:

> explicit compatibility checks and transparent failure reasons when a route
> cannot be used

There were none. The answer lived in **three places that never met**:

- selection — `subagents status`
- promotion — the published catalog
- the agent definition — `$CODEX_HOME/agents/`

Nothing joined them, so "why can't Codex delegate to this model?" was only
answerable by spawning one. And the tool the docs point at is no help:

```
$ checkAgentCapability("not-a/model")
{ "ok": true, "agentCapable": false, "verdict": "error", "detail": "codex exited 1" }
```

A typo, an unenabled provider, and a genuinely broken route all produce that
same line.

## `subagents explain`

```
$ bin/model-router codex subagents explain deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash
deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash cannot be spawned as a subagent.
  - deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash is hidden in the model picker, and a hidden model is never offered as a subagent.
    Unhide it in the Control Center's model list, or with ./bin/control picker set deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash show.
  - deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash is switched off as a subagent, which beats every mode including "all".
    Run ./bin/control subagents set deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash on.
  Child turns run at reasoning effort "max".
```

Read-only and quota-free. Per rule 6 of `docs/SUBAGENT-CERTIFICATION.md` — *a
control must produce the result its label implies* — this one reports, so it
promotes nothing and probes nothing.

Blockers come back in an order where fixing the first unblocks the rest:

```
unknown_route → provider_disabled → model_hidden → explicitly_off
→ not_selected → agent_definition_missing
```

`model_hidden` is deliberately ahead of `not_selected`: hidden beats every mode,
so naming the switch first would send someone to a control that cannot take
effect.

An unknown slug says **which half** is wrong:

```
opencode-go/not-a-real-model → "opencode-go is a known provider, but it serves
  no model called not-a-real-model." → curate-models opencode-go
gpt-6-astra                  → "...A subagent model is a routed provider/model
  slug, never a native one."
```

`agent_definition_missing` is the "the switch did nothing" case the
certification doc warns about — promoted in state, with no file for Codex to
spawn by name.

`--json` returns the same answer structured, for the Control Center and scripts.

## The certification line the issue asked us not to blur

> I am not asking Codex to silently treat an uncertified model as a native v2
> subagent.

So `explain` says where a v2 claim came from, because the three sources are not
worth the same:

```
note: opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash is offered because you selected it, which is
  a statement of intent rather than evidence that it can hold Codex's native child
  role. Streaming and tool calls do not prove delegation works.
  To gather that evidence, run ./bin/control subagents certify opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash.
  It spends real quota on this route's provider and on a native parent turn.
```

A registry-certified route and a locally five-check-verified route each say so
instead. A test asserts the prose never leaks `multiAgentVersion`, `v2_agent` or
`encryptedRelay` — rule 7: the reader should not need to know the machinery.

## A real bug the suite found on the way

**A configured subagent effort made its agent definition permanently drifted.**

`syncRoutedCodexAgents` writes the effort:

```js
const definition = routedAgentDefinition(model, { effort: subagentEffort(model.slug) });
```

`routedCodexAgentStatus` computed the expected contents **without** it. The two
therefore differ by exactly the `model_reasoning_effort` line, so every model
with a subagent effort set read as `stale` forever: doctor reported drift,
`--fix` republished byte-identical contents, and the next check reported it
again.

This is a defect *of* the independent-effort capability #804 asks about, so it
belongs here.

It hid because the existing test reads the operator's own settings — it passed
or failed depending on whether the machine running it happened to have an effort
configured. On mine, `grok-oauth/grok-4.5` did:

```
+ current: 1,          - current: 2,
+ stale: [ 'grok-oauth/grok-4.5' ]
+ ok: false,           - ok: true,
```

The new regression runs in a child with `CODEX_ROUTER_STATE_DIR`, `CODEX_HOME`
and `MODEL_ROUTER_MULTI_AGENT_STATE` set from the start (`MULTI_AGENT_STATE_PATH`
is resolved at module load, so setting them afterwards would not isolate
anything), and fails against the previous code.

## Testing

`test/subagent-explain.test.mjs` — 14 cases: every blocker, their ordering,
the three unknown-slug shapes, the definition-on-disk round trip, the three
certification sources, the off-ladder effort note, and the prose contract.

`test/codex-agent-catalog.test.mjs` — the isolated effort round-trip
regression, which fails without the status fix.

Driven by hand as a user through the full remediation chain on a scratch state
directory:

```
proven-mode refusal → subagents set … on → "no agent definition" → republish
→ "can be spawned (agent name: router_opencode_go_deepseek_v4_1_flash)"
```

and the effort really lands in the file Codex reads:

```toml
model = "opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash"
model_reasoning_effort = "high"
```

One wrong instruction was caught that way and corrected before commit —
`picker show <slug>` is really `picker set <slug> show`.

subagent, multi-agent, codex-agent-catalog, state-owner and doctor suites are
**145/145**. `npm run check` is clean.

## Not in this PR

The registry gains no `multiAgentVersion: "v2"` entry and no `v2_agent/`
application. Nothing here promotes a route or claims one is certified — that
still needs the five-check run and the review gate, exactly as #804 asked.

title: fix: preserve OpenRouter streaming usage through LiteLLM
body:
## Summary
- Add OpenRouter to the existing choice-bearing streaming usage normalization used by Z.ai and OpenCode Go.
- Preserve authoritative usage when it shares a Chat Completions chunk with choices, by splitting it into the usage-only chunk LiteLLM preserves.
- Add factory-driven tests for text/tool choices, positive and zero usage, cache details, missing usage, content-type gating, and usage-only terminals.

## Why
Codex uses reported input tokens for its context meter and compaction decisions. During investigation of Union Alpha through OpenRouter, greetings reached Codex with zero input tokens despite substantial input. This patch addresses the usage-preservation path, not the model context-window metadata.

A synthetic loopback experiment using the real router and API forwarder with the installed LiteLLM 1.96 library behind a test gateway wrapper located a loss inside Chat-to-Responses translation: supplied input/output usage of 50,000/8 became 10/2 when usage shared a choice-bearing terminal chunk. A separate usage-only terminal control preserved the counts. Enabling this gate preserved 50,000/8 through every observed hop. This was synthetic evidence, not a raw live OpenRouter capture, and did not use the deployed LiteLLM proxy service.

A live headless greeting subsequently changed from 0 input / 8 output before the patch to 171,832 input / 12 output after it, without router-estimated input usage. The operator also confirmed that the Desktop context meter resumed reporting input usage. These were separate turns, not a byte-identical replay; raw live upstream frames were not captured.

## Scope and related work
- Follows the same normalization precedent as #458 and #316; complements the request-side include_usage change in #346.
- Related upstream issue: BerriAI/litellm#36168.
- Does not include Union Alpha registration or Messages changes proposed in #805 and #798. Open PRs were checked for overlap with these two files.
- Does not explain or fix the separately observed high Union Alpha input count versus DeepSeek, reduce actual context consumption, or establish universal compaction correctness.
- Reuses the existing transform, including its cache-alias handling; no new inference, model parameters, dependency changes, or credentials.

## Verification
- node --test test/zai-cache-usage.test.mjs: 11 passed, including a fresh pre-commit run.
- Negative control: removing the OpenRouter gate produced six expected failures; restoring it passed all 11.
- npm run check: passed in the isolated contribution worktree.
- git diff --check: passed; independent read-only review found no blocking defects.
- Synthetic pinned-LiteLLM experiment and separate live observations described above were performed during investigation; the temporary end-to-end harness is not checked into this two-file PR.
- Full npm test did NOT complete: bounded attempts encountered Antigravity/secret-setup failures and timed out. Baseline attribution is unknown. The operator reported a live-router interruption during those attempts; the cause was not established. The full suite was not rerun. Publication and the final focused transform test required no router restart or service operation.

title: Bound image references when a route has no documented image-token bound
body:
Bound image references in the prompt-token estimate, so a resold model's screenshot is no longer charged as prose.

## What happens today

When a routed response arrives without usable usage — the router records `input_tokens: 0` for it — `estimateInputTokens` supplies a substitute (the `ZERO_INPUT_ESTIMATE` path). Where that usage is lost is not established here, and the provider's own accounting may well be correct; what this change addresses is the substitute the router then builds. That estimate counts an image reference's payload as text unless `maxImageTokensForRoute` supplies a per-image bound, and the only bound that existed covers `provider === "deepseek"` with the three documented Flash model names.

A route that resells DeepSeek Flash through another provider — for example `provider: "openrouter"`, `upstreamModel: "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash"` — gets no bound at all, so the image's base64 is charged as prose. Measured with the router's own exports:

    2.7 MB data:image/png;base64 screenshot, resold route, no bound       -> 819,328
    same body, native deepseek route (1024 bound applies)                 ->   1,060
    text-only control, 100k characters                                    ->  30,334

A client reads that usage to decide when to compact. One screenshot is therefore about 80% of a 1M-token window, so together with the surrounding conversation it crosses a 900k compaction threshold and the session compacts after nearly every screenshot instead of only when it is genuinely full.

## Change

`maxImageTokensForRoute` now returns a conservative default (4096) when the route is not one of the three documented direct DeepSeek Flash models, instead of returning `undefined`. Those three keep their documented 1024, now a named constant, and the discount still applies only to a recognised `input_image` part inside a real `message` or `function_call_output` content array — a pasted JSON example, tool schema, unknown field, ambiguous `file_id`+`image_url`, assistant-role content and `tools` example are all still counted whole.

The estimate is only there to keep a false zero from being believed and to stay roughly right; six figures for an image is far outside that error budget, while a few thousand tokens is inside it.

With the change the same body estimates at 4,132 (4,163 with a short instruction line), and the native DeepSeek route is unchanged at 1,060.

## Test

`test/response-usage.test.mjs` gains a regression case for the resold route (a 2.7 MB image must estimate under 20,000), and the existing route-bound test is updated to the new contract.

    node --test test/response-usage.test.mjs     # on Node 22.19 or newer
    -> tests 47, pass 47, fail 0        (46/46 at the base)

Full suite on the patched tree against the same suite at the base: identical failing-test sets, 25 failures in both (Electron process-tree, desktop-panel, macOS recovery, control-center and connector-setup among them; all of them fail on this machine at the base too), 4121 tests baseline vs 4122 patched.

## One caveat for reviewers

Run the tests on Node 22.19 or newer, which is what the installer requires. On Node 20 the `JSON.parse` reviver has no `context.source`, so the discount silently no-ops. On that runtime the patch is worse than the base rather than merely different, because the bound is added while the payload is not discounted; the base itself reports 42/46 there rather than 46/46. That is why the checks above are pinned to a supported Node.

## Not fixed here

- `routedRequestFits` (`src/router.mjs`) compares the same estimate against candidate windows, so an image-bearing request can be refused failover with `context-too-small` although the request is really a few thousand tokens. Same root cause, different symptom, and it is a routing gate rather than an accounting path — worth its own change and test.
- `estimateGeminiTokens` (`src/gemini-shape.mjs`), which answers `countTokens` in `src/gemini-surface.mjs`, divides serialized `contents` by 4, so an inline image's base64 is counted as text there too.

Prepared with an assistant operating this account, at the account owner's request.

title: [Bug]: GitHub Copilot Responses stream fails when response IDs change
body:
### What happened?

## Summary

When routing `github-copilot/gpt-5.6-luna` through Codex, the assistant starts producing a response, but the stream disconnects a few seconds later.

Codex reports:

```text
unexpected status 502 Bad Gateway:
The internal Responses stream ended before response completed.
stream disconnected before completion:
stream closed before response.completed
```

## Environment

- OS: macOS
- Client: Codex desktop app
- Provider: GitHub Copilot
- Model: `github-copilot/gpt-5.6-luna`
- codex-router local commit: `<redacted>`
- LiteLLM: `1.96.0`

The model was added as a user-curated model through the normal GitHub Copilot provider configuration. No source files were locally modified.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure the GitHub Copilot provider.
2. Curate or add a GitHub Copilot model named `gpt-5.6-luna`.
3. Select `github-copilot/gpt-5.6-luna` in Codex.
4. Send a simple prompt, for example: `Reply with exactly OK.`
5. The response text is displayed, but the turn later fails when the stream should finish.

The same behavior was reproduced through the local API forwarder at `127.0.0.1:4203`.

## Observed behavior

The local router emits an error event after forwarding the response text:

```text
{
  "type": "error",
  "code": "invalid_responses_stream",
  "message": "The Responses completion used a different response ID."
}
```

LiteLLM then reports:

```text
litellm.MidStreamFallbackError:
litellm.APIError: Response API in-stream error
```

## Root cause investigation

A direct request to the GitHub Copilot Responses endpoint returns HTTP 200 and does produce a terminal `response.completed` event.

However, the response IDs are not stable across the stream. The following events use different response IDs:

```text
response.created
response.in_progress
response.completed
```

The IDs have been redacted here, but they are different in the actual response.

The generic Responses stream validator in:

- `src/openai-adapters.mjs`
- `src/api-forwarder.mjs`

stores the ID from `response.created` and rejects `response.completed` when its ID differs:

```js
if (state.responseId &&
    data.response.id &&
    data.response.id !== state.responseId) {
  return invalidStream(
    state,
    "The Responses completion used a different response ID.",
  );
}
```

This replaces the valid terminal event with `event: error`. LiteLLM has already started returning HTTP 200 and forwarding output tokens, so it cannot convert this into a normal pre-stream error. The Codex client therefore sees a disconnected stream without `response.completed` and reports a 502.

The issue also occurs with different reasoning efforts (`low`, `medium`, and `max`), so it does not appear to be caused by the selected reasoning effort.

## Expected behavior

The GitHub Copilot provider should either:

1. normalize Copilot's per-event response IDs into a valid Responses stream; or
2. use a provider-specific compatibility mode that does not reject Copilot's changing response IDs while preserving the normal validation for other providers.

The current official `main` branch still applies the generic Responses stream transform to GitHub Copilot without a provider-specific exception:

https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/blob/main/src/openai-adapters.mjs#L496-L500

https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/blob/main/src/api-forwarder.mjs#L1532-L1534

No credentials, full prompts, API keys, or unredacted response IDs are included in this report.

### Which app do you route through?

Codex

### Platform

macOS

### Doctor output or support bundle

_No response_

title: fix: opt-in withholding of Codex app-connector tools on routed chat providers
body:
## Problem

Codex registers every installed app connector (Airtable, Notion, Slack, GitHub,
Canva, Figma, Gmail, Drive, ...) as an eager namespace on routed requests:
nothing carries `defer_loading` and no `tool_search` control is sent. A live
capture of a one-word turn (DeepSeek on OpenCode Go, Union Alpha on OpenCode Go
Messages) showed 38 tool entries across 25 namespaces with no deferral marker
at all. `flattenNamespaceTools` flattens Codex's whole connector registry into
the prompt: 576 provider-facing tools, ~1.09 MB of JSON Schema, ~200,000 input
tokens billed before the model reads the first word. Connectors disabled in
the Codex UI are still sent. This cost is silent to the operator. Native
(Responses-native) models don't pay it, because they take the deferred/code-mode
path Codex already supports.

## Change

`CODEX_ROUTER_APP_CONNECTORS` opts in to withholding these tools, in three modes:
- unset (default): unchanged behaviour, every connector declared eagerly.
- `none`: withholds every `mcp__codex_apps__*` namespace from a routed
  chat/messages surface, whether or not Codex marked it deferred and whether or
  not a search relay exists.
- a comma-separated list (e.g. `airtable,gmail`, trimmed, case-insensitive,
  unknown ids ignored): keeps those connectors eager and withholds the rest.

`mcp__codex_app` (threads, automations, navigation), `collaboration`, the
repls, the template picker, `image_gen`, and every plain tool always stay
eager. A withheld connector keeps its namespace registration, so stored calls
are still renamed outbound and restored inbound. Its definition is re-declared
the moment a stored `function_call`, a forced `tool_choice`, or an
`allowed_tools` entry names it, so an in-progress session never cites a tool
the request doesn't declare. That restoration is charged against a bounded
provider's tool ceiling like any other definition (a Groq surface that can't
hold them all still fails locally), and it is repaired again for routes whose
validators reject a sibling `$ref` (Kimi). The variable is read per request, so
no restart is needed. Responses-native routes are unchanged. Default behaviour
is unchanged.

## Measurements

Captured fixture: 576 tools / 1,091,492 bytes -> 76 tools / 121,002 bytes with
`none` (most of the remainder is the app snapshot the router injects itself).

Live before/after:
- DeepSeek fresh turn: 253,813 -> 45,576 input tokens.
- Union Alpha on OpenCode Go Messages: 241,388 -> 41,019 input tokens.

## Tests

Ran the five test files touched by this change:

```
node --test test/namespace-relay.test.mjs test/chat-tool-surface.test.mjs \
  test/namespace-relay-routing.test.mjs test/codex-app-tools.test.mjs \
  test/namespace-relay-custom.test.mjs
```

217 pass, 0 fail. The full suite was not run locally. On unmodified `main`,
four pre-existing/environmental failures are seen and are unrelated to this
change:
- `chatgpt-profile-switch` crash-boundary: 180s timeout.
- `login-free-app-server`: EPERM on Windows temp cleanup.
- `desktop-panel`: missing playwright.
- `catalog-publication-lock` and `config-manager`: pass in isolation.

## Open question for the maintainer

Whether to flip the default to `none` later, once operators have had a chance
to see the token savings against their own connector usage.
