title: fix(router): deliver the subagent handoff to Console Go Responses
body:
### What is broken

A Codex subagent pinned to a Console Go Responses route cannot be spawned. The
parent's first item is a native `agent_message`, Console Go rejects the item's
discriminator, and the child dies before it reads its task:

```
{"model":"muse-spark-1.3-contributor","error":{"param":"input[4]",
 "type":"invalid_request_error","message":"Upstream request failed:
 [invalid_request_error] `input[4]` did not match any supported type"}}
```

Measured on `opencode-go-responses/muse-spark-1.3-contributor` at router
0.6.0 (`5e1b49e6`). All three subagent roles fail identically -- the index
moves with the transcript, the rejection does not.

### Why

`agentMessagesAsUserMessages` already exists for exactly this, but
`zenFreeCompatibleInput` only reaches it for the free Zen pair. The paid
Console Go route keeps the native item, so the strict upstream sees a type it
does not implement. The payload is not encrypted either: Codex stores the
readable handoff under `agent_message.content[].encrypted_content`, and the
value is a plain string rather than a Fernet token.

### The change

`consoleGoCompatibleInput` renders a non-Fernet `agent_message` payload as text
through the existing `normalizeAgentMessageForNative`, then presents the item
as the ordinary user message Console Go accepts. It is wired into both entry
points -- the ordinary routed turn and routed compaction -- so a child can be
spawned, resumed, and compacted on these routes.

The gate is `needsConsoleGoResponsesToolCompatibility`, so `opencode-go`,
`opencode-go-messages`, paid Zen, and every other Responses provider keep
their current wire payload byte-for-byte. A native Fernet token is left
untouched rather than rendered as ciphertext.

### Regression test

`test/routing.test.mjs` gains "a routed subagent handoff reaches Console Go as
a user message". It posts the handoff to a Console Go route against a mock
gateway and asserts the upstream body carries no `agent_message` and that the
non-Fernet payload arrives as readable `input_text`.

Verified both directions: the test passes on this branch and fails on
`5e1b49e6` with `the native agent_message discriminator reached the strict
upstream`. `npm run check` passes.

### Live evidence

Before the change, a direct request to the router carrying the same
`agent_message` item returned `400 input[4] did not match any supported type`.
After it, the same request returns `200` and the model answers with exactly the
marker the payload asked for.

Then with real Codex subagents, one per role:

| Role | Task | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fast_explorer | list the `.toml` files in the agents directory | correct |
| code_worker | count usage-event rows, two independent methods | correct |
| deep_reasoner | analyse this patch and cite line numbers | correct |

All three children recorded
`opencode-go-responses/muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, every request in the
sequence returned 200, and no Console Go request has returned a non-200 since
the change.

### Relationship to existing guidance

`AGENTS.md` ("Routed subagent regression prevention") already requires the
reverse direction -- a non-Fernet `encrypted_content` part of an
`agent_message` rendered as `input_text` before a native Responses endpoint.
This applies the same rule to the Console Go Responses surface.

title: Z.ai Coding GLM-5.3-Flash can compact-loop because the 400K threshold is below the subagent tool-surface floor
body:
## Summary

`zai-coding/glm-5.3-flash` inherits the 400,000-token auto-compaction threshold that was originally chosen from OpenCode Go observations. On current Codex Desktop subagents, that threshold can sit **below the normal post-compaction request floor** once the full agent tool schema is reattached.

The result is a deterministic compact loop:

```
ordinary child turn (~450K-474K input)
-> Codex compacts successfully (~35K-55K compacted history)
-> next ordinary child turn reattaches the tool surface (~450K+ again)
-> immediately above the 400K threshold
-> compact again
-> repeat
```

This is provider-specific evidence for Z.ai Coding and is distinct from #820's Union Alpha reserve discussion and #266's zero-token estimate bug.

## Environment

- Windows Codex Desktop: `26.915.4065.0`
- Desktop-owned app-server: `0.155.0-alpha.9.2`
- codex-router live runtime: `0.5.1` plus selected merged backports
- clean reference investigated at `5e1b49e6e3fea1ada57f0e7fa6ca7612e9d17300`
- route: `zai-coding/glm-5.3-flash`
- advertised context: 1,000,000
- current auto-compact: 400,000
- effective Codex context event: 950,000

No synthetic provider probe was used; the measurements below came from naturally occurring routed subagent traffic.

## Evidence

Two independent Flash child tasks showed the same sequence repeatedly.

Representative provider-reported ordinary-turn input counts:

- 436,200
- 450,196
- 454,565
- 458,562
- 463,584
- 468,299
- 472,092
- 474,443

The router ledger contains **19 successful Z.ai Coding Flash requests above 400K**. The maximum observed successful prompt was **474,443 input tokens**, with 7,252 output tokens and HTTP 200.

After each successful compaction, Codex's token event dropped to roughly 35K-55K. But the next ordinary child turn immediately returned to roughly 450K-474K because ordinary turns reattach the large tool schema while the compaction request itself omits live tools.

The child rollout records contain valid top-level `compacted` records with small replacement histories, and projection/integrity checks have zero gaps, duplicate ordinals, or backward ordinals. So this is not transcript/projection corruption.

## Root cause

The Z.ai Coding descriptor currently says:

```json
"contextWindow": 1000000,
"autoCompact": 400000
```

The 400K threshold was copied from the same-model OpenCode Go conservative pin. Current Z.ai Coding traffic disproves 400K as a usable threshold for this client/tool surface: the provider repeatedly and successfully serves requests above it.

Because compaction omits the live tool schema, it reduces the history but cannot reduce the ordinary-turn static tool prefix. If that ordinary-turn floor is already above `autoCompact`, every successful compaction recreates the condition that triggered it.

## Proposed provider-specific fix

Raise **only** `zai-coding/glm-5.3-flash` to:

```json
"autoCompact": 500000
```

and bump its comp hash.

500K is deliberately conservative:

- it is the smallest round threshold above the measured 474,443-token successful floor;
- it still reserves half of the advertised 1M window;
- it does not change OpenCode Go, OpenRouter, Z.ai API, Ollama Cloud, or Command Code thresholds without provider-specific evidence.

A regression test should make the threshold provider-specific rather than asserting 400K for every Flash route.

I have a tested patch ready: syntax checks pass and the relevant registry/catalog/agent suite passes 134/134.

title: fix: defer Z.ai Coding Flash tools and raise compaction floor
body:
## Summary

Fixes #846.

This PR addresses the reproduced Z.ai Coding GLM-5.3-Flash compact loop at both layers:

1. the route's 400K auto-compaction threshold sat below its demonstrated successful ordinary-turn floor;
2. Flash lacked the standalone tool-discovery metadata already proven on full-size Z.ai Coding GLM-5.3, so Codex eagerly attached a very large direct tool/schema surface; and
3. once standalone discovery was enabled, Z.ai/LiteLLM returned bridged special function calls with `namespace: null`, while the response relay accepted only an omitted namespace. That prevented valid `tool_search` calls from being restored to native Codex `tool_search_call` items.

## Reproduction

On Codex Desktop `26.915.4065.0` / app-server `0.155.0-alpha.9.2`, two independent `zai-coding/glm-5.3-flash` child threads repeatedly showed:

```
ordinary turn (~436K-472K provider-reported input)
-> compact
-> ~35K-54K compacted turn
-> next ordinary turn returns to ~450K
-> compact again
```

The append-only router ledger contains **19 successful Z.ai Coding Flash requests above 400K**. The highest observed successful prompt was **474,443 input tokens** with non-empty output and HTTP 200.

The compacted rollout records themselves are valid and small; projection checks show no gaps, duplicate ordinals, or backward ordinals. This is not transcript corruption.

The full-size `zai-coding/glm-5.3` precedent in #297 is directly relevant: enabling `searchTool.mode = "standalone"` reduced a tool-heavy fresh-session surface from roughly 491K to 82K while preserving deferred MCP discovery and V2 subagents.

## Changes

Scoped route metadata for **`zai-coding/glm-5.3-flash`**:

- `autoCompact: 400000 -> 500000`
- enable `searchTool: { "mode": "standalone" }`
- use the already-proven Coding Plan GLM behavior template: `gpt-5.6-sol`
- use the `efficient-agentic` instruction overlay
- bump `compHash`
- document why this provider differs from the other Flash routes
- add provider-specific regressions

500K is deliberately conservative: it is the smallest round threshold above the measured 474,443-token successful floor and still reserves half of the advertised 1M window. Other Flash providers retain their separately proven 400K thresholds.

Response relay:

- treat provider `function_call.namespace === null` as the same unqualified wire identity as an omitted namespace
- apply this only at the provider-facing response boundary; native restored identities stay strict
- cover tool-search, custom-tool, function-relay, plain-identity, and raw-codec paths
- add streamed and non-streamed `tool_search` regressions plus custom-tool coverage

This PR deliberately **does not** add checked-in `multiAgentVersion: "v2"`. Repository policy requires an accepted exact-route `v2_agent` proof artifact; family similarity and successful ordinary tool turns are not sufficient evidence.

## Live verification

Installed Z.ai Coding Flash at max reasoning:

- basic response — HTTP 200
- streaming — HTTP 200
- forced function call — HTTP 200
- stateless tool-result continuation — HTTP 200
- compaction — HTTP 200
- subagent-capability tool calling — HTTP 200
- subagent-capability streaming — HTTP 200

Generated Codex catalog after refresh:

- `supports_search_tool = true`
- `context_window = 1000000`
- `auto_compact_token_limit = 500000`
- text + image input
- behavior base instructions match the full-size Coding Plan GLM execution template apart from model identity
- `comp_hash = zai-coding-glm-5-3-flash-v4`

### Deferred discovery A/B

Before the relay fix, a live Flash request correctly called the provider-facing `tool_search` function but the router returned:

```json
{"type":"function_call","name":"tool_search","namespace":null}
```

instead of native `tool_search_call`.

After the relay fix, the same two-turn live probe passes end to end:

1. Flash calls the bridged search control.
2. Router restores native `tool_search_call` with `execution:"client"`.
3. A synthetic search result exposes only `mcp__calendar.delete_event`.
4. The next Flash turn calls `delete_event` in namespace `mcp__calendar` with the requested id.
5. Both turns return HTTP 200.

That verifies deferred discovery itself, rather than only the metadata flag.

## Tests

- Flash + namespace/custom relay focused suite: **146/146 pass**
- installed live-router namespace relay suite after surgical backport: **119/119 pass**
- `npm run check` — pass in upstream worktree and installed live router
- `git diff --check` — pass
- broader registry/catalog/agent/native-drift/tool-surface suites — pass
- full repository `npm test` was run. One untouched Antigravity onboarding assertion fails with `null !== 1`; running that exact test against untouched current `main` reproduces the identical failure, so it is baseline/environmental and unrelated to these changed files. Hosted CI remains authoritative for that unrelated test.

No provider keys, prompts, private thread ids, or capability-bearing router URLs are included here.

title: fix: stop the bundled skill documenting a subagent pin the router removed
body:
## Problem

An explicit `spawn_agent.model` is kept; only a call that omits the model inherits the routed parent. That behavior shipped in #742, together with a rewrite of `.claude/skills/codex-subagents/SKILL.md` and an update to `docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md`.

Two places kept describing the behavior #742 removed:

- `skills/codex-router/SKILL.md`: "In-session subagents are always pinned to the routed parent's model because their tool arguments are model-generated and must not silently cross a provider or billing boundary."
- `src/namespace-relay.mjs`, the comment above `SPAWN_MODEL_TOOLS`: "An in-session subagent is always pinned to the routed parent: its model argument is generated by the parent model, not an independent user choice..."

The first one is not internal documentation. `skills/codex-router/SKILL.md` is installed into every user's `~/.codex/skills/codex-router/`, so it is what an operator, or a delegated agent reading its own instructions, sees while diagnosing a child that ran on the wrong model. It says the router discards the override on purpose.

## Why nothing caught it

The suite exercises the rewrite, not the prose describing it. `test/subagent-model-inherit.test.mjs` covers the keep-or-inherit split at the wire level and passes on both sides of the drift.

## Change

- Correct the skill's inheritance paragraph: an explicit `spawn_agent.model` is kept, delegating to another model means naming it, only an omitted model inherits the parent, and Codex validates the name against what it advertises for `spawn_agent`.
- Correct the comment above `SPAWN_MODEL_TOOLS` to match.
- Add `test/subagent-override-docs.test.mjs`, a source assertion over the two shipped skills and that comment, so the stale claim cannot come back silently.
- CHANGELOG entry under Unreleased.

No behavior change. In particular this does **not** touch `sanitizeSpawnAgentModel`, which still clears a model outside the client's advertised enum, after which the call inherits the parent; that guard is #632's and stays as it is.

## Not in this PR

The `subagents explain <model>` command that the troubleshooting path really wants is #804, still on `feat/804-subagent-explain` and not on `main`. Nothing here depends on it.

## Testing

- `node --test test/subagent-override-docs.test.mjs test/namespace-relay.test.mjs test/subagent-model-inherit.test.mjs` -- **150 pass, 0 fail**, including the two new assertions.
- `npm run check` -- syntax checks clean, `v2-agent applications valid (7)`.

title: Bound the image payload on the routed request path
body:
## Why

A conversation replays every image it still holds on every following turn, so a
session that works from screenshots grows until one request crosses the
provider's per-request image ceiling and the turn fails outright. Measured on
OpenRouter from this host on 2026-09-17: about 12MB of decoded image content was
accepted and about 31MB was refused with `HTTP 413: Downloaded image content
cannot exceed 30MB`. The reference incident was a session that had accumulated
1,791 image references before its turns started failing - a stalled agent, not a
slow one.

The per-image token estimate added in #813 bounds what one image is charged, but
nothing bounded how many images ride along. This bounds the payload itself.

## What it does

On the routed request path (`prepareRoutedRequest`), after tool-result aging,
the payload is bounded before it leaves:

- **Byte budget: 20MB of decoded image content** (`IMAGE_PAYLOAD_BUDGET_BYTES`),
  deliberately below the provider's 30MB ceiling so a provider that counts
  differently, or the text of the same request, still fits.
- **Token budget: 128K image tokens** (`IMAGE_PAYLOAD_BUDGET_TOKENS`), charged at
  the route's per-image bound (`maxImageTokensForRoute`: 4096 on a resold route,
  1024 on the three documented direct DeepSeek Flash models). Bytes bound the
  request; tokens bound the recurring per-turn bill that a byte cap alone does
  not, since under 20MB a hundred small screenshots still ride along and are
  charged again every turn.
- Oldest image references become short text receipts until the turn fits both
  budgets; **the newest two images are always kept**, even if one of them would
  exceed the budget alone.
- Images inside tool results are bounded too. Remote `https` image URLs are
  **not** measured (only `data:image/` references are); Codex sends data URLs, so
  that path is not reachable today, but it is a known limit if a surface ever
  forwards a remote image.
- The counts - `imageReferencesSeen`, `imageReferencesDropped`,
  `imageBytesSaved`, `imageTokensSaved` - are recorded on the usage event.

The bound is a flat constant rather than a fraction of the route's context
window on purpose: a bigger window does not make an image cheaper, it only
delays compaction, and what is being bounded is recurring spend per turn.

## Known gap (deliberately not covered here)

Only the routed path is bounded in this change. There are three `ageToolResults`
call sites in `router.mjs` - the routed path, the native path (the `else` branch
of `if (route)`, around line 4337) and the compaction path - and only the routed
one bounds images. The
native and compaction paths age tool results by size and leave images entirely
unbounded. That is not cosmetic: the native path leaves as a stateless full
conversation, so an old image costs its full size on every turn of that path
too, which is the same failure this change addresses. Those two paths are
knowingly left for a follow-up PR rather than wired blind here, because the
native path was not exercised in this change.

## Notes for review

- `...imageBudget` is spread on all five usage-event rows, not just the success
  row, so the counts survive on the error and retry rows. It is `undefined` on
  paths where the bound did not run, and spreading `undefined` adds nothing.
- The trim summary log line stays inside the existing `if (!QUIET)` gate.
  Nothing upstream hard-sets `CODEX_ROUTER_QUIET`, so the gating is correct for
  every deployment.
- The per-image default comes from `DEFAULT_IMAGE_TOKEN_BOUND` in
  `prompt-image-usage.mjs` (added in #813) rather than a second local 4096.

## Tests

`node --test test/prompt-image-budget.test.mjs` - 11/11.
`node --test test/response-usage.test.mjs` - 47/47.
Run under the runtime's Node v24 (the `JSON.parse` reviver `context` argument the
estimate path uses needs Node 21+; system Node 20 gives false failures there).

title: fix: inject the configured subagent effort into named spawn_agent calls
body:
## Problem

A routed session that spawns a subagent with an explicit `model` but no
`reasoning_effort` leaves the child at that model's catalog default.
Router-published agent definitions carry the operator's configured depth
(`subagentEffort`), but only routed models get a definition. Native entries
(for example `gpt-5.6-luna`) have none, so a child spawned from a DeepSeek
session silently ran at `medium` even though the operator had configured
`high` for that model.

## Change

`injectSessionModelForSpawnCalls` now fills in the operator's configured
per-model subagent depth when a `spawn_agent` call names a model and does not
pass `reasoning_effort`. Explicit effort still wins, an unconfigured model is
left untouched, and `create_thread` / unnamed spawns keep their current
behavior.

## Verification

- `node --test test/subagent-model-inherit.test.mjs`: 21 pass (5 new cases).
- `node --test test/subagent-*.test.mjs`: 98 pass.
- `node --test test/namespace-relay.test.mjs test/namespace-relay-custom.test.mjs test/namespace-relay-routing.test.mjs`: 165 pass.
- Live check after restart: a DeepSeek parent spawning `gpt-5.6-luna` without
  an effort now records the child session at `high`; the same call before the
  change landed at the catalog default (`medium`).

title: fix: restart wedged LiteLLM gateway after liveness failures
body:
## Summary

Fixes the "502 Bad Gateway / the upstream refused the connection" failure on `http://127.0.0.1:4202/v1/responses` for models routed through the local LiteLLM gateway.

## Observed failure (Windows)

On Windows, LiteLLM's uvicorn accept loop can die while the Python process keeps running:

```
OSError: [WinError 64] The specified network name is no longer available
Accept failed on a socket ... laddr=('127.0.0.1', 4200)
```

The wedge was triggered by a mid-stream upstream reset (`MidStreamFallbackError` / `ConnectionResetError(10054)`). After that the process stayed alive but the listener on `127.0.0.1:4200` was gone, so every routed request failed with `connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4200` and the router answered 502 until a human restarted the service.

## Root cause

`superviseGateway` only reacted to the child **process exiting** (`waitForExit`). A process that is alive with a dead/unresponsive listener never exited, so it was never recovered.

## Fix

- Poll the gateway's own `/health/liveliness` after it has been healthy once.
- After `CODEX_ROUTER_GATEWAY_HEALTH_FAILURES` consecutive failures (default `3`, env `CODEX_ROUTER_GATEWAY_HEALTH_FAILURES`), terminate the still-running child and reuse the **existing bounded, backed-off restart path**.
- Interval configurable via `CODEX_ROUTER_GATEWAY_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS` (default `15000`).
- Existing behaviour is unchanged when no `healthCheck` is supplied (all prior tests still pass).

## Files

- `src/gateway-supervisor.mjs` — liveness watchdog + env limits
- `src/start.mjs` — supplies the short 4s gateway liveness probe
- `test/gateway-supervisor.test.mjs` — regression test proving a live process with an unresponsive listener is stopped and replaced

## Verification

- `node --test test/gateway-supervisor.test.mjs` → **9 pass / 0 fail**
- `node scripts-check.mjs` → syntax checks passed
- Live recovery observed in production after deployment:

```
LiteLLM gateway stopped answering health checks (3 consecutive liveness failures); terminating the still-running process before restarting it.
LiteLLM gateway is healthy again after 2 restart(s).
```

- Direct request to the previously failing endpoint now succeeds:

```
POST http://127.0.0.1:4202/v1/responses
  model=opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash
→ HTTP 200, status=completed
```

title: Add, edit, and curate custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints from Control Center
body:
## What this does

Generic providers already carried everything an operator needs — an address, a protected key file, `/models` discovery, curation into the picker, and `<provider>/<model>` slugs that cannot collide — but they existed only on the command line. `providerOnboardingSnapshot()` walked the checked-in registry alone, so nothing in the desktop app could see one.

**Models → Custom → Add endpoint** now takes a name, a base URL, a Chat Completions or Responses choice, and an API key. Each endpoint then owns a chip whose menu can:

- add models from the endpoint's own catalog,
- add one **By name**, for a private or preview id the catalog never lists,
- remove a model,
- edit the address, protocol, or key,
- remove the endpoint with its key and models together.

Endpoints ride in their own `customEndpoints` array rather than among `providers`, so the tray and guided setup cannot mistake one for a checked-in provider they may select.

## Supporting fixes

- **`providers generic credential ID set --stdin`.** The existing hidden prompt opens `/dev/tty`, which an Electron child does not have.
- **`generic-providers` joins control.mjs's restart-bearing set.** It republishes the overlay and restarts the router exactly as `credential` does, but ran under the 850-second budget, so `assertRestartingPublicationAllowance` refused every add with "The model-overlay deadline cannot preserve publication and the full router readiness allowance" before anything was written.
- **`providers generic add-model`** registers an upstream id the endpoint does not advertise. Nothing verifies it, exactly as nothing verifies a base URL.
- **`safeFailure()` keeps the sentence.** A crashing router child used to surface Node's whole uncaught-exception report in the UI — file, source excerpt, caret, stack — with the message buried inside. Redaction is unchanged, and a child that failed without throwing is still shown whole.
- **A saved endpoint reports whether it answers.** Adding or editing runs one `GET /models`, so an unreachable host, a typo, or a rejected key is named in the dialog rather than showing up later as an empty model picker.

## Design note

This builds the Custom card on generic providers rather than on the `custom` per-model-endpoint container. The container keeps a checked-in model naming its own endpoint; generic providers already own discovery, curation, credential storage, and slug uniqueness, and nothing writes per-model endpoint entries today. Reviewers who would rather see the container extended instead should say so — the UI is not coupled to the choice.

## Testing

- `npm run check`, plus `tsc --noEmit` and the syntax checks in `apps/control-center`.
- 225 tests across `generic-providers`, `control-center-electron`, `provider-onboarding`, `curate-models`, `registry`, and `control`: all pass.
- New tests cover the `--stdin` credential path (and that it never falls back to the prompt), `add-model` including duplicate and usage refusals.
- One existing assertion in `control-center-electron` was updated: the connections summary now counts chips rather than every directory row, because endpoints are reached through the Custom chip instead of sitting beside it.

**Not yet verified:** the UI flow has not been exercised end to end against a live endpoint. The endpoint I set up for this work is unreachable from my network (a VPN blocks it), so add, edit, remove, and curate were exercised through their router commands and unit tests rather than by clicking through the app against a responding server.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Clamp stale native reasoning effort after model switches
body:
## Problem

Codex can apply a newly selected native model before it replaces the previous model's reasoning effort. When the old model supports `minimal` and the new model does not, native passthrough forwards an invalid model/effort pair and ChatGPT rejects the whole turn with HTTP 400.

This was not isolated to one model. The reporter's local session history contained 89 identical upstream validation failures: 67 on GPT-6 Astra, 12 on GPT-5.6 Luna, and 10 on GPT-5.6 Sol. The recorded turn context already contained `reasoning_effort: minimal`; router timing showed the native OpenAI request returning 400, so localization was not involved.

## Change

- Read the target native model's current account-catalog reasoning ladder, with the captured native catalog as the offline fallback.
- Keep supported efforts byte-for-byte unchanged.
- Clamp only known Codex effort names to the nearest declared rung at or below the requested level; a request below the model floor lands on that floor.
- Preserve unknown values so the upstream validator can still expose real client/schema drift.
- Fail open when model metadata is missing or unreadable.
- Log each model/field/from/to repair once per router process.

The normalization runs after an extended-window alias is translated back to its native base model and before the request is serialized for ChatGPT. It covers both the nested Responses spelling and the flat compatibility spelling.

## Verification

- `npm run check` passes.
- Five focused unit cases pass.
- The native routing regression passes through a mock ChatGPT endpoint and proves `minimal -> low`, supported `high` unchanged, unknown `future` unchanged, and reasoning summary preserved.
- Full suite on the patched tree: 4,398 tests, 4,353 passed, 13 failed, 32 skipped.
- The same six affected test files on an untouched `origin/main` worktree produce the exact same 13 failures. They are host-state failures from the Chinese Control Center locale, inherited proxy/OpenRouter environment, and installed Codex alpha behavior; this change adds no failures.

Prepared with an assistant operating this account, at the account owner's request.

title: fix: bound the upstream connect phase and derive the retry budget from it
body:
## What

`src/upstream-retry.mjs` lists `UND_ERR_CONNECT_TIMEOUT` as retryable, but the loop's pre-retry budget was a fixed 5s while the socket was allowed undici's 10s default to connect. By the time the failure arrived the attempt had already spent the budget, so no retry was ever started and the blip was relayed to the client as a 502.

Measured on 2026-09-21: one incident logged **454 connect timeouts and zero connect retries**, each failure costing its caller ~10.2s. A blackholed address measured 10.0s to fail.

## Change

- `fetchDispatcherOptions()` carries an explicit `connectTimeout` (3s; `CODEX_ROUTER_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`, clamped 0.5–30s) and races the resolved addresses (`autoSelectFamily`, 250ms per attempt) instead of serializing one dead anycast address in front of a healthy one.
- `src/upstream-retry.mjs` derives its default budget from that same bound (`3 x connectTimeout`, 9s by default) so the two cannot drift apart again. A fixed budget against a configured connect bound was the actual defect.
- Worst case for a request that does fail is unchanged at ~10s — three bounded attempts plus backoff, where one undici-default attempt used to be. A *slow* failure is still relayed untouched: a 504 the edge spent half a minute producing is not retried.
- `AGENTS.md` rule 3, `CHANGELOG.md` and `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md` updated; the troubleshooting entry tells a bound that is too small apart from a network path that is actually broken.
- The spawned-router test waits now tolerate a loaded host (5s → 30s, still polling at 50ms and still failing immediately when the child exits), because that gate was itself timing out under load and blocking the very fix it guards.

## Verification

- New tests: a bounded connect timeout is affordable for every retry (three attempts under the default budget and backoff); a connect timeout that outlives the budget is still relayed; the dispatcher carries the configured bound and clamps the override; the retry budget covers every bounded attempt it allows. Existing tests for relayed bytes, aborts and slow failures are unchanged.
- `node --test test/fetch-transport.test.mjs test/native-retry.test.mjs` → 32/32.
- Blackholed connect (`10.255.255.1:443`) measured **3.5s** with the new bound, against **10.0s** before.

## Risk

A connect timeout cannot double-execute work: no connection was established, so nothing was sent. The existing `canRetry`/`headersSent` backstop is untouched, and the budget still refuses slow failures.

title: fix: keep startup gates from killing the service on a loaded host
body:
## What

Three startup gates treated a scheduling artifact as a defect, and a one-minute task heartbeat turned each failure into a loop that could not converge:

1. **The gateway config ACL hardening was fatal.** `writeLiteLlmConfig()` hardened four files per start through a short-lived PowerShell helper and threw when that helper timed out. On a busy host every start died there.
2. **The interpreter probe was fatal on a timeout.** `venvRuntimeProblem()` already documents that a `spawnSync` timeout "is not proof of a broken virtual environment", but `start.mjs` threw on it anyway.
3. **The gateway's cold start was allowed 300s.** A starved Python import can take longer; the launching scheduled task then relaunched `start.mjs` after each failure and killed the in-flight import — the failure mode the code's own comment warns "loops forever".

Measured on 2026-09-21: the router was down for ~40 minutes on a host that was busy with unrelated work, because each attempt killed the previous import at the 300s mark.

## Change

- `src/litellm-config.mjs`: the ACL hardening is attempted, warned about on failure, and never fatal on the startup path. The files still inherit the owner-only ACL of the state directory they are written into, and callers that must not continue without the hardening still receive the error.
- `src/venv-runtime.mjs`: new `isTransientVenvProblem()`; `src/start.mjs` logs a warning for a timed-out probe and lets the gateway's own readiness gate be the judge. A genuinely broken environment (missing interpreter, non-zero exit) is still fatal.
- Cold-start allowance raised from 300s to 900s in `src/start.mjs`, with the matching waits in `src/service.mjs`, `src/service-readiness.mjs`, `src/router-restart.mjs` and `src/wait-health.mjs`, and the `src/health-backoff.mjs` comment updated to match.

## Verification

- `node --check` on every touched file; focused test set 78/78 (`node --test test/responses-heartbeat.test.mjs test/empty-completion-router.test.mjs test/fetch-transport.test.mjs test/native-retry.test.mjs`).
- With the change: a cold start on a loaded host completes instead of being killed mid-import; a start after the ACL helper times out proceeds with a warning.
- Simulated a fresh upstream checkout and rebuilt on top of it: the resulting tree is identical across two independent hosts.

## Risk

The longer allowance only changes how long a start waits for a gateway that is still initializing — a broken environment still fails, and the readiness gate that decides "healthy" is unchanged. The ACL change keeps the attempt; it only stops a transient timeout from taking the whole service down.

title: feat(i18n): complete the zh-TW interface for the Control Center and tray panel
body:
## What this changes

Completes the Traditional Chinese (zh-TW) interface for both desktop surfaces. Pages the earlier localization pass had not reached still rendered hardcoded English while the language was set to zh-TW: the whole Settings "ChatGPT accounts" section, every action label behind `runAction` and the optimistic toggles, the model directory, the shared formatters in `lib.ts`, and the tray panel's status, usage, connections, vision, local-model, and Ollama-catalog surfaces. The Windows tray context menu was English too, because the main process owns no dictionary of its own.

## Details

- **Dictionaries.** EN and ZH_TW both define every key: 1188/1188 in the Control Center and 386/386 in the panel. The other locales keep their existing overlays and fall back to English for the new keys, which is what they rendered before this change. The panel's key test now states that contract explicitly: zh-TW must stay complete, and another locale may omit a key because `t()` inherits the English source text.
- **Shared helpers.** `effortLabel` moves into `lib.ts` so the Models, Local, and Settings pages agree. The panel's Ollama-catalog "fit" column keeps a stable id for sorting and translates only the label beside it, so wording can no longer reorder the list.
- **Tray menu.** The context menu is built in the main process, which has no dictionary, so the renderer hands it the two labels it already resolved over a validated `setTrayLabels` IPC channel. English stays as the pre-render default for a tray-only launch.
- **Provider plan notes.** The panel's zh-CN-only note table becomes a per-language table and gains zh-TW.
- **Fixed in passing:** the zh-TW `models.subagentSummary` entry appended the English plural "s" to a Chinese sentence.

## Tests

- Source-copy assertions that pinned English strings to page sources now check the key the page renders plus its dictionary entry. The same stale marker fix is applied in `test/chatgpt-session-desktop.test.mjs`.
- The panel suites declare the language they assert on: `test/panel-ui.test.mjs` pins `en`, and the browser E2E passes `locale: "en-US"`. Both previously compared translated labels against English expectations, so they failed on a machine whose locale is not English.
- New: the tray context menu follows the interface language the renderer resolved.

## Verification

`npm run check`, plus the control-center, panel, and desktop-panel browser E2E targets, pass locally on Windows.

## Unrelated note

While rebuilding the packaged companion on Windows, `codex-router.ps1`'s Control Center update transaction could not complete: `Restore-ControlCenterTaskSnapshot` compares the task SDDL byte-for-byte, but Windows normalises the DACL (`D:AI` plus ACE reordering) as soon as the task is re-registered, so the restore never matches. Out of scope for this PR; happy to open a separate issue with the reproduction.

title: fix(win): recover the Control Center task when Task Scheduler rewrites its DACL
body:
## Problem

`tray install` / `tray rebuild` could not complete on Windows. `Recover-ControlCenterUpdateTransaction` and `Restore-ControlCenterTaskSnapshot` compared the tray task's stored security descriptor with the pre-transaction snapshot **byte for byte**, but Task Scheduler rewrites that descriptor when it registers a task: a DACL holding an inherited ACE gains the auto-inherited flag, and the ACEs are stored in canonical order.

Measured on Windows 10, for the same task:

```
recorded: O:<user>G:<users>D:(A;ID;0x1f019f;;;BA)(A;ID;0x1f019f;;;SY)(A;ID;FA;;;<user>)(A;;FR;;;<user>)
stored  : O:<user>G:<users>D:AI(A;;FR;;;<user>)(A;ID;0x1f019f;;;BA)(A;ID;0x1f019f;;;SY)(A;ID;FA;;;<user>)
```

Same owner, same group, same four ACEs, yet the check failed. Because the check lives in the recovery path, the rollback reported *its* SDDL error instead of the real failure, the journal stayed at phase `recovering`, and every later tray mutation failed at the same step.

## Fix

Compare the security identity rather than the two SDDL strings:

- owner and group SIDs,
- the DACL's remaining flags, with only the auto-inherited marker dropped,
- the ACE set, by each ACE's binary form (type, flags, mask, identity), order-insensitively.

Still refused: a different owner or group, a protected DACL, a null DACL where the other side has one (a missing DACL grants everyone full control; an empty one grants nobody), and an added, removed, or altered ACE. Any descriptor that cannot be parsed or read is treated as different, so the check stays fail-closed.

Both APIs are read the way Windows PowerShell 5.1 exposes them, which the test matrix now pins down:

- the parameterless `GenericAce.GetBinaryForm()` overload does not exist there, so the buffer-taking overload is used (a first cut used the parameterless one, threw for every ACE, and silently accepted every descriptor),
- `RawSecurityDescriptor.Control` is not populated for a descriptor parsed from an SDDL string, so the DACL flags are read from the `D:` section instead,
- wrapping a null `DiscretionaryAcl` in `@()` iterates once as a single null entry, which refused two identical DACL-less descriptors.

## Verification

On Windows, with the real stuck journal in place:

- `tray start` completed, recovered the transaction, and deleted the journal.
- `tray rebuild` then ran build -> install -> start to completion ("Companion rebuilt, installed, and started") with no rollback package left behind. Re-run after the last edit: same result, no journal, no leftover backup.

`npm run check` passes. `test/tray-service-windows.test.mjs` passes, including a new PowerShell-driven matrix that extracts the shipped helpers and asserts three accepted descriptors (identical, canonicalised, both without a DACL) and seven refused ones (added ACE, removed ACE, weakened ACE, protected DACL, other owner, missing DACL, unreadable descriptor).

Also in this PR: the "install refuses before the tray has been built" guard skips when the checkout already contains a built companion, which is the premise its own comment states. Every developer who has run the packager otherwise sees it fail.

## Note

This is independent of #857 (the zh-TW interface work); it only touches `codex-router.ps1` and its Windows tray test. Environment-only failures seen while testing this on Windows and left alone: the installer tests that shell out to `sh` (absent here), and the browser E2E, which needs the root Playwright dependency.

title: [Provider]: xAI Grok 4.7 (grok-4.7)
body:
## Provider and model ID

title: Native-model requests with string input or stream:false return bare upstream 400s ("Input must be a list" / "Stream must be set to true")
body:
### What happened?

Requests to native (ChatGPT-plan) models through `/v1/responses` fail with bare upstream errors when the client uses shapes the OpenAI Responses API normally tolerates:

1. `"input": "some string"` → `HTTP 400 {"detail":"Input must be a list"}` (the ChatGPT backend requires array-form input; the OpenAI public API accepts both).
2. Non-streaming requests (`"stream"` unset/false) → `HTTP 400 {"detail":"Stream must be set to true"}`.

The real Codex client always sends array input and always streams, so production traffic is unaffected — but anything else speaking the Responses API to the router (scripts, probes, proxies relaying third-party clients) gets an unhelpful 400 that names neither the model nor the requirement.

### Environment

- codex-router main @ `5e1b49e6`, Linux and macOS alike
- Fresh state dir, native session enabled, account authenticated

### Reproduction

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4202/v1/responses \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALLER_SECRET" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-5.6-sol","input":"Reply with exactly OK","max_output_tokens":400}'
# -> 400 {"detail":"Input must be a list"}

# same body with array-form input but no "stream": true
# -> 400 {"detail":"Stream must be set to true"}
```

### Suggestion

Normalize in the native forwarder: wrap string `input` into the array message form, and either honor non-streaming by buffering the SSE stream into one JSON response (the generic-provider path already assembles SSE for non-stream callers — jev-codex-router does exactly this for its caller edge) or return a router-authored 400 that states the requirement. Happy to send a PR for the input normalization if useful.

title: fix(responses): preserve diagnosed stream failures with typed failure events
body:
When a routed Responses stream stops after announcing a valid response, the client can discard the router diagnosis and show a generic premature-EOF error. Preserve that diagnosis with a schema-valid `response.failed` event using the response identity and next sequence observed on the final bytes delivered to the client.

The observer forwards bytes unchanged and keeps only bounded metadata. It runs after rewrites, held empty completions and heartbeat, isolates discarded retry attempts, and suppresses a duplicate failure only when the client consumes an existing terminal event. Missing or untrustworthy metadata keeps the existing generic error frame. Shared chat and JSON error paths keep their existing behavior. No global `[DONE]` marker is added.

Validation on the final version combined with main:

- Node 22.19: 920/920 tests across 33 test files; `npm run check` passes.
- Installed Codex 0.156.1: 20/20 isolated parser controls; five regressions fail before the terminal-consumption repair and pass afterward.
- Locked OpenAI 2.53.0 and LiteLLM 1.96.0: 10/10 actual SDK consumer controls.
- Native buffered response, Claude, Gemini and WebSocket: 4/4 compatibility controls. Gemini retains its existing OTHER classification without the diagnostic text.
- Independent review plus final range review covers every changed hunk; no remaining scoped findings. All fixtures use isolated state and local synthetic responses.

Client retry policy remains client-controlled. Generic fallback does not guarantee Codex shows the diagnosis, and prompt EOF is required. Native CI passed on Linux, macOS and Windows, including all three locked Python protocol jobs, both Electron jobs, the native macOS build, discovery and the formula check. The merged tree exactly matches the reviewed and tested candidate.

title: fix(guard): scale the pre-content budget with the request size
body:
## What

The pre-content budget is flat (30s default) while the prefill it has to cover scales with the prompt. A 577k-token request legitimately spends 70–130s before its first content byte, so the guard classified a working turn as an *empty completion* and the client received an explicit `precontent_limit` 502 — while identical requests succeeded whenever the prefill happened to fit the budget.

Measured 2026-09-21 on a routed client running a large repository context: 502s at 18.8s / 116.7s / 127.8s alternating with successful turns at 74s / 13s / 11s, all on the same model and prompt shape.

## Change

- New `preludeBudgetMs({ baseMs, requestBytes, perThousandTokensMs, maxMs })` in `src/empty-completion-guard.mjs`: adds 150ms per estimated 1k tokens (4 bytes/token) on top of the configured base, bounded by a ceiling (default 600s) that never drops below the operator's base. A missing, negative, or non-numeric size leaves the base untouched.
- `createResponsePipeline(contentType, preludeMs)` takes the budget, and `handleResponses` computes it once per request from the decoded body length and passes it to both the first and the retry pipeline. The Grok stall bound is unchanged, and the guards attached to the streams keep their byte bounds.

## Verification

- New unit test: scaling, the ceiling, the operator-base-wins case, and that a missing/negative/NaN size never shrinks the budget.
- 56/56 focused tests (`pipe-response`, `empty-completion-guard`, `empty-completion-guard-deepseek`); 39/39 integration (`empty-completion-router`).
- A scratch checkout 13 commits behind upstream rebuilt with this patch plus five unrelated local patches: focused gates 78/78.

## Risk

Large requests now wait longer before the router declares an empty completion (by design). Small turns keep the fast failure: the allowance starts at the configured base. The budget only grows — `Math.max(base, …)` means a configured base is never reduced by the clamp.

title: fix: keep one chat tool name standing for exactly one tool
body:
## Why

Two halves of the same collision, pulling in opposite directions. Both are about one flattened wire name standing for two different tools.

### Half one: an unbounded chat provider publishes two identities under one name

`chatProviderToolSurface` asks `flattenNamespaceTools` for deterministic collision aliases on the Groq route only:

```js
const expanded = flattenNamespaceTools(merged.tools, { aliasCollisions: true });
```

with a comment saying why — *"Groq has no OpenCode-style length bound, but it still needs deterministic aliases when two distinct native identities have the same flattened wire spelling."* Command Code gets the same protection for free, because its 64-character bound forces an alias on any duplicate. Every other chat-completions route reaches the branch above it and is handed `{}`, so `initializeNameAliases` returns `undefined` and no aliasing happens at all.

The shape is not hypothetical — it is the one `test/chat-tool-surface.test.mjs` already covers for Groq (*"Groq aliases a plain flattened spelling away from its injected app identity"*). Codex injects its app tools as a `codex_app` namespace **and** sends the flattened spelling, so a client carrying `codex_app__create_thread` beside the namespaced `create_thread` has two distinct native identities with one wire name. On `main`:

| provider | tool list sent upstream | two stored calls | both restore to |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `groq` | `…_f16801fcc6ec`, `…_c2dda340660e` | stay distinct | the right identity each |
| `commandcode` | `…_f16801fcc6ec`, `…_c2dda340660e` | stay distinct | the right identity each |
| `deepseek` | `codex_app__create_thread` **twice** | collapse to one name | `codex_app/create_thread` |
| `openrouter` | `codex_app__create_thread` **twice** | collapse to one name | `codex_app/create_thread` |
| `zai`, `moonshot` | `codex_app__create_thread` **twice** | collapse to one name | `codex_app/create_thread` |

Three consequences, in order of how quietly they fail:

1. The tool list carries one name twice. Strict OpenAI-compatible validators reject that outright.
2. The client's own `codex_app__create_thread` is unreachable for the turn — every call to the name comes back under the namespaced identity.
3. A **stored history** call the client made against its own tool is restored under the namespaced identity, which Codex dispatches somewhere else.

### Half two: the alias defeats "live top-level schemas win"

`flattenToolSearchHistory` states its own rule: *"Live top-level schemas win on a name collision."* It implements it by comparing the discovered tool's **provider-facing** name against the live tools' provider names.

On a route that aliases, the discovered tool is handed a different name, so it stops colliding — and the stale searched schema is declared beside the live one. That is already true on `main`, for exactly the two routes that alias:

```
main, a live `mcp__calendar__create_event` plus a search result that rediscovered it:

groq          declares mcp__calendar__create_event, mcp__calendar__create_event_35a0874e7141, mcp__calendar__delete_event
commandcode   declares mcp__calendar__create_event, mcp__calendar__create_event_35a0874e7141, mcp__calendar__delete_event
deepseek      declares mcp__calendar__create_event, mcp__calendar__delete_event
openrouter    declares mcp__calendar__create_event, mcp__calendar__delete_event
```

Two definitions of one tool go to the model, and the stale one — the whole reason the rule exists — is listed first in the search output.

So fixing half one on its own would spread half two to every route. They are one change.

## What changed

**`chat-tool-surface.mjs`** — the non-Groq branch asks for the same collision aliases, keeping the length bound orthogonal:

```js
return flattenNamespaceTools(providerTools, {
  aliasCollisions: true,
  ...(BOUNDED_TOOL_NAME_PROVIDERS.has(providerId)
    ? { maxNameLength: BOUNDED_TOOL_NAME_LENGTH }
    : {}),
});
```

**`namespace-relay.mjs`** — the shadow check compares the live tools' own **wire** spellings, snapshotted before any discovery mints an alias (beside the existing `initialNameAliases` snapshot, which is there for the same reason):

```js
const liveWireNames = new Set(NAME_ALIASES.get(namespaces)?.wireOwners?.keys() || []);
…
const shadowedByClient = (visibleNames.has(name) || liveWireNames.has(wireName)) && !priorOwner;
```

With no relay, `liveWireNames` is empty and the condition is exactly what it was, so nothing changes on a route that does not alias.

After both, all four providers agree on both questions, using the aliases Groq and Command Code already minted (`_f16801fcc6ec`, `_c2dda340660e` — same digests, since the alias is derived from the native identity and not from the route).

## Asking for the aliases costs nothing

`aliasCollisions` only reaches `assignProviderName` with `forceAlias` when two identities share a wire name; every unique name is reserved as itself first. Measured rather than asserted: **20,000 generated collision-free tool lists** (plain tools, namespaces, long names, varied shapes) produce a **byte-identical flattened list** with and without the flag — 0 differ.

## Verification

- Three new cases in `test/chat-tool-surface.test.mjs`, all three failing on `main`:
  - `every chat provider aliases a plain flattened spelling away from its app identity` — the Groq test's scenario, run on `deepseek`, `openrouter`, `zai`, `moonshot`, asserting no duplicate name upstream, distinct history names, and both calls restoring to their own identity.
  - `a live top-level schema wins over a discovered one on every chat route` — the same four plus `groq` and `commandcode`, which fail this on `main` today.
  - `collision aliases are the same on a bounded and an unbounded provider`.
- `node --test test/chat-tool-surface.test.mjs test/namespace-relay.test.mjs test/namespace-relay-routing.test.mjs test/namespace-relay-custom.test.mjs test/routing.test.mjs test/tool-arguments.test.mjs test/search-capability.test.mjs` — 362/362.
- `npm run check` passes.
- Property run over 3,000 generated tool lists on both branches: every provider-visible name unique, every name inside the declared bound, aliases unchanged by reordering the list, and every call restored to its native identity — 13,364 restores, 0 failures.
- Each before/after measured by running `main`'s copy of the modules in a worktree beside this branch.

## One thing I did not change

`flattenToolSearchHistory` keys `definitionOwnersByName` — discovered-versus-discovered precedence — on provider names, and I left that alone. Two discoveries that alias apart really are different tools, so provider names are the right key there; only the client-shadow check is asking "did the client already publish this spelling?"

title: fix: add up the billed counts of both attempts at one turn
body:
## Why

`mergeTokenUsage` says what it is for:

> Add up the usage of two attempts at the same turn. A turn the router had to send twice cost twice; the meter has to say so, or the retry marker names a turn whose reported spend still looks like one attempt.

It adds up `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `totalTokens`, the cache count, the reasoning count and the retry count — and drops `billedInputTokens` and `billedOutputTokens`, the two fields that carry what was actually billed. The one-sided branch keeps them, because it spreads the surviving attempt through:

```js
const a = { inputTokens: 50000, outputTokens: 100, totalTokens: 50100,
            billedInputTokens: 150000, billedOutputTokens: 135 };
const b = { inputTokens: 51000, outputTokens: 100, totalTokens: 51100,
            billedInputTokens: 151000, billedOutputTokens: 135 };

mergeTokenUsage(a, b)          // { inputTokens: 101000, outputTokens: 200, totalTokens: 101200 }
mergeTokenUsage(a, undefined)  // …, billedInputTokens: 150000, billedOutputTokens: 135
```

So the pair is reported with **less** information than either attempt alone.

`normalizeTokenUsage` reads these from the wire (`billed_input_tokens` / `billed_prompt_tokens` / `billedInputTokens`), and `provider-usage.mjs` — the Usage view and the tray totals — reads them back:

```js
const inputTokens = nonnegative(event.billedInputTokens ?? event.inputTokens);
```

That `??` is the whole point of the field: it exists for providers that meter spend separately from the prompt they report. Grok OAuth is one — `selectedRetryUsage` sends `billed_prompt_tokens` beside `prompt_tokens`, and `test/provider-usage.test.mjs` already asserts that a row carrying `billedInputTokens: 301_000` aggregates as 301,000. With the merge dropping it, the `??` falls through to the reported count on exactly the turns where the two differ:

```
main    Usage view reports  input=101000  output=200
branch  Usage view reports  input=301000  output=270
        upstream actually billed  input=301000  output=270
```

A retry is not an unusual case here — `observeRejectedRetryUsage` exists because "rejected retries are still upstream requests and may be billed", and it drains the rejected attempt through the ordinary observer specifically so its counts reach this merge.

## What changed

The two counts merge the same way `cachedInputTokens` and `reasoningTokens` already do: absent when neither attempt reported one, summed when either did. Ten lines, one function, no call site touched.

## Verification

- Two new cases, both failing on `main`:
  - `billed counts are added up like every other measurement` (`test/response-usage.test.mjs`) — summed on both sides, carried through from one side, absent when neither reports, and a measured `0` surviving rather than becoming absent.
  - `a retried turn's billed spend survives the merge into one row` (`test/provider-usage.test.mjs`) — the merge output fed straight into `aggregateProviderUsage`, mirroring the existing Grok row above it.
- `node --test test/response-usage.test.mjs test/provider-usage.test.mjs test/usage-events.test.mjs test/context-window-drift.test.mjs test/grok-run-report.test.mjs test/grok-oauth-turn.test.mjs test/subagent-turns.test.mjs test/control-center-usage.test.mjs` — 154/154.
- `npm run check` passes.
- Before/after measured by running `main`'s copy of the module in a worktree beside this branch.

## `progressOnlyRetried` is dropped too, and I left it

The same merge drops `progressOnlyRetried`, which `context-window-drift.mjs` and `provider-usage.mjs` both read as a disqualifier. I did not restore it here, because doing so needs a decision I should not make on your behalf.

The guard is:

```js
if (event?.progressOnlyRetried === true && event?.billedInputTokens === undefined) return undefined;
```

`billedInputTokens === undefined` is standing in for "`inputTokens` is a sum, not a single attempt" — true for the row shape `selectedRetryUsage` produces, where `inputTokens` is deliberately the *selected* attempt. `mergeTokenUsage` sums `inputTokens`, so a merged row carrying both the marker and a billed count would be **accepted** as a capacity measurement it is not, and the drift check would tell the operator to raise a `contextWindow` that is already right — the exact outcome that module's comment spends a paragraph warning about.

This change does not move that either way: with the marker still absent, the guard does not fire on a merged row today and does not fire after it. Restoring the marker means also deciding whether `mergeTokenUsage` should adopt `selectedRetryUsage`'s convention (selected prompt in `inputTokens`, aggregate in the billed fields) or whether the drift guard should name the "this count is a sum" condition directly instead of inferring it. Happy to open either as an issue, or as a PR if you say which.

title: fix(win): pin the logon task to the VBScript engine
body:
## What

`taskAction()` registers the logon task's action as `wscript.exe //B //NoLogo "<launcher>"`. Those flags configure the host; neither says which script engine loads the file, so Windows still resolves the launcher through the machine's `.vbs` association. On the machine this was found on, that association belongs to an editor rather than Windows Script Host, so the logon task fired, reported success, and the router never started -- no console, no error, nothing in the task history.

The action now passes `//E:VBScript`, which selects the engine explicitly, so the launcher runs whatever the association says. The render tests cover both hosts, and `cscript.exe` carries the same flag for parity.

## Rebased after review

- Dropped the task-descriptor commit. #858 landed the semantic comparison as `Test-SameControlCenterTaskSecurity`, so that half was redundant here; this branch no longer touches `codex-router.ps1` or `test/tray-service-windows.test.mjs`.
- Moved the changelog entry into `changelog.d/win-logon-vbscript-engine.md`.
- Updated the stale comment in `src/service-windows.mjs` that still described the action as `wscript.exe //B //NoLogo`.

## Verification

- `node --test test/service-render.test.mjs test/tray-service-windows.test.mjs` -> 49 pass, 0 fail, 18 skipped (unrelated platform gates).
- `npm run check` passes, including `changelog fragments valid (11)`.

title: fix(meta): break recursive tool schemas inside namespace entries
body:
## Problem

The direct Meta Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor route carries `toolSchemaRecursion: "flatten"`, and the api-forwarder applied that repair -- but only to top-level `type: "function"` tools. Meta is a Responses-native endpoint, so the router deliberately keeps Codex's `type: "namespace"` entries, and the recursion lives inside those children: the `codex_app` and connector app toolsets, where `$defs` re-enters itself (`__schema0`, the Gmail-style `MessagePartRequest.parts`).

So the repair ran, the forwarder's log stayed silent, and Meta still answered HTTP 400 `Recursive JSON schemas are not currently supported` on tool-bearing turns. Only some turns died, which made it read like a stale config rather than a gate that did not cover the shape.

The router gate (`needsNonRecursiveToolSchemaCompatibility`) does not name the direct Meta routes, so `repairToolSchemaRoots(tools, { nonRecursive: true })` never runs for them and namespace children keep their cycle.

## Fix

The gate now also honours a route's own `toolSchemaRecursion: "flatten"`, so a route that documents the limitation opts into the repair in the shape its endpoint validates. Moonshot-flavored routes stay excluded: a blanked cycle-closing ref there has to keep the type it declared, which the shared non-recursive pass does not recover, and those routes already run their own pass.

This also closes the same latent gap on `opencode-go-responses/muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, which carries the flag without being named in the gate. Sibling Meta routes keep their payloads until their own endpoint proves the restriction, as #792 decided.

Related: #792 (the original direct-Meta repair, closed) and #844 (the OpenRouter variant, open).

## Verification

New test in `test/namespace-relay-routing.test.mjs`: `direct Meta Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor breaks recursive refs inside namespace tools`. It drives the real router against a mock gateway and asserts the body the gateway receives, with `meta/muse-spark-1.3` (no flag) as the control.

- Fails without the gate change: `actual: { '$ref': '#/$defs/__schema0' }`, `expected: {}`.
- Passes with it: definitions and the acyclic `$ref` survive, both the `items` and `additionalProperties` cycle edges are blanked, and a flat function tool in the same request is repaired too.
- `node --test test/namespace-relay-routing.test.mjs` -> 35 pass, 0 fail.
- `npm run check` passes.

title: fix(meta): repair a replayed function call whose arguments string is empty
body:
## Problem

Meta validates a replayed function call's `arguments` as JSON and refuses the whole request with HTTP 400 "`arguments` must be valid JSON" before inference. The turn is lost -- and because the call stays in the transcript, every later turn of that thread dies with it.

Measured live on a Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor thread that had called an MCP tool without arguments:

- the model emitted `search_code` with `arguments: ""`, and the MCP server answered `pattern is required`,
- Codex recorded the call and its output faithfully,
- the next request died on replay, and the thread could not continue.

The same thread shows this is not a relay problem: other calls in the same response arrived with valid JSON, including `{}` for genuinely no-argument tools.

## Fix

Meta-bound requests turn an absent, empty, or whitespace-only `arguments` string on a replayed `function_call` into `{}` -- what the call meant and what the endpoint accepts -- and report each substitution on stderr rather than quieting it.

Deliberately narrow: a non-empty string that is not JSON is a different failure and is left exactly as it arrived, so a truncated call is never rewritten into a call the model did not make.

## Verification

New test in `test/generic-routing.test.mjs`: `Meta replaces a replayed empty function-call argument string, and only that`, against a mock upstream.

- Fails without the fix: `actual: ''`, `expected: '{}'`.
- `""` and `"   "` reach the upstream as `{}`.
- `'{"pattern":"x",'` (unparseable, non-empty) and a valid payload pass through byte-identical.
- `node --test test/generic-routing.test.mjs` -> 8 pass, 0 fail.
- `npm run check` passes.

title: [Bug]: ClinePass catalog entries drop supported_reasoning_levels and Codex refuses to parse them
body:
### What happened?

Selecting a ClinePass model makes Codex fail to load that catalog entry with `missing field supported_reasoning_levels`. The same catalog loads every other routed provider.

The registry fragments already declare a ladder. For example `config/clinepass/kimi-k3.json` has `defaultEffort: "high"` and a single `reasoningLevels` entry. `routedModel()` in `src/catalog.mjs` copies those onto `default_reasoning_level` and `supported_reasoning_levels`, then deletes both keys when `requestProfile === "clinepass"`:

```737:741:src/catalog.mjs
  // ClinePass strips these unsupported request controls, so Codex must not offer them.
  if (model.requestProfile === "clinepass") {
    delete next.default_reasoning_level;
    delete next.supported_reasoning_levels;
  }
```

That deletion is locked in by `ClinePass routed models omit the unsupported reasoning-effort selector` in `test/catalog.test.mjs`, which asserts both keys are absent. No other `requestProfile` takes this branch, which is why only ClinePass entries fail.

Current Codex requires `supported_reasoning_levels` on every catalog model. An absent key is a serde `missing field` error, not "no effort selector". The catalog already treats other required keys this way: `supports_parallel_tool_calls` is always written, and `apply_patch_tool_type` uses `null` rather than omitting the key, because omission makes the catalog unparsable.

The request-side strip should stay. `src/api-forwarder.mjs` still deletes `reasoning_effort`, `thinking`, and `top_p` for `requestProfile === "clinepass"`, and ClinePass does not accept those controls. The catalog field and the forwarded parameter are separate: the entry has to remain schema-valid, and the forwarder should keep dropping the controls the upstream rejects.

**Expected:** a published ClinePass model parses like every other routed model. `supported_reasoning_levels` is present. Codex does not send an effort ClinePass will reject.

Codex

macOS

title: fix(reasoning): replay a thinking model's own reasoning to satisfy the tool-call contract
body:
## What

opencode's Go plan (and DeepSeek's own API) rejects a thinking-mode assistant tool call whose `reasoning_content` is missing:

```
HTTP 400 — Upstream request failed: [invalid_request_error]
The `reasoning_content` in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API.
```

`ensureToolCallReasoningContent()` already guarantees the *field* exists (#809), but an empty string is not the contract. Measured live on the Go plan, 2026-09-21, identical tool-call history:

| request | result |
| --- | --- |
| `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, no `reasoning_content` | **400** |
| `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, `reasoning_content: ""` | **400** |
| `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, the model's own reasoning replayed | **200** |
| `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, tool history with the same session's reasoning | **200** |
| `deepseek-v4-flash`, `glm-5.2` (no replay contract) | 200 |
| any of the above without tool-call history | 200 |

The client cannot always supply the text: a compacted history, a stateless tool-result replay, or a client that does not echo reasoning items never saw it. The router did stream it.

## Change

New `src/chat-reasoning-replay.mjs`:

- **Remember**: `createReasoningReplayTap()` is a read-only `Transform` added to the relay, for contract models on Chat Completions SSE only. It re-emits every byte unchanged, buffers `delta.reasoning_content` and the tool-call ids of the turn, and on the turn's end stores the reasoning against those ids.
- **Replay**: `reasoningForToolCalls()` is consulted from `ensureToolCallReasoningContent()`. A turn that already carries reasoning is returned untouched; a turn whose reasoning was lost gets the remembered text; only when nothing is remembered does the previous empty-string behaviour apply.
- Tool-call ids are stable in history, so the match survives compaction.

## Cost and safety (deliberately no regression)

- Only models where `requiresReasoningContentOnToolCalls(model)` is true pay for the tap; every other route is byte-for-byte the previous path.
- The tap pre-checks each chunk with a substring test before any JSON parsing, and keeps at most one turn's text in memory.
- The cache is a Map with LRU eviction by entries (512) and total characters (400k); reasoning is stored whole or not at all — a truncated replay is not the same reasoning, and the model reads it as prose it once wrote.
- Nothing on the wire changes, so upstream prompt prefixes and their cache hits are untouched; a turn that already has reasoning is never rewritten.
- Every failure inside the tap is swallowed: observation cannot disturb the relay.

## Verification

- `test/chat-reasoning-replay.test.mjs` (6 tests): per-id store/lookup, empty and id-less no-ops, eviction by entries and by characters, the tap remembering a streamed tool-call turn while forwarding every byte unchanged, the tap staying silent without tool calls, and the replay/never-rewrite pair.
- Existing suites unaffected: `commandcode-forwarder` and `grok-oauth-forwarder` return exactly the same pass/fail counts with and without this change on this checkout (the failures are pre-existing environment drift, verified by running the same files against the unmodified file).
- A scratch checkout 5 commits behind upstream rebuilt with this patch plus eight unrelated local patches: gates 84/84.

title: fix(deepseek): normalize replayed reasoning for the thinking contract
body:
## Problem

DeepSeek's thinking endpoint applies an all-or-nothing reasoning contract to replayed histories. Two distinct rejections show up on real Codex sessions routed through `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash`:

- `HTTP 400: The ` + '`reasoning_text`' + ` in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API` — an assistant turn whose reasoning is missing
- `HTTP 400: No tool output found for tool call ...` — a reasoning part sitting between a tool call and its output breaks the pairing

Both are structural mismatches between what Codex records and what the contract expects, so any long mixed-model or compacted conversation eventually dies when it fails over to, or is routed onto, this model.

## Root cause

Reproduced deterministically by replaying a real session's history (479 items: 248 reasoning, 90 tool calls, mixed providers) captured from a live thread:

1. **Two reasoning shapes, one reader.** Codex records reasoning both as `{content, summary}` (what `deepSeekResponsesInput` reads) and as `{summary_text, raw_content}` (the native shape it silently drops). The thread's reasoning was roughly half of each, so half of the thinking turns went bare.
2. **Displaced reasoning.** A model that thinks between issuing a tool call and the result arriving leaves reasoning items inside the call/output exchange; DeepSeek then cannot pair the outputs.
3. **All-or-nothing.** Even with every recorded reasoning replayed, turns that never had reasoning (compaction, foreign providers) stay bare — and once *any* turn carries `reasoning_text`, bare turns are rejected. (A history with no reasoning at all is accepted, verified live.)

## Fix

Three normalizations in `deepSeekResponsesInput`, none of which changes bytes for well-formed inputs:

- read `summary_text` / `raw_content` alongside `content` and `summary`;
- hoist displaced reasoning to the head of its owning assistant turn (idempotent, input never mutated);
- insert an explicit placeholder reasoning part before assistant turns left bare in a history that otherwise carries reasoning. Histories with no reasoning at all are untouched.

## Test plan

- [x] New unit tests: native shape replay, hoist out of tool exchanges, placeholder insertion, idempotency, input immutability
- [x] `node --test` on all DeepSeek-related suites: 121 tests pass (routing, v4.1-flash, tool-message-compat, empty-completion-guard, chat-reasoning-replay)
- [x] Live against the public endpoint: the captured 479-item mixed-model history goes from 400 to 200 (served 1397 output tokens, prefix cache intact)
- [x] Live regression: fresh simple histories, thinking effort variants, and tool-call histories all 200

Related to #872 (which replays a thinking model's *own* reasoning from a stream tap for opencode's Go plan); this covers the input-side shapes and placement for the direct DeepSeek Responses endpoint, where the reasoning was never this model's to cache.

title: Add StepFun as a first-party provider (global + China platforms)
body:
StepFun (阶跃星辰) serves the same OpenAI-compatible API from two consoles, so it ships as two providers rather than one with a region switch:

| Provider | Endpoint | Key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stepfun-api` | `https://api.stepfun.ai/v1` | `STEPFUN_API_KEY` |
| `stepfun-api-cn` | `https://api.stepfun.com/v1` | `STEPFUN_API_CN_KEY` |

Each console issues its own key, so the two are credentialed and enabled separately and can both be active at once. The China entry carries a `planNote` naming where to create its key, which `providers enable`, `doctor` and the tray all print.

## Models

Both platforms publish three routes over `/chat/completions` with a top-level `reasoning_effort`:

| Model | Context | Input | Efforts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `step-5-preview` | 1M | text + image | low / medium / high |
| `step-3.7-flash` | 256K | text + image | low / medium / high |
| `step-3.5-flash-2603` | 256K | text | low / high |

Every window, ladder, modality and price comes from StepFun's published model and pricing pages rather than being inferred from the ids ([Step 5 Preview](https://platform.stepfun.ai/docs/en/guides/models/step-5-preview), [Step 3.7 Flash](https://platform.stepfun.ai/docs/en/guides/models/step-3.7-flash.md), [Step 3.5 Flash](https://platform.stepfun.ai/docs/en/guides/models/step-3.5-flash.md), [pricing and rate limits](https://platform.stepfun.ai/docs/en/guides/pricing/details.md)). The million-token route compacts at 900,000 like every other one in the registry.

## Why the `-api` suffix

Beyond matching `kimi-api` / `zai-api`, the bare `stepfun` id is deliberately left unreserved. A checked-in provider id that collides with an entry in an operator's `generic-providers.json` makes `parseGenericProviderDocument` reject the **whole** document — every generic provider is dropped, not just the colliding one, and its stored `credentialRef` becomes unreachable. Operators who already added StepFun as a custom endpoint keep working configuration.

## Provider checklist

- **One-click install** — selectable via `install.sh --providers` / `providers enable`, reported by `doctor` (verified: both appear, and an existing generic `stepfun` still reports its bound credential alongside them).
- **Tray setup** — `provider-onboarding` renders both as `kind: "api"` / `action: "add-key"`, the hidden credential path; the key never transits chat, logs or arguments.
- **Plan entitlement** — `planNote` on the China provider.
- **Usage** — StepFun publishes `GET /v1/accounts`, so `stepFunBalanceMetrics` feeds the tray a real balance card (prepaid/postpaid, cash and voucher split, CNY on the mainland host) instead of falling back to router traffic. A custom base URL is never sent that request.
- **Icon** — the official favicon, already white-on-transparent as the Island bezel needs, with its source recorded in `PROVIDER-ICON-SOURCES.md`; both regions share the one asset.

Also updated: Control Center branding, README and docs-site provider tables, changelog, and the discovery workflow's scoped secrets.

## Not claimed here

- **No live request has been made** on either platform. Everything is verified against the registry loader, `doctor`, the onboarding snapshot and mocked fetches; the wire itself is unproven until someone stores a key and runs `./bin/test-model 'stepfun-api/step-5-preview' --live --yes`.
- **StepFun is deliberately absent from the `chat-reasoning` replay contract.** Its docs return reasoning as a `reasoning` field rather than `reasoning_content` and say nothing about replaying it through tool-call loops. That table takes live evidence only — which is also why the existing `commandcode/step-3.7-flash` route is not in it.

## Testing

`npm run check` passes. 111/111 across `registry`, `provider-catalogs`, `provider-branding`, `provider-account-usage` and `model-discovery` on this branch rebased onto `main`. The full suite's four failures are pre-existing and unrelated: `desktop-panel` (playwright not installed), `login-free-app-server` "preserved custom provider" ×2 (a known local-only failure), and one `antigravity-oauth-probe` flake that passes 15/15 in isolation.

title: chore: write changelog entries as fragments
body:
## Summary

Changelog entries move from a shared `## Unreleased` section to one file per change under `changelog.d/`, folded into `CHANGELOG.md` at release.

## Why

Every change appended its bullet to the top of the same section, so two branches that shared no source file still collided there. `.gitattributes` answers that with `CHANGELOG.md merge=union` — which resolves a local `git merge`, and does nothing on GitHub, because **GitHub's server-side merge does not run `.gitattributes` merge drivers**.

So a pull request reports `CONFLICTING` on github.com while merging cleanly on a maintainer's machine, and every merge to `main` re-conflicts every other open pull request. That is not theoretical: today it cost three already-green pull requests (#869, #866, #865) a full re-push and CI cycle each, twice — once when an unrelated merge landed mid-review, and again after each of their own merges. With 13 pull requests open it taxes all of them.

The `.gitattributes` comment already observed that "of ten conflicting pull requests, seven conflicted on this file and nothing else." The union driver was the right idea; it just never applied where the conflicts were being reported.

A fragment per change removes the shared line instead of resolving it. Two pull requests writing two different files have nothing to collide on.

## What changed

- `changelog.d/` holds one bullet per change, with `README.md` documenting the format and the reasoning.
- `scripts/assemble-changelog.mjs` folds fragments into `## Unreleased` and deletes them. `--check` validates without writing; `--dry-run` reports what it would move.
- `scripts/changelog-fragments.mjs` holds the logic, so the assembler and the tests share one implementation.
- `npm run check` now validates fragment shape, so a malformed fragment is caught in review rather than by whoever cuts the release.
- `AGENTS.md`, `.gitattributes` and a new PR template record the rule and — importantly — that a `CONFLICTING` status on a CHANGELOG-only overlap is not evidence of a substantive conflict.

Assembly is sorted by filename, so the result is byte-identical on every machine.

## Compatibility

Editing `CHANGELOG.md` directly still works and the union driver stays, so the 13 pull requests already open are unaffected and need no rebase for this.

## Verification

- `node --test test/changelog-fragments.test.mjs` — 9/9. Covers folding, ordering, dry-run, the README not being treated as an entry, idempotence with no fragments, and fail-closed behavior on a malformed fragment or a missing `## Unreleased` heading (writing nothing in both cases).
- Real round-trip against the actual `CHANGELOG.md`: assembled correctly under `## Unreleased`, fragment removed, then reverted so this PR ships the fragment rather than the assembled entry.
- `node scripts-check.mjs` clean; full suite 4570 tests. Three failures beyond the four known machine-local ones (`namespace-relay`, `process-tree`, `router-resilience`) were contention in the parallel run — all 165 pass in isolation, and this change touches only scripts and docs.

The API profile keeps `xhigh` only when the model declares it, so Grok 4.5 still clamps that rung to `high`. Neither route advertises the Grok 4.6 Fast tier, and neither is marked as a native v2 subagent.

Sibling catalogs (OpenRouter, OpenCode Go, Command Code, Nous) are left unchanged until those providers list `grok-4.7`.
