title: feat(models): ship Grok 4.7 and the MiMo-V2.6 series
body:
xAI published `grok-4.7` on 2026-09-21 and Xiaomi published the MiMo-V2.6 series on 2026-09-22. This registers every route each provider's own live catalog lists, taking windows, modalities, and effort ladders from that catalog rather than from the family name.

## Grok 4.7 — six routes

`grok-oauth`, `grok-api`, Command Code (`xai/grok-4.7`), Nous Research and OpenRouter (`x-ai/grok-4.7`), and opencode Go's Responses surface. 500,000-token window, text + image, compacting at 440,000 like the rest of the family.

No route claims `multiAgentVersion: "v2"`. That needs an accepted `v2_agent/` artifact in the same pull request, and it is not inherited from the certified 4.5 siblings. `grok-oauth/grok-4.7` does not inherit 4.6's Fast service tier either.

## MiMo-V2.6 — fourteen routes

Pro, Flash, and Pro-UltraSpeed on Xiaomi's own API, Command Code, the Nous Portal, and OpenRouter; opencode Go carries the Pro and Flash ids its catalog lists. Xiaomi publishes reasoning as a **toggle**, not an effort ladder, so each entry keeps the single `high` rung every other MiMo route uses — OpenRouter's records for these ids support `reasoning` but specifically not `reasoning_effort`.

The 1,048,576-token window is each provider's own published figure and compacts at 900,000, which still reserves the full 131,072-token output limit. The two opencode Go routes keep the 1,000,000 their V2.5 siblings use, because OpenCode publishes no limit for a paid Go id.

UltraSpeed is the same Pro answers generated faster at ten times the token price, and its picker description says so. `mimo-v2.6-flash-free` is curatable on the anonymous OpenCode routes but stays on conservative metadata, because its published 200,000-token window cannot reserve room for its own 32,000-token output limit — the same rule `mimo-v2.5-free` already follows.

## One list for the Grok OAuth adaptations

The bridge pinned its workarounds to the literal slug `grok-oauth/grok-4.6` in eight places across the forwarder, the router, the tool facade, the structured-patch and patch-hook experiments, and request diagnostics, so adding a Grok model meant finding all of them. `src/grok-oauth-routes.mjs` now holds that list once.

The two facts the registry already knows — whether a route has an `xhigh` rung and whether it offers a service tier — are read back off the model entry the way `hostedSearchEnabledFor` always was. A second Grok model now joins by declaring its own capabilities, and a workaround is widened only where the behaviour was actually observed.

## The audit caught an inherited assumption

Checking every new entry against current provider documentation turned up a defect in the **existing** `openrouter/grok-4.6`: its ladder was copied from Command Code's entry — that commit says "matching Command Code, not Nous Research's xhigh-ladder route" — rather than read from OpenRouter, so it published low/medium/high.

OpenRouter documents `xhigh` in the accepted effort vocabulary and maps an unsupported rung down instead of rejecting it; its `/models` records for both `x-ai/grok-4.6` and `x-ai/grok-4.7` advertise `reasoning_effort`; and xAI documents `xhigh` as native to both models. Both OpenRouter entries now carry the fourth rung. Command Code publishes no parameter metadata at all and stays conservative — now recorded as its own reason rather than as the precedent another route was copied from.

## Verification

- `npm run check` clean; suite 4527/4571, with only the two failures this machine always has (no playwright, no `codex` binary). Every other failure passed on isolated re-run — `routing.test.mjs` goes 152/152 alone.
- `grok-oauth` is the one route with no model-list endpoint to confirm against, so it was checked live. `bin/test-model grok-oauth/grok-4.7 --live --yes` passes basic response, streaming, tool calling, stateless tool result, and compaction. **That is the ordinary compatibility probe and says nothing about the native v2 child role.**
- All four rungs checked live with `--effort=RUNG`; `xhighEnabledFor` confirms 4.7 sends `xhigh` rather than clamping it the way 4.5 does.
- New regression tests: `test/grok-4.7.test.mjs`, `test/mimo-v2.6.test.mjs`.

### Known evidence gaps

title: fix(catalog): publish hidden models after visible ones for the desktop picker
body:
## Problem

Selected routed models (here `stepfun-api/step-5-preview`, earlier `opencode-go/mimo-v2.6-pro`) were missing from the ChatGPT desktop model picker, though `codex app-server` `model/list` returned them with `hidden: false` — from both the CLI and the desktop's bundled binary.

Root cause, read from the desktop bundle: the picker's query calls `model/list` with `{includeHidden: true, cursor: null, limit: 100}` and never follows `nextCursor`; hidden entries are filtered out only afterwards. Codex serves the list in `priority` order, and the published catalog interleaved hidden routes (149 of 173 entries on this host) with visible ones, so Step 5 Preview sat at entry 107 and was cut off.

## Fix

`publishHiddenAfterVisible` (`src/catalog.mjs`) renumbers every `visibility: "hide"` entry into a band after the highest visible priority, preserving their relative order. It runs on the final published catalog after picker visibility is applied.

- Visible priorities are untouched, so the picker order and the spawn_agent override window (AGENTS.md step 5) don't change. Hidden models are never spawn overrides.
- Array order in the file is unchanged, since Codex renders by `priority`.

## Verification

- New regression test in `test/catalog.test.mjs` (120 hidden routes + visible models past entry 100 → all visible models land on the first 100-entry page, visible priorities unchanged).
- `test/catalog.test.mjs` + `test/control.test.mjs`: 105/105 pass on a clean `main` base; `node scripts-check.mjs` passes.

title: fix(opencode-free): refuse the free ids OpenCode serves only to its own client
body:
## What prompted this

A check on whether MiMo-V2.6 is free on OpenCode. It is — `mimo-v2.6-flash-free` is in Zen's live catalog, models.dev publishes it at $0 (200,000 context / 32,000 output, empty `reasoning_options`), and it was already listed as curatable by #879. Flash only; there is no free Pro or Pro-UltraSpeed.

It does not work through this router.

## The finding

`opencode run -m opencode/mimo-v2.6-flash-free "Reply with exactly: ROUTE_OK"` answers `ROUTE_OK` from inside the OpenCode client. The same request from here is answered:

```
FreeTierError: OpenCode's free tier can only be used from within OpenCode
```

Probed 2026-09-23 against `https://opencode.ai/zen/v1` in the shape the router uses — no credential, since `opencode-free` is in the registry's `ANONYMOUS_ENDPOINTS`, plus the `x-opencode-session` header this repository attaches, Chat Completions for the primary ids and Responses for the Muse pair:

| id | result |
|---|---|
| `big-pickle`, `mimo-v2.5-free`, `mimo-v2.6-flash-free`, `muse-spark-1.2-contributor-free`, `muse-spark-1.3-contributor-free`, `nemotron-3-ultra-free`, `nemotron-3.5-lightning-free` | `FreeTierError` |
| `deepseek-v4-flash-free` | cleared the gate (upstream was down at probe time) |
| `hy3-free`, `laguna-s-2.1-free` | `ModelError: not supported` — withdrawn from the catalog |

So curating any of the first row produced a picker entry that fails on its opening request — the exact outcome the unverified-protocol refusal beside it exists to prevent.

## What changed

- `OPENCODE_FREE_CLIENT_GATED` in `src/opencode-curation.mjs` names the gated ids, and curation refuses them with a reason that says the cause is OpenCode's access policy, not a router compatibility limitation — otherwise the message reads as a missing feature somebody could wait for this repository to ship.
- Recorded per id, never as a provider-wide rule: `deepseek-v4-flash-free` cleared the same gate on the same run and stays addable.
- Discovery reports a gated id under `blocked` with that reason instead of offering it under `addable`; `doctor` says so where it suggests curating the free tier for failover.
- **The refusal reaches only a fresh candidate.** `normalizeCurationModels` resolves every stored row through the same function, so blocking those would strand an operator's existing entry short of its documented provider — the Muse migration to `opencode-free-responses` and the window/ladder upgrades both run there. A gated id keeps its place in `responsesModels`/`primaryModels`; what the gate withholds is the route's first appearance.

`hy3-free` and `laguna-s-2.1-free` are recorded as withdrawn in the module comment but left listed. Discovery reads the live catalog, so it cannot offer a withdrawn id whatever this file says, and their records still serve entries curated before the withdrawal — delisting them would only cost the repository its worked examples of a documented free window.

## What this deliberately does not do

Getting past the gate would mean reproducing whatever identifies OpenCode's own client. That is circumventing a provider access control stated in its own error, not fixing a compatibility problem, so it was left alone and `AGENTS.md` now says not to.

## Tests

`curate-models`, `model-discovery`, `registry`, `model-discovery-audit`, `untrusted-model-discovery`, `discovery-mode` — 136/136. New coverage: every gated id is refused with the FreeTierError reason on both providers of the pair while `deepseek-v4-flash-free` is not; a gated id already curated still resolves to its documented route and keeps its metadata upgrade; scripted curation exits non-zero naming the id; discovery splits `addable` from `blocked`.

Two scripted-curation tests lost fixture ids that are now unaddable. The documented-window case moved to `laguna-s-2.1-free`, and the Muse profile/modality assertions they carried are already covered against stored entries by "OpenCode Free curation migrates Muse to Responses" and "OpenCode Free Muse Spark routes document text and image input".

A 22-suite parallel run showed 8 failures in `test/routing.test.mjs`; that file passes 153/153 on its own, so it is loopback-port contention rather than this diff.

title: refactor(effort): move the effort clamp into a module its tests can import
body:
## What

^Gpi-forwarder.mjs starts a server at import time, so its pure effort clamp could not be unit-tested. declaredEffort and EFFORT_LADDER move unchanged into src/effort-ladder.mjs, and the forwarder imports them. No behaviour change.

## Why it matters

The clamp decides whether a user's chosen reasoning depth survives. The catalog advertises only the rungs the installed Codex build can parse (0.141 has no `max`, so it clamps down to `xhigh`); the forwarder is what turns that back into the model's own top rung. If a registry entry declares a single rung, every `max`/`xhigh` silently collapses to that rung and the model runs shallower with no error — measured 2026-09-22 on the opencode DeepSeek entries, whose provider advertises low/high/max.

## Tests

`test/effort-ladder.test.mjs` pins the composition: Codex's clamped `xhigh` reaches a model declaring low/high/max as `max`; a single-rung declaration collapses (kept as a test so the failure mode stays visible); lower rungs land on the nearest declared rung at or below them; an unparseable request falls back to the declared floor. 4/4 pass.

No behaviour change, no new dependency, no wire change.

title: Show the connection being made while a provider key publishes
body:
## The gap

Saving a provider credential runs one router command (`control credential <id>`) that writes the key, enables the provider, **and** republishes every installed client's catalog under a single lock. Only after it resolves does the snapshot refresh and the provider's routes flip from blocked to usable.

The credential dialog closes the moment you submit. So for the length of that command the Models page is byte-identical either side of the key being accepted — the chip is still grey, the routes still offer "Connect", and the only feedback anywhere is the small spinner in the title bar. Reported as "after I add the api key it doesn't seem like it renders the models in realtime".

## The change

A per-provider mutation is tracked for the whole credential transaction. Key save, OAuth sign-in and disconnect all run through `runProviderCredentialAction`, so all three report. It is cleared in the `finally` of the same `await` that already reconciled the snapshot — on failure too — so the placeholder gives way to the real routes and never back to the state it replaced.

- **The chip** moves onto the connections strip immediately with a spinner and "Connecting…" / "Disconnecting…" in place of the enabled dot, and is disabled so a second mutation cannot race the first. Placement is optimistic; the count is not — a provider still publishing sits among the chips without being counted as connected.
- **Every route waiting on that provider** swaps its Connect button for the same word plus a `SkeletonBlock` sized to the switch that is about to appear. This reuses the vocabulary the pending add-models rows already established, and keeps the slot the same height, so nothing on the row moves when the wait starts or when it ends.
- Strings in en / zh-CN / zh-TW; other languages fall through to English via the partial overlays.

## Verification

New renderer test `saving a provider key shows the connection being made before it lands` drives the real flow against a mock delayed by 1500ms and asserts:

- the connecting chip appears within 1200ms, carries `data-state="connecting"`, `aria-busy`, and is disabled;
- the connected count does not move;
- the waiting route loses its Connect button and gains the label plus the skeleton;
- a route whose own provider is untouched keeps its button;
- both placeholders are gone once the command returns, with no renderer errors.

`npm run check` and the full control-center suite pass in a clean worktree off `main`: 116 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped.

title: feat(models): let the operator delete locally curated models
body:
## Why

`addProviderModels` has always accepted any catalog provider, but removal was gated to custom endpoints, whose slugs happen to encode their upstream id. A model curated onto an ordinary provider — OpenRouter, DeepSeek, StepFun — could be published from the app and then never taken back.

Removal itself already worked. `curate-models --remove` prunes the `user-models.json` overlay and republishes every installed client, and by construction it can never touch a checked-in route. What was missing was a way to reach it, and the data to know which routes it applies to.

## What changed

**The missing signal.** The registry merge is the only place that still knows which side a route came from — both are normalized into the same shape afterwards. `mergeUserModels` now records that as `LOCAL_MODEL_SLUGS`, and `routerCatalogSnapshot` carries it into the snapshot as `local: true`. It is never set on a route this checkout ships.

**IPC.** New `removeLocalModels` handler, not gated by provider kind. It resolves each slug against the overlay rather than deriving an upstream id from it — an ordinary provider's public slug does not encode one, and the entry's own provider may differ from the family primary that curation takes (`opencode-free-responses` publishes under `opencode-free`). A checked-in slug has no overlay entry and is refused, so nothing can be "removed" only to reappear on the next publication. This also reaches an entry the merge skipped, which a slug-derived removal could never find.

**UI.** A locally curated route is tagged `Local` and carries a delete control, behind the same confirmation the disconnect flow uses. Multi-route families get a trailing actions column, rendered only for families that actually have a local route so every other family keeps its existing column widths. Single-route families get it in the details panel — without that second path a model like `stepfun/water18-0910` would have had no surface at all. Strings in en / zh-CN / zh-TW.

**`curate-models --dry-run`.** `--no-apply` reads like a rehearsal but only defers publication — it persists the overlay, so a removal run under it really deletes. That behaviour is deliberate and documented, so it is unchanged; `--dry-run` is the actual rehearsal, planning the same curation and writing nothing. It is rejected alongside `--apply`/`--no-apply`.

## Verification

- 176 tests pass, 0 fail (1 Windows-only skip) across the curation, registry, IPC and i18n suites. Renderer typechecks and builds.
- New coverage: the dry run writing nothing and its flag guard; `LOCAL_MODEL_SLUGS` marking overlay entries and never a checked-in slug; the IPC handler's resolution and its comma/authority guards; a renderer test that the delete appears on the local route alone and fires only after confirmation.
- Driven by hand against the built renderer with the test fixture: the control appears on the local route only, and confirming calls `removeLocalModels(["opencode-go/ox-alpha"])`. Doing this caught a real bug — the fixture stub had been placed behind a `?customEndpoints=1` gate, which would have failed this test in CI.
- Resolution checked against a real 6-entry overlay: both routable local models map to the correct family-primary command, and a checked-in slug is refused.

title: DeepSeek V4 Pro: allow Low reasoning in Codex picker; beware UTF-8 BOM when editing registry JSON on Windows
body:
## Summary

On Windows with codex-router 0.6.0 and Codex CLI 0.155.1, the routed model `deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro` was published to Codex Desktop with:

- `default_reasoning_level: high`
- supported levels: `high`, `max`

As a result, Codex Desktop only exposed High for DeepSeek V4 Pro.

I verified that changing the DeepSeek registry entry to Low/High works correctly and Codex Desktop then exposes **Low (Ligero)**.

## Working registry definition

In:

`config/deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro.json`

the model can use:

```json
{
  "defaultEffort": "low",
  "reasoningLevels": [
    {
      "effort": "low",
      "description": "Low reasoning"
    },
    {
      "effort": "high",
      "description": "Deep reasoning"
    }
  ]
}
```

After regenerating the Codex catalog, the resulting `merged-models.json` correctly contains:

```json
"default_reasoning_level": "low",
"supported_reasoning_levels": [
  {
    "effort": "low",
    "description": "Low reasoning"
  },
  {
    "effort": "high",
    "description": "Deep reasoning"
  }
]
```

Codex Desktop then allows selecting **Low / Ligero** for DeepSeek V4 Pro.

## Important Windows / PowerShell gotcha

While testing this, PowerShell rewrote the JSON file as UTF-8 **with BOM**. Node then failed to parse the registry with:

```text
Unexpected token '﻿', "﻿{
    "v"... is not valid JSON
```

The registry parser in `model-registry.mjs` uses JSON parsing that rejects the BOM.

Writing the file as UTF-8 **without BOM** fixed the issue. For example:

```powershell
$p="$env:LOCALAPPDATA\codex-router\config\deepseek\deepseek-v4-pro.json"
$c=Get-Content $p -Raw
[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText($p,$c,(New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding($false)))
```

After that, importing `model-registry.mjs` showed the model in memory with `defaultEffort: low` and Low/High reasoning levels, and running:

```powershell
node "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\codex-router\src\catalog.mjs"
```

regenerated the catalog successfully.

## Verified routing

DeepSeek routing itself was already working correctly through the router (`provider=deepseek`, HTTP 200). This issue is specifically about the reasoning-effort metadata exposed in the Codex picker and the Windows BOM pitfall when editing registry JSON.

## Suggested changes

1. Consider changing the checked-in DeepSeek V4 Pro registry metadata from High/Max to Low/High (or otherwise expose Low in the picker).
2. Consider making registry JSON parsing tolerant of a leading UTF-8 BOM, since Windows/PowerShell users can easily produce BOM-encoded JSON while editing configuration files.

title: [Bug]: Grok OAuth drops xAI encrypted reasoning, so Grok 4.7 stops reasoning after two tool rounds and can loop
body:
### What happened?

On the Grok OAuth route, Grok stops reasoning after a few rounds of tool calls, even at `xhigh`. With no reasoning, it plans in visible text ("next I'll check…"), and in long agent loops that text can degenerate into one sentence repeated for minutes. The stream stays HTTP 200 with deltas flowing, so no stall guard or timeout ever fires.

**Expected:** a multi-round tool loop keeps reasoning, the way it does in the official Grok CLI.

**Cause:** xAI returns each turn's reasoning as a `reasoning` output item with `encrypted_content`. On `grok-oauth/*`, the path is Codex (Responses) → LiteLLM (Chat Completions) → `grok-oauth-forwarder` → xAI (Responses). The Chat hop cannot carry `encrypted_content`, and `toResponsesRequest` on `main` (a684a3e6) sends no reasoning history at all. Later requests therefore contain the model's past tool calls but none of its reasoning. Grok 4.7 then stops reasoning from about the third round.

#### Evidence

**1. Controlled A/B, straight against xAI, synthetic prompt only.**

- Setup: Grok 4.7, `xhigh`, `store:false`, one `exec_command` tool, an 8-module audit task, fake tool outputs.
- Each arm runs the same live loop and differs only in what it does with the previous turn's `reasoning` item.
- Headers match the forwarder's.
- Values are reasoning tokens per step, from `usage.output_tokens_details`.

| Previous reasoning sent back as | rep 0 | rep 1 | rep 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| full item with `encrypted_content` | 77, 147, 126, 966, 1426, 1383, 8, 2 | 77, 158, 252, 293, 71, 3, 704, 2 | 77, 104, 86, 263, 1224, 77, 2, 7 |
| dropped (what `main` does) | 76, 87, **0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0** | 72, 55, **0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0** | 76, 363, **0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0** |
| summary only, no `encrypted_content` | 74, 346, **0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0** | 74, 363, **0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0** | 75, 60, **0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0** |

- With a single prior tool round, 8 of 9 runs across the three arms still reason; the effect appears after two rounds.
- Grok 4.6 in the same small loop still reasoned with the item dropped. In long real sessions it degrades too; see (2).

**2. Aggregate from my own router usage events.**

- Grok 4.7: 97.6% of responses to a tool result have `reasoning_tokens = 0` (1,352 responses, all at `xhigh`).
  - First turns of a session always reason.
  - Turns right after a new user message reason 72% of the time.
- Grok 4.6: the zero-reasoning share grows with input size. It is 3% at 50–100K and 15% at 200–300K in early September, and 17% / 81% since 2026-09-11.

**3. Ruled out** by replaying one real stuck request directly to xAI, 3 runs each, 0/3 reasoning in every variant:

- the `x-grok-exact-repetition-check` header;
- the tool count (286 → 3);
- the Codex base prompt / `model_switch` instructions (down to a one-line prompt);
- `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]` on its own;
- the size of tool outputs (context cut to ~28K tokens);
- the assistant's prior visible text.

**4. What happens when it degrades.** Two runaway turns in my history were both zero-reasoning responses to a tool result.

- One ran for 11 minutes: a ~60-character progress sentence repeated about 2,000 times (~15 MB of SSE), until the parent interrupted.
- One produced 77K output tokens and ran until the context was nearly full. Codex then recorded it as a completed turn.

#### Fix I am running locally (happy to open a PR)

A small store in the forwarder:

- After a response completes, remember its certified `reasoning` items (`id`, `summary`, `encrypted_content`), keyed by `(x-grok-session-id, first tool call_id)`.
- The same call IDs come back verbatim in the next Chat request, so `toResponsesRequest` re-inserts those items in front of the matching `function_call`s.
- Also set `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]`.
- Bounded: 4,096 entries, 6 h TTL, LRU.
- On a miss (restart, eviction, rewritten history), it falls back to today's behavior.
- Failed or incomplete responses are never remembered.
- Env switch to turn it off.

Results with it:

- Through the forwarder: 14/14 steps reasoned (off: 8 of 10 later steps at 0).
- Through the full Router → LiteLLM → forwarder chain: 14/14 steps reasoned, 42 cache hits / 0 misses.

A longer-term alternative is a Responses-native hop for Grok that carries `encrypted_content` end to end, so Codex holds it.

**Also worth considering (separate):** a guard on exact visible-text repetition that cancels the upstream and ends the turn with a terminal error. Nothing on this route bounds a stream that keeps emitting deltas. The official CLI has its own doom-loop handling; this route has none.

### Which app do you route through?

Codex (Desktop, Codex CLI 0.155.0-alpha.16), with Grok 4.7 used as a sub-agent.

### Platform

macOS (Apple Silicon); Grok CLI 1.0.40 OAuth session.

### Doctor output or support bundle

Not attached: this is not an install problem. My install carries local modifications; the A/B in (1) was run directly against the xAI Responses endpoint, so it does not depend on them. `main`'s forwarder request builder has no reasoning handling, which corresponds to the "dropped" arm.

title: fix(grok): carry xAI encrypted reasoning through the OAuth tool loop
body:
Fixes #888.

## Problem

xAI returns each turn's reasoning as an opaque `reasoning` item with `encrypted_content`. Grok 4.7 keeps reasoning through a tool loop only when that item comes back in the next request.

On `grok-oauth/*`, the request crosses a Chat Completions hop (LiteLLM → `grok-oauth-forwarder`) that cannot carry the item. `toResponsesRequest` sends no reasoning history at all. As a result, Grok 4.7 stops reasoning from about the third tool round, even at `xhigh`. It then plans in visible text, and in long agent loops it can repeat one progress sentence until interrupted.

Live A/B against xAI (synthetic prompt, same loop, only the carried reasoning differs; details in #888):

| Previous reasoning sent back as | Steps that reasoned |
|---|---|
| full item with `encrypted_content` | 24/24 |
| dropped (current `main`) | 0/18 from step 3 |
| summary only | 0/18 from step 3 |

## Change

- New `src/grok-reasoning-carry.mjs`: a bounded in-memory store (4,096 entries, 6 h TTL, LRU) for the forwarder.
  - After a response **completes**, the forwarder keeps that response's reasoning items that carry `encrypted_content`.
  - They are keyed by the conversation id the forwarder already derives (`conversationId`) and by the call ID of the response's first tool call.
- `toResponsesRequest` takes an optional `recallReasoning(callIds)`.
  - For an assistant message with tool calls, it places the recalled items in front of that turn, which is the order xAI produced them in.
  - It also sets `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]`.
- The same call IDs come back verbatim in the next Chat request, so no extra protocol is needed.

## Safety

- The items are xAI's own bytes. The router never authors or edits reasoning text.
- A miss (restart, eviction, rewritten or compacted history, another conversation) sends no reasoning, exactly as today.
- Failed, incomplete, or missing-terminal responses are never remembered.
- `CODEX_ROUTER_GROK_REASONING_CARRY=0` turns it off.
- `/health` on the forwarder reports `reasoningCarry` stats.
- No change to other providers or to the Responses-native routes.

## Tests

- `test/grok-reasoning-carry.test.mjs`:
  - store bounds, TTL, eviction, and session isolation;
  - request placement, and that a miss invents nothing;
  - an end-to-end forwarder loop against a mock xAI covering carry, cross-conversation isolation, and a failed response not being replayed.
- Negative control: reverting only `src/grok-oauth-forwarder.mjs` fails the placement and end-to-end cases.
- All `grok*`/forwarder test files: 287/287 pass. `npm run check` passes.
- Full suite locally: 3 failures and 1 cancellation in `desktop-panel`, `login-free-app-server` and `search-sidecar`. They reproduce identically on unmodified `main` (a684a3e6) on this machine, so they are environmental and unrelated.
- Live verification with a real Grok OAuth session, synthetic 7-step tool loop through Router → LiteLLM → forwarder with this change: 14/14 steps reasoned, 42 carry hits, 0 misses. With the carry off: 8 of 10 steps after step 2 had zero reasoning.

## Docs

- AGENTS.md: a Grok entry next to the existing interleaved-thinking reasoning-replay rule.
- CHANGELOG: an Unreleased entry.

title: fix: let a loaded host record the service process identity
body:
writeServiceProcessState() runs before anything else starts, and it needs
processStartIdentity() plus processCommandLine(), both of which spawn
powershell.exe with a five-second budget and no retry. It then writes the
record through writePrivateJson(), whose ACL hardening allows fifteen seconds
and throws. Both are fatal, so a host whose powershell.exe is merely cold
cannot start the router at all.

Measured 2026-09-23, on a Windows boot under logon load: the ACL helper logged
`spawnSync powershell.exe ETIMEDOUT` twenty-two times in one boot window, so
every powershell.exe spawn was exceeding fifteen seconds while the identity
probe allowed five. start.mjs could not record its own identity, refused to
run without a stoppable process record, and the task's one-minute heartbeat
relaunched it into the same failure for forty minutes while the desktop client
showed "Reconnecting... waiting for network". The same probes measure 0.9-1.6s
on an idle host, which is why this only ever appeared after a restart.

A timeout is the one probe outcome that is not evidence about the process: the
child never ran. It is now retried once, at the same 45s allowance the
interpreter probe in start.mjs already has, and the probe resolves the absolute
system PowerShell so a PATH entry cannot decide whether the router can prove
which PID it is about to signal. A probe that answered -- including an absent
process -- is never retried, so the identity guarantee itself is unchanged.

The wider budget is opt-in, and only the service-process record asks for it.
Every other caller of these probes runs inside a bounded operation: a Windows
service stop that declares 15s, and a restart phase that reserves 10s for the
process-owner check and must still leave the router's own readiness allowance
intact. Widening the default there would let a slow probe outlive the deadline
of the operation that asked for it, so `service restart` could report failure
after it had already restarted the service, and the outer operation deadline
could kill the child mid-stop. The default therefore stays exactly what it was,
and a test asserts it.

The record write opts into hardenFailure: "warn". It carries a PID, an identity
string, paths and ports, never a credential; what makes it safe to act on is
the verification in serviceProcessOwns, not its secrecy, since a hand-edited
record for another checkout is rejected on sourceRoot, stateDir, command line
and identity before any PID can be signalled. The fallback ACL is the state
directory's inherited one, not an owner-only one. The default stays "throw", so
every credential write still fails closed.

title: fix(windows): verify service shutdown and preserve probe outcomes
body:
Windows service commands could report a completed stop when process, command-line or port probes had not answered, and a failed scheduled-task query could leave the minute heartbeat enabled. An early install failure could also run recovery before shutdown had been verified.

Preserve answered process absence separately from unknown query failures. Strict lifecycle reads reject corrupt or malformed process records. Stop, restart, uninstall and install refuse uncertain registration/ownership/port state, retain the record, and never start a replacement over an unverified tree. Disable the heartbeat before shutdown; a successful root-task enumeration establishes true absence and permits recorded orphan cleanup. Recovery is allowed only after verified shutdown. Runtime probes share bounded deadlines, while existing cold-start settings and record-hardening behavior stay intact. Startup diagnostics name the failing probe without printing its contents.

Validation: parent and independent reviewer both ran the four focused suites, with 113 passes and four native-Windows skips; the parent also ran adjacent shared process/startup/tray consumers, with 85 passes and four existing platform skips. The new complete-source regressions fail against main in 55 cases and pass after repair. Fault injection covers unavailable/malformed scheduler answers, all four lifecycle commands, orphan trees, reused PIDs, real record-validation errors, failed port checks, disabled-heartbeat ordering, early setup failures, verified registration recovery and bounded slow probes. Native PowerShell tests query only the test process or override a cmdlet inside a child process. No installed service is mutated locally.

Repository checks and whitespace checks pass. All 74 final hunks across eight changed files were inspected; the review evidence matches the committed candidate. Native Windows and full platform CI remain required before merge.

title: fix(install): stop counting orphaned crash reporters as a running client
body:
## Problem
After ChatGPT.app / Codex is fully quit, macOS keeps its Chromium crash reporter alive, reparented to launchd:

```
/Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Frameworks/Codex Framework.framework/Versions/153.0.8010.53/Helpers/browser_crashpad_handler
```

That path matches `/Codex Framework/`, so `bin/install` printed "Codex is running right now (PID 71348 and 1 other process) … Fully quit and reopen it" for an app that had been closed for hours.

## Fix (`src/client-restart-notice.mjs`)
- **Crash reporters are never counted**: `browser_crashpad_handler`, `chrome_crashpad_handler`, `crashpad_handler.exe`, and `--type=crashpad-handler` children, on macOS, Linux, and Windows alike.
- **A listing made only of helpers counts as not running.** Helpers are Electron `* Helper (…).app` processes, anything under a framework's `Helpers/` directory, and processes started with `--type=`. Such a listing is left over from an app that already quit. When the main process is running, it is still what the notice names.
- **Windows Cursor paths:** the Cursor pattern now accepts the closing quote that `Win32_Process` puts around an executable path containing spaces. Without it, a running Cursor on Windows was never matched.

## Tests
New cases in `test/client-restart-notice.test.mjs`:
- orphaned crashpad handlers only → no processes, "Codex is not running"
- main app + crashpad handlers + renderer → names PID 4242 and ignores the crash reporters
- helper-only leftovers → not running
- Windows: an orphaned `crashpad_handler.exe` and a `--type=crashpad-handler` child are ignored, and a quoted `Cursor.exe` main process is named

`node --test test/client-restart-notice.test.mjs` passes 11/11 and `test/control-center-harness.test.mjs` passes 19/19. On the host that showed the bug, the live probe now returns `[]` and "Codex is not running".

title: fix(startup): back off only transient automatic failures
body:
Repeated automatic launches can keep spending the same startup probe budget while a loaded host remains temporarily unavailable. Add a private, bounded cooldown for classified transient failures before the automatic service becomes fully ready.

The delay grows through 1, 2, 4, 8 and 15 minutes. The record stores a fixed reason, count and timestamps. Explicit manual start/restart clears the record before stopping and again after the old process is verified stopped. Foreground supervision remains immediate; full managed readiness clears the cooldown. Configuration, credential, ACL and ownership-mismatch failures keep their strict fatal behavior, and runtime failures after readiness cannot seed a new cooldown.

Propagate the exact 0/1 disable setting through Linux, macOS and Windows service renderers. Treat an installed automatic cooldown as temporary only when readiness and process evidence confirm that state; preserve the existing refusal on unknown ownership.

title: fix(transport): name refused loopback hosts so the local hint fires
body:
## Problem

When the router's own LiteLLM gateway on `127.0.0.1:4200` is down, Codex shows:

> unexpected status 502 Bad Gateway: The local router could not complete the request: the upstream refused the connection. If this network needs an outbound proxy, set NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 …

This happened live on 2026-09-23. The gateway restarted 11 times under a load average of ~300 on 18 cores, and each time it missed its startup health deadline.

The message is wrong in two ways: it doesn't say which host failed, and it tells the operator to reconfigure a network that is working. `transport-failure.mjs` already has a hint for loopback hosts ("one of this install's own processes … run ./bin/doctor --fix"), but it never fired.

## Cause

When a socket connection is refused, Node's error carries `address` and `port`, **never** `hostname`:

```
Error ECONNREFUSED {"address":"127.0.0.1","port":4299} | connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4299
```

`transportFailureHost()` only read `hostname`, and `connect ECONNREFUSED host:port` didn't match any of `HOST_PATTERNS`. So the host fell back to "the upstream", `localTransportHost()` returned false, and the code picked the proxy hint. The unit tests still passed because their fixtures set a `hostname` field that real errors don't have.

## Fix

- Read `address` when `hostname` is missing.
- Add a `connect E… host:port` message pattern as a fallback.
- Replace the fixtures that set a fake `hostname` with the shape Node really produces. Add a test that does a real refused `fetch`, so the fixtures can't drift from reality again.

The same failure now reads: `127.0.0.1 refused the connection. That is one of this install's own processes, not the network: run ./bin/doctor --fix.`

## Testing

- `node --test test/transport-failure.test.mjs`: 14/14 pass. Without the `src` change, 4 fail: the two corrected fixtures and both new tests.
- `test/model-failover*.test.mjs` timed out after 10s in 19 tests on the author's machine. Untouched `main` had more of the same timeouts at the same load (35 failures), so the machine is the cause, not this change. CI is the clean check for those.

Not addressed here: the LiteLLM startup health deadline under extreme load, which is why the gateway kept failing to come back.

title: fix(gateway): don't kill a starved LiteLLM on liveness timeouts
body:
## Problem
A `stepfun-api/step-5-preview` turn sat on "Working for 5m 29s" with no actions and then failed with `502 Bad Gateway: ... the upstream refused the connection`. The router log shows the chain:

1. The machine's load average was about 340–380 on 18 cores, mostly from headless-Chrome capture jobs.
2. LiteLLM was healthy and streaming the step-5 turn, but it missed three 4 s liveness probes because the probes timed out. The watchdog then killed it (`stopped answering health checks (3 consecutive liveness failures)`), which cut the stream off partway through its reasoning.
3. The replacement could not finish importing within the 300 s cold-start budget under the same load. It was killed and re-imported from scratch (`did not come back: ... connection was refused`), over and over. Every routed request got `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4200` and a 502.

## Fix
- `health-probe.mjs`: the timeout error now carries `probeOutcome` (`timeout` / `refused` / `answered`). The startup probe already made this distinction internally.
- `gateway-supervisor.mjs`: only conclusive failures (a refused port or a bad answer) count toward the 3-failure fuse. That is still enough to catch the Windows dead-accept-loop case the watchdog exists for. Timeouts need `CODEX_ROUTER_GATEWAY_HEALTH_STALL_FAILURES` in a row (default 20, about 5+ minutes), which still ends a truly wedged event loop.
- A replacement that is still running when its health budget runs out gets up to 3 budgets before it is stopped. It is no longer killed partway through its import.

## Tests
- New: timeouts wait for the stall fuse while refusals trip the short one; the stall fuse is read from the environment; a replacement that is still starting is waited on, not killed; `probeOutcome` is tagged.
- `node --test test/{fatal-exit,gateway-restart,health-backoff,gateway-supervisor,health-probe}.test.mjs`: 45/45 pass.

title: fix(reasoning): capture JSON tool-call reasoning for replay
body:
## Problem

The Chat Completions forwarder remembers `reasoning_content` from SSE responses, but LiteLLM's Responses adapter can request a non-streaming JSON completion. On that path, a thinking model's tool call is returned successfully without its reasoning being cached. The following tool-result turn then has no exact reasoning to replay, and OpenCode Go DeepSeek rejects it.

## Change

- Observe complete JSON Chat Completions responses for models with the existing reasoning replay contract, keyed by each returned tool-call ID.
- Bound capture at 4 MiB, decode UTF-8 strictly, and skip malformed or incomplete choices. Relay response bytes unchanged and retain the upstream JSON `Content-Type`.
- Add a two-request forwarder regression proving the next tool turn receives the original reasoning, plus malformed, oversized, invalid UTF-8, and multiple-choice cases.

This is based directly on upstream `main` and does not include fleet-specific persistence or failover patches.

## Verification

- `node --test test/chat-reasoning-replay.test.mjs test/go-json-replay-forwarder.test.mjs` — 11 passed.
- `npm run check` — passed.
- A separate installed-router canary using `opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash` at max completed a tool call and returned a final answer after the corresponding local fix was deployed.

title: fix: registry BOM, Grok xhigh, native generic clients, Responses reasoning, uninstall skills
body:
## Summary

Five independent fixes, one commit each, found while triaging the open issues. They can be reverted one at a time.

- **#887 (part b): registry and `user-models.json` saved with a UTF-8 BOM** (28f7799)
  - Before: Notepad or PowerShell `Set-Content` writes a leading BOM. The registry loader then failed with `Unexpected token`, and `readUserModels` silently returned `[]`, which hid every curated model.
  - After: both loaders strip a leading BOM before `JSON.parse`.
  - Part (a) of #887, offering Low reasoning on DeepSeek V4 Pro, is **not** changed. The repo's own evidence disagrees on whether the model supports it, and DeepSeek's docs need checking first.
- **#861: `grok-api/grok-4.7` `xhigh`** (3e0220f)
  - Before: the `xai-reasoning` request profile clamped every effort outside low/medium/high to `high`, so Grok 4.7 offered `xhigh` in the picker but silently ran at `high`.
  - After: `xhigh` is kept when the model declares it; Grok 4.5 still clamps to `high`.
  - This is the one part of #878 (credit @ringomax) that `main` didn't already have.
- **#862: native requests with string `input` or `stream: false`** (6100787)
  - Scope: callers that use the router key or no auth, the same rule the existing native normalization follows.
  - A string `input` becomes one user message.
  - A request without `stream: true` is sent upstream as a stream and folded back into one JSON response by the new `src/native-buffered-response.mjs`. A failed or cut-off stream returns a 502 with the reason.
  - Codex turns are untouched. A client with its own ChatGPT credential still gets the upstream 400s.
- **#840: reasoning replayed as visible text on generic Responses routes** (b6bb8cf)
  - Before: `carryReasoningThroughInput` also ran on native `openai-responses` routes. It rewrote reasoning that came before a tool call into assistant `output_text`, and copied reasoning into the visible answer.
  - After: it runs only on Chat Completions routes.
  - Behaviour change: built-in Responses providers (Copilot, Meta) now receive reasoning items unchanged before tool calls, instead of as text.
- **`bin/uninstall`: skill removal is best effort** (30ab1ea)
  - Before: under `set -eu`, a failed `skills-install.mjs uninstall` (for example a symlinked skills root) aborted the script. The `codex` shim and the background service were left behind.
  - After: skill removal is best effort. This mirrors the install-side fix in #891.

title: Windows: gateway supervisor stalls forever after liveness-triggered restart (awaits exit of killed child with no timeout)
body:
## Summary

On Windows, the LiteLLM gateway supervisor stalled after its first liveness-triggered restart. The gateway stayed down on port 4200 until I restarted the service by hand. The router on 4202 stayed up, so every routed request failed with a 502 for more than 20 minutes. Native OpenAI models kept working because they do not go through the gateway.

- Version: `0.6.0`, `c1112001` (main, 2026-09-22)
- OS: Windows 11, Task Scheduler service
- Workload: one long Codex session on `openrouter/stealth/space-bunny-alpha`, with about 250K–400K cached tokens per request

## What the log shows (`~/.codex/codex-router/router.log`)

Requests were healthy until 13:07 UTC:

```
[codex-router] timing at=2026-09-24T13:07:11.611Z model=openrouter/stealth/space-bunny-alpha provider=openrouter status=200 total_ms=58348 ...
[codex-router] LiteLLM gateway exited (code=null, signal=null); restarting in 1000 ms (restart 1 of 5). The router stays up; requests fail with an upstream error until it answers again.
[codex-router] LiteLLM gateway stopped answering health checks (3 consecutive liveness failures); terminating the still-running process before restarting it.
[codex-router] timing at=2026-09-24T13:08:38.464Z model=openrouter/stealth/space-bunny-alpha provider=openrouter status=502 total_ms=149151 ...
[codex-router] request failed: TypeError: fetch failed <- Error: read ECONNRESET (ECONNRESET)
[codex-router] request failed: TypeError: fetch failed <- Error: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4200 (ECONNREFUSED)
... (the same ECONNREFUSED 502 on every routed request from here on)
```

After the "terminating the still-running process" line, the supervisor never logged again. There was no `is healthy again`, no `did not come back`, no `restart 2 of 5`, and no `not restarting it again`. Nothing listened on 4200. Codex showed:

```
Unexpected status 502 Bad Gateway: The local router could not complete the request: the upstream refused the connection. If this network needs an outbound proxy, set NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 ...
```

About 20 minutes later, the old `litellm.exe` and two `python.exe` processes were still alive. `node src/service.mjs restart` replaced them, and 4200 came back straight away.

For comparison, an earlier incident in the same log recovered normally (`did not come back ...`, `restart 2 of 5`, ..., `is healthy again after 5 restart(s)`). This time the loop stopped before it reached `start()`.

## Where I think it hangs

`src/gateway-supervisor.mjs`, in the `unhealthy` branch:

```js
if (outcome.kind === "unhealthy") {
  log(`${label} stopped answering health checks ...; terminating the still-running process before restarting it.`);
  if (isRunning(current)) stop(current);   // current.kill("SIGTERM")
  await waitForExit(current, label);       // no timeout, no escalation
}
```

`waitForExit` in `start.mjs` resolves only on the child's `exit` event. The last log line comes just before this `await`, and no later line appears, so the supervisor seems to be stuck here. The `exit` event for the killed child never arrived. The gateway child is the `.venv\Scripts\litellm.exe` launcher, which runs `python.exe` underneath. The hung process was the same one whose listener had already died (the WinError 64 / dead-accept-loop case the watchdog comment describes). I have not confirmed why a single `kill("SIGTERM")` did not end it. The launcher-plus-python tree is my best guess.

The other stop path (`stopChildren`) escalates to `SIGKILL` after `SIGKILL_AFTER_MS`, but the supervisor's stop path has no such escalation.

## Suggested fix

- Bound the post-stop wait in the `unhealthy` branch. Race `waitForExit` against a timeout, then escalate: `SIGKILL`, and on Windows a tree kill (`taskkill /PID <pid> /T /F`) so the python grandchild goes too.
- If the old process still cannot be confirmed dead, log that. Then either try `start()` anyway (the port bind will say whether 4200 is free) or return `exhausted: true`, so the service exits and Task Scheduler restarts everything. Either outcome is better than a silent, permanent stall. It would also keep rule 3 in the file header ("Never silent").

A regression test could use a fake child whose `kill()` does not emit `exit`, and assert that the supervisor either restarts or exhausts within a bounded time.

title: feat(failover): let a model stay selectable while opting out of automatic failover
body:
## Let a model stay selectable while opting out of automatic failover

### Contract

| `failoverCandidate` on a `user-models.json` entry | Visible in model picker | Explicit routing (by slug) | Automatic failover candidate |
|---|---|---|---|
| absent (every existing entry) | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged (yes, as today) |
| `true` | yes | yes | yes |
| `false` | **yes** | **yes** | **no** |

### Motivation
Some routes should be available when the operator picks them by hand but must never absorb other
models' traffic: for example a local or subscription-backed executor registered as a generic
provider, which may be slow, single-concurrency or best-effort. Today such a model is ranked like any
other enabled model, so a quota failure elsewhere can silently move a turn onto it.

### Previous behaviour
Every listed, enabled model is an automatic candidate for quota failover, compaction attempts and
compaction overflow. The only ways to keep one out are:
- hiding it, which also removes it from the picker;
- pinning a failover chain, which freezes every other model's failover order;
- turning failover off globally.

Generic providers are never `keyless`, so the existing "a model served from this machine is never
chosen automatically" rule does not cover them.

### New behaviour
- `rankFailoverCandidates` skips any model with `failoverCandidate: false`. The check runs before a
  named chain is applied, so an old chain entry cannot bring the model back. All three automatic
  paths (quota failover, compaction attempts, compaction overflow) go through this function.
- Picker publication, explicit routing by slug and every other code path are untouched: the field is
  read in exactly one place.

### Type validation
`modelProblem` refuses a non-boolean `failoverCandidate` with
`model <slug> has an invalid failoverCandidate`, so a typo such as `"no"` cannot silently leave a
route eligible. The entry is skipped and the reason is reported like other invalid user models.

### Backward compatibility
- Field absent: ranking is identical. A test compares absent and `true` against the current order.
- Curation already keeps existing entries byte-for-byte, so the field survives re-curation, provider
  edits, catalog refreshes and restarts (verified on a running install).
- No schema version bump. Older builds ignore the field, so the model simply stays eligible there.

### Documentation
- README, failover section: a short paragraph on opting a route out.
- `changelog.d/failover-candidate-opt-out.md` fragment; `CHANGELOG.md` is not edited.

### Tests
- `test/model-failover.test.mjs`, ranking:
  - a `failoverCandidate: false` model is never offered;
  - a named chain cannot bring it back;
  - absent and `true` rank exactly as before.
- `test/failover-candidate-registry.test.mjs` (new), registry validation, loading the registry in a
  fresh process against a temporary state directory:
  - `false` survives loading;
  - absent loads unchanged;
  - a non-boolean value is refused with a skip reason.
- Against unpatched `src/`, the three behaviour tests fail and the compatibility test passes, as
  expected.
- Both files together: 57/57 pass.

### `npm run check`
PASS (syntax checks, v2-agent applications, changelog fragments).

### Full `npm test`
Not fully green on the machine used, and neither is `main` on that same machine, so the result is
reported against a `main` baseline run there:

| | tests | pass | fail | cancelled | skipped |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `main` (baseline) | 4659 | 4619 | 5 | 1 | 34 |
| this branch | 4665 | 4556 | 2 | 73 | 34 |

- The +6 tests are the new ones, and all pass.
- **Failures:** none of the failing or cancelled tests touch failover or the model registry. They are
  environment-dependent:
  - real installed `codex-cli` app-server versions;
  - guided-setup dependency installation;
  - `control-center-electron.test.mjs`, which cancels in cascade with "event loop has already
    resolved".
- **The branch-only cancellations are that one Electron file.** Re-run in isolation it passed 75/75
  on this branch, and on `main` the same isolated file cancelled 72, so it is flaky on both sides.

No merge requested: happy to adjust naming (e.g. a provider-level default) if you prefer a different
shape.

title: fix(routing): open the message envelope on every Chat Completions route
body:
## Summary

On codex-cli 0.156.1, routed OpenRouter turns log `ERROR codex_core::util: OutputTextDelta without active item`. Reproduced live on `openrouter/mimo-v2.6-flash` and `openrouter/stealth/space-bunny-alpha`.

**What the router relayed:** I captured the stream between Codex and the live router with a loopback tap. For the answer turn that follows a tool call, the reasoning item opens and closes correctly at `output_index` 0. The assistant's `response.output_text.delta` events then arrive:
- for the message item `gen-…`,
- still at `output_index` 0,
- with no `response.output_item.added` and no `response.content_part.added` before them.

The part then closes as `reasoning_text`. Codex logs one error per delta. In the tool-call turn, a message that was never opened is also closed at index 0 after the `function_call`.

**Where it comes from:** the LiteLLM bridge itself. I drove the pinned LiteLLM offline with a synthetic OpenAI-compatible stream (reasoning chunks, then content). `litellm.aresponses(..., use_chat_completions_api=True, stream=True)` emits exactly this shape whether the reasoning arrives as `reasoning` or as `reasoning_content`. No provider quota is involved, so any Chat Completions route whose reply starts with reasoning is affected.

**The fix:** `src/zai-responses-compat.mjs` already repairs this exact shape (AGENTS.md, gateway section, item 9), but only for Z.ai.
- A new `messageEnvelopeCompatTransform(provider, contentType)` attaches that repair to every `protocol: "openai"` (default) route.
- Excluded, as the reasoning-summary repair already does: direct `deepseek` (it has its own bridge repair), `openai-responses` providers (they skip the bridge) and native traffic (no route).
- Anthropic Messages routes are also excluded: they arrive message-first and I have no capture showing this shape there.
- The old Z.ai-only factory, and the second `zai-coding` branch in `router.mjs`, are gone.

**Hardening needed before widening it.** The full suite caught the first problem.
- Framing is now byte-level. The old `StringDecoder` framing rewrote invalid UTF-8 to U+FFFD, which broke "router response pipelines preserve ambiguous provider bytes exactly" once the stage ran on generic routes. Unchanged blocks are now relayed as the original bytes. A frame that is not valid UTF-8 turns rewriting off for the rest of the response. This is the same rule the item-lifecycle normalizer follows.
- Content parts of an item that was opened as something other than a message are never adopted as a message envelope.

**Why not in `item-lifecycle-normalizer.mjs`:** that stage is reorder-only by contract ("blocks pass through byte-for-byte; only their order changes"). The problem here is a missing envelope, not an ordering problem, and the repo already had a dedicated repair for it.

**Known, unchanged:** on a tool-call turn, LiteLLM still closes an empty message after the `function_call`. The router relayed it before this change too, as a bare `done` labelled `final_answer`. It is now a complete, well-formed item at the next index. Dropping it would be a separate change.

## Verification

- **Live oracle:** I ran a worktree router on a spare port beside the live service, using the live gateway and forwarders, with the same `codex exec` repro. `OutputTextDelta without active item` count: **2 → 0** on `openrouter/mimo-v2.6-flash` and **0** on `openrouter/stealth/space-bunny-alpha`. Answers `MIMO-OK PAPAYA` / `BUNNY-OK PAPAYA`. I re-ran mimo after the byte-framing change: still 0.
- In the relayed streams, the message now opens with `output_item.added` + `content_part.added` at `output_index` 1, after reasoning at 0. In tool turns it opens at 2, after the call at 1.
- New router test, "router gives OpenRouter Chat Completions text a message envelope after reasoning". It uses the pinned-LiteLLM shapes for the answer turn and the tool turn, and checks that every text/part event belongs to an item opened at its own index. **It fails without the `src/` change** with `response.output_text.delta without an active item`.
- New unit tests: factory scope, the live OpenRouter shape, invalid UTF-8 relayed byte-exact, other items' content parts not adopted.
- `npm run check`: passes.
- `npm test`: 4607 pass, 6 fail. All six fail identically on unmodified `origin/main` on this machine:
  - `desktop-panel`: Playwright is not installed.
  - two `login-free-app-server` "preserved custom provider" cases, and "real Codex app-server completes signed-out turns…".
  - two `setup-node-deps` guided-setup cases.

## Changelog

`changelog.d/chat-message-envelope-repair.md`

title: fix(grok): carry xAI encrypted reasoning through the OAuth tool loop
body:
Fixes #888. Supersedes #889 — **the fix is @JamesTsai0128's work**, carried here unchanged with their commits and authorship intact. This branch only adds what `main` started requiring after #889 was opened.

## Why a second pull request

#889 reports CONFLICTING on github.com. The two sides overlap on exactly two files:

| File | Overlap |
|---|---|
| `src/grok-oauth-forwarder.mjs` | none — `main` never touched it |
| `AGENTS.md` | three-way merges clean |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | **the whole conflict** |

`.gitattributes` carries `CHANGELOG.md merge=union`, which resolves locally and does nothing on GitHub's server-side merge — the exact failure [changelog.d/README.md](../blob/main/changelog.d/README.md) was added to `main` to end. So #889 merged clean on a maintainer's machine while GitHub refused it, and every merge to `main` re-conflicted it.

This branch is #889's commits merged onto current `main`, with the `CHANGELOG.md` bullet moved to `changelog.d/grok-reasoning-carry.md` verbatim. The source diff is byte-identical to #889.

## The bug

xAI returns each turn's reasoning as an opaque `reasoning` item with `encrypted_content`. Grok 4.7 keeps reasoning through a tool loop only when that item comes back in the next request. On `grok-oauth/*` the request crosses a Chat Completions hop (LiteLLM → `grok-oauth-forwarder`) that cannot carry it, and `toResponsesRequest` sent no reasoning history at all. Grok 4.7 stopped reasoning from about the third tool round even at `xhigh`, planned in visible text, and in long loops could repeat one progress sentence until interrupted.

## The change

- `src/grok-reasoning-carry.mjs`: bounded in-memory store (4,096 entries, 6 h TTL, LRU), keyed by conversation id, first tool call id, and model.
- `toResponsesRequest` takes `recallReasoning(callIds)`, places recalled items in front of the turn that produced them, and sets `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]`.
- Only completed responses are remembered; a miss sends no reasoning, exactly as before.
- `CODEX_ROUTER_GROK_REASONING_CARRY=0` disables it. `/health` reports `reasoningCarry` stats.

## Verification on this branch

- `test/grok-reasoning-carry.test.mjs`: 4/4 pass.
- All `grok*` + `*forwarder*` test files: **315/315 pass**.
- `npm run check`: passes, fragments valid (8).
- Full suite: **4609/4646 pass**. The failures are `desktop-panel` (playwright absent) and two `codex-cli … preserved custom provider` cases, all of which reproduce identically on unmodified `main` on the same machine.

**Negative control** — `main`'s `src/grok-oauth-forwarder.mjs` with only the new store module added, so just the forwarder wiring is missing:

```
✔ store keeps only certified encrypted reasoning, keyed by session and first call
✔ store scope includes the model, so another Grok model never receives the reasoning
✖ toResponsesRequest puts carried reasoning in front of the turn that produced it
✖ forwarder returns xAI's encrypted reasoning on the next tool-loop request
```

Both behavioral tests fail without the forwarder change and pass with it, so this reproduces #888 rather than passing either way.

## What is not verified here

These are mock-xAI tests. They prove the encrypted item is sent back on the next request; they do not prove Grok 4.7's reasoning survives 20+ rounds against the live API. That rests on @JamesTsai0128's live A/B in #888 (24/24 steps reasoned with the item carried, 0/18 from step 3 without, summary-only no better), which has not been independently re-run here.

title: fix(search): retain operation timeout until sidecar settles
body:
## Problem
`AbortSignal.timeout()` uses an unreferenced timer. If a search-sidecar provider adapter never settles and there are no other active event-loop handles, Node exits before that timer fires and before the pending operation delivers its prescribed `search_sidecar_timeout` error. On Windows Node 22, the existing `retry policy is bounded by one operation deadline and cancellation` regression was independently reproducible as `cancelledByParent` / `Promise resolution is still pending but the event loop has already resolved`.

## Fix
Use a referenced, bounded timeout backed by an `AbortController` for each provider attempt and retry delay. Release each timer when the relevant attempt or retry finishes. Existing parent-signal cancellation behavior and overall operation deadline remain unchanged. Includes the required changelog fragment.

## Verification
- Isolated regression before patch: 6 passed, 1 cancelled.
- Isolated regression after patch: 7 passed, 0 failed/cancelled.
- Related search files (`search-sidecar`, `search-sidecar-control`, `search-capability`, `chat-wire-search-history`): **26 passed, 0 failed/cancelled**.

title: fix(ci): install router runtime dependencies for packaged Electron smoke

title: fix(images): bound compaction's image payload and resend on provider refusal
body:
## Problem

A screenshot-heavy session on `openrouter/stealth/space-bunny-alpha` stalled for good with:

```
unexpected status 413 Payload Too Large: openrouter rejected the request ... (HTTP 413: Downloaded image content cannot exceed 30MB)
```

The usage ledger shows the cause. Turns up to 405 were bounded normally (31 images seen, 9 dropped, 10.9MB saved). At ~858k estimated tokens Codex auto-compacted, and every attempt from 406 on was a 413 with **no image stats at all** plus `toolResultsShaped` — i.e. the compaction path. `summarize()` aged and RTK-shaped tool results but never ran `boundImagePayload`, so the summary request carried all ~31MB of screenshots. Codex retries compaction before every following turn, so the session could never take another turn. (The original budget commit 19b7b096 explicitly left compaction unbounded.)

## Fix

1. **One reduction step for every provider-bound request.** `prepareProviderInput()` runs tool-result aging and the image budget together; routed turns, failover hops and compaction all go through it, so a path can no longer skip the budget.
2. **Resend on refusal.** The 20MB budget is a measurement, not the provider's contract. A 400/413 whose body names image content (`isImagePayloadRejection`) is answered by resending the same model the same request with half the image payload, oldest first, up to twice (`tighterImageBudget`), keeping the newest two images. Applies to turns and compaction; each resend is logged (not QUIET-gated). A refusal that can shed nothing more is surfaced unchanged.

Native ChatGPT traffic is unchanged.

## Tests

- `prompt-image-budget.test.mjs`: rejection classifier (OpenRouter wording, too-many-images, per-image cap; negatives for the router's own 413, unsupported-image 400, 429), halving until only the protected newest remain, zero-token routes.
- `routing.test.mjs`: compaction bounds 40 images to 32 + 8 receipts and meters them (fails on main: all 40 forwarded); a mock gateway refusing >5 images with OpenRouter's 413 is retried `[10, 5]` → 200 on both `/responses` and `/responses/compact`.
- Local: routing, prompt-image-budget, compaction-checkpoint, compaction-limit, tool-result-aging, usage-events all green; `npm run check` green. `model-failover-router` timed out on child `/health` waits locally under a load average of ~190–260 — relying on CI for that file.

title: Fix compaction against generic OpenAI-Responses gateways that reject non-streaming requests
body:
## Summary

With a generic OpenAI-Responses provider (custom `--base-url`, `--adapter openai-responses`), every auto-compact eventually failed with:

```
HTTP 400: Stream must be set to true
```

`summarizeWith()` sent the compaction summarizer with `stream: false`. Some Codex-LB style gateways reject non-streaming requests outright. Because compaction reruns before each following turn once the context is full, the session wedges: every turn re-fails until the thread is abandoned.

Changes in `src/router.mjs`:

- Compaction streams **only for generic providers** (`providerForModel(route)?.generic === true`). Every other route keeps the plain non-streaming call it already worked with — no behavior change for built-in providers.
- New `responsesSseToResponse()` unwraps the terminal `response.completed` event into the same shape the non-streaming path parsed, so text extraction and usage metering are unchanged. It follows real SSE framing: multi-line `data:` payloads joined with `\n`, CRLF tolerated, comment/id/retry lines ignored.
- Gateways that end the stream without a terminal event: the answer is rebuilt from accumulated `response.output_text.delta` text plus the last-seen usage. Verified live against such a gateway — a real ~258K-token compaction streamed for 443s and completed `200` with 401 output tokens.
- A `response.failed` / `response.incomplete` terminal — or a later `completed` after one — poisons the attempt: no delta fallback, and the caller classifies it as a failed attempt (status 502) so it flows through the existing failed path: `failed[]` metering, image-rejection retries, `gatewayErrorStatus`, `classifyRoutedFailure`, provider cooldowns, and context-length failover — instead of a hard short-circuit.

Plus the changelog fragment (`changelog.d/generic-compaction-streaming.md`); `CHANGELOG.md` untouched.

## Verification

- `npm run check` → syntax checks passed, v2-agent applications valid, changelog fragments valid
- `node --test test/compaction-checkpoint.test.mjs test/compaction-limit.test.mjs` → 34/34 pass
- `npm test` (full suite) → [runs locally; results noted in comments]
- Live end-to-end against a gateway that rejects non-streaming requests: compaction previously died with 400 on the first attempt; with this change it streamed to completion (443s, 200, 401 output tokens)
- Two rounds of adversarial review on the diff (SSE framing edge cases, usage metering, failure/failover classification, scoping) — all findings addressed

## Changelog

Fragment added: `changelog.d/generic-compaction-streaming.md` (validated by `npm run check`).

title: fix: deliver Azure Sol subagent tasks to curated Luna
body:
## Summary

Azure KMAMC Responses could return a Fernet-shaped opaque `spawn_agent.message`. A native Luna child cannot decrypt an Azure-origin value, and the router's routed-child native relay could return 502 (`Native collaboration payload relay omitted the task payload`) before the child ran any tool.

For the Azure KMAMC Responses route only, this change removes Codex's private `encrypted` annotation from the `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, and `followup_task` schemas. It aliases the configured `collaboration` namespace to Azure's accepted `agents` namespace on the provider-bound declaration, matching history and tool choice, then restores Codex's namespace on the response. A completed call gets the empty plaintext marker only for a nonempty JSON string message that is not Fernet-shaped. An omitted Azure spawn model remains absent so Codex's configured curated Luna default wins. Other provider/tool schemas retain their prior treatment. The branch also includes Azure image-generation tool filtering, which is absent from current `main` and needed at the same request boundary.

The repair originated in local commits `70dc75f5` and `63755b9c`; `f3c1c295` adds the changelog fragment and `18d7d1a1` integrates current upstream `main`.

## Reproduction

1. Configure the router's Azure KMAMC Responses route and Codex `features.multi_agent_v2.tool_namespace = "collaboration"`; select `azure-kmamc/gpt-6-luna` / Max as the default subagent. Do not place credentials in command arguments or the PR.
2. On the pre-fix router, start a fresh `azure-kmamc/gpt-6-sol` Medium session and ask it to spawn a Luna Max child that calls a harmless shell command and returns a unique marker. The child fails before its shell call with `Encrypted function output content could not be decrypted or decoded`, or the routed-child relay reports the omitted-task 502.
3. On this repair, repeat in a fresh session. Inspect the parent `collaboration.spawn_agent` call for `encrypted_function_args: []`; inspect the child's own rollout for `input_text`, effective Azure Luna/Max identity, a real shell call, and the returned marker. Named roles, omitted-model default, two overlapping children, Azure-to-Azure, and native-Sol-to-curated-Luna controls were exercised during the local repair.

## Verification

- Original repair at `63755b9`: Azure compatibility and namespace relay tests **141/141**; encrypted-relay and compaction regression cases **2/2**.
- After integrating upstream `9fb6440d` at `18d7d1a1`: updated focused tests **142/142**, relay/compaction cases **2/2**, `npm run check` passed (syntax and 18 changelog fragments), `git diff --check` passed. The only merge overlap was the insertion beside upstream's DeepSeek forced-tool handling; both paths were retained.
- Fresh CLI Azure Sol Medium -> configured `verifier` ran `azure-kmamc/gpt-6-luna` Max and executed a shell tool. A fresh read-only-parent control selected the same child under an effective read-only sandbox; a disposable write attempt was denied. The verifier role's read-only setting alone did **not** override a writable parent sandbox. These are local runtime observations, not a claim of long-duration reliability or fresh live execution of the post-merge commit.
- Full `npm test` on this Windows host is **not green or complete**: an earlier attempt was interrupted after at least 2,736 tests and 87 reported failures, 67 of them `cancelledByParent`. Three Antigravity assertions pass individually; POSIX `sh -n` fails individually because `sh` is unavailable here. An unrelated profile-switch test times out even alone (20-second focused and 120-second file runs), and its test/source files are unchanged from upstream. These examples do not classify every failure. Please use CI to assess the final integrated branch; do not infer a green full suite from the focused results.

## Security / review notes

No credential store, caller key, authorization header, or user configuration is changed in this PR. The existing forwarder strips caller `authorization`/`x-api-key` and supplies only the selected provider credential. Plaintext child-task text necessarily reaches the Azure endpoint and local Codex runtime records; it must not contain secrets. The empty marker plus restored `collaboration` identity uses the current Codex structured plaintext dispatch/redaction path. The Fernet-shaped exclusion matches the observed opaque format, not a general authenticated issuer-provenance guarantee; arbitrary configured namespaces require a separate Codex-side dispatch change. No ciphertext or credential is included in this PR.
