title: fix(responses): preserve UTF-8 across non-streaming chunks
body:
## Summary

Non-streaming Responses decoded each HTTP chunk independently. Splitting the UTF-8 bytes of `Çağrı` could return `��ağrı`; the same corruption could affect JSON-encoded tool arguments and metadata.

Use an incremental UTF-8 decoder and flush it at EOF before parsing. Keep the existing response validation, usage fields, and namespace restoration.

## Verification

- `npm run check` — passed.
- Focused adapter, namespace, generic routing, DeepSeek Responses, and forwarder diagnostics suites — 189 passed.
- The new regression fails on unchanged `main` and passes across every two-chunk byte split and one-byte chunks, covering two-, three-, and four-byte characters.
- Full root suite (`node --test --test-timeout=600000 --test-concurrency=2 test/*.test.mjs`, with inherited proxy settings cleared) — 5,273 passed, 42 skipped, 5 failed. All five failures reproduce on unchanged `main`: the durable login-lease fixture, Linux GUI lifecycle verification, and three Vertex discovery cases blocked by provider-host DNS.

- GitHub CI: Ubuntu and macOS root tests, Electron tests on Linux and Windows, and Homebrew formula validation passed ([run](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/38518174981)). The remaining Windows root and native macOS jobs are still running.

## Changelog

`changelog.d/responses-json-utf8.md`

title: fix(claude): abort Responses requests when clients disconnect
body:
## Summary

Claude Code cancellation after the request body finished did not abort the canonical Responses request. The handler only listened for the request body's `aborted` event, so an upstream generation could continue after the client disconnected.

Abort on an unfinished response connection's `close` event, handle an already-disconnected caller before fetching, and remove both cancellation listeners after handling the response. Avoid writing an error to a destroyed connection.

## Verification

- `npm run check` — passed.
- Final Claude surface/cancellation, launcher/configuration, agent bridge, and HTTP resilience suites — 27 passed.
- All three cancellation regressions fail on unchanged `main`: before upstream headers, during a JSON body, and during an SSE body. With the fix, the upstream socket closes and the handler releases its listeners.
- Normal JSON and SSE completion controls retain their answer and terminal behavior.
- Full root suite (`node --test --test-timeout=600000 --test-concurrency=2 test/*.test.mjs`) — 5,270 passed, 42 skipped, 12 failed. The same 12 failures occur on unchanged `main` in this environment: login-lease/GUI lifecycle, inherited proxy fixtures, and Vertex DNS. The proxy baseline fixtures pass when the inherited proxy opt-in is cleared.

- GitHub CI: Ubuntu root tests, Electron tests on Linux and Windows, and Homebrew formula validation passed ([run](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/38518177451)). The remaining platform jobs are still running.

## Changelog

`changelog.d/claude-client-cancellation.md`

title: fix(usage): apply billed-token fallback before merging retries
body:
## Summary

When one retry attempt omitted a billed token component, `mergeTokenUsage` counted that attempt as zero for the component. For example, an attempt reporting 100 input tokens plus an attempt reporting 250 billed input tokens became 250 instead of 350, although the provider aggregate counts the same attempts separately as 350.

Apply billed-to-raw fallback to each attempt before adding. Preserve explicit billed zeroes, leave billed fields absent when neither attempt reports them, and retain the raw usage totals.

## Verification

- `npm run check` — passed.
- Usage, provider totals, hourly events, Control Center usage, and routing suites — 261 passed.
- Final usage/provider unit suites — 72 passed.
- The new aggregate regression fails on unchanged `main`. It checks both attempt orders, input/output partial billing, explicit zeroes, fully billed/raw controls, repeated merges, provider/model totals, daily buckets, and the rolling total.
- Full root suite (`node --test --test-timeout=600000 --test-concurrency=2 test/*.test.mjs`) — 5,265 passed, 42 skipped, 13 failed. Twelve failures also occur on unchanged `main` in this environment (login-lease/GUI lifecycle, inherited proxy fixtures, and Vertex DNS). The additional Grok one-line retry fixture passed on isolated rerun and in the complete Grok forwarder rerun — 72 passed.

- GitHub CI: Ubuntu root tests, Electron tests on Linux and Windows, and Homebrew formula validation passed ([run](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/38518181117)); the separate Grok apply_patch protocol workflow also passed. title: fix(qwen): preserve checkpoint state and scope final guidance
body:
Spark Default missed the Qwen checkpoint adapter because eligibility recognized only the concrete Qwen slug. Valid checkpoints followed by restored content also missed continuation guidance. Both omissions could discard useful file findings, prior fixes, and dependencies from the intended handoff behavior.

Both explicitly scoped Qwen aliases now adapt canonical local compaction into a nine-section working-state ledger, recognize checkpoints before restored content, and receive ordinary-turn guidance for self-contained final answers with concrete changes, verification, and genuine remaining actions. Continuation follows the latest actual request and distinguishes recorded evidence from fresh verification. Custom compact prompts, enforced nontext formats, remote compaction, unrelated routes, and original input order retain their existing contracts.

The prompt extracts recorded state rather than solving the task again. Public Codex, Qwen Code, and archived Claude references and license notices are recorded in `config/qwen-compaction/PROVENANCE.md`. Synthetic fixtures and an opt-in local evaluator are included.

Validation:

- [x] 23 adapter and mocked-router tests covering both aliases, released `post_turn` metadata, restored/multipart input, format boundaries, immutability, and failover scoping.
- [x] 17 evaluator/scorer/transport tests; without optional local Python, 15 pass and two explicitly skip. Windows shell transport is explicitly unverified.
- [x] `npm run check` and whitespace checks.
- [x] Adjacent router/reasoning/failover suites: 58 passed; one optional pinned LiteLLM check skipped.
- [x] Independent compatibility against a private copy of an older router: 34 adapter/reasoning tests and 13 synthetic wire cases on both older and fresh source.
- [x] Local model completed two valid candidate compactions, retaining all ten file topics and earlier fixes in one synthetic history.
- [x] Completed-task and explicit open-item controls produced substantive answers with evidence, owners, and dependencies. These controls used the prior continuation block; final-response guidance is unchanged.
- [ ] Generic status/recap acceptance: **failed**. The exact request "Give me the current result and remaining work." repeatedly produced only a promise to verify disk, including a controlled replay changing only continuation guidance. Normal termination below the output cap rules out truncation for that specific failure.
- [x] Surgical activation on the older installed router preserved unrelated changes, replaced the listener, and returned healthy. Exact six runtime hashes matched the reviewed candidate.
- [x] Two synthetic HTTP requests through the installed Spark Default route completed: canonical nine-section compaction retained the corrected fictional path and passed-versus-unrun evidence; resumed final returned the requested marker, path, 4/4 tests, browser not run, and no invented follow-up. These requests do not constitute real Codex app end-to-end retention proof.

This remains a draft because general recap reliability is unresolved. The deterministic integration fixes and bounded guidance have independent source/compatibility acceptance; the failed recap criterion is not accepted as fixed.

Evaluation inherits server sampling defaults with medium effort and bounded test output allowances. Candidate checkpoints still showed redundant content, status/verification wording errors, an inferred path, and role-attribution drift. Baseline extraction exhausted its allowance, so no valid paired retention score or quantitative improvement is claimed. There is no claim of lossless memory, general long-context reliability, or Codex/Claude-equivalent quality. Full unrelated repository tests and Windows shell transport were not run.

title: Fix ChatGPT logins for distinct users sharing a workspace
body:
## Summary

Adding a second ChatGPT user from the same workspace fails login finalization because the router treats `tokens.account_id` as the whole login identity. The workspace ID can be shared by distinct users.

Track an optional user ID from the existing ID token alongside the workspace ID. Apply that identity consistently during discovery, completed-login recovery, switching, crash recovery, removal checks, and usage selection. Existing profiles and transaction journals without a user ID remain supported, and duplicate logins for the same user remain rejected. Model catalog refresh also refuses publication when the bearer session changes during the request.

No new dependencies or changes to OAuth credentials, login flow, routing headers, or UI copy.

## Verification

- New shared-workspace regression reproduced the identity-conflict failure before the fix.
- Focused account/profile/usage/catalog/desktop-panel suites: 114 passed, 1 skipped (Windows-only ACL test).
- `npm run check`: passed.
- Live local recovery: three distinct saved users report usable; original active selection and all credential bytes unchanged. Control panel shows all three Ready and no conflict banner.
- `npm test`: full suite is not green in this local environment. The signed-out real Codex app-server integration (`requests.length` is 2 rather than 1 for preserved custom providers) and two Vertex catalog/discovery assertions also fail when run from an untouched archive of upstream `8c5c1288`. The complete account/profile/usage/catalog/desktop-panel subset above passes after the final changes.
- `git diff --check`: passed.
- Independent review: identity attribution and legacy recovery findings addressed and re-reviewed.

## Changelog

Added `changelog.d/chatgpt-workspace-user-identity.md`.

title: Fix Grok tools, discovery, completion and request accounting
body:
Grok tool calls could lose arguments and schema constraints across the Responses/Chat bridge, and completed turns could trigger unnecessary recovery. This PR repairs those boundaries while keeping execution, approvals, and file validation in the client.

## Resulting behavior

- Preserve complete tool schemas, alternative operations, namespace identities, collisions, forced choices, discovery, and argument history. Grok gets typed patches and whole-line replacements; negotiated patch hooks retain the original arguments.
- Give current structured patches and legacy native-patch history separate provider identities. History retains exact bytes, call IDs, and results but is not callable. Preserve original client permissions in the tool reference.
- Emit initial tool-argument prefixes and only consistent terminal suffixes. Conflicting snapshots fail closed; malformed arguments are not repaired or replayed after output is committed. Facade schemas and compilers share their character/size/numeric constraints, and errors report only fixed tool/category labels.
- Accept successful finals in one generation; remove speculative progress-only recovery. Preserve valid tool-search actions and caller-owned app tools. Caller reasoning, service tier, output limits, and explicit parallel-tool policy survive the bridge.
- Separate estimated current context from cumulative billing, retain the required usage shape, and add bounded request-stage/tool-schema diagnostics. Context and compaction thresholds remain unchanged.
- Isolate native subagent relay headers and require one unambiguous payload after a successful terminal. Give compaction its own summarization instruction authority while retaining original instructions as quoted context.
- Fix atomic PID readiness publication in nested process tests. Add safe native Control Center launch-stage diagnostics for the still-unexplained macOS lifecycle timeout.

- Fix Node 24.22 skill publication by copying absent children under the exclusively claimed root. Preserve concurrent files across same-content conflicts and interrupted refreshes; fresh ownership generations and durable revocation prevent recovery from deleting conflicted replacements.

## Current verification

Current head: **7d63ba2e**, including current main **4f2774ca**. Merge conflicts are resolved; merge remains with the maintainer. The final full local Node 24.22 run passes: **5,987 passed, 64 skipped, zero failures**; `npm run check` passes. Remote CI has completed on this exact head: **16 successful checks, 2 intentional skips, zero failures**. Full tests pass on Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows; all Grok protocol jobs and the native macOS build pass.

- New opt-in `patch-feedback-v2` returns recognized invalid structured-patch arguments through a **denial-only native PreToolUse hook**. Valid operations compile into an ordinary native patch and retain the client's existing permission checks. The hook never returns `allow` or `updatedInput`, reads project files, or executes edits.
- The original upstream argument bytes and call IDs survive failed-call history. Unicode/size limits and transport contradictions still fail closed. No JSON repair, hidden generation, fabricated tool output, or replay of executed tools was added. The v1 serializer and v2 feedback have separate persistent opt-ins; activating v2 cannot activate v1 in old clients.
- Deterministic Router → locked LiteLLM → Grok forwarder → mock xAI → actual Codex checks pass: invalid encoded operations → native denial → corrected patch → final; absent/untrusted/changed hooks; outside-workspace denial under `never` and `on-request`; disconnect and duplicate completion without double application. Both Codex CLI 0.159.0 and the installed Desktop binary 0.164.0-alpha.11.1 pass. Codex 0.159 rejects retired `untrusted` approval policy before a turn; that case is not verified.
- The no-feedback negative control makes six transport attempts and fails; v2 completes the three scripted responses. This proves client feedback behavior, not a live Grok quality or latency improvement. No live provider generations were used.
- The full local suite passes on Node 24.22 with an isolated lockfile dependency tree. The macOS AirPlay fixture collision is fixed without changing runtime or timeouts; its **12 focused tests pass on both Node 24.22 and Node 26.7**. Compaction assertions locate the preserved call ID rather than assuming its position after instruction replay.
- Independent protocol review found and fixed a WebSocket capability downgrade and missing CI path filters. Separate activation flags and their cross-platform service rendering were also reviewed. No remaining blocking findings from that review.
- Local composite **bb3769b7** retains #1040 and the user's unrelated changes. The protected two-file v2 hook is installed and trusted by the Desktop app-server, Router was restarted with v2 enabled/v1 disabled, and core doctor checks pass. Existing Desktop children may retain the old endpoint; a full user-controlled Codex restart and fresh Grok chat are still needed for organic acceptance.
- Fresh GitHub Codex review and one retry both failed inside the review service with `An unknown error occurred` ([first attempt](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/pull/1031#issuecomment-6420986901), [retry](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/pull/1031#issuecomment-6421168891)). Neither attempt published new review findings or a completed review. GitHub Codex review remains blocked by that service failure; independent review, local protocol proof, and green CI are not a GitHub Codex approval. No additional retry or merge was performed.

## Evidence limits

The October 26 organic failure was `operations_invalid_json` in all three original upstream snapshots before local conversion. V2 changes how this validation failure returns to the client; it does not claim to prevent malformed upstream output or cover every facade argument error.

The two October 21 `invalid function relay arguments done` incidents completed upstream in one attempt and failed during local restoration. Retained logs do not contain the offending tool identity/arguments, so their exact cause is unproven. The new diagnostics make subsequent failures attributable without capturing their contents.

The previously authorized eight-call synthetic patch experiment produced **4/4 valid baseline and 4/4 valid candidate** results; it did not reproduce the incidents or demonstrate a lower organic failure rate. No additional live generations were used for this update. Earlier compaction and quality samples do not establish a general speedup or universal loop freedom.

Methodology and boundaries: [argument contracts](docs/grok-argument-contract-validation.md), [relay and compaction](docs/grok-relay-compaction-validation.md), [request diagnostics](docs/grok-request-diagnostics.md), [client edit scheduling](docs/codex-edit-concurrency.md), [earlier quality campaign](docs/grok-agent-loop-quality.md).

A Router restart loads server changes; the new v2 endpoint and trusted hook also require a fresh client process. Context settings remain unchanged. Local installation/health, CI, review, and merge are separate acceptance states.

title: fix(router): preserve local GLM reasoning effort
body:
## Summary

Local GLM routes can show low/high/max in the picker while every choice reaches the model as high. The selection can be stripped by the keyless-provider workaround or LiteLLM's filter for custom OpenAI model names; structured effort values from the Responses bridge also fall back to high in the GLM adapter.

Restrict removal to the actual keyless Ollama transport, carry selected GLM effort through LiteLLM's supported `extra_body` channel, and extract structured effort before applying GLM's declared ladder. The carry runs after subagent overrides and preserves other extension fields. It excludes native Responses, single-level GLM, other profiles, and Ollama. Existing effort clamps and omitted-effort defaults are unchanged.

## Verification

- [x] Reproduced effort loss with failing regressions and isolated router → locked LiteLLM → forwarder → mock upstream captures.
- [x] Independent review of the complete four-file diff.
- [x] Final focused regressions and `npm run check`; changelog validation passes.
- [x] Clean generated-config full-plane checks pass on locked LiteLLM 1.96.2 and an isolated production-source copy with LiteLLM 1.96.0: nine mock requests per version. Low/high/max arrive unchanged; medium maps to low; omission keeps high; tool IDs, results, reasoning separation, extension fields and subagent precedence survive.
- [x] A genuine six-case isolated Responses smoke passed six client requests and six upstream attempts with no retries: low/high/max wire effort, exact markers, terminal SSE, tool selection, and call-ID-preserving continuation all passed. The artifact SHA256 is `0ce319b9f2003f275e9c6c650b9b2c93595e79112976e953c6ae6b8e0bf3c256`.
- [x] The persisted independent-review receipt verifies the frozen v3 smoke, promotion, and production-verification source hashes and original 51/51 model-free result.
- [x] Production publication completed with journal phase `promoted` and forward state `ALL_POST`; bounded production verification passed 6/6, preservation passed, and final hardware health passed.
- [ ] All 407 stock test files completed with six CPU workers and the optional pinned-LiteLLM tests enabled: 5,413 tests, 5,371 passed, 6 failed, and 36 skipped in about 542 seconds (exit 1). Three timing or observation failures passed focused reruns: pinned reasoning replay, Electron SIGTERM cleanup, and deadline abort propagation. The signed-out app-server parent plus two preserved-provider subtests account for the other three reported failures; both root-openai fallback subtests passed. The preserved-provider case reproduced for both installed Codex builds: each made two WebSocket upgrades where the test expects one, while still producing one routed request. The relevant tests and dependency paths are unchanged, and focused triage found no direct dependency on the GLM hunks; the full suite is not green.

## Live GLM qualification

The authorized hardware transaction activated the pinned GLM root at `2026-10-18T04:08:31Z` with alias `glm-5.3-flash` and context 500000. One distributed peer failure during startup recovered through automatic container restarts. The preserved Qwen containers remain stopped and available for rollback.

The reviewed production-source copy with installed LiteLLM 1.96.0 passed the complete six-case isolated v3 transport smoke. Low/high/max arrived unchanged on the upstream wire, non-streaming markers matched exactly, the streaming marker completed with its terminal event, and tool continuation replayed the same stable call ID. Zero exposed reasoning on the two structurally valid tool cases is accepted; all four marker cases exposed positive separate reasoning in this run. Earlier failed smoke artifacts remain preserved.

Publication attempts 3 through 5 failed closed on a Hermes YAML parser false positive and then API-indirection ownership mismatch. Two reviewed helpers reconciled only those internal config bytes with private backups: five model keys were quoted without value loss, and one `api` scalar was normalized from an environment reference to the same managed endpoint already proven equal across config, marker, current-secret derivation, and `.env`. No source or ownership guard was bypassed.

Publication attempt 6 succeeded with forward state `ALL_POST`. The authorized router restart ran; Codex and Remote were not restarted at that publication boundary. Fresh router health was healthy with no degraded components, and installed source hashes match the reviewed postimages. The production verifier passed six sent and six completed cases with no retries, exact markers, terminal streaming, tools, same-ID continuation, and positive separate reasoning on all marker cases. Its `observed_upstream_effort` field is false, so the isolated smoke above remains the wire-effort evidence.

The final pre-restart preservation audit verified all 16 baseline entries, 15 protected dirty files, the two approved source postimages, unchanged install HEAD `b1ead7bcb09650b43e375c312daa6788390be131`, and original Codex PIDs 6474 and 56037 with their start times preserved. Final hardware health found both exact GLM candidate IDs running with unchanged restart counts 3/4 and start times, neither restarting nor OOM-killed, preserved Qwen IDs stopped, correct raw GLM identity and 500000 context, and explicit vLLM running/waiting counters `0/0` after production verification.

The frozen GLM-high raw run used the same fixture manifest and token caps as the earlier Qwen-medium and GLM-low runs. It made 16 requests without retries and passed 15/16, improving on low's failures in cases 2, 9, and 11. Case 6 omitted the actual ready URL and literal `open` and changed the required literal resume wording, while preserving the human owner, approval requirement, no-agent-tool boundary, and a resume instruction. Case 10 passed from the checkpoint generated by successful case 9; its frozen-fallback annotation is incorrect because of generic dependency bookkeeping, and the immutable artifact remains preserved with the discrepancy disclosed.

Observed end-to-end completion-token rates were Qwen medium 14.304 tokens/s serial and 60.143 tokens/s across four streams, GLM low 18.480 and 37.282, and GLM high 11.668 and 23.875. High used 1375 completion tokens over 117.843 seconds for serial cases 1-12 and 414 over 17.340 seconds for parallel cases 13-16; its per-case median was 14.157 with a 1.043-25.698 range. Valid quality-failed responses remain included. Completion tokens include reasoning, and full-response timing includes queueing, prefill, decode, and network. Two other requests were running before high, so these are uncontrolled single-run observations, not isolated decode throughput or a speed ranking. The frozen fixture caps match and model/effort profiles differ; cache/load and concurrent traffic were not controlled.

A separate reviewed GLM-high throughput probe stopped at idle preflight because metrics showed one running request and zero waiting requests. Its receipt records `status: blocked_busy` and `post_requests: 0`; it made no generation request or retry. No attributable server decode rate or server time to first token was obtained, so the figures above remain client-side end-to-end suite observations.

The stale startup-catalog diagnosis was correct: Codex 0.163.0 has no supported hot reload for its static model manager. The user authorized one managed app-server daemon restart, which changed the scoped control-socket owner from PID 56037 to PID 37759. Desktop PID 6474 retained its original identity and start time, and the desktop app was not quit. A fresh native WebSocket query now verifies Spark Default as `custom/spark-default` with the GLM description, default `low`, efforts `low`/`high`/`max`, and text-only input. Remote status then passed with `status: ok`, `connectionState: connected`, `environmentName: homelab`, and `errorCode: null`. This later restart is separate from the earlier publication restart and pre-restart preservation audit. The frozen raw GLM-low evaluation remains 12/16 strict checks, including the real case-2 instruction and truncation failure. Actual Codex compaction, full 500000-token retention, concurrency stability, coordinated reboot recovery, and model-wide quality remain unqualified. The broad router suite also remains 5,371 passed, 6 failed, and 36 skipped. These findings are preserved in [homelab-flux #36](https://github.com/roccolangeweg/homelab-flux/pull/36). Both PRs remain draft and unmerged.

title: fix: recognize generic providers in subagent diagnostics
body:
`subagents explain` reports `provider_disabled` for an enabled, usable generic provider because it checks only the built-in provider selection. The route can be available while the diagnostic tells the operator to enable it again.

Use `genericProviderConfigured` for runtime generic providers and retain canonical provider-family selection for built-ins. This changes the explanation only, not route selection, credentials, or subagent enablement.

- Exercise the actual CLI with isolated state and synthetic endpoint metadata. Check enabled and disabled generic providers, a missing credential reference, built-in families, visibility, explicit disablement, missing agent definitions, and unchanged state files.
- Three of the seven new tests fail on the current main branch before the fix. All 40 focused and adjacent tests pass afterward on Windows with Node 24.19.0.
- `npm run check` and `git diff --check` pass. No live provider call is needed for these tests; the full test suite has not been run.

Test command: `node --test test/control-subagent-explain.test.mjs test/subagent-explain.test.mjs test/generic-runtime-registry.test.mjs test/provider-selection.test.mjs`

title: fix: preserve Windows AppData paths in private ACL helpers
body:
The sanitized environment passed to Windows PowerShell omits APPDATA and LOCALAPPDATA. This loses an isolated caller profile and can redirect PowerShell module-discovery cache files into the working directory.

Preserve those two public paths in the existing allowlist. Provider/caller credentials and NODE_OPTIONS remain excluded; ACL requirements and helper timeouts are unchanged.

Validation:

- Both actual synchronous and asynchronous helper launches preserve isolated paths while filtering synthetic secrets; both written files remain owner-only.
- Full file-security test file: 9 passed, one POSIX-only assertion skipped on Windows.

This is independent of #1009 and does not include private-writer consolidation.

CI evidence (2026-10-18):
- [Upstream CI](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/39110070775): Linux 5,367 passed / 42 skipped; macOS 5,368 passed / 41 skipped; Windows 5,269 passed / 130 skipped. All three suites have zero failures. Both Electron jobs and formula metadata also passed.
- The native macOS lifecycle smoke failed waiting for Control Center `true/true/true`, with no running/ready/visible process recorded. The identical timeout already occurs in main builds [39054169527](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/39054169527) and [39054151934](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/39054151934); the native application and CI smoke sources are unchanged between those baselines and this PR. Existing logs do not establish the lower-level launch cause.
- [Fork verification of the exact PR source](https://github.com/TruthNian/codex-router/actions/runs/39111346806) passed the same native macOS job, including universal build, signing and full lifecycle smoke. Checkout was pinned to `fed1dd4a369f62bb59c4c9bad56cbb072ae600c5`; only the fork-only validation workflow differs, with no application or test source changes.
- A single targeted upstream rerun was denied; this contributor has read access to the upstream repository. The upstream native check therefore remains failed and is not being represented as green.

title: test: bound skill-install concurrency workers and guarantee cleanup
body:
When concurrent skill-install fixture setup fails, its workers can remain alive. Attaching exit observation late can also miss an already exited child and strand the test runner.

Observe close immediately after spawn, bound setup and exit waits, preserve diagnostic stderr tails, and always retire owned workers in finally. Replace a fixed staging sleep with an explicit release handshake; the second child must observe actual lock contention and cannot stage while the first owns the lock.

Validation:
- The filtered concurrency case and the preceding three cases pass together.
- Complete skill-install file on Windows: 40 passed; four platform-specific cases skipped, with the repository's existing per-test deadline.
- Forced setup failure: the old fixture remains alive until an external eight-second deadline terminates its tree. The fixed fixture preserves the failure and exits in about 0.35 seconds with its worker gone.

Production skill installation, ownership and lock policy are unchanged.

CI evidence (2026-10-18):
- [Upstream CI](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/39113111654) passed all three main test suites, both Electron jobs, formula metadata and deterministic discovery/security checks.

The fork-only workflow changes the checkout pin and selects that job; application/test sources are unchanged.
- The upstream native check remains failed. This supplementary run is not presented as a repair of the existing launch failure.

title: test: reserve bounded port capacity for large integration suites
body:
Adding integration-test consumers shrinks every equal-sized port block, so a large existing suite can exhaust its allocation even though its own demand has not changed.

Allow a suite to declare a bounded reservation before dividing the remaining ports among ordinary consumers. Reserve the routing suite's existing 256-port capacity, preserve disjoint credential-lease/managed/ephemeral exclusions, and reject invalid or oversubscribed reservations, including malformed, negative, fractional and empty declarations.

Validation:
- All three growth/invalid/oversubscription controls fail against unmodified main.
- Final capacity, actual lease isolation and pool tests: six passed, including growth from 60 to 230 ordinary consumers. Undeclared consumers use the guaranteed 32-port minimum; the reserved routing suite still draws 200 distinct ports.
- The unchanged allocator and routing suite passed the comprehensive 170-case run. Only allocator/lease test assertions were extended afterward; their final focused rerun passes all six cases.
- An earlier Windows repeat encountered four five-second fixture startup timeouts. Those four cases pass separately on main and this branch, and the final complete rerun passes. No test deadline was increased; the timeout evidence is retained.

Only test port allocation changes; production ports and request behavior are unchanged.

title: test: isolate subagent explanation fixtures from execution order
body:
The reasoning-effort explanation case depends on a previous test having published an agent definition. Running it alone therefore reports an unspawnable route and fails for fixture ordering rather than reasoning behavior.

Give each relevant case its own published or absent definitions, restore effort through a test hook, and clean up the owned scratch root.

Production explanation and spawning behavior are unchanged.

title: test: reset owned log fixtures before support-bundle cases
body:
A preceding failed operation can leave router.log in the shared scratch state. The support-bundle privacy test then fails with EEXIST while arranging its directory fixture, before reaching the omission assertions.

title: fix: keep rejected tool streams terminal in Codex
body:
When a provider emits a rejected tool call after output has already been committed, the Router currently reports a generic stream failure. Codex can treat that failure as retryable, regenerate the turn repeatedly, and eventually show only `stream closed before response.completed`.

This preserves the local diagnostic code and classifies committed namespace-relay and invalid-function-argument rejections as terminal using the existing `localRejection` contract. The client receives `response.failed` even when response identity metadata is missing. Tool validation stays strict, unsafe completed items remain withheld, and ordinary transport failures retain their retry behavior.

Adapted from the approach in #1022 to current main's existing terminal-failure API. This is a separate change from #1031; it does not resolve why the original provider tool arguments were invalid.

### Validation

- Reproduced the namespace integration and end-of-stream helper failures on unmodified main, then verified both regressions pass with the fix.
- Focused suites: 167 passed; an additional full Router regression verifies malformed function arguments after visible output terminate without retry or failover.
- `npm run check`: passed. Final full isolated `npm test`: **5,376 passed, 0 failed, 37 skipped**, including the pinned offline LiteLLM interpreter.
- Updated the native signed-out test for Codex 0.163: it may retire an unused authenticated WebSocket before opening the turn connection. The test still requires exactly one upstream generation, now validates every connection's authentication, and requires a completed turn without error/retry notifications. The previous connection-count assertion failed on this installed client; both native cases now pass.
- Installed official Codex CLI `0.163.0-alpha.10.2`, isolated HOME/CODEX_HOME, synthetic loopback provider, no live quota: exercised actual `endStreamedResponse` output with missing identity metadata through HTTP/SSE and the Router WebSocket bridge. In both transports, `server_error` dispatches twice with one configured retry; terminal local rejection dispatches once and reports `willRetry=false`.
- Native cancellation check on the same revision: cancelling a partial function call closes the WebSocket and aborts the local upstream before continuation; no command executes, the completed assistant item survives, the incomplete call is absent from resumed context, and the next turn completes. Ordinary native cancellation emits no `response.interrupt` frame, so this is evidence for close/reconnect only.
- Independent read-only review of failure classification and diagnostic privacy: no findings.

No installation or service restart is included. Maintainer retains merge control.

title: test: separate Node fixture startup from HTTP readiness
body:
The router and request-diagnostics functional suites start a five-second readiness deadline immediately after spawning a child, so Node initialization and HTTP readiness compete for one setup allowance. Main run [39184637964](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/39184637964) expired in request-diagnostics-router.test.mjs with no child stderr. That old log cannot distinguish child initialization, binding, parent scheduling or a blocked HTTP probe. Each fetch also lacks its own abort bound, so the nominal deadline does not bound an accepted connection that never answers.

Introduce a shared test-only Node fixture helper. Its preload reports initialized, entering listen(), and listening phases through the owned IPC channel. Initialization has a finite 15-second allowance; the existing five-second HTTP readiness budget begins after the listener is observed. Each probe and its complete body are bounded by the remaining budget. Early exits, signals and failed probes report phase, elapsed/CPU timings, last HTTP status and a bounded stderr tail, with caller URLs redacted. Starts exceeding the former five-second threshold remain visible as warnings even if readiness succeeds. Apply this to the two affected suites, preserving their environments, transport preload arguments, authentication and routing assertions.

Validation:
- Final-source local regression: 179 passed, zero failures or skips. npm run check passed; changed helper/fixture syntax and changelog checks passed after the final diagnostic additions.
- [Latest-head upstream CI](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/39195770816) passed on Windows, Linux and macOS, including both Electron jobs and the native macOS lifecycle job. No fork substitution was needed.
- Fault regressions cover initialization longer than the HTTP budget, a never-listening child, an initialization crash, a response that sends headers then stalls its body, and HTTP 503. Slow successful initialization must retain its phase/CPU warning.
- CPU-limited Windows fault injection reproduces the original readiness failure. With external tracing disabled at the same owned-job rate400, unchanged main fails and the final patch completes the original success/failure/cancel assertions. A control restoring the initialization cap to five seconds still fails, so initialization headroom is an explicit part of the contract correction, not a demonstrated startup speedup. More severe rate50 throttling still exceeds the finite warm-up allowance and fails with phase information.
- All 17 changed hunks reviewed. Changes are limited to tests and one changelog fragment.

Supplementary baseline measurements: an exact-main [Windows full-suite phase run](https://github.com/TruthNian/codex-router/actions/runs/39190990002) passed 5,271 tests with 130 platform skips. A separate [600-start baseline sample](https://github.com/TruthNian/codex-router/actions/runs/39194163996) at the existing two-file concurrency measured median458ms, p99 563ms and maximum735ms, with no pre-listen helper process launches. Node24.21.0 and the Windows image match the historical failed job. These fresh VMs did not reproduce that historical stall. Neither successful sampling nor injected CPU starvation establishes which host resource or process caused that particular incident; the confirmed repair is the readiness-contract and observability defect.

title: fix(macos): observe startup without launching GUI query helpers
body:
The native macOS smoke can fail before the real Control Center starts because its lifecycle observer repeatedly launches that same Electron application with `--query-lifecycle`. A query process registers with LaunchServices even though it never owns a window and exits immediately. If it overlaps the native host's `NSWorkspace.openApplication` request, the request can fail with `NSCocoaErrorDomain 256`, underlying `NSOSStatusErrorDomain -600`. Polling then keeps reporting `running=false, pid=null, ready=false, visible=false, updatedAt=null` because no real application session started.

Use one Node-only lifecycle query entry point in CI, the signed-release smoke, and the macOS rebuild probe. It reuses the packaged handler's existing path selection, schema/size validation and live-PID check. Existing readiness flags, exact-bundle checks, bounded polling, child quit/reopen, outer quit, swap recovery and cleanup remain in place.

### Causal evidence

- [Launch-phase experiment](https://github.com/TruthNian/codex-router/actions/runs/39202889176): the original query-based observation reproduced the all-null timeout without an injected delay. The native host received reopen, requested the child, and got Cocoa error 256; no non-query Electron entry occurred. Three interleaved observations without GUI helpers opened normally. Holding a registered query briefly reproduced the same failure.
- [Unmodified-package control](https://github.com/TruthNian/codex-router/actions/runs/39204147756): reuse the previously built, signature-verified app without changing its executable or `app.asar`. Stop its actual query process at an AppKit-registration barrier (`finishedLaunching=false`), then call the same NSWorkspace API. It returns 256 -> -600; after the query exits, the same bundle opens successfully. This separates the LaunchServices collision from application compilation, renderer readiness and source instrumentation.
- [Registration-order control without pausing queries](https://github.com/TruthNian/codex-router/actions/runs/39206379873): wait only until the exact query PID registers with AppKit (`finishedLaunching=false`), then issue one NSWorkspace open request. All 8 trials fail with 256 -> -600, while all query processes exit normally with status 0. A separate [immediate-overlap control](https://github.com/TruthNian/codex-router/actions/runs/39205913379) opened successfully in 8/8 trials. This pins the triggering order without relying on a stopped or modified query. The same runs verify the PR helper blob against the real packaged handler: live-hidden and post-quit JSON agree.
- The new test executes the actual CI observer under a child-process guard, with a positive control proving the guard detects a GUI-helper launch. Against main `0a0fdce1`, the four state-observation cases fail specifically on attempted subprocess creation. The release/rebuild wiring check also fails. With this patch, all six pass.

### Validation

- Local adjacent regression: 171 passed, 16 platform/dependency skips; two initial shell-syntax failures were caused by `sh` missing from the local command PATH, and passed after using the existing Git shell.
- `npm run check`, the new helper's syntax check, shell syntax and complete hunk review passed.
- [Upstream CI](https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/actions/runs/39204625341) passed on the final commit `1cef4c52`: Linux 5,381 passed / 41 skipped; macOS 5,382 passed / 40 skipped; Windows 5,282 passed / 130 skipped. Both Electron packages, the universal native macOS build/seal/lifecycle job, formula checks, discovery and GitGuardian passed. Manual Homebrew installation and live catalog audit retain their expected skips.
- The real signed/notarized release was not invoked; its changed observer uses the same helper whose real packaged-state parity was verified above. Signing, notarization and publication steps are unchanged.

The historical #1035/#1036 logs did not retain the underlying NSWorkspace error, so they cannot independently prove that every old timeout had this cause. This patch removes the causally reproduced query/open collision; it does not claim that every possible macOS startup failure is fixed. No startup timeout is extended, and the native/Electron launch implementation is unchanged.

title: chore(deps): bump undici from 8.11.2 to 8.12.2
body:
Bumps [undici](https://github.com/nodejs/undici) from 8.11.2 to 8.12.2.
Release notes

Sourced from undici's releases.

v8.12.2

Security fixes

High severity

Denial of service via TLS 1.2 certificate-changing renegotiation

CVE-2026-87018 · GHSA-qrxm-fqhp-jwvm

A malicious or compromised HTTPS server could crash the Node.js process by initiating TLS 1.2 renegotiation and presenting a different, CA-trusted certificate whose hostname did not match the requested host. The resulting socket error reached an assertion in undici's HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 connection handling. This release handles post-connect certificate errors without terminating the process.

TLS certificate validation bypass through dropped Agent options

CVE-2026-109383 · GHSA-2m5v-pch6-74hx

Agent used a JSON-based clone for constructor options, which silently removed function-valued TLS options such as checkServerIdentity. Applications relying on custom certificate or public-key verification could therefore accept a certificate that the callback was intended to reject. This release preserves TLS options when creating per-origin dispatchers.

Cache poisoning and cross-user disclosure through cross-origin redirects

CVE-2026-109829 · GHSA-4w7w-5xrc-9h26

When an originless Agent combined redirect and shared-cache interceptors as compose(redirect(), cache()), a response from a cross-origin redirect could be stored under the original URL. This could allow persistent cache poisoning or disclosure of user-specific responses to later callers. This release verifies the response origin before caching and preserves redirect-hop cache-control policy.

Denial of service through excessive Content-Encoding values

CVE-2026-109869 · GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c

A malicious HTTP server could crash the Node.js process by returning more than five content codings and closing the connection before sending the body. Although fetch() rejected the response, an error from an orphaned internal stream could remain unhandled. This release validates the content-encoding chain before creating the body stream and aborts oversized chains safely.

Medium severity

Denial of service through the decompress interceptor

CVE-2026-87029 · GHSA-55wc-3pg8-jfw6

An exception thrown by a downstream response handler from an asynchronous decompression callback could escape as an uncaught exception. A server could trigger this when decompress was composed with a handler such as dump with a size limit. This release converts downstream handler exceptions into per-request errors.

Subresource Integrity bypass with non-lowercase algorithm tokens

CVE-2026-109841 · GHSA-f72v-6w45-q472

fetch() treated valid mixed-case or uppercase SRI algorithm tokens, such as SHA256, as unknown and could accept a response whose body did not match the configured digest. This release normalizes algorithm tokens before validation and digest selection.

Denial of service through unbounded EventSource parser state

CVE-2026-109924 · GHSA-4qv8-2p9j-2685

A malicious Server-Sent Events endpoint could exhaust process memory by sending many tiny data: fields without completing an event, or by splitting an unfinished line across many chunks. This release bounds retained EventSource parser state, including field counts, buffered chunks, unfinished-line length, and retained field data.

title: [Bug]: Skill installation fails with ERR_FS_CP_EEXIST while publishing staged skills
body:
### What happened?

Skill publication fails on a destination directory that the installer itself has just created and marked for publication. In `publishStagedSkill`, the installer calls `mkdirSync(target)`, writes `.codex-router-publishing`, then calls:

```js
cpSync(staged.content, target, {
  recursive: true,
  force: false,
  errorOnExist: true,
});
```

title: [Bug]: Login-free native aliases can route GPT slugs to hidden paid presets
body:
## What happened

On Windows, a Codex request using a native GPT slug reached an OpenRouter paid preset that the user had never added or selected. The visible symptom was:

```text
402 Payment Required: ... Claude Fable 5.1 (OpenRouter)
You requested up to 65536 tokens, but can only afford 800.
```

The user's saved native catalog still contained the original OpenAI models. The merged picker entries had instead been replaced with external aliases and hidden.

The installed router was 0.5.1 at `3341ea0a`. The alias-selection defect is also reproducible on current `main`, `0a0fdce15b8325b10dd3f187c0acf1beed50dda4` (0.6.0).

## Relevant state, reduced to routing and selection fields

```json
{
  "enabled_providers": ["openrouter"],
  "picker": {
    "hidden": ["openrouter/claude-fable-5.1"],
    "visible": [
      "openrouter/minimax/minimax-m3:free",
      "openrouter/nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free"
    ]
  },
  "native_aliases": {
    "gpt-6.1-sol": "openrouter/claude-fable-5.1"
  },
  "merged_entry": {
    "slug": "gpt-6.1-sol",
    "display_name": "Claude Fable 5.1 (OpenRouter)",
    "visibility": "hide"
  }
}
```

The user-model overlay contained only the two free routes. Fable came from the checked-in preset. The config backup from the affected period had `model_provider = "codex-router"` and `model = "gpt-6.1-sol"`, which puts catalog generation into login-free mode. These observations do not establish which action enabled that mode.

## Root cause

`buildLoginFreeCatalog()` filters configured providers, then calls `buildNativeAliasAssignments()` with every configured route. Picker hidden/visible policy is applied only after aliases have already been allocated and written. The router resolves those aliases independently of picker visibility.

Consequently, a hidden paid preset can consume the first native allowlist slot while an explicitly selected free model is left outside it. Hiding the resulting picker entry does not prevent a request with that native slug from reaching the paid preset.

Native GPT slots representing external models are intentional in login-free mode. The defect is allocating them to hidden or unselected models. Ordinary signed-in publication should continue to preserve the real native entries.

## Reproduction without provider requests

1. Supply one listed native slot, such as `gpt-5.5`.
2. Supply an external route list with hidden Fable first and a selected `:free` route second.
3. Apply picker state with Fable hidden and only the free route visible.
4. Build/publish a login-free catalog.

Current behavior: the native slot maps to Fable; the later picker overlay hides the slot but leaves the alias routable. Expected: only the selected route can receive that slot. An explicit empty selection should allocate no aliases.

## Proposed fix and validation

Apply the same hidden/explicit visible policy before native-slot assignment, retaining canonical routes for the existing publication overlay and preserving legacy hidden-only picker behavior. Add unit regressions and a subprocess publication test covering login-free aliases and subsequent ordinary signed-in publication.

The original implementation fails both selection regressions with the native slug mapped to Fable. No real model request or credit purchase is needed to reproduce this.

Related native-catalog work exists in #46/#47 and #666, but those address authentication probing or native cache freshness. Searches across open/closed issues and PRs did not find this hidden-preset alias-allocation case.

title: fix: honor picker selection when assigning login-free native aliases
body:
## Summary

Fixes #1047.

Login-free catalog publication assigned native GPT slots before applying picker selection. A hidden paid preset such as Fable could receive `gpt-6.1-sol` even when only free models were selected; the later overlay hid the entry but left its alias routable.

Filter alias candidates by hidden state and, when present, the explicit visible allowlist before allocating slots. Keep canonical routes for the existing overlay and retain legacy hidden-only picker behavior. Ordinary signed-in native publication stays on its existing path.

This addresses the unexpected route that led to the reported OpenRouter 402. It does not change credit limits, infer what enabled login-free mode, or treat login-free slots as real OpenAI models.

Release notes

Sourced from mcp's releases.

v1.30.0

Maintenance release of the 1.x line. 2.x is the current line; 1.x docs are at https://py.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/v1/.

A few defaults changed in this release. If you run a server or client on 1.x, skim these first:

Behaviour changes

HTTP client redirects are only followed within the endpoint's origin (#3448)

  • streamable_http_client and sse_client follow a redirect only if it stays on the same scheme, host and port (or upgrades http to https on the same host).
  • A redirect anywhere else now fails the request with httpx.HTTPStatusError. If that other URL is the server you meant, use it as the endpoint URL.
  • The follow_redirects setting on an httpx.AsyncClient you pass in is no longer used for MCP requests, so you don't need it for the trailing-slash redirect any more.
  • OAuthClientProvider applies the same rule to its own requests.

Idle Streamable HTTP sessions now expire (#3426)

  • A stateful session with nothing in flight for 30 minutes is closed. The client's next request gets a 404 and it has to initialize again.
  • Clients that keep the GET stream open (the SDK's client does) are not affected.
  • A server also holds at most 10 000 sessions at once; beyond that, new sessions get a 503.
  • To turn either off: FastMCP(..., session_idle_timeout=None, max_sessions=None).

The OAuth client checks the authorization server's issuer (#3431)

  • Authorization server metadata whose issuer doesn't match the server it was fetched for is now rejected with OAuthFlowError: Authorization server metadata issuer mismatch.
  • Client registrations are now remembered per issuer; if the server later points at a different authorization server, the client registers again.
  • If protected resource metadata can't be fetched because of a 5xx/429, the flow now stops instead of falling back to the legacy endpoints.

Two new DeprecationWarnings (#3431, #3451)

  • ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider / PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider without issuer=. Pass your authorization server's issuer URL.
  • AuthSettings with resource_server_url set but validate_token_resource unset. Set it to True or False.
  • Both keep working as before in 1.x; this mostly matters if your tests turn warnings into errors.

New

  • AuthSettings.validate_token_resource: only accept tokens your TokenVerifier reports as issued for this server (#3451).
  • issuer= on ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider and PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider (#3431).
  • session_idle_timeout= and max_sessions= on FastMCP (#3426).

title: fix: recover aged tool output without rerunning tools
body:
When old tool output is omitted, the current receipt tells the model to repeat the original tool call. Re-execution can change data or repeat a write, and the retention module currently supplies no runtime writer or model-usable reader.

This change commits an exact, private snapshot before replacing any output. Receipts supply a read-only local command with paginated text, literal search and SHA-256 verification. Full output remains until a successful reader call returns a signed proof in tool-result history; it is bound to the conversation and system/developer permission context and expires after 30 minutes. An available shell alone is insufficient: Windows workspace sandbox validation reproduced EPERM against owner-private snapshots. Sandboxes retain full output with no permission changes or automatic escalation. Missing execution tools, storage/ACL failures, lock contention, capacity limits or corrupt existing snapshots leave the full result intact. Tool-less compaction summarizers also retain exact output because they cannot follow a readback command.

Snapshots use install-keyed, conversation/call-scoped handles. Replayed originals renew their inactivity lease; expired, purged or corrupt snapshots explicitly report unavailable evidence. Explicit purge shares the writer lock. No HTTP content endpoint or automatic execution of an original tool is introduced. Only text received by Router can be recovered; prior tool-host truncation remains outside this boundary.

Validation:
- Expanded related suites: 435 passed, 4 platform/environment skips, no failures.
- Final recovery/policy regressions: 24 passed, covering exact Unicode/CRLF paging, restart readback, search, expiry, corruption, capacity, ACL/disk fault injection and writer/purge contention.
- Final related runtime/compatibility suites: 354 passed.
- HTTP integration verifies full passthrough before readback proof, omission only after proof, and full passthrough on an actual filesystem failure. Forged, expired and cross-context proofs are rejected.
- `npm run check` and `git diff --check` passed.
- Windows installed validation: real GLM-5.3 sandbox-denied and full-access controls passed. Both emitted their original output only once and deleted the emitter. The denied reader left all original evidence intact; the permitted reader retrieved the exact proof and only then enabled omission. A same-session follow-up began with the old result already omitted and successfully read it again. Independent rollback rehearsals and post-deploy HTTP/model/WebSocket checks passed.

CI follow-up: updated the four legacy routing fixtures to perform real CLI readback before expecting omission and to retain exact tool-less compaction input. The full routing suite passed 164/164. All four updated regressions fail at their intended assertions on the unmodified main baseline (negative control). No production code or workflow was changed by this follow-up.

title: feat: support a persistent compatibility-layer opt-out
body:
An installation using native GPT and Responses-native providers currently has no persistent way to refuse the LiteLLM compatibility layer: source installation, startup, or forced dependency repair can provision or execute it again. Add a private, versioned `compatibility-layer.json` policy, controlled by `control compatibility-layer status|on|off` (with a dependency-free command for fresh checkouts).

Explicit opt-out filters compatibility-dependent routes from effective catalogs and dependency planning, rejects their IDs and aliases before upstream delivery, sends remaining Responses routes through the existing API forwarder, and skips Python provisioning/probes/launch in both installers and doctor repair. Missing policy preserves existing behavior; invalid explicit policy disables compatibility. Health confirms policy adoption before publication, and updates/rollbacks refuse older revisions that cannot honor an explicit opt-out.

Stored model definitions, provider selections, credentials, and native vision bridging remain available. Cached environments are retained for recovery. The existing full Homebrew formula keeps its build-time Python dependencies; this change controls runtime behavior and source installation, as documented in `docs/compatibility-layer.md`.

Validation (head `1eb8e46881ffd3468d9c7775ec84de36a308ed32`):
- All 16 applicable CI checks pass; 2 conditional jobs (live provider catalog audit and manual Homebrew install) skip as configured. Linux: 5,384 passed / 45 skipped; macOS: 5,385 passed / 44 skipped; Windows: 5,289 passed / 130 skipped. Zero failed tests on all three platforms. Native macOS tray/widget, unified app, Electron builds, dependency matrices, syntax, and audit checks also pass.
- Both real installers exercised with isolated command-recording fixtures, including forced repair, invalid-policy refusal, enabled Python provisioning positive controls, and a regression detector which rejects the original installers.
- A real isolated core stack starts with an absent gateway binary, completes HTTP, SSE, WebSocket, tool-history and remote-compaction requests, and rejects disabled requests without upstream delivery.
- Adapted onto the existing Windows integration without replacing prior fixes: 258 runtime checks and 61 lifecycle checks passed (11 host skips). Deployed with independently rehearsed rollback; real GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3 and Grok-4.6 streams completed. Doctor: 37 checks, no failures. title: Fix ERR_FS_CP_EEXIST in skill publication on Node 26+
body: Fixes #1046 ## Problem Skill publication fails with `ERR_FS_CP_EEXIST` on Node.js v26.12.0 when copying staged skills to the target directory. The issue occurs in `publishStagedSkill` in `src/skills-install.mjs` at line 809. The function creates a target directory with `mkdirSync`, writes a `.codex-router-publishing` marker file, then calls: ```js cpSync(staged.content, target, { recursive: true, force: false, errorOnExist: true }); ``` On Node.js v26.12.0, `cpSync` with `errorOnExist: true` throws `ERR_FS_CP_EEXIST` ("Target already exists") when the destination directory already exists, even when copying contents *into* it. This behavior differs from earlier Node versions (22.x) where `errorOnExist` only checked individual files. ## Solution Copy each entry from `staged.content` into the target directory individually, rather than copying the directory as a whole: ```js for (const entry of readdirSync(staged.content)) { const sourcePath = path.join(staged.content, entry); const targetPath = path.join(target, entry); cpSync(sourcePath, targetPath, { recursive: true, force: false, errorOnExist: true }); } ``` This approach: - ✅ Works on both Node 22.x and Node 26.x - ✅ Preserves collision protection (`errorOnExist: true` still prevents overwriting individual files) - ✅ Maintains all existing ownership and safety guarantees - ✅ All 44 tests in `test/skills-install.test.mjs` pass ## Testing Verified on Node.js v22.23.4: - All 44 skill installation tests pass - No regressions in concurrent installs, ownership checks, or collision handling

title: fix: clean up supervised children after a failed spawn
body:

title: fix: reject generation redirects without replaying consumed requests
body:
## Summary

A generation endpoint can consume a POST and then redirect it. Following that redirect and treating a later connection failure as an unsent original request can replay the consumed generation.

Refuse generation redirects before following or relaying their Location, using the existing native redirect boundary. The API forwarder returns a typed HTTP 400 endpoint configuration error, which LiteLLM does not retry as a transient 5xx. Vision preserves raw and encoded refusals instead of retrying the read or switching engines. Ordinary errors and the Local/Grok long-idle transport budgets retain their existing behavior.

The policy deliberately includes same-origin generation redirects: a 3xx response does not prove the original POST was unconsumed. Configure the final API endpoint. This retains the submitted policy; collaborator feedback requests maintainer confirmation before merge.

## Current main integration

Rebased onto `44cc7b0bf2cac42c16e302f0c5a28bdb40e8c6c9`, including #1069. Responses-native models now go directly to the API forwarder. The vision regression previously overrode only its gateway URL, so the normal text turn could reach an installed default API port and return 401.

Both Router fixtures now explicitly select their owned API and health URLs. Default fixture API URLs point to a separate owned 401 sentinel, and cleanup asserts that it received no requests. Removing the vision API override reproduces `401 != 200` against that sentinel, without contacting an installed Router or forwarder. The corrected case still requires one consumed vision request, no second-engine request, one successful text request and zero redirected-target calls.

## Verification

- Current head `72a2c3e010812ff210eacf923cbf77b805c47176`: 140 related cases passed, no failures or skips. Includes all nine redirect cases, actual per-model direct Responses routing, transport selection, native replay behavior, vision, Fetch transport and the newly merged process-output capture tests.
- The installed LiteLLM loopback-only probe passed with two retries configured and exactly one origin request. It blocks external DNS/connections, uses synthetic credentials and installs nothing.
- API coverage includes Responses, Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages across 301/302/303/307/308. Raw and encoded vision refusals, credential-pool non-rotation, sanitized errors and unchanged ordinary error classification are covered.

title: [Bug]: Completed function_call with empty arguments bypasses JSON guard and poisons Codex thread history
body:
## Summary

The fix for #797 / #800 still permits a **completed** `function_call` with `arguments: ""`. That value is valid as a *streaming placeholder*, but it is not valid JSON for a finished tool invocation. Codex stores the unusable call and subsequent `Continue` and `/compact` attempts receive HTTP 400 when the same history is replayed.

Reproduced on **24 October 2026** with `opencode-go-responses/muse-spark-1.3-contributor` (OpenCode Go, Responses route). The issue remains on GitHub `main` at `9945d74354ab07942f171be329cf81c9478fc5e2`.

## Reproduction / retained evidence

A completed `exec_command` is recorded in Codex's response history with:

```json
{"type":"function_call","name":"exec_command","arguments":"","call_id":"call_example"}
```

Codex cannot run it and records a matching `function_call_output`:

```text
failed to parse function arguments: EOF while parsing a value at line 1 column 0
```

Following turns then fail when this pair is replayed:

```text
HTTP 400: `arguments` must be valid JSON
```

The command was **never executed**. The problem persists for both ordinary continuation and manual compaction, so an otherwise useful thread becomes unusable.

## Root cause

In `src/invalid-function-call.mjs`:

```js
export function functionCallArgumentsAreJson(value, { allowEmpty = true } = {}) {
  if (typeof value !== "string") return true;
  if (allowEmpty && value.trim() === "") return true;
  try { JSON.parse(value); return true; } catch { return false; }
}
```

`inspectFunctionCallArguments()` calls this without overriding `allowEmpty`. Both `findUnusableCompletedFunctionCall()` and `findUnusableFunctionCallArguments()` consequently accept `arguments: ""`, despite being completion/history checks.

This edge case was excluded from the earlier non-empty malformed-JSON fix described in #797, making it a separate regression.

## Expected behaviour

1. Keep allowing empty arguments in opening/partial streaming frames.
2. Require parseable JSON when a `function_call_arguments.done`, `output_item.done`, or completed response snapshot arrives. Withhold the entire unexecutable tool call and use the existing bounded failure/retry path.
3. Reject stored invalid history locally instead of attributing an upstream HTTP 400 to the provider.
4. For an already poisoned history, optionally recover **only** a confirmed unexecuted pair: adjacent `exec_command` with `arguments: ""` and matching `function_call_output` whose text is precisely the native parser error above. Omit both from the forwarded request in memory, leave the on-disk transcript intact, and continue rejecting every other malformed case. Do not invent command arguments.

## Local fix and verification

A narrow local patch on the installed router now passes `{ allowEmpty: false }` for completed/history inspection and adds the exact-pair recovery described above. It has **not** been pushed or proposed as a PR.

- `test/invalid-function-call.test.mjs`: **15 passed**.
- Focused mocked router integration checks in `test/model-failover-router.test.mjs`: **4 passed**.
- Repository syntax/configuration checks and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Managed router restart completed and `/health` returned `ok: true`, with no degraded dependencies.
- No live provider calls were used in the regression tests.

Relevant files: `src/invalid-function-call.mjs`, `src/router.mjs`, `test/invalid-function-call.test.mjs`, `test/model-failover-router.test.mjs`.

Environment: Codex on Windows with WSL Ubuntu, Node 22.22.2, router checkout initially at `592be375`. The exact private thread identifiers, prompts and paths are intentionally omitted.

title: Refuse empty function_call arguments for tools that take inputs
body:
Fixes #1066.

A routed model could complete a `function_call` with `arguments: ""`. The JSON check let that through, so Codex stored a call it couldn't parse, and every later turn on the thread failed.

## Behavior
- **Response (stream and non-streaming):** a completed function call with empty or whitespace-only arguments is relayed only when the tool was declared this turn, or loaded earlier by `tool_search_output`, with a schema that takes no inputs (no `parameters`, or no properties and no required fields). For any other tool the item is withheld and the turn fails with `invalid_function_call_arguments`, the same as truncated JSON. Opening frames and in-progress snapshots may still be empty. Namespaced tools are matched by namespace and name.
- **History:** a stored empty call to a tool known to take inputs is refused with a 400. Tools missing from this turn's inventory are still allowed, because they may have been removed since the call ran.
- **Recovery for threads already broken:** an empty-argument call whose only output is exactly Codex's `failed to parse function arguments: EOF while parsing a value at line 1 column 0` never ran. The router leaves that pair out of the forwarded request in memory, so it does not invent arguments and does not change stored history.

## Verification (Node 22)
- `npm run check` passes. Full `npm test`: 5775 passed, 0 failed, 68 skipped.
- `test/invalid-function-call.test.mjs`: 22 passing, including 10 new tests.
- Real stack (LiteLLM, api-forwarder and router) against a mock upstream that emits empty-argument calls:
  - **main:** the Responses route relays `exec_command("")` with `response.completed`, and poisoned history is forwarded unchanged.
  - **This branch:** `exec_command("")` is refused with 502 `invalid_function_call_arguments`. `ping_now("")`, a tool that takes no inputs, still completes. On both the Responses and Chat routes, poisoned history is forwarded without the pair and the turn completes. A stored empty `exec_command` call with any other output is refused with a 400.

title: Bound supervisor teardown so a lost child exit can't hang the router
body:
Fixes #1020.

**Problem.** On shutdown, the supervisor in `src/start.mjs` waited on `Promise.all` of every child's exit. If a child's exit was never reported (the Windows report in #1020), the supervisor hung forever, so the service manager never restarted the router.

**Fix.** The teardown now waits at most `SIGKILL_AFTER_MS + 5s` (`src/bounded-teardown.mjs`). If a child still hasn't reported its exit by then, the supervisor logs why and exits non-zero so the service manager restarts it. When every child exits normally, nothing changes.

**Verification (Linux, Node 22).**
- `test/bounded-teardown.test.mjs` has three tests: a drained teardown returns true; an exit that never settles returns false within the bound; a real spawned supervisor-style script holding a live handle exits with code 1 instead of hanging.
- The startup lifecycle fixture now mocks the new module.
- Real-stack check (LiteLLM + forwarder + router against a mock upstream): after one served turn, I SIGKILLed the router child. On both main and this branch the supervisor exits in about 13s with the same code, so normal crash handling is unchanged.
- I couldn't reproduce the lost exit event on Windows itself here.

title: fix: preserve certifi 2026.10.23 across gateway reinstallations
body:
## Summary

Updates and repairs install the checked-in Python lock, which can restore certifi 2026.7.22 after an operator has updated the local environment. Make certifi a direct security pin and regenerate both the universal lock and Homebrew resource.

```diff
- transitive certifi==2026.7.22
+ direct certifi==2026.10.23, with matching lock and Homebrew hashes
```

2026.10.23 removes the compromised emSign roots covered by [GHSA-6q48-6c7w-9gw2](https://github.com/certifi/python-certifi/security/advisories/GHSA-6q48-6c7w-9gw2) while retaining the unaffected G1 root restored in [certifi#440](https://github.com/certifi/python-certifi/pull/440). Related: #1053; this proposal uses 2026.10.23 on current main and includes a matching-stamp downgrade regression.

## Evidence

Tested head: `75fe65b2adc8fb4c98006911928c4b8eaa2dee87`, base: `2e3fd008a130d5adf3e2a4b690780abcdb3e4602`.

- **Before:** the lock and Homebrew resource select 2026.7.22; certifi is absent from the direct requirements checked by the installation fingerprint.
  **After:** a fresh, cache-disabled, hash-checked install on macOS arm64 / Python 3.12.16 installs 2026.10.23. Only certifi changes version among 111 locked projects.
- `node --test test/python-lock.test.mjs test/install-plan.test.mjs test/homebrew-formula.test.mjs`: **30 passed**. Includes detection of an installed 2026.7.22 even when its dependency stamp matches.
- Negative controls: removing the direct pin or restoring 2026.7.22 makes the new security-floor test fail. A cache-disabled reinstall without hashes is rejected.
- Fresh environment: `uv pip check` passes for 106 installed packages. The repository verifier checks all five direct pins, imports, 43 LiteLLM requirements including 30 proxy-extra requirements, and a real localhost `/health/liveliness` response (**HTTP 200**).
- `npm run check` and `git diff --check`: passed. Requirement files and formula were regenerated with the existing project tools. Installer commands and hash enforcement are unchanged.

Draft pending the existing cross-platform CI and maintainer review. The full Node suite, Windows/Linux execution, and a complete Homebrew install were not run locally; no cross-platform or release qualification is claimed.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** Two-way for source changes. Reverting the pin/lock would permit the older certificate bundle again, so retain the security floor if an unrelated installer change needs rollback.

**Blast Radius:** Installation. The shared Python environment and Homebrew resource change one package; provider configuration, credentials, and installer control flow are unchanged. Maintainers own merge/release approval after the existing CI matrix; this PR does not switch an active installation to a fork.

title: Search sidecar: Keenable as an opt-in second adapter (roadmap P07)
body:
Roadmap item P07 asks for more trusted search-sidecar adapters without weakening the per-model opt-in or the transport boundary. I'd like to propose Keenable Search as a second, opt-in adapter. Perplexity stays the default.

The policy change, in plain terms: `TRUSTED_SEARCH_ORIGIN` in `src/search-sidecar-policy.mjs` becomes a two-row table, one exact origin and fixed path per adapter. The Perplexity row is today's rule, unchanged. The Keenable row is `https://api.keenable.ai`, with path `/v1/search/public` when no credential is bound and `/v1/search` when one is. Allowing no credential is the only relaxation, and only for that row, because Keenable's API works without a key (a key only raises rate limits).

Everything else stays as it is: enabled `openai-chat` descriptor, `allowPrivate: false`, no extra path or query, the DNS-pinned redirect-refusing transport, and the shared result URL, DNS and credential checks. `search-sidecar set` records the adapter from the descriptor's exact origin in the binding's existing `adapter` field, and the catalog, doctor, control and request path all check against that recorded adapter, so neither adapter can be reached through the other's descriptor.

Keenable takes one query per request, so a multi-query turn sends one request per query, in order, under the same deadline. Each request carries a fixed `X-Keenable-Title: codex-router` header, which the keyless path requires; it names the app, not the user or machine.

I have this on a branch with unit, control, capability and router-path tests next to the Perplexity ones, docs (en, zh-CN, ja) and a changelog fragment. A live keyless run through `router.mjs` returned 8 results per query. If you would rather keep a credential required for every adapter, I can make Keenable key-only instead.

Disclosure: I work at Keenable, which runs this search API.
